title: 3.3.1 AUTOMATING ADMINISTRATIVE TASKS

paragraphs.text:
The integration of AI in school administration offers potential to
optimize the “back-office” functions of schooling, transitioning from
manual oversight to data-informed management. Advancements in AI-
powered assistants and algorithms allow institutions to streamline labor-
intensive processes such as enrollment, scheduling, and 24/7 student support.
These systems can identify patterns in student attendance, resource allocation,
and academic performance, generating reports that were previously labor-
intensive to compile. Also, the integration of automated communication
systems facilitates a responsive environment, enabling schools to maintain
real-time engagement with teaching staff and parents through personalized
notifications. 54

In Türkiye’s education system, the administrative workload
placed on school leaders may impact their ability to prioritize effective
leadership . As occurs elsewhere, school principals and their deputies often
spend a substantial portion of their day managing bureaucratic tasks within
centralized systems such as e-Okul (school information system used to track
student information from initial registration to graduation) and MEBBİS
(centralized information management system) leaving less time for mentoring
teachers and focusing on pedagogical improvement. AI systems can automate
many of the repetitive tasks associated with platforms like data entry and
attendance tracking. This automation offloads a portion of the administrative
workload from school principals, their deputies, and teachers. An AI-powered
assistant would not replace existing information systems but enhance them to
streamline processes for school staff. Specific examples include:

•
Automated data analysis instead of manual review : While e-Okul al-
ready centralizes student information, an AI assistant could proactive-
ly analyze such data. Instead of school administrators and teachers
manually searching for trends, the AI tools could automatically flag a
student whose grades are declining across multiple subjects, identify
a teacher who is not performing, or recognize an entire group strug-
gling with a specific concept. For a school, the AI assistant could create
automated weekly summaries on teacher performance metrics, atten-
dance rates, and other key indicators, saving hours of manual data
compilation; nevertheless, the adoption of these tools also depends
on addressing algorithm aversion, as administrators and teachers may
feel that automated metrics overlook the contextual information that
only human oversight can provide.
•
Automated and tailored communication : An AI assistant can improve
the communication features of the e-Okul Parent Information System
(VBS). It could automatically produce and send tailored weekly prog-
ress reports to parents in Turkish, emphasizing both achievements and
areas for improvement. The AI assistant could also manage schedul-

title: 3.3.2 AI-POWERED PREDICTIVE DETECTION SYSTEMS AS A KEY ADMINISTRATIVE TOOL

paragraphs.text:
The school dropout rate is a growing concern in Türkiye.
Demographic and socioeconomic data reveal that school dropout risk in
Türkiye is higher among girls and adolescents aged 15–17, particularly those
in large households or those balancing caregiving and labor responsibilities.
Statistics indicate that engagement in agricultural work increases the
probability of dropout by 30.6%. 56 Moreover, a recent report from Türkiye’s
Parents’ Association identifies two main factors contributing to this trend:
first, the socioeconomic considerations related to school expenses that may
affect enrollment; and second, shifting perceptions regarding educational
outcomes. The intersection of these factors may influence the educational
pathways of young people.

A critical AI tool in education management is the development of
early warning systems (EWS) to identify students at risk of dropping out .
These systems represent a strategic shift towards early intervention through
the analysis of real-time data from existing platforms like e-Okul, including
academic performance, attendance records, and disciplinary issues. An
AI-powered EWS can detect students at risk long before they disengage,
allowing school leaders to act decisively and enhancing conventional Early
Warning Systems, which have already proven successful in reducing dropout
rates, by improving both the precision and speed of identifying at-risk

title: 34 Artificial Intelligence in School Education in Türkiye

paragraphs.text:
students. 57 The effectiveness of an AI-powered EWS is dependent on two
critical administrative functions:

•
Data governance : The predictive accuracy of an EWS depends on the
quality and timeliness of the data obtained. School administrators in
Türkiye have to be responsible for guaranteeing that student data en-
tered into the national Education Management Information System
(EMIS) is consistent, correct, and updated. This process requires es-
tablishing protocols for data management at the school level and en-
suring compliance to feed the system with reliable information.
•
Operationalizing insights : An alert from an EWS is valuable if it acti-
vates an effective response. The main responsibility of school lead-
ership is to design the framework that follows an alert. This process
involves creating intervention pathways, allocating resources, and em-
powering staff to provide targeted support. Without this framework,
the EWS risks becoming an information tool with no practical impact.

Türkiye is moving beyond theoretical models and has been
working to implement its own national EWS to reduce school dropout .
This system, as announced by the Ministry of National Education , is designed
to identify students at risk of disengagement by tracking key metrics like
absenteeism and grades. By integrating AI in EWS directly into its robust
educational data infrastructure, Türkiye’s administrators can leverage real-
time information to intervene early and provide targeted support. 58 For
example, when an AI system detects correlated anomalies such as a decline in
cross-disciplinary academic performance and attendance frequency, the EWS
can generate an automatic alert for school administrators. This process allows
leadership to transition from reactive monitoring to proactive intervention
through targeted counseling. This strategic deployment demonstrates a
commitment to addressing the dropout issue through the usage of data-
driven technology to ensure students remain in the education system.

Finally, the implementation of EWS demands responsible
leadership . School administrators must ensure the AI models are transparent
and can be explained to parents and teachers. They must also be vigilant
in detecting potential biases in the algorithms to prevent the perpetuation
of inequities against students from certain socioeconomic or regional
backgrounds and alert the Ministry of National Education in such cases. An AI-
powered EWS is not just a technological tool but a management strategy that,
when implemented responsibly, can improve student retention, and ensure
equitable support for every student.

title: 4. Challenges for the private sector

paragraphs.text:
Based on structural and economic conditions in Türkiye, the
challenges for the private sector and EdTech industry in adopting AI for
education are diverse . Consistent with global trends where technological
advancement often outpaces policy development, Türkiye’s EdTech sector
navigates an evolving regulatory landscape that seeks to keep pace with
rapid AI innovation. While the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy sets a
broad vision for expansion into sectors like education, 59 EdTech firms lack
precise legal guidelines regarding high-risk AI classifications. Below, the
report discusses the main challenges that private firms need to navigate to
fully implement AI tools for education: regulatory uncertainty, low AI literacy
among teachers, limited data access, and infrastructure gaps.

title: 4.1 REGULATORY UNCERTAINTY

paragraphs.text:
The private sector in Türkiye operates within a complex regulatory
environment, shaped by frequent legislative changes and uneven
implementation across ministries. According to the OECD Regulatory
Policy Outlook 2025 , 60 Türkiye’s regulatory framework has experienced
several reforms, yet challenges continue: stakeholder consultation is not
systematic, ex‐post evaluation of regulations is not formally established, and
ministries have discretion in the interpretation and enforcement of rules. The
OECD report also highlights that regulatory uncertainty and administrative
complexity remain key barriers to private investment and market entry in
Türkiye, affecting fast‐moving digital sectors such as EdTech and AI‐enabled
services. As a result, companies might face higher transaction costs,
unpredictable approval pathways, and difficulties scaling solutions nationally.

The regulatory environment for AI in education in Türkiye remains
nascent and evolving, creating uncertainty for EdTech companies .
Türkiye’s government has taken important steps toward establishing a national
AI governance framework and MoNE has developed the Artificial Intelligence
in Education Policy Document Action Plan , 61 presenting a forward‐looking
and comprehensive vision for incorporating AI into Türkiye’s education
system, as well as commitments to ethical AI, teacher capacity building,
and personalized learning. However, these frameworks remain essentially
strategic rather than operational, limiting their its practical implementation.
The absence of clear pathways in the field of AI for education also complicates
partnerships with public schools, where administrators may be reluctant to
adopt tools that could later be deemed non‐compliant.

Türkiye is increasingly adopting a governance model based on
coordination in the field of artificial intelligence in education. ETKİM,
operating under the General Directorate of Innovation and Educational
Technologies of the Ministry of National Education, serves as an interface
between public policies and private sector innovation. This unit works to
ensure the alignment of EdTech initiatives with national priorities, guide pilot
implementation processes, structure public-private partnership models, and
create suitable testing environments for scalable solutions. This structure
contributes to the concretization of the regulatory framework not only through
normative documents but also through application-based coordination
mechanisms. Consequently, the AI ecosystem in education in Türkiye is
gradually evolving towards a more holistic management model between
central policy documents and innovative actors in the field.

title: 4.2 LOW AI LITERACY AMONG TEACHERS

paragraphs.text:
A persistent challenge is the low level of digital literacy among
teachers, limiting confidence to meaningfully integrate AI into their
teaching practice . Although Türkiye has made progress in digital infrastructure,
many educators lack the pedagogical and technical knowledge required to
meaningfully integrate AI into teaching and learning. Research on teachers’
digital skills in Türkiye indicates that approximately 70% of educators operate
at only basic or intermediate levels of digital pedagogy, despite growing
awareness of the need for digital transformation in schools. 62 A recent study
of 221 pre‐service teachers in Türkiye found that only the technical dimension
of digital literacy significantly reduces AI‐related anxiety, indicating that future
teachers’ confidence in using AI depends on their ability to understand and
operate technologies. 63

The limited digital and AI literacy among teachers could create an
adoption gap, slowing both classroom adoption of AI tools and the ability
of EdTech to scale AI solutions. Insufficient digital and AI competencies
among teachers creates a structural challenge for the EdTech ecosystem:
schools may be hesitant to adopt AI‐powered tools as teachers do not feel
confident using them. To avoid the adoption gap, the MoNE together with
the EdTech ecosystem should invest in training, onboarding, and ongoing
teacher support.

Türkiye is in fact taking important steps to strengthen teachers’
AI literacy by pairing innovation with large‐scale teacher training and
support . The Ministry of National Education has developed an AI Teacher
Assistant to ease teachers’ daily workload through automated lesson planning,
assessment creation, and classroom management support. Also, the MoNE
is strengthening teachers’ AI readiness through the Teacher Information
Network (ÖBA) , which has already trained more than 157,000 teachers in AI,

title: 4.3. LIMITED DATA ACCESS

paragraphs.text:
Protecting the personal data of Türkiye’s more than 18 million
students and one million teachers is a core priority for the Ministry of
National Education (MoNE) . The Law on the Protection of Personal Data
(KVKK) 65 establishes strong principles for the processing, storage, and transfer
of personal data, including sensitive categories such as educational records,
biometric information, and online identifiers. 66 While the KVKK emphasizes
data localization for regulatory compliance, true system effectiveness
depends on pairing these requirements with robust technical safeguards
and enforcement capacity to ensure superior privacy outcomes. Ensuring
compliance with KVKK also means that AI‐enabled assessment tools must be
carefully monitored before deployment to prevent unlawful processing or
automated decision‐making risks.

Türkiye’s commitment to data protection restricted the use of
international cloud based AI services . KVKK’s provisions limit cross border
data transfers and impose strict obligations on data controllers, including
public institutions and private EdTech providers. While KVKK was initially
seen as more restrictive than the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation
(GDPR) due to its dependence on explicit consent for international transfers 67 ,
the 2024 amendments to the KVKK (Law No. 7499, effective June 1, 2024)
introduced a more structured, three-tier framework under a revised Article
9. Regular or repeated cross-border transfers may now proceed based on
adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses, or binding corporate rules,
with explicit consent no longer serving as a valid mechanism for ongoing
international transfers. Despite these advancements, high compliance
burdens still drive Turkish EdTech developers toward locally hosted, custom
LLMs over global infrastructure. While this localization safeguards data
sovereignty, it inflates costs and slows technology adoption. Moving forward,
the ecosystem could benefit from evaluating how to maintain linguistic and
cultural alignment —which does not strictly require data localization— while
ensuring educational tools remain performant. Exploring hybrid architectures
could provide a path to balance security objectives with the need for Türkiye’s
EdTech industry to remain competitive.

64 Sümeyye, E. et al., (2025). Interview conducted to the Department of AI and Big Data Ap-
plications and AI in Education Initiatives. Ministry of National Education – Republic of Türkiye

text:

students and one million teachers is a core priority for the Ministry of
National Education (MoNE) . The Law on the Protection of Personal Data
(KVKK) 65 establishes strong principles for the processing, storage, and transfer
of personal data, including sensitive categories such as educational records,
biometric information, and online identifiers. 66 While the KVKK emphasizes

depends on pairing these requirements with robust technical safeguards

compliance with KVKK also means that AI‐enabled assessment tools must be

title: 4.4. INFRASTRUCTURE GAPS

paragraphs.text:
Türkiye’s government has made progress in expanding digital
infrastructure through large‐scale initiatives . In Türkiye, through the FATİH
Project, a total of 665,000 interactive whiteboards have been installed in
classrooms and internet access has been provided to schools, thereby
promoting equality of opportunity in education, improving technological
infrastructure in schools, and expanding the effective use of information
technology tools in the teaching and learning process. 68 69 More recently,
the World Bank highlights that Türkiye is upgrading digital platforms and
rolling out an AI‐enhanced version of EBA to support personalized learning
nationwide, provide targeted professional development for teachers, promote
entrepreneurship by supporting students and EdTech start‐ups. 70 These
initiatives represent substantial progress toward a modern digital ecosystem.

Also, the Safe Schooling and Distance Education (SSDE) project
has been instrumental in strengthening Türkiye’s digital infrastructure.
The Ministry of National Education (MoNE) upgraded EBA’s technical
features and user capacity during the pandemic to ensure the platform
remains resilient even under peak demand. After the emergency, the SSDE
project has continued to enhance the EBA platform into a sophisticated
LMS by integrating advanced technologies such as AI and gamification.
This software transformation is supported by a robust physical infrastructure
rollout, which includes establishing EBA connectivity in 3,500 IT classrooms
in disadvantaged districts and equipping 45,000 classrooms with modern
smartboards to facilitate blended learning. 71

Despite major national investments, Türkiye still faces structural
digital infrastructure gaps that constrain the reach of private‐sector AI
solutions. OECD analysis shows that digital divides persist across education
systems and are below the OECD average, especially in regions where
broadband access, device availability, and school‐level digital capacity remain
uneven (See Table 7). 72 Disparities are more pronounced in socio‐economically
disadvantaged and rural areas, where schools report insufficient equipment
and limited capacity to use digital tools effectively.

For AI‐enabled EdTech solutions that depend on stable

title: 5. Key takeaways: AI for education in Turkiye

paragraphs.text:
Takeaway 1 - Proactive government leadership and a national strategy : Türkiye’s
approach to AI in education is not ad-hoc; it is guided by strong and systemic leadership from
the Ministry of National Education (MoNE). Comprehensive national policies like the National
Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2021-2025) and the AI in Education Policy Document and Action
Plan (2025–2029) provide a clear roadmap. These plans need to be aligned with homegrown,
context-specific tools such as the EBA Student Assistant and the AI Teacher Assistant,
demonstrating a commitment to building an educational technology ecosystem.

Key priority
Specific steps moving forward

Ensure coherence
between national AI
strategies and the
actual tools deployed in
schools, by strengthening
governance structures
that coordinate MoNE,
EdTech firms, and
universities.

1. Create a National AI-in-Education committee to align the
National AI Strategy, the AI in Education Action Plan, and
MoNE’s digital platforms (EBA, MEBBİS, ÖBA).
2. Develop a unified technical architecture for all AI tools
used in schools to ensure interoperability.
3. Institutionalize a sandbox for AI innovation, allowing com-
panies to test tools with anonymized datasets under MoNE
supervision.
4. Publish annual progress reports tracking implementation,
adoption, and impact of AI tools across provinces.

Takeaway 2 - The strategy is “AI as an assistant,” not a replacement : Across all
applications, the model for AI integration is to empower, not replace, educators. AI is positioned
as a personalized support for students, a time-saving assistant for teachers in lesson planning
and content creation, and a tool for administrators to automate bureaucratic tasks. This
viewpoint ensures that the unique skills of critical thinking, creativity, and human connection
remain at the center of education.

Key priority
Specific steps moving forward

Reinforce the pedagogical
role of teachers in an
AIenabled classroom and
promote AI literacy among
teachers and students
so they can use tools
responsibly.

1. Develop national design guidelines for AI tools that ex-
plicitly define what tasks AI should and should not per-
form in classrooms.
2. Integrate AI‐supported pedagogy modules into teach-
er training programs, focusing on co‐teaching models
(teacher + AI assistant).
3. Incorporate AI literacy within the curricula, teaching re-
sponsible use, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and aca-
demic integrity.

Takeaway 3 - Human oversight is a non-negotiable principle : While AI offers
powerful tools for automating grading and providing feedback, the “human-in-the-loop”
principle is essential. Teachers must have the final say on student evaluations to ensure fairness,
empathy, and contextual understanding. Any AI assessment system must be transparent,
examined for bias, and compliant with Türkiye’s data protection laws (KVKK).

Key priority
Specific steps moving forward

Strengthen transparency
and accountability in all
AI‐supported assessments,
while ensuring compliance
with KVKK and ethical AI
standards.

1. Develop a national framework for AI in assessment, in-
cluding transparency requirements and audit procedures.
2. Mandate bias testing reports for any AI tool used in grad-
ing or student evaluation.
3. Provide KVKK-compliant data governance templates for
schools and EdTech companies to ensure lawful process-
ing of student data.

title: 42 Artificial Intelligence in School Education in Türkiye

paragraphs.text:
Takeaway 4 - AI is being deployed to tackle critical systemic challenges : The
integration of AI is strategically targeted at some of Türkiye’s most pressing educational issues.
The development of a national Early Warning System (EWS) aims to proactively address the
significant student dropout rate by identifying at-risk students through data analysis. This
strategy shifts the administrative focus from reaction to prevention, showcasing AI’s potential
to drive systemic improvement and enhance educational equity.
Specific steps moving forward

Key
priority

Use AI to address
structural
inequities, not just
classroom‐level
tasks. Strengthening
data infrastructure
is key to support
predictive analytics.

1. Define national indicators for dropout risk, combining academic,
behavioral, and socio‐emotional data.
2. Train school counselors and administrators on interpreting risk
scores and designing targeted interventions.
3. Integrate EWS outputs into MoNE’s case‐management systems,
ensuring follow‐up actions are tracked and evaluated.
4. Develop a national research partnership with universities to
continuously refine predictive models and monitor unintended
consequences.

Takeaway 5 - Success hinges on teacher development : Technology alone is
insufficient. The long-term success of AI depends critically on robust and continuous professional
development for teachers through platforms like ÖBA. Educators must evolve their teaching
methods, moving away from tasks that AI can easily replicate and toward assignments that
demand higher-order skills like critical analysis and creativity. Equipping teachers with the skills
and confidence to integrate AI effectively is the most important factor for a successful digital
transformation.
Specific steps moving forward

Key
priority

Build AI‐ready
teaching
competencies across
all provinces and
shift pedagogy
toward higher‐order
skills that AI cannot
replicate.

1. Expand ÖBA’s AI training modules into a structured, multi‐level
certification pathway (beginner → intermediate → advanced).
2. Integrate AI competencies into pre‐service teacher education,
ensuring new teachers enter the system AI‐literate.
3. Develop model lesson plans and classroom scenarios showing
how teachers can use AI for differentiation, feedback, and proj-
ect‐based learning.
4. Ensure rural and disadvantaged schools receive targeted sup-
port to avoid widening the digital divide.

Takeaway 6 - Strategic alignment through innovation hubs : An important innovation is the
establishment of ETKİM (Education Technology Incubation and Innovation Center) at the METU
Teknokent campus. This center acts as a strategic bridge between the Ministry of National
Education (MoNE) and the private sector. By fostering a “homegrown” innovation model, ETKİM
ensures that digital and AI for education tools are developed with a deep understanding of
local linguistic diversity and pedagogical needs, allowing for seamless integration into national
platforms like EBA.
Specific steps moving forward

Key
priority

Scale the “test-bed”
model to bridge the
gap between EdTech
innovation and
classroom reality

1. Expand the Professional Learning Lab infrastructure to allow
more teachers and academics to provide real-time pedagogical
feedback during the product development phase.
2. Establish a procurement pipeline for successful ETKİM gradu-
ates, ensuring that high-performing local AI tools are prioritized
for national scaling within EBA.

Future investment and strategic policy should prioritize specialized EdTech applications. As
demonstrated by successful local examples like EBA Student Assistant, value is generated by
applying AI directly to specific classroom needs. ETKİM should be the primary vehicle for this
focus, leveraging its strategic position to scale its “test-bed” model and ensure local EdTech
innovation is seamlessly integrated into national platforms like EBA.

paragraphs.text: White Paper

text: White Paper

title: Introduction

paragraphs.text:
AI cluster deployments are approaching scales where physical infrastructure becomes a primary
design constraint. Fiber count, building layout, breakout strategy, optical reach, and power density all
influence deployment feasibility, facility design, operational efficiency, and future expansion. A scalable
physical network architecture must accommodate growth without introducing unnecessary complexity
into the cabling plant. Growth involves more than increasing fiber count. Larger deployments
introduce additional requirements in network topology, infrastructure organization, and facility design
that influence long-term operational flexibility. The paper focuses on the back-end scale-out fabric,
where fiber density, optical connectivity, and physical network architecture have the greatest influence
on deployment scale and long-term infrastructure design.

title: Purpose of This Paper

paragraphs.text:
This white paper is the second installment in AFL’s series on architecting AI infrastructure at scale. The
first paper ( Architecting AI at Scale ) established a three-layer cabling framework comprising backbone
trunks, zone cabling, and equipment cords together with a set of design principles intended to
simplify deployment and support long-term scalability. This paper applies those principles to a practical
16K-XPU back-end network using commercially available optical connectivity technologies. The
objective is to demonstrate how a consistent physical architecture can support current deployments
while remaining adaptable to future compute generations. The paper highlights how infrastructure
requirements change at key scaling thresholds and how design decisions made today reduce the need
for disruptive physical modifications as cluster architectures evolve.

title: Core Design Principles

paragraphs.text: The design philosophy remains straightforward:

-
Zone cabling should perform adaptation and redistribution
-
Equipment cords should complete the final device connection
-
Backbone trunks should deploy the highest fiber count practical for the link and remain
simple, permanent, and application-agnostic

When these responsibilities remain separated, the same physical fiber plant can support scale-out,
storage, front-end networking, and future workload requirements without fundamental changes to
the underlying infrastructure. When these responsibilities become intertwined, changes in compute
architecture can force extensive redesign of the physical plant, increasing complexity, cost, deployment
risk, and time-to-deployment.

One further discipline is added to the framework: all cabling is panel to panel. Within that framework,
panels hold and protect connections but do not adapt, break out, or redistribute fibers. As a result,
cassettes or modules do not appear in either reference design. Instead, topology-driven fiber
rearrangement (including the mesh between switch tiers and the distribution of accelerator lanes
across fabric planes) is implemented in factory-terminated zone cables and equipment cords rather
than panels or trunks.

title: Terminology

paragraphs.text: Two conventions apply throughout this paper and the remainder of the series.

XPU: The Generic Accelerator
This series uses XPU as the generic term for an AI accelerator. XPU covers GPUs, TPUs, and
custom accelerator silicon. The physical connectivity problem (lanes, fibers, connectors, reach) is
the same regardless of what compute sits at the end of the fiber.

T0, T1, T2: Numbered Switch Tiers
This paper names the switch tiers of the scale-out fabric T0, T1, and T2, counting up from the
accelerator. T0, or leaf, is the first switch an XPU lane reaches. T1, or spine, is the next tier
up. T2, or core, is the third tier. The numbered convention is vendor-neutral, extends naturally
as fabrics grow deeper, and avoids terminology that varies between vendors and between
InfiniBand and Ethernet practice.

title: Cluster Scale

paragraphs.text:
The worked example in this paper examines a 16,384-XPU AI training cluster. This scale represents a
practical deployment boundary for a two-tier Clos fabric using current-generation switch silicon and
commercially available optical connectivity. The reference architecture demonstrates how a consistent
physical infrastructure supports high-density AI deployments while maintaining operational simplicity
and providing a foundation for larger cluster architectures.
The companion paper extends the same architectural principles to a 128K-XPU deployment, where
larger scale introduces additional considerations including three-tier fabrics, campus topology, inter-
building connectivity, and higher-density physical infrastructure.

title: Node Architecture

paragraphs.text:
Cluster size is only one dimension of the problem. Node architecture also drives physical infrastructure
requirements. An eight-XPU node and a seventy-two-XPU node create different demands on fiber
density, breakout strategy, rack design, network topology, and where scale-up networking transitions
into scale-out networking. This white paper series works through both examples and concludes with
a forward-looking discussion of the larger node architectures that future compute platforms are
expected to introduce. The goal is to show how changes in node architecture influence every layer of
the cabling system, from rack-level connectivity through to campus-scale network design.

title: Design Assumptions

paragraphs.text:
The worked examples apply the design defaults established in part one of the series: single-mode fiber
throughout, high-fiber-count backbone trunks with Type B polarity, SpiderWeb Ribbon ® (SWR ® ) cable
construction, factory-terminated assemblies, direct panel-to-panel zone distribution, and a design
objective of minimizing separable connections within each channel. SWR ® is AFL’s high-density ribbon
cable construction, enabling very high fiber counts within a reduced cable diameter. While SWR ® is the
reference construction throughout, the architectural principles apply equally to conventional ribbon
and discrete fiber cable constructions. These assumptions provide a consistent baseline for evaluating
cluster architectures at different scales.

title: Scope: Back-End Network

paragraphs.text:
This paper focuses on the back-end scale-out network and the supporting fiber infrastructure.
Compute platform selection, switch ASIC decisions, firmware configuration, and transport protocol
optimization are considered only when directly linked to cabling design. The emphasis is on translating
cluster-scale requirements into practical decisions involving fiber, connectors, panels, pathways, and
network architecture. Readers will gain an understanding of the fiber architecture decisions associated
with current cluster scales, the constraints that emerge as deployments grow, and the design principles
that maintain flexibility across multiple generations of compute infrastructure.

title: Node Size

paragraphs.text:
The node is the unit the fiber plant must serve. Node size determines where scale-up copper ends
and scale-out fiber begins, how much fiber lands at each rack, and what the zone cabling looks like.
Fundamentally, the cluster-level fabric design stems from node design, node density, and total node
quantity, rather than the reverse.

Three node classes cover current deployments and the systems expected over the next generation of
AI infrastructure. The dividing line between classes is the scale-up domain: the set of XPUs sharing a
coherent memory fabric and communicating over the highest-bandwidth interconnect available.

-
Chassis-based nodes contain the scale-up domain within a chassis
-
Rack-based nodes contain the scale-up domain within a rack
-
Multi-rack nodes extend the scale-up domain across multiple racks, at which point scale-up traffic
becomes an optical networking consideration

title: Small: Chassis-Based Node

paragraphs.text:
The chassis-based node typically comprises eight XPUs within a single chassis, with scale-up
connectivity delivered through a passive copper backplane. Scale-out connectivity is provided through
eight NICs operating at 400G or 800G. Typical deployments place two to four nodes within each rack,
producing power densities measured in tens of kilowatts per rack. Fiber lands at the node only for
scale-out, storage, and front-end network traffic. The scale-up domain never leaves the chassis and
never traverses a fiber connector.

title: Medium: Rack-Based Node

paragraphs.text:
The rack-based node uses the full rack as the scale-up domain, with up to seventy-two XPUs linked
through dedicated scale-up switch trays over passive copper. Scale-up traffic still avoids fiber, but the
scale-up domain now occupies the whole rack rather than a single chassis. Scale-out traffic exits the
rack on fiber at one or two ports per XPU, producing fiber counts an order of magnitude higher than
the chassis-based node. Power density exceeds 100 kilowatts per rack and requires liquid cooling,
significantly influencing data hall layout.

title: Large: Multi-Rack Node

paragraphs.text:
In multi-rack nodes, the scale-up domain spans the XPUs of several racks (typically two or three today,
more in future generations). Optical scale-up interconnect carries scale-up traffic between racks at
distances measured in meters. Under this model, every XPU is served by one set of fibers for scale-
up traffic and another set for scale-out traffic, both operating at speeds that current optics support
through dense parallel ribbon connectivity. Fiber count per node increases substantially.

The progression between node classes is not linear. Moving from a chassis-based node to a rack-
based node, copper holds the scale-up domain while the fiber plant serves scale-out, storage, and
front-end traffic. The transition from a rack-based node to a multi-rack node introduces fiber into the
scale-up domain itself. The cabling architecture absorbs this transition without structural change: the
backbone remains unchanged, the zone layer assumes additional mesh and breakout responsibility,
and equipment cords remain close to the device. The three-layer framework’s ability to absorb capacity
is what provides long-term value across generations of cluster architecture.

title: Scale-Out Fabric

paragraphs.text:
The scale-out fabric is aligned across four planes. Each plane is an independent, non-blocking, two-
tier Clos fabric: T0 switches face down to the XPUs and up to the T1 switches. The planes never mix.
Traffic that enters plane 2 at an XPU leaves plane 2 at an XPU.

Each XPU presents one 400G-DR4 fabric port. The DR4 transceiver breaks out into four 100G lanes,
and the fabric assigns one lane to each plane. That breakout is the plane-distribution mechanism:
every XPU touches every plane through a single transceiver and a single MPO-8 connector. Each XPU
therefore connects to each of the four planes with one 100G lane (16,384 T0-facing endpoints per
plane) and all four planes remain independent and symmetrical.

XPU Server Tray with four 400G-DR4 Ports

XPU Server Tray with 4X 400G-DR4 ports, each with four optical lanes of 100G, connecting to four individual switches,
representing the four planes. A detailed explanation of the physical implementation of meshing, including shuffle cables,
striping, and plane distribution, is provided in the Meshing in AI and Hyperscale Data Centers white paper.

The cluster is organized in pods. A pod is sixteen racks of four nodes: 512 XPUs. The 16K cluster
comprises 32 pods. Each pod holds its own per-plane T0 switches, and same-indexed XPUs converge
on a common T0 switch within each plane, keeping intra-pod XPU collectives to a single hop.

The reference design uses 32-port switches. Each port carries a 400G-DR4 transceiver with breakout
capability to four 100G lanes — 128 lanes per switch, split 64 down and 64 up. At that radix a plane
needs eight T0 switches per pod: 256 T0 switches and 128 T1 switches per plane, or 1,024 T0 and
512 T1 switches across the four planes. From the cabling standpoint the relevant fact is that the
lane count carries through unchanged: 16,384 T0–T1 lanes per plane, matching the 16,384 DR4
transceivers on the XPU face (65,536 lanes across the four planes).
400G-DR4 was selected for three reasons:

-
400G-DR4 uses parallel single-mode optics, sharing fiber type and polarity convention with the
rest of the plant
-
400G-DR4 breaks out cleanly into four 100G lanes, allowing each XPU port to distribute across
the four planes
-
400G-DR4's 500-meter reach covers any distance within a single-hall 16K cluster

title: Cabling From the XPU Up

paragraphs.text:
The cabling design philosophy should follow in the direction the fibers run: from the XPU port, up through T0, to T1.
Three equipment layers carry the channel. Equipment cords make the port connections. Zone cables carry fiber between
panels and hold the topology. Trunks carry fiber between zones and consist of Type B, point-to-point connectivity. Panels
sit between the layers as simple MPO-8 pass-through adapter fields. Nothing is spliced, patched through modules, or
reorganized mid-channel.

title: XPU to T0

paragraphs.text:
Each XPU port lands on an MPO-8 equipment cord (eight fibers, Type B, factory terminated)
running from the NIC to the rack panel, typically one to three meters, routed for airflow and
serviceability. A rack of four nodes presents 32 fabric ports: 256 fibers.

From the rack panel, a single 288F zone cable carries the rack’s fabric fibers to the pod’s T0 zone
panel: 256 fibers in use, 32 spare, 36 MPO-8 connectors per end. The mesh is implemented in
the equipment cord between the T0 zone panel and the T0 switches.

The four lanes of every XPU port emerge on four different connectors, one per plane. The panels
at both ends pass the connectors straight through.

Storage and front-end fibers use similar cabling practices at lower fiber counts. Storage NICs
(typically two per node, two fibers each) and front-end connectivity (up to two 400G-DR4 ports
per node, eight fibers each) route on 144F cables toward their own aggregation zones, sharing
pathways and panel discipline with the fabric while remaining separate from the back-end
fabric’s plane-meshed topology.

title: T0 to T1: Backbone Trunks

paragraphs.text:
Backbone trunks are the permanent infrastructure: cables installed once between the pod zones
and the network zone, for the life of the building.

Each T0 switch presents sixteen 400G-DR4 uplink ports: 128 fibers. One 144F trunk per
T0 switch carries those uplinks to the network zone (128 fibers in use, 16 spare, 18 MPO-
8 connectors per end, patched into simple MPO pass-through panels at both ends). Where
pathway consolidation is preferred, one 288F trunk serves a pair of T0 switches. The trunk itself
is Type B polarity end to end, no redistribution.

At 1,024 T0 switches, the trunk plant is 1,024 × 144F (or 512 × 288F): roughly 131,000 T0–T1
fibers, matching the XPU face.

title: Where the Mesh Lives

paragraphs.text:
The Clos topology requires every T0 group to connect to every T1 group — the 4×4 mesh. The
backbone does not commit to that pattern; trunks stay domain-neutral and Type B. The panels
do not implement it; they pass connectors through. The mesh is built into the zone cabling
at the network zone: factory-terminated assemblies whose T1-side connectors regroup the
arriving trunk fibers so that each T1 switch receives lanes from every T0 group in its plane, in a
consistent, documented pattern.

This is the paper’s architectural commitment in one sentence: meshing is done in the equipment
cords, and zone cabling never in panels or trunks. The connectivity patterns supporting this
approach are covered in detail in the Meshing in AI and Hyperscale Data Centers white paper.

The XPU-to-T1 path comprises two optical channels. Each channel crosses two separable panel
connections - four end to end plus the transceiver interfaces. Reach is rarely the constraint inside
a cluster — DR4 covers 500 meters — but connector count against the optical power budget is.
Panel-to-panel cabling with no modules keeps that count at the minimum the topology allows.

title: Fiber-Count Cascade

paragraphs.text:
The cascade builds the physical bill of materials from the XPU upward. Each stage identifies the physical products required
and the associated connectivity between network tiers, providing an auditable framework for deriving cable quantities,
connector counts, fiber utilization, fiber-kilometers, and other deployment metrics.

-
Per XPU: One fabric port, 400G-DR4, eight fibers, one MPO-8
-
Per node: 8 XPUs × 8 fibers = 64 fibers for the back-end scale-out fabric
-
Per rack (four nodes): ~336 fibers comprising 256 back-end fabric fibers plus ~80 storage and front-end fibers, with
one 288F zone shuffle cable serving the back-end fabric, meshing across the four planes between the two T0 racks in
the pod; smaller cables serve the remaining networks
-
Per T0 switch: 16 ports down, 16 ports up — 128 fibers on each side, one 144F trunk per switch carries the uplinks
-
Per plane: 16,384 lanes, one per XPU — 32,768 fibers entering from the pods and 32,768 leaving toward T1,
non-blocking, so the counts balance
-
Across four planes: 131,072 fibers on the XPU-facing side of T0, matched by 131,072 on the T1-facing side, the
backbone carries the full fabric count

Roughly a quarter of a million fibers for one 16K hall, scale-out fabric alone. About 16,000 MPO-8 port terminations at
the XPU face to test and record. Every one of them factory terminated.

title: Conclusion

paragraphs.text:
The 16K-XPU reference architecture demonstrates that large AI training clusters can be deployed
using a consistent, scalable physical infrastructure based on commercially available optical
connectivity. The three-layer cabling framework, combined with panel-to-panel connectivity,
factory-terminated assemblies, and topology implemented within equipment cords and zone
cabling, produces a physical plant that remains simple to deploy, straightforward to operate, and
adaptable to future compute generations.
The worked example provides a practical reference design for a two-tier, 16K-XPU Clos
fabric. Every major design decision, from fiber counts and cable hierarchy through to plane
distribution and mesh implementation, supports a common objective of reducing operational
complexity while preserving long-term flexibility. The resulting architecture separates permanent
infrastructure from topology-specific connectivity, accommodating expansion without
fundamental backbone changes.
A 16K deployment is an important architectural milestone rather than the upper limit of
cluster scale. Larger deployments introduce additional design considerations involving rack-
scale compute, three-tier fabrics, campus topology, optical reach, and higher-density physical
infrastructure. The companion paper examines those changes and demonstrates how the same
architectural principles extend to campus-scale AI infrastructure while maintaining the consistent
physical framework established in this reference design.

title: Building AI Training Clusters at 16K Accelerators

paragraphs.text: White Paper

text: White Paper

title: Introduction

paragraphs.text:
AI cluster deployments are approaching scales where physical infrastructure becomes a primary
design constraint. Fiber count, building layout, breakout strategy, optical reach, and power density all
influence deployment feasibility, facility design, operational efficiency, and future expansion. A scalable
physical network architecture must accommodate growth without introducing unnecessary complexity
into the cabling plant. Growth involves more than increasing fiber count. Larger deployments
introduce additional requirements in network topology, infrastructure organization, and facility design
that influence long-term operational flexibility. The paper focuses on the back-end scale-out fabric,
where fiber density, optical connectivity, and physical network architecture have the greatest influence
on deployment scale and long-term infrastructure design.

title: Purpose of This Paper

paragraphs.text:
This white paper is the second installment in AFL’s series on architecting AI infrastructure at scale. The
first paper ( Architecting AI at Scale ) established a three-layer cabling framework comprising backbone
trunks, zone cabling, and equipment cords together with a set of design principles intended to
simplify deployment and support long-term scalability. This paper applies those principles to a practical
16K-XPU back-end network using commercially available optical connectivity technologies. The
objective is to demonstrate how a consistent physical architecture can support current deployments
while remaining adaptable to future compute generations. The paper highlights how infrastructure
requirements change at key scaling thresholds and how design decisions made today reduce the need
for disruptive physical modifications as cluster architectures evolve.

title: Core Design Principles

paragraphs.text: The design philosophy remains straightforward:

-
Zone cabling should perform adaptation and redistribution
-
Equipment cords should complete the final device connection
-
Backbone trunks should deploy the highest fiber count practical for the link and remain
simple, permanent, and application-agnostic

When these responsibilities remain separated, the same physical fiber plant can support scale-out,
storage, front-end networking, and future workload requirements without fundamental changes to
the underlying infrastructure. When these responsibilities become intertwined, changes in compute
architecture can force extensive redesign of the physical plant, increasing complexity, cost, deployment
risk, and time-to-deployment.

One further discipline is added to the framework: all cabling is panel to panel. Within that framework,
panels hold and protect connections but do not adapt, break out, or redistribute fibers. As a result,
cassettes or modules do not appear in either reference design. Instead, topology-driven fiber
rearrangement (including the mesh between switch tiers and the distribution of accelerator lanes
across fabric planes) is implemented in factory-terminated zone cables and equipment cords rather
than panels or trunks.

title: Terminology

paragraphs.text: Two conventions apply throughout this paper and the remainder of the series.

XPU: The Generic Accelerator
This series uses XPU as the generic term for an AI accelerator. XPU covers GPUs, TPUs, and
custom accelerator silicon. The physical connectivity problem (lanes, fibers, connectors, reach) is
the same regardless of what compute sits at the end of the fiber.

T0, T1, T2: Numbered Switch Tiers
This paper names the switch tiers of the scale-out fabric T0, T1, and T2, counting up from the
accelerator. T0, or leaf, is the first switch an XPU lane reaches. T1, or spine, is the next tier
up. T2, or core, is the third tier. The numbered convention is vendor-neutral, extends naturally
as fabrics grow deeper, and avoids terminology that varies between vendors and between
InfiniBand and Ethernet practice.

title: Cluster Scale

paragraphs.text:
The worked example in this paper examines a 16,384-XPU AI training cluster. This scale represents a
practical deployment boundary for a two-tier Clos fabric using current-generation switch silicon and
commercially available optical connectivity. The reference architecture demonstrates how a consistent
physical infrastructure supports high-density AI deployments while maintaining operational simplicity
and providing a foundation for larger cluster architectures.
The companion paper extends the same architectural principles to a 128K-XPU deployment, where
larger scale introduces additional considerations including three-tier fabrics, campus topology, inter-
building connectivity, and higher-density physical infrastructure.

title: Node Architecture

paragraphs.text:
Cluster size is only one dimension of the problem. Node architecture also drives physical infrastructure
requirements. An eight-XPU node and a seventy-two-XPU node create different demands on fiber
density, breakout strategy, rack design, network topology, and where scale-up networking transitions
into scale-out networking. This white paper series works through both examples and concludes with
a forward-looking discussion of the larger node architectures that future compute platforms are
expected to introduce. The goal is to show how changes in node architecture influence every layer of
the cabling system, from rack-level connectivity through to campus-scale network design.

title: Design Assumptions

paragraphs.text:
The worked examples apply the design defaults established in part one of the series: single-mode fiber
throughout, high-fiber-count backbone trunks with Type B polarity, SpiderWeb Ribbon ® (SWR ® ) cable
construction, factory-terminated assemblies, direct panel-to-panel zone distribution, and a design
objective of minimizing separable connections within each channel. SWR ® is AFL’s high-density ribbon
cable construction, enabling very high fiber counts within a reduced cable diameter. While SWR ® is the
reference construction throughout, the architectural principles apply equally to conventional ribbon
and discrete fiber cable constructions. These assumptions provide a consistent baseline for evaluating
cluster architectures at different scales.

title: Scope: Back-End Network

paragraphs.text:
This paper focuses on the back-end scale-out network and the supporting fiber infrastructure.
Compute platform selection, switch ASIC decisions, firmware configuration, and transport protocol
optimization are considered only when directly linked to cabling design. The emphasis is on translating
cluster-scale requirements into practical decisions involving fiber, connectors, panels, pathways, and
network architecture. Readers will gain an understanding of the fiber architecture decisions associated
with current cluster scales, the constraints that emerge as deployments grow, and the design principles
that maintain flexibility across multiple generations of compute infrastructure.

title: Node Size

paragraphs.text:
The node is the unit the fiber plant must serve. Node size determines where scale-up copper ends
and scale-out fiber begins, how much fiber lands at each rack, and what the zone cabling looks like.
Fundamentally, the cluster-level fabric design stems from node design, node density, and total node
quantity, rather than the reverse.

Three node classes cover current deployments and the systems expected over the next generation of
AI infrastructure. The dividing line between classes is the scale-up domain: the set of XPUs sharing a
coherent memory fabric and communicating over the highest-bandwidth interconnect available.

-
Chassis-based nodes contain the scale-up domain within a chassis
-
Rack-based nodes contain the scale-up domain within a rack
-
Multi-rack nodes extend the scale-up domain across multiple racks, at which point scale-up traffic
becomes an optical networking consideration

title: Small: Chassis-Based Node

paragraphs.text:
The chassis-based node typically comprises eight XPUs within a single chassis, with scale-up
connectivity delivered through a passive copper backplane. Scale-out connectivity is provided through
eight NICs operating at 400G or 800G. Typical deployments place two to four nodes within each rack,
producing power densities measured in tens of kilowatts per rack. Fiber lands at the node only for
scale-out, storage, and front-end network traffic. The scale-up domain never leaves the chassis and
never traverses a fiber connector.

title: Medium: Rack-Based Node

paragraphs.text:
The rack-based node uses the full rack as the scale-up domain, with up to seventy-two XPUs linked
through dedicated scale-up switch trays over passive copper. Scale-up traffic still avoids fiber, but the
scale-up domain now occupies the whole rack rather than a single chassis. Scale-out traffic exits the
rack on fiber at one or two ports per XPU, producing fiber counts an order of magnitude higher than
the chassis-based node. Power density exceeds 100 kilowatts per rack and requires liquid cooling,
significantly influencing data hall layout.

title: Large: Multi-Rack Node

paragraphs.text:
In multi-rack nodes, the scale-up domain spans the XPUs of several racks (typically two or three today,
more in future generations). Optical scale-up interconnect carries scale-up traffic between racks at
distances measured in meters. Under this model, every XPU is served by one set of fibers for scale-
up traffic and another set for scale-out traffic, both operating at speeds that current optics support
through dense parallel ribbon connectivity. Fiber count per node increases substantially.

The progression between node classes is not linear. Moving from a chassis-based node to a rack-
based node, copper holds the scale-up domain while the fiber plant serves scale-out, storage, and
front-end traffic. The transition from a rack-based node to a multi-rack node introduces fiber into the
scale-up domain itself. The cabling architecture absorbs this transition without structural change: the
backbone remains unchanged, the zone layer assumes additional mesh and breakout responsibility,
and equipment cords remain close to the device. The three-layer framework’s ability to absorb capacity
is what provides long-term value across generations of cluster architecture.

title: Scale-Out Fabric

paragraphs.text:
The scale-out fabric is aligned across four planes. Each plane is an independent, non-blocking, two-
tier Clos fabric: T0 switches face down to the XPUs and up to the T1 switches. The planes never mix.
Traffic that enters plane 2 at an XPU leaves plane 2 at an XPU.

Each XPU presents one 400G-DR4 fabric port. The DR4 transceiver breaks out into four 100G lanes,
and the fabric assigns one lane to each plane. That breakout is the plane-distribution mechanism:
every XPU touches every plane through a single transceiver and a single MPO-8 connector. Each XPU
therefore connects to each of the four planes with one 100G lane (16,384 T0-facing endpoints per
plane) and all four planes remain independent and symmetrical.

XPU Server Tray with four 400G-DR4 Ports

XPU Server Tray with 4X 400G-DR4 ports, each with four optical lanes of 100G, connecting to four individual switches,
representing the four planes. A detailed explanation of the physical implementation of meshing, including shuffle cables,
striping, and plane distribution, is provided in the Meshing in AI and Hyperscale Data Centers white paper.

The cluster is organized in pods. A pod is sixteen racks of four nodes: 512 XPUs. The 16K cluster
comprises 32 pods. Each pod holds its own per-plane T0 switches, and same-indexed XPUs converge
on a common T0 switch within each plane, keeping intra-pod XPU collectives to a single hop.

The reference design uses 32-port switches. Each port carries a 400G-DR4 transceiver with breakout
capability to four 100G lanes — 128 lanes per switch, split 64 down and 64 up. At that radix a plane
needs eight T0 switches per pod: 256 T0 switches and 128 T1 switches per plane, or 1,024 T0 and
512 T1 switches across the four planes. From the cabling standpoint the relevant fact is that the
lane count carries through unchanged: 16,384 T0–T1 lanes per plane, matching the 16,384 DR4
transceivers on the XPU face (65,536 lanes across the four planes).
400G-DR4 was selected for three reasons:

-
400G-DR4 uses parallel single-mode optics, sharing fiber type and polarity convention with the
rest of the plant
-
400G-DR4 breaks out cleanly into four 100G lanes, allowing each XPU port to distribute across
the four planes
-
400G-DR4's 500-meter reach covers any distance within a single-hall 16K cluster

title: Cabling From the XPU Up

paragraphs.text:
The cabling design philosophy should follow in the direction the fibers run: from the XPU port, up through T0, to T1.
Three equipment layers carry the channel. Equipment cords make the port connections. Zone cables carry fiber between
panels and hold the topology. Trunks carry fiber between zones and consist of Type B, point-to-point connectivity. Panels
sit between the layers as simple MPO-8 pass-through adapter fields. Nothing is spliced, patched through modules, or
reorganized mid-channel.

title: XPU to T0

paragraphs.text:
Each XPU port lands on an MPO-8 equipment cord (eight fibers, Type B, factory terminated)
running from the NIC to the rack panel, typically one to three meters, routed for airflow and
serviceability. A rack of four nodes presents 32 fabric ports: 256 fibers.

From the rack panel, a single 288F zone cable carries the rack’s fabric fibers to the pod’s T0 zone
panel: 256 fibers in use, 32 spare, 36 MPO-8 connectors per end. The mesh is implemented in
the equipment cord between the T0 zone panel and the T0 switches.

The four lanes of every XPU port emerge on four different connectors, one per plane. The panels
at both ends pass the connectors straight through.

Storage and front-end fibers use similar cabling practices at lower fiber counts. Storage NICs
(typically two per node, two fibers each) and front-end connectivity (up to two 400G-DR4 ports
per node, eight fibers each) route on 144F cables toward their own aggregation zones, sharing
pathways and panel discipline with the fabric while remaining separate from the back-end
fabric’s plane-meshed topology.

title: T0 to T1: Backbone Trunks

paragraphs.text:
Backbone trunks are the permanent infrastructure: cables installed once between the pod zones
and the network zone, for the life of the building.

Each T0 switch presents sixteen 400G-DR4 uplink ports: 128 fibers. One 144F trunk per
T0 switch carries those uplinks to the network zone (128 fibers in use, 16 spare, 18 MPO-
8 connectors per end, patched into simple MPO pass-through panels at both ends). Where
pathway consolidation is preferred, one 288F trunk serves a pair of T0 switches. The trunk itself
is Type B polarity end to end, no redistribution.

At 1,024 T0 switches, the trunk plant is 1,024 × 144F (or 512 × 288F): roughly 131,000 T0–T1
fibers, matching the XPU face.

title: Where the Mesh Lives

paragraphs.text:
The Clos topology requires every T0 group to connect to every T1 group — the 4×4 mesh. The
backbone does not commit to that pattern; trunks stay domain-neutral and Type B. The panels
do not implement it; they pass connectors through. The mesh is built into the zone cabling
at the network zone: factory-terminated assemblies whose T1-side connectors regroup the
arriving trunk fibers so that each T1 switch receives lanes from every T0 group in its plane, in a
consistent, documented pattern.

This is the paper’s architectural commitment in one sentence: meshing is done in the equipment
cords, and zone cabling never in panels or trunks. The connectivity patterns supporting this
approach are covered in detail in the Meshing in AI and Hyperscale Data Centers white paper.

The XPU-to-T1 path comprises two optical channels. Each channel crosses two separable panel
connections - four end to end plus the transceiver interfaces. Reach is rarely the constraint inside
a cluster — DR4 covers 500 meters — but connector count against the optical power budget is.
Panel-to-panel cabling with no modules keeps that count at the minimum the topology allows.

title: Fiber-Count Cascade

paragraphs.text:
The cascade builds the physical bill of materials from the XPU upward. Each stage identifies the physical products required
and the associated connectivity between network tiers, providing an auditable framework for deriving cable quantities,
connector counts, fiber utilization, fiber-kilometers, and other deployment metrics.

-
Per XPU: One fabric port, 400G-DR4, eight fibers, one MPO-8
-
Per node: 8 XPUs × 8 fibers = 64 fibers for the back-end scale-out fabric
-
Per rack (four nodes): ~336 fibers comprising 256 back-end fabric fibers plus ~80 storage and front-end fibers, with
one 288F zone shuffle cable serving the back-end fabric, meshing across the four planes between the two T0 racks in
the pod; smaller cables serve the remaining networks
-
Per T0 switch: 16 ports down, 16 ports up — 128 fibers on each side, one 144F trunk per switch carries the uplinks
-
Per plane: 16,384 lanes, one per XPU — 32,768 fibers entering from the pods and 32,768 leaving toward T1,
non-blocking, so the counts balance
-
Across four planes: 131,072 fibers on the XPU-facing side of T0, matched by 131,072 on the T1-facing side, the
backbone carries the full fabric count

Roughly a quarter of a million fibers for one 16K hall, scale-out fabric alone. About 16,000 MPO-8 port terminations at
the XPU face to test and record. Every one of them factory terminated.

title: Conclusion

paragraphs.text:
The 16K-XPU reference architecture demonstrates that large AI training clusters can be deployed
using a consistent, scalable physical infrastructure based on commercially available optical
connectivity. The three-layer cabling framework, combined with panel-to-panel connectivity,
factory-terminated assemblies, and topology implemented within equipment cords and zone
cabling, produces a physical plant that remains simple to deploy, straightforward to operate, and
adaptable to future compute generations.
The worked example provides a practical reference design for a two-tier, 16K-XPU Clos
fabric. Every major design decision, from fiber counts and cable hierarchy through to plane
distribution and mesh implementation, supports a common objective of reducing operational
complexity while preserving long-term flexibility. The resulting architecture separates permanent
infrastructure from topology-specific connectivity, accommodating expansion without
fundamental backbone changes.
A 16K deployment is an important architectural milestone rather than the upper limit of
cluster scale. Larger deployments introduce additional design considerations involving rack-
scale compute, three-tier fabrics, campus topology, optical reach, and higher-density physical
infrastructure. The companion paper examines those changes and demonstrates how the same
architectural principles extend to campus-scale AI infrastructure while maintaining the consistent
physical framework established in this reference design.

title: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

paragraphs.text:
Today, current AI systems can execute many tasks that were once the sole domain of humans,
including both routine and non-routine intellectual work. The increasing adoption of AI technologies
within workplaces is altering the way individuals utilise cognitive, socio-emotional, and physical
abilities to perform tasks across a broad range of occupations. This shift is reshaping the variety and
depth of different skills that are expected from workers.
Rising demand for cognitive skills

Studies highlight a growing demand for cognitive skills as a result of AI adoption, particularly those
associated with higher-order analytical abilities, critical thinking and problem solving. The depth of
cognitive abilities expected from workers is increasing and becoming more diverse, often leading to a
shift in the occupational structure towards roles that require advanced skills. This trend is likely to
persist and expand to a wider range of jobs, especially if the newly created jobs are concentrated in
the non-routine and the cognitive or metacognitive categories.
Human-AI collaboration and overseeing AI

The proliferation of AI-generated content is redefining the use of cognitive skills, moving away from
pure creation towards tasks such as editorial review and appraisal. This shift elevates the importance
of contextualising, overseeing, and making judgements, which are tasks that, so far, are better
performed by humans. Effective human-AI collaboration requires individuals to provide framing,
oversight, and context, which cannot be delivered without a strong area-specific expertise as well as
scientific and computational literacy, even for those in non-technical roles.
Further boost in the value of digital skills and hybrid roles

AI technologies are driving further demand for digital skills, both in terms of variety and depth of skills.
In particular, intermediate and advanced digital skills are required to integrate and use AI tools within
several sectors and occupations. This shift is reshaping what it means to be a digitally competent
worker, while also extending and deepening hybrid roles that combine traditional expertise with
computational skills. Digital and data literacies are prerequisites for effectively interacting with AI
systems.
Intensifying the value of socio-emotional skills

Despite advances in AI, the technology cannot still perform tasks requiring emotional intelligence and
complex human interaction. This limitation further heightens the importance of socio-emotional skills,
which remain uniquely human. Such skills are also essential for the fair and human-centric adoption of
AI, functioning as the human enablers of technological advancement while safeguarding ethical
principles.
Human strengths in an AI-driven workplace

Human cognition, emotion, judgement, and creativity are essential for a meaningful human-AI
collaboration. In a world where machines can process information rapidly, recognise patterns on a
large scale, and optimise routine decisions, the distinct strengths humans offer include the ability to
adapt to the unexpected, judge ethical implications, communicate across disciplines, and learn
continuously. This is part of a broader transition in how we value work, navigate uncertainty, relate to
others, and integrate meaning and fairness into technology-driven processes.
Shifts in manual skills and complementarities

relative importance of manual skills for routine activities. However, more refined manual skills for

performed by humans. Effective human-AI collaboration requires individuals to provide framing,
oversight, and context, which cannot be delivered without a strong area-specific expertise as well as
scientific and computational literacy, even for those in non-technical roles.
Further boost in the value of digital skills and hybrid roles
AI technologies are driving further demand for digital skills, both in terms of variety and depth of skills.
In particular, intermediate and advanced digital skills are required to integrate and use AI tools within
several sectors and occupations. This shift is reshaping what it means to be a digitally competent
worker, while also extending and deepening hybrid roles that combine traditional expertise with
computational skills. Digital and data literacies are prerequisites for effectively interacting with AI
systems.
Intensifying the value of socio-emotional skills
Despite advances in AI, the technology cannot still perform tasks requiring emotional intelligence and
complex human interaction. This limitation further heightens the importance of socio-emotional skills,
which remain uniquely human. Such skills are also essential for the fair and human-centric adoption of
AI, functioning as the human enablers of technological advancement while safeguarding ethical
principles.
Human strengths in an AI-driven workplace
Human cognition, emotion, judgement, and creativity are essential for a meaningful human-AI
collaboration. In a world where machines can process information rapidly, recognise patterns on a
large scale, and optimise routine decisions, the distinct strengths humans offer include the ability to
adapt to the unexpected, judge ethical implications, communicate across disciplines, and learn
continuously. This is part of a broader transition in how we value work, navigate uncertainty, relate to
others, and integrate meaning and fairness into technology-driven processes.
Shifts in manual skills and complementarities
Execution of simple manual tasks in controlled environments by AI-enabled robots is diminishing the
relative importance of manual skills for routine activities. However, more refined manual skills for

title: CHANGING LANDSCAPE OF SKILLS IN THE AGE OF AI | 05

paragraphs.text:
performing non-routine tasks are less affected. For example, robots can efficiently move goods along
predefined routes and handle uniform packages. However, human workers with refined manual skills
are needed to resolve issues. Human involvement continues to be essential in real-world dynamic
environments with unstructured tasks.
Emerging demand for technical AI skills/workforce

Perhaps the most immediate impact of AI has been the emergence of new demand for specialised
technical skills that were previously non-existent, that are necessary to develop, maintain, and
implement AI systems. As a result, the expanding 'AI workforce' now encompasses individuals with
varying levels of technical competency, ranging from highly sophisticated frontier AI researchers and
engineers to professional users who incorporate AI technologies into their daily work.
Small but growing size of the AI workforce

Research indicates that only a small share of the workforce is involved in the development and
professional use of AI technologies. Depending on the analytical methods and definitions applied, the
share of the AI workforce ranges from as little as 0.3% to as much as 5% of total employment, with
variations across countries and over time. Nevertheless, the demand for AI-related skills has
increased rapidly over the past decade, driven by the growing necessity to design, apply, and manage
these systems.
Profile of AI workforce, occupations and sectors

The majority of AI workforce are highly educated white men with prime working age, particularly visible
among AI developers. Specialised AI skills are found at the intersection of mathematics, science, and
computer science, with AI concentrated thus far in a few high-skilled occupations, notably
mathematician, actuary, statistician, software and application developer, ICT manager, and database
and network professional. The majority of the AI workforce is, therefore, among professionals and
associate professionals in ICT, finance and professional, scientific and technical fields, although AI
skill demand is gradually expanding to other sectors.
Proficiency levels of AI workforce

Technical AI skills can be understood as existing along a hierarchical spectrum. This ranges from
task-based familiarity with AI tools to sophisticated competencies in AI development and engineering.
The 'AI developer' profile is the most clearly defined, focusing on designing and building AI systems.
Meanwhile, the 'AI user' profile encompasses workers with varying degrees of technical skills, from
those capable of redesigning or implementing AI tools to non-specialist users who interact with AI-
enhanced systems. Consequently, AI skills are categorised from basic to intermediate and advanced
levels, each building upon the previous.
Emergence of AI literacy as a foundational skill

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into our daily lives and workplaces, the need for individuals to
comprehend and safely use AI tools in an ethical manner has emerged as a new fundamental skill. AI
literacy is now regarded as a core requirement for the new digital era, enabling individuals to exercise
agency and participate fully in AI-enhanced environments. It is vital not only for workers who interact
directly with AI technologies, but also for all citizens affected by the expanding reach of these tools in
government services, media, privacy, finance, healthcare, and education.
Three domains of AI literacy to learn

AI literacy encompasses three closely linked domains. The first is technical literacy, which involves a
basic understanding of how AI systems function, including familiarity with machine learning,
algorithms, and data-driven technologies. The second domain is analytical and data literacy, or the
capacity to interpret and assess AI outputs in real-world situations. The third domain is ethical and

title: CHANGING LANDSCAPE OF SKILLS IN THE AGE OF AI | 06

paragraphs.text:
societal literacy. As AI becomes woven into work and everyday life, individuals must be aware of
issues related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, fairness, and
sustainability.
Integrating AI literacy into education and training

Embedding an AI competence framework into initial and continuous education and training is
considered essential to prepare current and future generations for an AI-driven world. There have
been efforts to operationalise AI literacy as a structured, teachable, and measurable competence,
integrated across the curriculum as a transversal skill from primary to higher education, as well as
adult learning programmes and workplace training. Various frameworks are now available to support
the teaching and learning of AI to students, teachers, and adults.
Policy responses to low levels of AI literacy and skills

As current levels of AI literacy among workers remain low, several countries have incorporated AI
skilling into their national AI strategies and actions. Also, short and diverse learning pathways exist for
workforce AI skilling, including employer-led training, collaborations between academia and industry or
bootcamps. However, the existing supply of training may be insufficient to meet the growing and
rapidly evolving demand, particularly for general AI literacy. Policies need to expand AI literacy
programmes to reach more diverse groups, as most workers will require the skills necessary to use
and interact with AI systems to stay employable and autonomous in the AI-driven world of work.

Revising occupational standards, qualifications and curricula and adapting quality
assurance

Adjusting occupational standards and learning outcomes to reflect changing workplace realities has
become a necessity. Learners and workers not only need general AI literacy, but also sector- and
occupation-specific guidance on how AI changes workflows, decision-making processes, quality
standards and human interaction within specific occupations and sectors. The growing use of AI
technologies in education and workplace also requires significant adaptation of assessment,
certification and quality assurance systems in education. However, successful integration of AI-related
competences into education and training systems depends heavily on the preparedness of teachers,
trainers and institutions.
Beyond AI: Future-readiness and empowerment

AI is not the sole force transforming labour markets. Given multiple disruptions, the concept of ‘future-
ready skills’ has emerged, emphasising the need for individuals to adapt and thrive in a rapidly
evolving world. As information becomes more accessible, the focus shifts from simply acquiring
knowledge to developing ‘wisdom’ through robust foundational skills, socio-emotional learning, and
future-readiness. These broader skillsets are essential not only for handling more complex workplace
tasks but also for empowering citizens in an uncertain future.
Developing human capabilities in an AI-powered future

An AI-powered future calls for citizens who are resourceful, resilient, and adaptable to perform
effectively in different work-related settings. This requires a shift in focus from teaching specific
skillsets to the cultivation of broader human ‘capabilities’. Such capabilities go beyond particular skill
domains and underpin human agency and the ability to learn, apply, and adapt knowledge and skills
for future needs. Capabilities are built within skills ecosystems – coordinated through life-course
education and training investments, firm practices, labour market institutions, and social dialogue.
Ethical AI governance and robust workplace safeguards are as critical as investment in skills to
enhance human capabilities.
