title: 1 Introduction: Why ICT co- ordination?

paragraphs.text:
Despite having had a transformative impact on society and the daily lives of billions, the extent that digital
tools have shaped education is an open question. Research on teachers’ use of digital tools tends to point
to a variable picture, with secondary analysis of PISA 2022 data suggesting some very digitally-engaged
teachers who make regular use of digital tools, some very digitally-disengaged teachers, and then a larger
group in the middle of these extremes (Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025 [1] ). It can be argued that, in general,
there is a somewhat surface-level presence of technology in the classroom. For some time now, it seems
that technology for communication purposes is most common, but its use for more conceptual
understanding is far less common (Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025 [1] ; OECD, 2020 [2] ).

In one respect a degree of caution in the use of digital tools can be valuable. The moderated use of digital
tools, where the presence of analogue methods accompanies digital tools, seems important based on the
latest evidence on certain digital tools (Forsström et al., 2025 [3] ). There are tentative signs that countries
are also mindful of an unfettered, all-encompassing digitalisation of classrooms, as reflected in attention
to mobile-phone use in schools and classrooms (OECD, 2024 [4] ). Indeed, a recent literature review of five
digital tools and their use in the classroom suggested that digital tools are not a panacea that can single-
handedly unlock higher student outcomes (Forsström et al., 2025 [5] ). Digital tools require careful
implementation by teachers, where professional judgement by teachers of their timing, relevance and
purpose are all essential (Forsström et al., 2025 [3] ).

That said, when used with a meaningful pedagogical intention, the literature indicates that digital tools can
have significant impact on a range of student outcomes (Forsström et al., 2025 [3] ). Moreover, classrooms
remain an essential space for students to learn about how to effectively use and apply tools. Students can
build essential knowledge about how certain technologies function, including their limitations and
affordances, and develop a mastery of the appropriate application of these technologies. In particular,
classrooms can support the equitable development of this type of digital literacy. Rather than leaving the
development of students’ digital literacy to chance and the opportunities that their backgrounds may, or
may not, afford, classrooms are a means of helping to ensure the equitable access to learning opportunities
on and using digital tools. In this respect, teachers can help to mitigate the development of digital divides
that may arise and exacerbate inequalities, both in the immediate- and long-term.

evolve. It means that there is always a need to critically engage with what is and is not possible and to ask

research on digital tools is still developing, due to the time demands of collecting rigorous evidence and
the relative infancy of many tools. In this respect, there is a need for a constant and critical engagement
with digital tools and their role in education.

tools have shaped education is an open question. Research on teachers’ use of digital tools tends to point
to a variable picture, with secondary analysis of PISA 2022 data suggesting some very digitally-engaged

paragraphs.text:
Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ). In particular, attention on ICT co-ordination has grown as the picture has
become clearer that the application of digital tools needs to be thoughtful, measured and organised through
a set of several individuals. Moreover, that this application depends on an often incomplete or evolving
picture of what technologies may be able to effectively do, this makes the effective identification and critical
engagement with such technologies even more important and thus heightens the importance of clear co-
ordination efforts. As the power of technologies grows, so too do the potential opportunities and challenges.
Co-ordination is important for enabling schools to be responsive to these changes in an efficient, equitable
way. Indeed, it is important to emphasise here that while attention has primarily focussed on formal co-
ordinator roles, it is wrong to view these as the sole agents at work. Digitalisation is not simply outsourced
to co-ordinators for them to address, but effective integration of digital tools into classroom and the
processes of schools is a collective effort and responsibility. Co-ordinators are the agents that can help to
spearhead and streamline this process, identifying the risks and the opportunities in their context and
building the capacity of their colleagues to make sure nobody is left behind.

This working paper aims to present a short overview of the literature on ICT co-ordination at the school
level. It focusses in particular on the role of ‘ICT co-ordinators’. Different terminologies have been used in
the literature and across contexts to describe this role, such as ‘ICT mentor’, ‘ICT manager’ and ‘digital
pedagogues’ (Letnes, 2025 [7] ), all of which reflect compelling aspects of this broad, important and still
poorly understood role. The term ‘ICT co-ordinator’ is relatively common in the literature and is adopted
here for ease, while acknowledging the variation that may exist in different systems.

This working paper aims to provide a rapid survey of the literature in what is a still relatively nascent field
but, accordingly, also fast-moving as new and varied contexts are studied (e.g. Gustafsson, Olofsson and
Bergström, 2024 [6] ; Letnes, 2025 [5] ). The authors have prepared this paper in the knowledge that the ideas
it presents may well change and evolve in the future as new findings emerge; indeed, it is hoped that our
collective understanding will progress and certain ideas that are put forward here are challenged and
refined.

This working paper draws upon the evolving work of the OECD project “Resourcing School Education:
Policies for the Digital Transformation of Education and Future-Readiness of Teachers”. This includes its
work to understand the use of digital tools in classrooms and their potential. In particular, this work is
synthesised alongside some of the literature for an ongoing project supporting Bulgaria and Slovakia,
funded by the European Union via the Technical Support Instrument, and implemented by the OECD in
cooperation with SG REFORM from the European Commission.

This working paper first elaborates on the context of digitalisation in classrooms and schools to help frame
why effective ICT co-ordination is so important. It then turns to consider in more detail the tasks that are
typically encompassed by ICT co-ordination. A key rationale here is that ambiguity in the role of ICT co-
ordination significantly impairs its effectiveness (León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada,
2019 [6] ; Letnes, 2025 [7] ). This detailed review hopes to alleviate this risk by allowing for more detailed and
precise discussions around the role. The paper then turns to consider some of the key features of the
surrounding policy environment that can support effective co-ordination. The paper concludes with an
overview of how co-ordination is approached in different systems, both in terms of more team-based
approaches and those that concentrate on single co-ordinators.

title: 2 Trends shaping the use of digital tools in schools

paragraphs.text:
At the end of the 2010s, the OECD undertook a large-scale video study of teaching. Working with eight
different countries and economies, the study deployed a mixed methods design, including the direct
observation of some 75 teachers in each system, to understand the presence and effect of certain practices
in mathematics classrooms (OECD, 2020 [2] ). One notable finding was that the use of technology was
primarily reserved for communication purposes in the classroom. More recently, even after various
technological developments, secondary analysis of the OECD’s PISA 2022 data painted a similar picture
(Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025 [1] ). Four distinct groups of teachers were identified using cluster analysis:

•
The “minimally engaged” who rarely use digital tools for their work.

•
The “moderately engaged” who use digital resources for a relatively narrow set of activities, mostly
focussed on instructional design rather than direct applications in the classroom.

•
A second group of “moderately engaged” teachers who mostly use digital resources for
pedagogical activities involving direct interactions and student support.

•
The “highly engaged” who make frequent of digital tools for the full spectrum of activities in and
outside of the classroom.

Broadly speaking, this suggests that it is relatively common to see technology used for communication –
such as illuminating an idea through a PowerPoint or the use of a smart whiteboard or projector – but less
common to see technology used for advancing conceptual understanding, such as modelling a particular
phenomenon or highlighting patterns. This latter form of more engaged use of technology occurs with some
teachers – and indeed highly engaged teachers can be found in every country analysed using PISA 2022
data – but not all teachers (Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025 [1] ). Indeed, the proportion of this type of teacher
in the teacher population varies across countries.

The use of digital tools in the classroom is also not only a question of how technology is used in pedagogical
processes with students, but also how it supports and informs the various steps that lead to these
processes. For instance, preparing lessons and resources can be shaped by technology too. A recent
report by Estyn in Wales (UK), who inspect quality and standards in education and training in Wales (UK),
noted the promising potential of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly Generative AI, to positively impact
teachers’ workload (Estyn, 2025 [8] ). Their thematic report is based on a survey to some 300 practitioners
in Wales (UK) and visits to a broad range of some 20 schools for conversations with different stakeholders,
including leaders, teachers and pupils. They highlight consistent reporting from teachers of AI being an
effective support that can reduce workload in areas such as lesson planning, resource creation and
differentiation of learning materials. AI can be an effective “starting point” for teachers in their planning and
preparation, that they can then apply their judgement to (p.12). Indeed, there are promising signs from
emerging empirical evidence that Generative AI has the potential to deliver significant productivity gains.

a 31% reduction in lesson and resource planning time (OECD, 2026 [9] ). These efficiencies are driven by

As the OECD’s recent Digital Education Outlook noted, secondary science teachers in England reported

AI’s versatile functionality, with research suggesting it can fulfill four primary roles: serving as an

paragraphs.text:
information hub, generating personalised materials to support group work, providing feedback to teachers,
and acting as a peer contributor in collaborative tasks.

This also raises the question of the extent that digital tools are used beyond the classroom in the broader
functioning of the school. A range of administrative processes are an established part of school life in many
systems, from a range of monitoring efforts (e.g. attendance, performance, participation) to communication
efforts (e.g. with parents, across teachers). Effective ICT co-ordination in this area could be highly
significant. Administrative tasks are a considerable demand on teachers and can be a notable source of
stress for many. The OECD’s Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) 2024 (OECD, 2025 [10] )
reports that on average, a one standard-deviation increase in hours spent on marking, administrative tasks
or communicating with parents by full-time teachers is associated with over a 10% standard deviation
decrease in teacher well-being. It is therefore unsurprising that consideration of how technology may
alleviate some of these administrative requirements and support greater efficiency has fallen on the radar
of certain policymakers. For instance, in England (UK) a bespoke task force has been established to
investigate how workload can be streamlined through the use of digital tools (OECD, 2024 [11] ). Similarly,
there has been considerable investment in systems such as Australia, where its Workload Reduction Fund
has seen some 30 million Australian dollars committed by the government to pilot innovative projects to
reduce workloads and maximise how teachers and leaders use their time (Australian Government,
2026 [12] ).

While there are promising signs that the careful integration of digital tools into teachers’ and school leaders’
tasks such as lesson preparation processes may have positive impacts, it is worth highlighting that more
research is still needed. As Estyn’s report in Wales (UK) notes, the exploration of AI and its applications in
schools is nascent. Furthermore, it is characterised by some individual staff members who are actively
engaging in exploring AI – echoing the ‘highly engaged’ cluster of PISA 2022 mentioned previously – but
that strategic implementation at the school-level is far more limited (Estyn, 2025 [8] ). Similarly, there are ad-
hoc examples of schools using AI to alleviate routine tasks – such as letter writing, report writing, or drafting
of school policies – but that this is not systematic and also non-exhaustive (Estyn, 2025 [8] ). This suggests
that co-ordination efforts may have to attend to ensuring the benefits of improved effectiveness in certain
tasks are equally shared among staff and schools. Similarly, it is also important to note that this shift toward
automation is balanced by ongoing concerns that overreliance on AI could undermine teacher autonomy
and professionalism (OECD, 2026 [9] ). This further reiterates the importance of helping teachers and school
leaders to develop their ability to critically and carefully engage with the implementation of digital tools, as
discussed further below.

title: The central role of the teacher in effectively using digital tools in classrooms

paragraphs.text:
While the field remains in a state of evolution, it is noteworthy that the latest research suggests that the
potential of technology to impact student learning goes hand-in-hand with effective pedagogy. A recent
review of five digital tools highlighted the centrality of the teacher in the effective use of each tool. The
review suggests that effective pedagogical use of technologies in the classroom is essential, and that the
mere presence of certain technologies does not automatically guarantee their success (Forsström et al.,
2025 [5] ).

•
For instance, regarding programming and robotics , research suggests that programming
education has the potential to significantly develop computational thinking, creativity and problem-
solving skills. Effective learning environments for these tools are shaped by collaborative
environments and strategies encouraging students to reflect on their learning processes. Teachers
play a crucial role in managing cognitive demands and guiding exploration, particularly when
moving to text-based languages that present greater complexity.

•
Media production and literacy tools can substantially enhance language and literacy
development, particularly benefiting students from less stimulating home environments. That said,
teachers need to make strategic use of digital methods of learning alongside analogue methods,
while also managing the risks of distraction that certain tools may pose (e.g. using social media
platforms or video streaming services). They may also need to ensure that engaging multimedia
integration is not heightening cognitive load unnecessarily.

•
Game-based learning (GBL) has the potential to enhance motivation, engagement and critical
skills development such as problem-solving and collaboration. The teacher is significant in helping
to align games with learning goals by selecting suitable games. They may also need to address
technical barriers or provide scaffolds for certain games.

•
Through its offer of immersive learning experiences, extended reality and simulations – including
formats such as augmented (AR), virtual (VR) and mixed reality (MR) – can support conceptual
understanding, notably in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) subject.
But there is also a notable risk of cognitive overload with such tools and the use of scaffolds by
teachers to guide students’ engagement with extended reality and simulations is important.
Teachers are also important in terms of connecting learning from such experiences with students’
prior knowledge and making connections for coherent learning experiences.

•
Finally, regarding artificial intelligence and learning analytics , AI-powered tools, such as
intelligent tutoring systems and natural language processing, provide immediate feedback to both
students and teachers, enabling timely interventions. But teachers’ involvement is essential in
interpreting AI feedback. AI-enhanced collaborative tools (e.g. chatbots) can also support balanced
group participation and communication, though teachers play an important role in building an
understanding of the limitations (e.g. potential biases) of such tools and fostering students’ critical
digital literacy.

Similarly, the OECD’s recent Digital Education Outlook reiterates the important role of teachers in effective
implementation with Generative AI. It highlights that general-purpose GenAI carries risks for learning, and
that it must be used with pedagogical purpose or redesigned as specific educational GenAI tools (OECD,
2026 [9] ). The Outlook notes studies that provide empirical evidence that using GenAI with pedagogical
intent can improve learning and foster skills like critical thinking, creativity and collaboration. Some of the
ways this pedagogical intent manifests are through scaffolding students’ iterative exploration and critical
reflection when using GenAI tools.

Looking across these tools and research studies, some common patterns can be identified in terms of the
type of practices teachers are making use of in their role. It is helpful to adopt the OECD’s Schools+
taxonomy of high-quality teaching here (OECD, 2025 [13] ), which organises teaching into five core goals,
with twenty practices organised within these. Combining this taxonomy with the review of digital tools by
Forsström and colleagues (2025 [3] ), the following features of pedagogy stand out:

•
Ensuring cognitive engagement: Teachers manage cognitive load by attending to appropriate
levels of challenge in any tasks using digital tools. This includes carefully stepped progression of
difficulty with teachers steadily lifting scaffolds for students depending on how students apply
themselves to using certain tools. Part of the managing of cognitive load is also ensuring sufficient
practice opportunities for students to build fluency. Teachers may draw upon first-hand experiences
of students using tools directly, as well as highlight real-world connections between tools and other
applications, to foster students’ engagement.

•
Crafting quality subject content: Teachers facilitate clear explanations and expositions of new
tools, such as by providing worked examples of how tools work and can be applied. This may also
include explicitly highlighting certain limitations or risks (e.g. ethical, bias). Teachers can also make
connections with larger abstractions in the content beyond certain tools.

Similarly, the OECD’s recent Digital Education Outlook reiterates the important role of teachers in effective
implementation with Generative AI. It highlights that general-purpose GenAI carries risks for learning, and
that it must be used with pedagogical purpose or redesigned as specific educational GenAI tools (OECD,
2026 [9] ). The Outlook notes studies that provide empirical evidence that using GenAI with pedagogical
intent can improve learning and foster skills like critical thinking, creativity and collaboration. Some of the
ways this pedagogical intent manifests are through scaffolding students’ iterative exploration and critical
reflection when using GenAI tools.
Looking across these tools and research studies, some common patterns can be identified in terms of the
type of practices teachers are making use of in their role. It is helpful to adopt the OECD’s Schools+
taxonomy of high-quality teaching here (OECD, 2025 [13] ), which organises teaching into five core goals,
with twenty practices organised within these. Combining this taxonomy with the review of digital tools by
Forsström and colleagues (2025 [3] ), the following features of pedagogy stand out:
•
Ensuring cognitive engagement: Teachers manage cognitive load by attending to appropriate
levels of challenge in any tasks using digital tools. This includes carefully stepped progression of
difficulty with teachers steadily lifting scaffolds for students depending on how students apply
themselves to using certain tools. Part of the managing of cognitive load is also ensuring sufficient
practice opportunities for students to build fluency. Teachers may draw upon first-hand experiences
of students using tools directly, as well as highlight real-world connections between tools and other
applications, to foster students’ engagement.
•
Crafting quality subject content: Teachers facilitate clear explanations and expositions of new
tools, such as by providing worked examples of how tools work and can be applied. This may also
include explicitly highlighting certain limitations or risks (e.g. ethical, bias). Teachers can also make
connections with larger abstractions in the content beyond certain tools.

paragraphs.text:
•
Providing social-emotional support: Teachers actively attend to developing particular skills,
such as collaboration, resilience, self-regulation, that students may need for working on certain
tools. Also, they are mindful of the need for human interaction alongside certain tools (e.g. mixed
reality) to avoid over-reliance.

•
Fostering classroom interaction: Teachers facilitate effective student collaboration through
monitoring and task design. Teachers blend this type of facilitation with more explicit instruction or
whole-class discussion depending on the class’s needs.

•
Using formative assessment and feedback: Teachers make use of real-time feedback and data
to adjust their teaching to allow for responsiveness and proactiveness in attending to
misconceptions or learning gaps. Teachers also support students to make use of this data, to allow
for metacognition and progress.

One interesting feature here is how teachers are a common presence. At times, they may be playing a
more direct role in building understanding, such as through quality worked examples and the careful
sequencing of content. At other times, they may be acting more as facilitators in the classroom by nurturing
the social-emotional skills that students need for working effectively in groups or by guiding students as
they experiment with certain tools and their applications. These are shaped by the particular context of the
classroom and, in particular, the students’ levels of prior knowledge.

This picture of strategic, careful application of digital tools is echoed elsewhere. Secondary analysis of
PISA 2022 data suggest that moderate learning time with digital technologies is associated with positive
outcomes (Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025 [1] ). On average across the OECD, use of digital devices is
associated with an increase in students’ perceived quality of their mathematics lessons, as well as a
number of things that are indicative of positive teaching behaviour (e.g. student support and cognitive
activation). Moreover, the moderate use of digital devices in learning is also associated with better
performance in mathematics as measured by PISA. However, beyond that moderate use, the association
with academic performance becomes negative. This invites consideration of some of the challenges that
teachers face, which the aforementioned secondary analysis also shines a light on. The use of digital
devices is also associated with a worse disciplinary climate and digital distractions. In this respect, teachers
face the challenge of balancing practices that can facilitate quality engagement with digital tools alongside
those of effective classroom management. This is important context for understanding the contours of the
type of support that teachers may need, including the role that ICT co-ordinators may play.

title: The nature of preparation and guidance

paragraphs.text:
This raises the question of what is the surrounding infrastructure that supports teachers in their use of
digital tools. A recent OECD policy survey highlighted that regarding teacher professional learning few
countries require teachers to engage in continuous professional learning on digital education (OECD,
2025 [14] ). However, many systems have sought to encourage it, mostly by ensuring the provision of
professional learning in this space and removing any potential barriers to teachers’ engagement with this
provision. Free professional learning opportunities are thus provided in 27 of 35 jurisdictions surveyed.

One interesting finding from secondary analysis of PISA 2022 data suggest that teachers’ repeated
exposure to learning opportunities on digital tools may be particularly important. Analysis found that,
consistently across countries, teachers who received training in the use of ICT in their initial education
make more use of ICT later on (Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025 [1] ). However, there was nearly the same
level of use among teachers who only received professional development on the topic later on. The highest
level of use among those who received both, suggesting that there’s an important role for professional
learning at all stages of the teacher career. This heightens the importance of how learning opportunities in
schools are facilitated. It also suggests that attending to use of digital tools in the transition period from
initial teacher education through potential induction phases may be important too. This is particularly

relevant seeing that induction, according to the latest TALIS 2024 findings, is an increasing feature in many
systems (OECD, 2025 [10] ).

The question of which particular forms of professional learning are most impactful when it comes to digital
tools is an open question. Do digital tools demand the same sorts of active ingredients that has been
identified as essential for effective professional learning, or are there some areas of particular variation?
This is an area that demands further research. A recent OECD Policy Perspective noted that there are,
some tentative signs from certain studies that there is indeed overlap between what makes effective
professional learning and what makes effective professional learning on digital tools (OECD, 2025 [14] ). For
instance, features such as ensuring a sustained focus and concrete individual guidance have been noted
as significant in a large-scale survey of literacy teachers in the United States (Hutchison, 2012 [15] ).

Building on the aforementioned literature review of digital tools and the demands they pose for teachers’
pedagogy, it is also possible to identify certain features of teacher professional learning that may be
especially significant. The impact of digital tools on students' learning and motivation relies heavily on
teachers’ practices, choices and competencies. One common theme is that teachers’ selection of tools,
specifically the purposes for which the tools are used, the timing of their use and the educational objectives
they support, is essential (Forsström et al., 2025 [3] ; Forsström et al., 2025 [5] ). This suggests there is a need
for dedicated work on subject-based applications alongside the development of some technical knowledge
around different tools and the goals they can help achieve. Indeed, the latter may be particularly significant
for engaging students in understanding themselves and how and when to apply tools, including the ethical
risks of certain tools. In this respect, teachers’ digital literacy must be furthered if the digital literacy of
students is to also be enhanced (Estyn, 2025 [8] ; Forsström et al., 2025 [5] ). A further pattern across the
review of tools was the importance of managing students’ cognitive load, particularly during transitions to
more complex tools, such as by designing effective scaffolds. This may demand opportunities to see
tangible examples of such scaffolds and how teachers can responsively adapt them to student needs as
they progress.

Accordingly, looking across these patterns, it can be hypothesised that the following may be significant for
effective professional learning on digital tools:

•
Incorporate particularly clear, subject-specific examples or modelling of how particular digital tools
can be applied.

•
Support technical knowledge of how certain tools work, particularly for imparting to students and
for their critical, engaged use of tools.

•
Provide space for iterative, collaborative experimentation among colleagues and accompanying
feedback or reflection.

•
Dedicate time to content and intra-subject discussion to map tools to the curriculum and objectives.

•
Make use of coaching and expert support (e.g. so-called “highly engaged” teachers or ICT co-
ordinators).

These demonstrate, in general, good alignment with what has been identified as being significant features
of effective professional learning, with some particular emphasis on certain features. They point to the
importance of co-ordination efforts in a school to support professional learning efforts, with the strong focus
on in-school collaboration in particular suggesting that localised expertise and orientation may be needed.

They also point to the role of central system actors. A key first step, as noted, may be pursuing further
research to better understand how to provision and deliver impactful professional learning. In particular,
tangible examples of effective programmes could be especially relevant to school and system leaders

learning that can make it impactful (Sims and Fletcher-Wood, 2020 [16] ). This is particularly important
considering that changing teaching practice is typically hard as, due to the sheer complexity of teaching,
teachers’ behaviours often are deeply ingrained. Teachers may have certain practices that are essentially

levers may further incentivise engagement with professional learning and teachers’ attention to digital
matters in their teaching. At the same time, such levers may not, on their own, be automatically effective.

was impactful and shaped teachers’ day-to-day teaching. There is a risk that completing professional
learning becomes the primary objective, rather than the application of learning to one’s practice to

title: An evolving world of technology

paragraphs.text:
The OECD’s Trends Shaping Education 2025 highlighted the ubiquitous nature of digital technology in our
societies (OECD, 2025 [19] ). Moreover, this is a picture that is not standing still; the presence of so-called
‘frontier technologies’, including artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things, or mixed realities in the
form of augmented and virtual reality, means that what is possible and may be possible is shifting and thus
constantly changing the way we work, learn and communicate.

One common theme that stands out here is that the digitalisation of life and work has placed a greater
need for people to develop their digital literacy. This includes the ability to appropriately use and apply
digital tools to different situations, as well as understanding key new technologies such as how to use AI
responsibly and ethically. For instance, the skills to critically evaluate digital content, protect one’s privacy,
and use tools to support outcomes without excessive use that harm’s one’s well-being are all increasingly
important (Forsström et al., 2025 [5] ). Moreover, as outlined further below, without the equitable
development of this, it risks some people falling behind and struggling to keep pace with the evolving digital
trends in our societies. One key question that the OECD’s Trends Shaping Education poses is “Can
education prepare students for an increasingly digital future by embedding digital literacy into curricula and
teachers’ initial and continuing learning?” (OECD, 2025, p. 51 [19] )

It is in this context that the work of ICT co-ordinators is under particular scrutiny. Embedding digital literacy
into curricula is a large-scale challenge that stretches from policymakers to the classroom. Curricula are
often talked of in terms of the ‘intended’ curriculum – which is often shaped by experts and policymakers
in terms of what is expected to be covered – and the ‘implemented’ curriculum – which is the actual
manifestation of the intended curriculum in the classroom. The latter is more variable and mediated by the
teacher who does the implementing. Education systems across the OECD have updated their curricula to
integrate learning goals for students’ digital skills (Boeskens and Meyer, 2025 [20] ), though this is in terms
of the ‘intended’ curriculum and attention on how this manifests in the actual ‘implemented’ curriculum
remains important. This is particularly important when digital skills are not systematically assessed in many
countries. ICT co-ordinators have the potential to shape this mediation process by working with teachers
on the development of the implemented curriculum. This is particularly the case due to co-ordinators’
potential role in capacity-building and developing the digital literacy of teachers themselves through
continuing learning.

As mentioned, the world of digitalisation is also a dynamic space of change. The importance of co-
ordination can surface particularly at the frontier of change in the latest technologies. This is a space that
is fast-moving and often harder for policymakers and researchers to attend to. For instance, a policy survey
on systems’ regulation of digital education noted that guidelines on emerging technologies (e.g. generative
AI) are less frequent and guidance on emerging issues like algorithmic bias remain an exception (Boeskens
and Meyer, 2025 [20] ). Co-ordination may be important for building responses to these types of technologies.
Indeed, without this type of effective co-ordination, there is a risk of some schools affronting certain
challenges more effectively than other schools. Accordingly, there is a risk of digital divides developing
which is a growing risk and challenge for systems, and one where ICT co-ordinators are key actors, as
outlined further below.

title: Preventing digital divides and equity gaps

paragraphs.text:
Effective ICT co-ordination can also have considerable ramifications for fostering equity and inclusion in
schools and systems. On one level this is about quality digital infrastructure for all. This touches upon both
the identification and procurement of the right tools, including in a cost-efficient manner, but also the
maintenance of this infrastructure. This type of technical co-ordination that often occurs ‘behind-the-
scenes’ of the final classroom manifestation, such as setting up digital infrastructure and trouble-shooting
problems, can be important for streamlining the use of tools and creating the space for individual teachers
to concentrate on their use. While the degree of central support for these aspects (Boeskens and Meyer,
2025 [20] ), particularly the question of deciding on which technologies to procure, can vary across countries,
school-level digital co-ordination is important for creating and maintaining a functioning digital infrastructure
for all.

However, as the OECD’s Trends Shaping Education has noted, the digital divide has gone beyond just the
historic question of connectivity to being about the degree that one can benefit from online information and
services (OECD, 2025 [19] ). In this respect, in education this means that schools and teachers having access
to the relevant information on the type of digital tools that can be effectively used is key. Several
considerations appear particularly important here:

•
As noted, the effective use of digital tools hinges upon the careful judgement of teachers. This is
underpinned by their own digital literacy and how they develop their pedagogical skills. Equitable
opportunities for teachers to develop this type of digital literacy is therefore significant. In schools,
quality digital co-ordinators can be important in a capacity-building role here, be that by directly
facilitating training themselves, supporting the identification of relevant opportunities, or creating
knowledge exchange of best practices with other schools and stakeholders.

•
Moreover, certain tools appear particularly valuable for students with special educational needs.
For instance, research suggests that augmented reality (AR) can enhance academic and
developmental outcomes in students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual and
developmental disabilities (IDD) (Forsström et al., 2025 [5] ). A further example is how digital writing
instruction can provide essential scaffolding and support, particularly for students facing learning
challenges (Forsström et al., 2025 [5] ). Again, ICT co-ordination may be significant here in terms of
identifying such opportunities and working with teachers as well as relevant support staff to enable
effective implementation that can foster greater equity.

•

support students in environments with limited digital infrastructure (OECD, 2026 [9] ). Small

to better formalise the role of the ICT co-ordinator and develop policy solutions that support them to
effectively fulfill their important role.

Finally, a further strand to the question of preventing digital divides is the risk of certain schools being left
behind due to the speed of change. ICT co-ordinators may also serve as a key connection node in an ever-
changing environment to ensure the communication of accurate, up-to-date information. As previously
noted, nearly all countries have developed central strategies to guide digital education (Boeskens and
Meyer, 2025 [20] ), but how long will these strategies remain valid in a changing digital context? When they
do evolve and change, it is through formal co-ordinator roles that such information may be diffused to avoid
the widening of digital divides due to outdated information. The recent advent of Generative AI is a case
in point; for instance, in their recent study of schools in Wales, the Welsh inspectorate Etsyn noted the
importance of ensuring schools had the relevant information for ethical, safe use, such as on the statutory
duties around use of AI for administrative work (Estyn, 2025 [8] ). In this respect, the notion of school-level
co-ordination may miss the fact that actually this co-ordination is also an important cog in the wider system-
level co-ordination of digital policies and ensuring that this co-ordination is a force that nurtures and furthers
equity in the digital space. This invites deeper consideration of the tasks that underpin ICT co-ordination,
as the next section discusses in more detail.

These examples capture how, when it comes to equity, effective digital co-ordination can prevent digital

implementation of certain solutions. In contrast, the absence of effective ICT co-ordination may prove
harmful and actually foster digital divides. This adds to the significance of efforts, as set out further below,

title: 3 Co-ordinating ICT in schools: Key theoretical lenses

paragraphs.text:
The rise in ICT co-ordinators in many settings has been a response to the increasing potential and
importance of technology in education, as well as the accompanying risks that technology poses. The
challenge of effectively navigating these in integrating ICT into schools has seen ICT co-ordinators enter
the picture and grow in prominence (León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ).
ICT co-ordinators have come to be seen as important actors in supporting the effective integration of ICT
in schools to positively contribute to students’ learning outcomes, be that directly or indirectly.

It is in this context that the OECD recently began a project, funded by the European Union via the Technical
Support Instrument, and implemented by the OECD in cooperation with SG Reform of the European
Commission, looking into ICT co-ordination in Bulgaria and Slovakia, with a focus on team-based
approaches. This section presents some of the literature that has been thus far consulted for this work.

This section outlines, first, four broad thematic areas that constitute effective ICT co-ordination. For each
of these four areas, the particular tasks that may constitute them are set out. Here, these outlines are
shaped by the varying attention certain areas have received due partly to the evolving nature of needs in
schools too. Hence, it is perhaps not surprising seeing the challenge of integrating digital technologies
effectively into classrooms as set forth previously that attention to the pedagogical strand of co-ordination
is less well-developed than that of the technical strand. This reflects the greater historical concentration of
co-ordinators on technical tasks rather than pedagogical ones (Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] ; Woo and Law,
2020 [22] ).

More broadly, in general the research base remains shaped by the relatively nascent nature of the position
of ICT co-ordination and its constantly changing demands (León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and
Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ). Indeed, the latter, as set forth previously, is significant because it means
information may quickly become outdated; for instance, the question of AI and cybersecurity is now a key
challenge for co-ordinators (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ), and this raises the question of how
best to make use of primary data collected in very different technological contexts (e.g. Tondeur, Cooper
and Newhouse, 2010 [11] ). Further challenges include a greater attention at the primary than secondary and
vocational school levels (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ), while with regard to empirical studies
these are in some instances quite small in scale; Woo (2020 [24] ) for instance studied eight digital literacy
coaches in Singapore in private international schools, while Avidov-Ungar and Hanin-Itzak (2019 [25] )
studied 24 co-ordinators in Israelian elementary schools.

There are also gaps in terms of research in different contexts, which is significant considering that
contextual factors – as set out below – can heavily shape how co-ordinators work. In general, the literature
base stems from only a few contexts. For instance, a systematic literature review on ICT integration - which
often touches upon the role of the co-ordinator - found that there is a notable representation of studies
from Spain, Belgium and the United States (Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] ). Meanwhile, recent studies in
different contexts – such as those in more decentralised systems for co-ordination (e.g. Gustafsson,
Olofsson and Bergström, 2024 [22] ; Letnes, 2025 [5] ) – have richly highlighted different challenges that co-
ordinators may face.

These two points around the context of research and the sample sizes invite consideration of the challenge
of generalising knowledge in this space. The four areas discussed below seek to synthesise across these
different challenges in the research base to present a more coherent if still developing picture of co-
ordination. While there is no single consensus with regard to the role of ICT co-ordination (Woo and Law,
2020 [22] ; Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] ), these four broad areas appear to offer a promising direction forward
for framing the co-ordination role in the face of today’s demands when it comes to ICT in schools.

After addressing these four conceptual task areas, this section then turns to consider how specific roles
may be created to cater to these thematic areas. This structure is informed by the fact that one key
message from the relatively young field of research on ICT co-ordination is that ambiguity around roles
and functions can reduce the effectiveness of ICT co-ordinators (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada
and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ). At the same time, co-ordination can look very different in different systems
based on their policy environment, from their available human and financial resources to their degree of
centralisation or decentralisation. These types of contextual factors are borne in mind as the section turns
to consider different approaches and their relative advantages and disadvantages.

title: An emerging four-part model of co-ordination

paragraphs.text:
Although a relatively young field, the question of what constitutes ICT co-ordination has undergone some
notable changes. A key foundational distinction has been between the technical and pedagogical aspects
of co-ordination. This distinction can be seen in some of the earliest studies examining ICT co-ordination
in schools (Tondeur, Cooper and Newhouse, 2010 [27] ). At the same time, it is worth noting that within this
there is variability and the extent that co-ordinators have focussed on substantial pedagogical change is
an open question that has started to receive more attention, with some arguing that attention on pedagogy
has historically been confined to more superficial, simple tasks than more complex, substantive
pedagogical change across a school (Letnes, 2025 [7] ; León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐
Estrada, 2019 [6] ), as discussed further below.

Coupled with these two key features, there has been growing attention to the role of ICT co-ordinators as
planners or managers. For instance, Woo (2020 [24] ) notes that attention on this idea of planning policies in
schools and monitoring these policies has also featured in several different typologies of the ICT co-
ordinator’s role.

More recently, a four-part model has emerged that further elaborates on this three-part model (see
Table 3.1). This sees the technical and pedagogical strands remain constant, but sees greater clarity
added to the space of planning and managing. A detailed study of the Flemish Community in Belgium
clarifies these four key thematic areas that underpin co-ordination (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels,
2024 [23] ):

•
Technical tasks (e.g. hardware and software, first line support etc.)

•
Pedagogical (e.g. integration in the classroom, curricula, training, innovation etc.)

•
Policy and vision (e.g. developing a vision, financial advice, motivating/sensitising colleagues)

•
Administrative tasks (e.g. inventories, following up on orders, managing users etc.)

This focus on four areas has a strong link in previous focusses on three areas. The policy and vision can
be seen to overlap with attention to deriving careful planning, which is also informed by administrative work
too such as procurement. As the authors note, the pedagogical and technical aspects of co-ordination form
the core of ICT co-ordination but are supported by the policy/vision and administrative domains too. Each
of these four areas are set out below in more detail.

text:
Pedagogical co-ordination focusses on supporting the effective integration of digital tools into teachers’
pedagogy. It is thus primarily concentrated on the classroom, and this can move between more
individualised co-ordination to teachers and particular classes, and more whole-school co-ordination
around how digitalisation is used in pedagogy. In particular the latter, as noted, has received greater
attention in recent years. This seems a product of both the need to more systematically consider digital

paragraphs.text:
tools as they have evolved, but also the relatively limited attention on this in the co-ordinator’s role, with it
primarily dwarfed by trouble-shooting technical issues or attending to more superficial pedagogical tasks.
Some of the main pedagogical tasks that are identified across the literature include:

•
Identifying needs

•
Curating appropriate tools and resources

•
Building teachers’ capacity to use digital tools

One aspect of pedagogical co-ordination is understanding different needs. This is a key foundation for
being able to provide the co-ordinated support below if tools are to be appropriate and effectively used.
Understanding needs may occur at different levels, such as the needs of individual teachers and classes,
as well as the needs of the school in terms of, for instance, a school development plan. This may also be
about diagnosing the needs of a system, and thus knowing the curricula demands too. Indeed, co-
ordinators may need to be able to look across both the intended and implemented curricula. In sum,
diagnosing the needs across the school is important for being able to accurately know what co-ordination
is needed. Notably this may overlap with how policy and vision is defined below, with this needs
assessment identifying the current situation and the vision encompassing where the school wants to
eventually be.

Co-ordination can also play a role in curating particular tools or applications to identify the most relevant
ones for teachers. This builds on the aforementioned diagnosis, trying to match needs to particular digital
solutions. Curation is also about making judgements on quality. Thus, co-ordination may demand a degree
of critical evaluation of tools to gauge their appropriateness. It may also demand co-ordinators remain
attuned to how tools evolve and if particular tools have, for instance, an increasing evidence base of their
effectiveness. Indeed, a degree of research literacy may be one important competency in this aspect of
co-ordination and one worth understanding further in the future – particularly as some schools establish
additional roles focussed on supporting school engagement with research (OECD, 2025 [13] ).

Capacity-building is widely identified as a key feature of pedagogical co-ordination. In essence, it centres
on enhancing teachers’ knowledge and skills for being able to use digital tools. It is helpful to dig down
below the term ‘capacity-building’ to consider in a more granular way what this may actually mean:

•
Directly delivering or facilitating professional learning. One of the most effective forms of this may
be more close-hand support to teachers. Tondeur and colleagues (2010 [27] ) noted that where there
was evidence of a significant increase in the meaningful use of ICT in schools, there was a focus
from co-ordinators on capacity-building through one-to-one support to teachers and role modelling
and scaffolding. This echoes the growing literature on the potential benefits of coaching or
mentoring (Boeskens, Nusche and Yurita, 2020 [29] ). It may also be that professional learning to
groups of teachers is more efficient and appropriate for certain contents. Working groups or
communities of practice may be established in schools under the auspices of a co-ordinator, while
more whole-school formats of training or information sharing may be deemed necessary. In each
case, professional learning should endeavour to align with the literature on effective professional
learning, as discussed above in Section 1.

•
Creating relevant connections for knowledge exchange and peer collaboration or support. This was
also one feature that Tondeur and colleagues highlighted as being potential beneficial to support
meaningful ICT use in schools (2010 [27] ). Co-ordinators may facilitate connections with colleagues
in a school that can help respond to a particular need (e.g. encouraging a colleague to observe
how another teacher is using a particular tool). It may also be a means of sharing and furthering
innovations.

•
Signposting relevant learning opportunities for colleagues. As well as signposting connections to
colleagues within a school, co-ordination may identify learning opportunities that are delivered by
external providers that can meet teachers’ particular needs.

•
Undertaking formative assessment teachers. In this respect, pedagogical co-ordination can
function almost like a mentoring or coaching of teachers on digital matters. They may identify
particular needs and provide bespoke feedback to attend to any limitations or challenges.

Moreover, building on the discussion earlier of the types of practices teachers make particular use of during
the integration of digital tools, it is possible to identify some of the priority content areas that pedagogical
co-ordination could be concentrated around. Indeed, while pedagogical co-ordination should remain
context-specific and informed by the localised needs of teachers, as the first point above noted, the more
limited body of research on the pedagogical strand of ICT co-ordination – and according to certain studies
more limited attention to the most complex aspects of pedagogical co-ordination in the role (León ‐ Jariego,
Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ) – means that direction on shaping pedagogical co-
ordination can be valuable. The insights forthwith offer an indication of the pedagogical content areas that
could be initially considered alongside a needs-based assessment of teachers in a school:

•
How to align specific learning objectives in a subject’s sequence of work with particular digital tools
to help identify relevant (and non-relevant) opportunities for tools’ use.

•
How assessment data from particular digital tools (e.g. learning analytics, platforms) can be used
to proactively identify student needs and, accordingly, provide further feedback or adapt teaching
to students’ needs.

•
Developing classroom management strategies for avoiding distractions when using digital tools. In
particular, novice teachers typically report a need for more classroom management support
(OECD, 2025 [10] ) and, in this respect, may be particularly in-need of additional pedagogical
strategies.

•
Sharing and refining scaffolds that can be used with students to facilitate the appropriate level of
challenge in digital tools.

Lastly, one important underlying tension here to be mindful of here is the authority of the co-ordinator. This
surfaces in the literature, with Gustafsson and colleagues noting that (2024 [30] ) one challenge some co-
ordinators reported in their empirical study in Sweden was their overwhelming work with individuals who
came forward, seeking help from the co-ordinator. In contrast, reaching those that do not come forward
with specific problems can be far harder and very sensitive. Even then, the authors also note that
sometimes the problems that drive individual teachers to approach co-ordinators for help tend to be
relatively superficial and specific problems, such as trouble-shooting technical challenges with particular
tools or software. Similarly, in their detailed case studies of co-ordinators in private international schools,
Woo and Law (2020 [22] ) found co-ordinators could face resistance from colleagues when it came to going
beyond simple technical fixes to more substantial questions of pedagogy.

This points to the challenge co-ordinators face in the pedagogical space of bringing different types of
teachers onboard and fostering wider pedagogical change at a school-level. It also points to the close
relationship with policy and vision and school leaders, as this may shape how the importance of certain
pedagogical approaches is communicated, as well as the authority that the co-ordinator has to more
actively engage with teachers who may be reluctant to consider their digital pedagogy. Some have argued
that this aspect of collective pedagogical change has been under-attended to in the literature (Letnes,
2025 [7] ), arguably reflecting this tension of authority in the co-ordinator role as well as its evolving nature
and priorities. The question of collective change is considered in more detail in Section 5.

being able to provide the co-ordinated support below if tools are to be appropriate and effectively used.
Understanding needs may occur at different levels, such as the needs of individual teachers and classes,
as well as the needs of the school in terms of, for instance, a school development plan. This may also be

ordinators may need to be able to look across both the intended and implemented curricula. In sum,
diagnosing the needs across the school is important for being able to accurately know what co-ordination
is needed. Notably this may overlap with how policy and vision is defined below, with this needs
assessment identifying the current situation and the vision encompassing where the school wants to
eventually be.

ones for teachers. This builds on the aforementioned diagnosis, trying to match needs to particular digital
solutions. Curation is also about making judgements on quality. Thus, co-ordination may demand a degree
of critical evaluation of tools to gauge their appropriateness. It may also demand co-ordinators remain
attuned to how tools evolve and if particular tools have, for instance, an increasing evidence base of their
effectiveness. Indeed, a degree of research literacy may be one important competency in this aspect of

additional roles focussed on supporting school engagement with research (OECD, 2025 [13] ).

on enhancing teachers’ knowledge and skills for being able to use digital tools. It is helpful to dig down
below the term ‘capacity-building’ to consider in a more granular way what this may actually mean:
•

be more close-hand support to teachers. Tondeur and colleagues (2010 [27] ) noted that where there

from co-ordinators on capacity-building through one-to-one support to teachers and role modelling

groups of teachers is more efficient and appropriate for certain contents. Working groups or
communities of practice may be established in schools under the auspices of a co-ordinator, while
more whole-school formats of training or information sharing may be deemed necessary. In each
case, professional learning should endeavour to align with the literature on effective professional
learning, as discussed above in Section 1.
•

also one feature that Tondeur and colleagues highlighted as being potential beneficial to support
meaningful ICT use in schools (2010 [27] ). Co-ordinators may facilitate connections with colleagues
in a school that can help respond to a particular need (e.g. encouraging a colleague to observe
how another teacher is using a particular tool). It may also be a means of sharing and furthering
innovations.

title: Technical

paragraphs.text:
The technical aspect of co-ordination relates to the fact that using digital tools in a school partly depends
on having the right infrastructure to function. Moreover, this infrastructure may demand particular technical

text:
The technical aspect of co-ordination relates to the fact that using digital tools in a school partly depends
on having the right infrastructure to function. Moreover, this infrastructure may demand particular technical

paragraphs.text:
expertise. This is reflected in some of the main tasks of this aspect of co-ordination as identified in the
literature, which includes:

•
Establishing hardware and software

•
Attending to technical issues

•
Adapting infrastructure for continued efficiency and effectiveness

As noted, historically, the technical aspect has been suggested to be the most dominant aspect of the co-
ordinator’s role (Devolder et al., 2010 [28] ; Woo, 2020 [24] ). Thus, functioning essentially as a technician has
consumed most of the co-ordinator’s time and work.

A foundation of the technical role is establishing the hardware and software that underpins a school’s digital
infrastructure. As with the pedagogical role, this demands a degree of identifying what is needed and the
solutions that exist to this end. This may, however, stretch beyond just the classroom to also consider
wider whole-school systems, such as student performance management systems or centralised platforms.

It is important to note that the degree of autonomy that schools and ICT co-ordinators have to shape the
nature of their digital infrastructure may vary across systems. For instance, in many systems, schools
share responsibility for the procurement of digital devices or software. Central authorities support them by
offering guidance, negotiating with suppliers or establishing purchasing criteria (Boeskens and Meyer,
2025 [20] ). However, this is not the case in all systems and can vary by the type of digital tool being procured.
Both of these may heighten the role of ICT co-ordinators.

A key function of the technical role is attending in real-time to issues and fixing these. Digital infrastructure
may, in some contexts, be fragile and the timely reparation of this infrastructure important for keeping
learning going and schools functioning. This can be conceptualised as ICT co-ordinators providing digital
‘first aid’ or ‘firefighting’.

This also encompasses developing solutions to prevent future issues and, in that respect, adapting digital
infrastructure in a responsive, more sustainable way. This invites consideration of a final strand of the
technical role: that it may demand the development of new technological tools or services. This may take
the form of adapting existing digital infrastructure to make improvements or developing new solutions that
can meet particular needs. This demands a degree of innovation from co-ordinators, as well as relevant
technical knowledge.

A particular example of this that has emerged in the literature recently is that of cyber-security; because
this field may evolve and change, there is a need for a school’s digital infrastructure to be potentially
updated to respond to new risks (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ). Part of the adaptation that is
necessary in the role is thus ensuring the security – through backup and preventive measures – of the
digital infrastructure. Once again, this is a reminder of how this role can vary. Thus, most jurisdictions
provide central guidelines on cyber security in schools, but binding regulations are less widespread
(Boeskens and Meyer, 2025 [20] ). Guidelines on emerging technologies (e.g. generative AI) are less
frequent and guidance on emerging issues like algorithmic bias remain an exception.

title: Policy and vision

paragraphs.text:
A further aspect of effective co-ordination attends to policy and vision. This part of co-ordination can be
seen as encompassing the following core features:

•
Defining the objectives of co-ordination

•
Managing resources in an efficient and impactful way

•
Motivating and uniting staff and stakeholders

Clearly defining the policy and vision in a school underpins ICT co-ordination. This can help to orientate
co-ordination towards particular objectives. While the needs-based assessment is primarily focussed on
gauging information on where teachers are at in terms of their successes and shortcomings in using digital
tools, the vision can be seen as providing an indication of eventually what ICT co-ordination should look
like in the school.

This task of defining objectives may take a very literal and tangible form in terms of a concrete written
vision and strategic plan for ICT integration in a school. Co-ordinators can be key figures here, alongside
those of school leaders normally too. Sometimes referred to as a ‘digital education plan’, this can be seen
as an important document that outlines tangibly the key goals and actions for digitalisation in a school. As
set out below, certain systems like Portugal have heavily orientated their approach to co-ordination in
schools around this. Plans can take different forms (e.g. Vanderlinde et al., 2012a), but it is notable that
attending to both strategic and operational questions can be important (Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] ).

Furthermore, the plan needs to both foster ownership if it is to be effectively used, but also balance different
stakeholder needs. For instance, it may also include aspects of the school’s own ethos or vision for itself
as an institution and its students. Similarly, depending on the system, the plan may be informed by
guidance or requirements by the system. Co-ordinators may play a key role in building and uniting people
behind a vision and balancing different needs to foster collective ownership in a school. They may also
help this vision evolve and stay up-to-date with changing needs.

A further aspect of the policy and vision of ICT co-ordination relates to the management of resources. As
alluded to already, part of the technical co-ordination demands developing the digital infrastructure in the
school. While the technical co-ordination realises this development, one prior aspect of policy and vision
demands strategising this infrastructure and deciding on the resources that can go into it. The nature of
these resources can take many shapes – both financial as well as human resources – and are shaped by
those provided by system-level leaders. There may, thus, be differing degrees of autonomy in how these
resources can be used, but they remain essential to defining the wherewithal of the digital infrastructure
and the form that ICT co-ordination may take in a school.

Finally, an important part of co-ordinating a policy and vision for ICT co-ordination is that change in schools
demands stakeholder engagement that can motivate and co-ordinate people. For instance, there is a need
to bring people onboard to a vision of digitalisation in a school and also sustain their engagement with this
vision. There is also a need to build strong, trusting relationships that allow for open dialogue, feedback
and growth. These can be thought of as ‘change management’ skills and is an aspect of co-ordination that
has increasingly caught the attention of researchers. For instance, studies have documented the
importance of organisational and leadership aspects in the co-ordination role (Avidov-Ungar and Hanin-
Itzak, 2019 [25] ) and also the value of co-ordinator’s ability to lead change, such as through their
communication skills (Blau, Shamir-Inbal and Hadad, 2020 [31] ). Moreover, research has suggested that
this stakeholder engagement should be broad, with the early engagement of teachers crucial but so too
wider staff members, such as administrative staff (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ).

Notably, this aspect of engagement can be seen to include both motivating colleagues, but also external
actors – some of which are set out further below – who may also need motivating and bringing onboard to
the school’s vision. These external actors may be important for supporting both efficiency and
effectiveness.

Here, it is worth noting that the literature on change processes in schools has grown considerably in recent
years. Indeed, in the face of the aforementioned challenges of provisioning and delivering professional
learning that enhances practice, attending to the wider school environment that can effectively support
change is important. For instance, the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) in the United Kingdom
has developed and refined a guide for schools on how to select and embed evidence-informed approaches
in a school (Education Endowment Foundation, n.d. [18] ). While this focusses particularly on school-level
change initiatives, its insights point to some of the key considerations, particularly for leaders when working

the school. This is discussed further below but it is worth noting that the influence of policy and vision on
driving school-level change in terms of effective digital pedagogy is receiving increasing attention and may
be an important avenue for further research.

title: Administrative

paragraphs.text:
A fourth area of co-ordination relates to administrative tasks. This area tends to have some overlap with
that of technical co-ordination, as it is also primarily focussed on ensuring the smooth running of the digital
infrastructure of a school. Some of the key features include:

•
Supporting the logistics of the digital infrastructure

•
Facilitating internal communication

•
Handling external communication

One notable feature of the administrative work of co-ordination may include monitoring the digital
infrastructure and handling the various administrative tasks that underpin it. For instance, digital
infrastructure needs to be procured which can demand various legal and financial steps. This may demand
engagement with external providers and facilitating communication with them, such as following up on
orders or problems with providers. Similarly, digital infrastructure may demand certain forms of book-
keeping. Administrative co-ordination may help to streamline these processes by ensuring people are
prepared for this or have the relevant expertise for it.

One further part of the administrative role may be facilitating internal communication. Administrative tasks
such as administering the school intranet and managing user accounts can be an important part of allowing
effective communication between teachers and students in schools. This can also support efficiency, in
particular freeing up time for teachers to engage in more impactful initiatives. For instance, the school
intranet may demand posting curriculum resources or updates, and administrative co-ordination can attend
to this for teachers. Alternatively, it may be that certain software demand the creation of individual use
accounts and administrative co-ordination may undertake this rather than teachers for their individual
classes.

A final aspect may relate to outwards communication. Administrative co-ordination may include aspects
such as maintaining the school website and parental communication channels or managing social media
(León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ). In this respect, ICT co-ordination is an
important role for facilitating how a school can efficiently and effectively communicate with its wider
community. Again, these may demand a degree of technical co-ordination, but provided that there are no
problems then they are primarily tasks that can be implemented with minimal technical expertise.

The administrative area of co-ordination points the fact that ICT co-ordination is also partly about interacting
with external actors as well as internal actors in a school. This invites consideration of some of the key
additional actors that shape ICT co-ordination and which may need considering when designing effective
approaches to co-ordination.

prepared for this or have the relevant expertise for it.
One further part of the administrative role may be facilitating internal communication. Administrative tasks
such as administering the school intranet and managing user accounts can be an important part of allowing
effective communication between teachers and students in schools. This can also support efficiency, in
particular freeing up time for teachers to engage in more impactful initiatives. For instance, the school
intranet may demand posting curriculum resources or updates, and administrative co-ordination can attend
to this for teachers. Alternatively, it may be that certain software demand the creation of individual use
accounts and administrative co-ordination may undertake this rather than teachers for their individual
classes.
A final aspect may relate to outwards communication. Administrative co-ordination may include aspects
such as maintaining the school website and parental communication channels or managing social media
(León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ). In this respect, ICT co-ordination is an
important role for facilitating how a school can efficiently and effectively communicate with its wider
community. Again, these may demand a degree of technical co-ordination, but provided that there are no
problems then they are primarily tasks that can be implemented with minimal technical expertise.
 25
The administrative area of co-ordination points the fact that ICT co-ordination is also partly about interacting
with external actors as well as internal actors in a school. This invites consideration of some of the key
additional actors that shape ICT co-ordination and which may need considering when designing effective
approaches to co-ordination.

title: 4 Implementing ICT co-ordinators in schools and systems

paragraphs.text:
Considering the role of the ICT co-ordinator in isolation from the wider architecture at the school and
system levels that surrounds it is futile. There is a strong consensus in the research literature that the role
of the ICT co-ordinator is heavily shaped by the context in which it operates. This has been conceptualised
in different ways. Some, for instance, have referred specifically to the 'architecture for learning' that shapes
the way the role is embedded in existing organisational structures (Woo and Law, 2020 [22] ). Others have
noted that across the literature it is common to consider the degree of ICT integration at the levels of
teachers, schools and education policy (Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] ). This can be considered the micro, meso
and macro levels.

Neither of these provide a perfect fit for considering the role of the ICT co-ordinator but both of them can
be informative, as set forth in these next sections. The 'architecture' can be considered in terms of how the
role is established and embedded in a school, but also at the level of how the school typically works as an
organisational entity. In this respect, the way the role functions straddles both the micro and the macro
levels, with co-ordinators having connections to both individual teachers but also groups of teachers and
organisational processes. Meanwhile, the wider school environment is an important meso level factor.
There are also though wider system-level supports that co-ordinators draw upon, which can be considered
the macro level of operation. Indeed, this goes back to the tension raised earlier on that co-ordinators can
be local, regional and national actors, with the degree of emphasis on these varying depending on a system
but also in a more fluid way depending on the task the co-ordinator undertakes.

This section first considers approaches to co-ordination and task assignment, looking at how these may
be combined across different individuals. The subsequent sections turn to consider in more detail the
enabling factors for effective co-ordination, discussing the role of the school environment and culture, as
well as the more 'macro' level supports that may be established. It has been argued that both of these
have historically received less attention than the more micro factors (Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] )but there is
an increasing interest in this type of factors, particularly in the wake of the relatively limited levels of ICT
integration in schools.
