title: Approaches to co-ordination and task assignment in a school

paragraphs.text:
Having considered the primary thematic areas of co-ordination above, this invites consideration of how
these may actually manifest in terms of specific roles and strategies within a school. Broadly speaking two
broad approaches can be seen in co-ordination efforts:

•
One is that of a single, individual dedicated ICT co-ordinator role,

•
and the second is that of a team-based approach where multiple people are responsible for co-
ordination undertaking different tasks.

In each of these cases, it has been argued that a key feature is that any roles are formal and clearly defined
(Woo, 2020 [24] ). This is a concern that has been raised by some researchers and identified as an

impediment to the role of ICT co-ordinator. For instance, in their study of ICT co-ordinators in Andalusia,
Spain, León-Jariego, Rodríguez-Miranda and Pozuelos-Estrada (2019 [6] ) noted that there was a lack of
shared vision in what co-ordinators were orientated towards doing, reflecting an ambiguity in their role and
its function.

With regard to single co-ordinators, this approach is the more historically dominant format. As Rodríguez-
Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada and León-Jariego (2014 [26] ) noted, this became a common model across
Europe with the more widespread advent of digital technologies. It can be seen as a response to the
challenges of digitalisation as well as the scale of the change it presented, with the creation of the role of
an ICT co-ordinator helping to create a formal position responsible for overseeing this work. The co-
ordinator could serve as a focal point within the school as well as the system. This type of single individual
may be well-suited to certain schools, particularly those that are relatively small and where the digital
infrastructure is relatively contained too. It may also be more resource-efficient for some systems as it may
demand fewer financial resources than multi-person teams. There may also be some greater efficiency in
terms of decision-making processes (see Box 5.1).

A team-based approach centres on the formation of a dedicated team of individuals responsible for the co-
ordination of digital tools in their school. Each individual oversees a bespoke area of responsibility (e.g.
technical, pedagogical as set out above), though a key feature is that there is frequent, close collaboration
among the team members. The overarching goal of adopting a team-based approach is that it allows the
workload of ICT co-ordination to be spread out to different profiles. This is grounded in the argument that
co-ordination demands a range of skills (and arguably increasingly skills) – as the four areas outlined above
showed – and that someone who can effectively undertake all of these roles is extremely rare, if impossible
(Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ). A team-based approach may allow better engagement with
certain tasks. Hence, one notable concern here is for the potential for certain tasks to dominate the role at
the expense of others. This appears particularly the case with regard to pedagogical work which is perhaps
unsurprising seeing the challenges that have been outlined earlier on. Indeed, in their aforementioned
study of ICT co-ordinators in Andalusia, Spain, León-Jariego et al. (2019 [6] ) noted not only a lack of clarity
in roles but also suggested that this meant some pedagogical tasks were somewhat superficially
completed. Hence, co-ordinators did primarily focus on supporting ICT use in the classroom but in terms
of simple tasks that were quite similar to daily teaching activity. There was, hence, less focus on promoting
ICT use that engaged with more complex classroom tasks, and which may be more substantial.

It is also worth noting that some researchers have drawn attention to the relatively high turnover that
characterises the role of ICT co-ordinator (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ). This adds to the
challenge of hiring the right individual for the role, while there are also potential wider personal
characteristics to consider as set out below. A team-based approach may allow for more continuity in ICT
co-ordination in a school by fostering a degree of internal ‘institutional memory’ to be retained as co-
ordination is shaped by multiple people and their habitual ways of working. The role can be insulated from
some of the vulnerabilities that high turnover may bring. This could, at the same time, be a hindrance if
such co-ordination efforts were not working particularly well. Hence, a team’s way-of-working may become
deeply ingrained and lead to a degree of inertia that is hard to adjust. This may be a consideration at the
local level as the composition of teams is attended to, including the team’s mix of personal characteristics.

Finally, it is also worth noting that moving to a more team-based approach is also in line with the wider
literature on school leadership as demanding a ‘distributed’ approach that draws upon relevant expertise
within the school. Indeed, the idea of ‘networked’ leadership has also been discussed in the literature,
reflecting the fact that schools do not exist in isolation but are often connected to other actors or schools.
Hence, they exist within a network and leadership may also run across these connections. Indeed, this can
be seen in how some primary schools, for instance, may share particular technical ICT support staff due
to their smaller size.

title: Potential permutations to approaches

paragraphs.text:
Within these broad approaches, there are a range of permutations. Indeed, a recent OECD policy survey
noted that there is no single approach across countries. Figure 4.1 presents the number of jurisdictions
with dedicated staff positions with responsibility for the use of digital resources for teaching. There is rich
variation; some systems have part-time roles, others full-time roles, some make use of technical support
staff or external contractors, some systems’ positions are shaped by the school size or other school
characteristics, and some systems rely on the discretion of schools or local authorities (see Annex Table
7.2, Boeskens and Meyer, 2025 [10] ). It is also notable that despite the presence of multi-stage career
structure for teachers in many systems, according to the Policy Survey fewer than half (15 of 36 [42%])
have centrally defined staff positions with responsibilities related to the use of digital resources for teaching
(e.g. supporting teachers in integrating digital technologies into their practice). Some of the areas where
variation in approaches to school-level co-ordination roles may appear are further outlined in the next sub-
sections.

title: Part-time and full-time

paragraphs.text:
Co-ordination roles may be full-time or part-time roles. This may depend on the resources available, as
well as the nature of the job and the demands on the role. For instance, in smaller school settings the role
may be part-time, or, as set out below further, split in a role-sharing format. One point to highlight here is
that part-time can, itself, be very varied; the number of hours, or percentage of a workload, that is
consumed by co-ordination can vary greatly. It can allow for adaption to particular contexts.

Interestingly, it has been argued that a dedicated portion of some teaching time may be particularly
beneficial for pedagogical co-ordinators. This may allow for the co-ordinator’s knowledge to be mobilised
to impact students, for the co-ordinator to stay better attuned to the typical challenges of digitalisation and
pedagogy their colleagues encounter, and it may also be good for the credibility of ICT co-ordinators (Woo,
2020 [24] ).

Notably, this blend of part-time and full-time roles may co-exist; in team-based approaches there may be
dedicated full-time positions as well as those who participate in the team on a part-time role. It may be that,
for instance, a dedicated member of the school leadership team is responsible for ICT co-ordination and
has a certain number of hours for engagement in the ICT co-ordination team, or someone who is part of
the administrative staff.

title: Role-sharing

paragraphs.text:
It may be that certain roles are shared across a certain number of schools. For instance, this may be
particularly the case with regard to technical support and in relatively small schools. Technical support may
lend itself well to this, because certain technical issues may be able to be troubleshooted centrally and at
distance. Issues may also arise less frequently in smaller school settings or, seeing that the digital
infrastructure is often smaller and simpler, are in general less complex issues to solve and thus demand
less of a technical co-ordinator’s dedicated time. In this respect, working across multiple schools can create
a fuller workload for technical co-ordinators. Also, unlike pedagogical co-ordination which demands a
closer degree of interaction with teachers and their particular needs, the technical co-ordination tends to
focus on hardware and software that are largely similar across schools. That said, recourse to certain
emergency means of attending to technical issues may be important, with a shared role demanding a
degree of flexibility in terms of how the co-ordinator is made available to schools to efficiently respond to
their needs.

More broadly, technical co-ordination that involves engagement across multiple schools may allow for the
development of bespoke technical solutions that can be used in multiple settings, which may be more cost-
efficient (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ). It also has been argued that pooling resources
together across schools to hire a shared co-ordinator may mean greater resources that can attract
particularly high-quality candidates (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ).

This is particularly pertinent considering that education systems across the OECD currently face significant
gaps in the availability of technical assistance in schools. In PISA 2022, 41% of 15-year-old students
attended schools whose principal reported having insufficiently qualified technical assistant staff, on
average across the OECD (Boeskens and Meyer, 2025 [20] ). According to the OECD’s Policy Survey on
School Education in the Digital Age, out of 37 responding jurisdictions, six systems (16%) assign the
responsibility for the maintenance of digital education resources to technical support staff (at the lower
secondary level), which are sometimes shared between multiple schools. In nearly three-quarters of
responding jurisdictions (27 of 37 systems [73%]), assigning responsibility for the maintenance of digital
education resources is at the discretion of schools or local authorities (Boeskens and Meyer, 2025 [20] ).
Role-sharing may be a valuable area for further exploration for local authorities.

title: Multi-layered

paragraphs.text:
It may be that while there is a dedicated co-ordinator this person also relies on a range of supporting co-
ordinators. For instance, Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels (2024 [23] ) note that there may be one single ICT
co-ordinator, who delegates across several supporting technical co-ordinators – in the school or externally
as a form of outsourcing.

This has overlap with the idea of a team-based approach but specifically emphasises that individual co-
ordination areas are also potentially team-driven too. This may be particularly relevant in large schools or
affiliated networks of schools where there is a team of technical co-ordinators with a designated lead co-
ordinator that represents and oversees this team.

paragraphs.text: Regional and local levels

A final permutation to consider is how much emphasis is placed on the co-ordinator serving as a school-
level actor, or as a more regional – or even national – actors that works across schools. Woo and Law
(2020 [22] ) highlighted two levels of operation for co-ordinators: a more regional role that sees them work
primarily with leaders on their strategy, and then a more local, school-centred role that focusses primarily
on the capacity-building of teaching staff. Meanwhile, in their study of co-ordinators in public schools in
Hong Kong, Woo (2015 [34] ) noted that co-ordinators may navigate responsibilities at both the local, regional
and national level. The latter may be particularly informed by the size of a system and the number of co-
ordinators available.

This can be seen as a permutation of the above four-part model where the regional role sees a greater
emphasis on the tasks related to policy and vision, and the more localised role attends more to pedagogical
aspects. This may also combine with each of the three variation levels above. It could be, for instance, that
there is a full-time or part-time co-ordinator role that works on strategic oversight across multiple schools,
with an assigned individual co-ordinator in these schools under their guidance, thus creating a multi-
layered team. This captures the potential malleability in the approaches and how they can be potentially
adapted to different contextual needs, something that is considered in further detail later in this paper.

title: Effective collaboration in ICT co-ordination

paragraphs.text:
The question of how effective collaboration can be established between colleagues for ICT co-ordination
has received increasing attention in recent years. This is a relevant question in all systems and schools,
whether there is a single ICT co-ordinator model or a team-based one. That’s because the type of tasks
that are demanded for effective ICT co-ordination still demand the engagement of and collaboration with
other actors even if a single individual is primarily responsible for co-ordination efforts. For instance, the
aspect of policy and vision in co-ordination points to the fact that a single co-ordinator will still need to work
with members of the school leadership in designing ICT policies for the school. That said, in a team-based
approach, attention to how effective collaboration is promoted is particularly important.

The question of how effective collaboration can be established between colleagues for ICT co-ordination
has received increasing attention in recent years. This is a relevant question in all systems and schools,
whether there is a single ICT co-ordinator model or a team-based one. That’s because the type of tasks
that are demanded for effective ICT co-ordination still demand the engagement of and collaboration with
other actors even if a single individual is primarily responsible for co-ordination efforts. For instance, the
aspect of policy and vision in co-ordination points to the fact that a single co-ordinator will still need to work
with members of the school leadership in designing ICT policies for the school. That said, in a team-based
approach, attention to how effective collaboration is promoted is particularly important.

title: Organising collaboration

paragraphs.text:
Both Woo (2020 [24] ) and Desmedt and colleagues (2024 [23] ), in their studies of co-ordination in Singapore
and reviewing international practice for the Flemish Community of Belgium respectively, have looked into
some of the features that underpin effective teamwork. Looking across these, it is possible to synthesise
several key features that may be attended to for fostering effective collaboration:

•
Ensuring a clear division of tasks and assignment based on expertise. As mentioned, a
consistent argument across the literature is that ambiguity around roles and functions can reduce
the effectiveness of ICT co-ordinators (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada and León-Jariego,
2014 [26] ; Letnes, 2025 [7] ). In this respect, ensuring clarity from the beginning among the different
actors – whether it is multiple official ‘co-ordinators’ or a single co-ordinator working closely with
different colleagues – is a truly primordial foundation for effective co-ordination.

•
Attending to the processes for making decisions . This includes assigning responsibilities or
mandates and defining how certain decisions are reached. Processes may need to be
differentiated and multiple based on different types of decisions; for instance, certain decisions
(e.g. technical) may need recourse to a degree of swiftness, while others around the ICT policy or
plan need more iterative processes.

•
Defining the formal infrastructure of collaboration, such as the organisational units and their
interaction mechanisms. This includes defining which groups of stakeholders will meet, for what

purpose, and with what frequency. This may include the organisational units responsible for
management and making decisions, but also those who meet for consultation or collaborative
purposes.

•
Creating space for informal collaboration too. Opportunities for collaboration that are less formal
can also be significant for building a culture of exchange and innovation. For instance, this may
take the form of working group lunches.

Interestingly, with regard to this blend of formal and informal architecture, it appears that the establishment
of formal structures should not be under-estimated. Although working in a relatively unique setting of
private international schools, and with a small sample of co-ordinators (n=4), the in depth case studies of
Woo and Law (2020 [22] ) highlight the importance of attending to the structures surrounding co-ordinators,
especially those seeking to enact pedagogical changes. Formal structures that connected co-ordinators to
different teaching teams at different hierarchical levels in their school were essential, the authors argue,
for supporting instructional tasks in the co-ordinator’s role. In particular it is worth noting that the co-
ordinators examined by Woo and Law were relatively new in their role and hence ICT co-ordination was a
new school initiative. Formal structures may be particularly important in such contexts in this respect seeing
that the more tacit cultures that can facilitate collaboration and exchange may not be fully in place.

Regarding the delineation of structures, it appears that a particularly important consideration is clearly
defining the relationship between co-ordination efforts and school leadership. The engagement of school
leadership in digital co-ordination efforts is, across the literature, a significant consideration for its success
(Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] ; Woo and Law, 2020 [22] ). This may overlap with aspects above such as the
processes for making decisions or defining the formal infrastructure of meetings and communication. While
the specific approach can vary and be defined by individual schools, in general, an ICT co-ordinator should
have a defined channel of communication with school leadership, or a member of an ICT co-ordination
team will also be a school leader to be able to align policies and ensure effective communications. Beyond
these formal means of interacting around co-ordination efforts, it is important to note that leaders also play
a role in shaping the more general culture of a school – such as its disposition to learning and digitalisation
– and this is attended to more in the paper’s next section (5.Enabling effective co-ordination).

Finally, it is worth noting that it is possible to identify some overlap with wider research on effective
leadership. For instance, the importance of organising clear roles and routines of interaction and
collaboration stand out (Leithwood, Harris and Hopkins, 2019 [35] ). In general, it may be that there is value
in greater exploration between effective leadership and that of leading digital transformation; for instance,
one key feature of leadership is the use of data to drive change, though this is discussed less in the field
of implementing digital co-ordination.

digitalisation in a school, it is important to note that there remains, nonetheless, an important collective
responsibility too. Digital co-ordination is something that demands engagement, to differing extents, from
all those in a school. One risk in ICT co-ordination is that it may create a situation where responsibility for
digitalisation is essentially being too heavily outsourced. This may reduce the engagement of certain key
stakeholders and the effectiveness of co-ordination efforts. This can be a risk across both individual and
team-based approaches.

ordinator as solely responsible for digitalisation in the school, rather than it being something that remains
a collective endeavour being spearheaded by the co-ordination. The co-ordinator is helping to streamline
certain aspects of co-ordination (e.g. procurement) and serve as a source of inspiration (e.g. curating best
practices), but teachers still need to engage actively in thinking about how digitalisation intersects with their

paragraphs.text:
pedagogy. After all, a co-ordinator may be able to recommend certain digital tools for a teacher to use in
their classroom, but they won't have the same localised knowledge of a class’s needs like the teacher, and
the teacher's judgement in the application of these tools remains essential. In this respect, there is some
outsourcing of the cognitive load of digitalisation to the co-ordinator, but the cognitive load of certain
aspects - particularly pedagogical - rest primarily with the individual teacher. Otherwise, there is a risk
where capacity building is limited and digitalisation in the classroom ineffective. Indeed, this is a reminder
of the tricky balancing of how cognitive load is distributed in ICT co-ordination: effective co-ordination can
save time and resources by specialists taking on certain tasks in a school and undertaking these at scale,
but digitalisation is also challenging for all and tasks such as pedagogical integration demands critical
thinking from teachers alongside co-ordinations. This risk is a reminder of the importance of a system
communicating the responsibility of all teachers to actively and critically engage in the digitalisation
process. The vision of the system and the provision of professional learning opportunities are both
important here. For instance, systems such as Singapore leverage both individual digital co-ordinators in
their schools, but they also emphasise the active engagement of all teachers in the digitalisation process.

This is a risk that may also arise in team-based approaches too. Hence, a teacher may view digitalisation
as the responsibility of the group of co-ordinators and their individual role as limited. A further risk is that
the team-based approach leads to a situation where members of the team view responsibility as ultimately
falling on their team members. One team member may assume that someone else is overseeing a certain
task or handling a problem, meaning that these tasks or problems are not actually resolved in a timely,
efficient manner. To avoid this type of situation, clear division of tasks and regular communication are
especially important. It is also essential that the decision-making process is clear so that the way that
ultimate responsibility for certain decisions among the team is taken is well understood.

A final point to note here with regard to the risks of how cognitive load is distributed is that this may evolve
and change. Indeed, co-ordination approaches may evolve in step with the needs of a school or system.
This is an area where longitudinal research on co-ordination in schools is very much needed. It may be
that co-ordination efforts in certain school contexts may need to be more centralised and direct in terms of
a clearly designation co-ordinator or team of co-ordinators initially orientating teachers (e.g. providing
resources, suggestions for practice) and that over time, as teachers' capacity develops, co-ordination
becomes less centralised and orchestrated by an individual and team, and increasingly a collective, whole-
school endeavour. This may see teachers take on more of the cognitive load as their self-efficacy grows.

title: Resourcing the co-ordination roles

paragraphs.text:
Effective ICT co-ordination is shaped by how different resources are allocated. This can be highly variable
between systems. A key consideration is funding co-ordination hours, with the role typically demanding
either a reduction in workload or the funding of a full-time role.

In some systems, ear-marked funds can be drawn upon to cover the hours of ICT co-ordination. For
instance, in the Flemish Community of Belgium, all primary, secondary and adult education institutions can
access government funds to pay for ICT co-ordinators (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ). Notably,
these resources can be used individually by establishments or pooled with other schools. This reflects the
fact that ICT co-ordinators cost different amounts based on their level of qualification. This is an important
point that highlights how ICT co-ordination may, itself, have different gradations and allow for a degree of
career progression itself (see below).

In the Flemish Community of Belgium, schools can also assign hours to ICT co-ordination at their own
discretion from a wider pool of resources (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ). For instance, they
may assign a certain number of hours of a teacher to co-ordination, deducting this from their teaching
hours, or assign administrative staff’s time to co-ordination efforts. In each case, this balancing of hours is

shaped by the fact that this is an allocation of a finite number of hours and thus there may be trade-offs to
reallocating more staff hours to ICT co-ordination.

This raises the question of the type of incentives that attract people to the role of ICT co-ordinator and can
help to ensure the appropriate individual undertakes a particular role. The following levers are some of
these available to policymakers to shape how they attract quality candidates to the role. They are not
mutually exclusive and may be applied in different combinations.

•
Qualifications: It may be that certain qualifications serve as a prerequisite for undertaking a role.
For instance, in Estonia, the position of ‘Educational Technologist’ demands a specialised master’s
degree. This reflects the expertise that the role demands of mapping digital competencies in
school, developing digital learning materials and supporting the integration of the right technologies
into classrooms. Prerequisites can shape the quality of applicants to a position, but also shape the
number of applicants, with certain qualifications being a potential barrier if teachers do not see the
investment in the qualification as worthwhile. Indeed, it is worth noting that Estonia has a long and
established history of digitalisation in its school system.

•
Additional renumeration: An ICT co-ordinator role may be incentivised through financial
incentives. Co-ordinators may receive additional renumeration for their role. This potentially carries
high costs to a system, but it may also be a means of attracting quality candidates to the role.
Significant here may be the fact that certain expertise in the space of ICT can be very valuable on
the job market, and it can therefore be competitive hiring technologically-competent individuals to
roles such as a technical co-ordinator.

•
Learning opportunity: There may be particular professional learning opportunities that are offered
to ICT co-ordinators, such as bespoke training in preparation for the role (Avidov-Ungar and Hanin-
Itzak, 2019 [25] ). This type of opportunity to learn new content may be an important feature in
attracting individuals to the role, particularly seeing the timely nature of mastering digital
technologies and the personal interest some may have in the topic.

•
Formal recognition of role: Connected to this idea of a learning opportunity is how the formal
recognition of the role of ICT co-ordinator in the teacher career structure may be significant for
attracting candidates. For instance, this type of additional role may be a significant signal for
teachers that can serve a stepping stone for future roles. In particular, the recognition of the role
as part of the school leadership team may mean that it is a learning opportunity for teachers who
can gain exposure to the roles and responsibilities of leadership. Moreover, it has also been argued
that clearly defined roles may be important for the status and credibility of the co-ordination role
(Woo, 2020 [24] ). Policymakers may formalise co-ordination roles as valuable opportunities for
growth and development, and this may shape the attractiveness of the role. Indeed, it may be that
there is a degree of vertical progression within the role of ICT co-ordination, with different pay-
scales depending on one’s qualifications, or alternatively aspects such as one’s experience or
performance measures may be drawn upon.

•
Dedicated hours: The opportunity to dedicate a certain number of hours to ICT co-ordination may
be significant. Additional roles with dedicated time can be a way for teachers to diversify their
working hours and invest time in their passions. For teachers who are passionate about digital
tools, the opportunity to engage in working on this topic alongside other roles may be important for
attracting them to the role.

title: The role of individuals

paragraphs.text:
Within these models and co-ordination efforts, it is important to also note that ICT co-ordination remains a
fundamentally ‘human activity’. Hence, even with efforts to better define approaches and tasks, there
remains a degree of variability and unpredictability because ICT co-ordination is undertaken by individuals.

text:
Within these models and co-ordination efforts, it is important to also note that ICT co-ordination remains a
fundamentally ‘human activity’. Hence, even with efforts to better define approaches and tasks, there
remains a degree of variability and unpredictability because ICT co-ordination is undertaken by individuals.

paragraphs.text:
One lens to consider here is the actual ICT co-ordinator as an individual. Across the literature, hard-to-pin-
down features such as individuals’ mindsets, values and attitudes are noted as influencing ICT co-
ordination efforts. For instance, Avidov-Ungar and Hanin-Itzak (2019 [25] ) have researched features such
as co-ordinators’ motivation and prior knowledge and have argued that these are important influences on
the role. Woo (2020 [24] ) in their study of Singaporean co-ordinators notes the presence of certain
competencies like negotiation in influencing the work of co-ordinators. Indeed, some of the earliest studies
of the role have noted the importance of personal characteristics, with Tondeur, Cooper and Newhouse
(2010 [27] ) noting that some of the most successful co-ordinators were “enthusiastic, experienced and
respected staff members” (p.302). The aforementioned value of certain leadership qualities, such as
communication skills, is also worth noting here (Blau, Shamir-Inbal and Hadad, 2020 [31] ).

One challenge here is that the literature has primarily concentrated on personal characteristics in terms of
individual co-ordinators. Features that may be significant in terms of teams where, arguably, the human
aspect may be more complex as personal characteristics interact together, is a far less clear picture. This
presents some challenges for those engaged in defining the role and, crucially, appointing people to these
roles, as they must gauge not only the individual’s suitability for a role but also how they may interact with
other members of a co-ordination team. Further research on the influence of personal characteristics within
certain teams would be valuable for practitioners and policymakers alike.

Finally, a second lens of the ‘individual’ to attend to is that co-ordinators must also work with individual
teachers. This has received a considerable level of attention in the literature. It has been argued that the
concentration on enhancing the capacity of individual teachers has actually skewed attention from the
wider need for co-ordinators to foster sustainable school-level change (Letnes, 2025 [7] ; Sosa-Díaz et al.,
2022 [21] ). These are important arguments, and it does seem, as set out in the next section, that greater
attention to the wider meso-level factors of the school is important. At the same time, co-ordinators may
still have a close relationship with individual teachers. For instance, as set out above, assessing needs in
a school may constitute both an individual and collective assessment of staff, while capacity-building and
motivating staff may also demand a personal touch. In this regard, individual teachers and their
characteristics also shape the way that co-ordinators work and the effectiveness of certain relationships.
Certain tasks of co-ordination are highly relational, and in this regard heavily influenced by the individuals
in these relations.

attention to the wider meso-level factors of the school is important. At the same time, co-ordinators may
still have a close relationship with individual teachers. For instance, as set out above, assessing needs in
a school may constitute both an individual and collective assessment of staff, while capacity-building and
motivating staff may also demand a personal touch. In this regard, individual teachers and their
characteristics also shape the way that co-ordinators work and the effectiveness of certain relationships.
Certain tasks of co-ordination are highly relational, and in this regard heavily influenced by the individuals
in these relations.

title: 5 Enabling effective co-ordination

paragraphs.text:
While this paper has primarily concentrated on the specificities of the ICT co-ordinator role, this section
shall now turn to consider more of the role’s integration within the school and system environment. As
noted, the co-ordinator role(s) does not exist in a vacuum but is heavily shaped by the school context it
operates within, as well as the type of system-level expectations and supports that surround it. Strategically
attending to these contextual factors at the meso and macro level is essential for ensuring successful ICT
integration in schools and systems (see Figure 5.1).

This section first turns to examine the integration of the co-ordinator role in a school and its wider
organisational and cultural processes. It then zooms out to consider the wider system-level supports that
can help co-ordinators to thrive.

title: School-level integration

paragraphs.text:
As mentioned earlier, two levels of school-level architecture can be considered. One is that of how the
actual co-ordinator works and is connected to other units in a school (Woo and Law, 2020 [22] ).This has
been discussed above in terms of co-ordinators’ tasks and how they may function as part of a team.
Another level which has not always been attended to in the literature is the school’s broader architecture
and how it typically works in terms of organisational processes and norms.

Indeed, there is a perceptible increase in attention to actors such as school leaders as well as the type of
tasks that co-ordinators complete in relation to mobilising people and driving school-level change. More
than a decade ago, Vanderlinde, Aesaert and Van Braak (2014 [36] ) noted that the process of ICT integration
in schools is a fundamentally school-level social phenomenon, rather than dependant on individual
teachers. This idea has taken a strong foothold in the literature and is reflected in how co-ordination is
increasingly considered as a contextually-situated role. Moreover, attending to the relationship between
the ICT co-ordinator role and the school environment appears particularly significant considering that some
have argued that schools are increasing in their autonomy and responsibility, and thus may play an
outsized role in shaping the effectiveness of the ICT co-ordinator role (Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] ).

This section begins by considering the influence of school leadership teams in shaping ICT integration,
before turning to consider additional actors that may be significant for the effective implementation of
change in a school.

title: School leadership teams

paragraphs.text:
School leaders are a natural starting point for considering how ICT co-ordination is implemented in a
school. It has already been noted that school leaders play an important role in co-ordination efforts of the
digital infrastructure of a school. In particular, there may be close collaboration between ICT co-ordinators
and the school leadership team, or it may be that a member of the school leadership is responsible for
overseeing ICT co-ordination and attending to aspects such as policy and vision.

Beyond these more formal roles or structures, it is important to note that leadership in a school heavily
shapes the broader environment within which ICT co-ordination occurs. Schools are complex spaces that

are shaped by different structures, processes and norms. ICT co-ordination exists within this environment
and must co-exist alongside these different structures, processes and norms, which may also be
supporting other priorities and goals than just digitalisation. School leaders play an outsized role in shaping
this broader school environment.

One fundamental aspect of this school environment is the type of learning culture that leaders foster. For
instance, while hard to define and pinpoint, a school’s culture shapes how colleagues may collaborate
together, how willing they are to adopt change, or how likely teachers are to take risks and innovate in their
teaching. Blau, Shamir-Inbal and Hadad (2020 [31] ) have argued that collaborative activities seem easier to
integrate in schools with a collectivist culture. Leaders play an important role in shaping the school’s
learning culture and ethos, defining not only the general ethos or vision of the school but also embodying
this through their daily interactions with colleagues.

Connected to this is not only the question of a learning culture, but the organisational infrastructure which
underpin how a school typically works on a day-to-day process. Leaders shape the structures and
processes with regard to who colleagues interact with and how they do so. Again, this is somewhat
intangible and can evolve in its own organic way too. Nevertheless, the importance of the formal
connections between different organisational units in a school has already been discussed above.
Accordingly, it is important to acknowledge that school leaders are very influential in determining these
units and the connections between them. They may have the power to adjust these, and this may
subsequently shape ICT co-ordination efforts.

A further aspect of leadership that frequently surfaces in the literature relates to the type of vision that
leaders set forth. This has been already discussed in detail in relation to the ‘policy and vision’ task of the
ICT co-ordinator role, but it is important to note how central school leaders are in this work of defining any
digital education plan or vision. Sosa-Diaz and colleagues’ (2022 [21] ) systematic literature review highlights
that the active support of leaders in a school’s efforts to integrate ICT is essential for any efforts’ success.
Leaders can help give credence to this plan, but they also have an important oversight in terms of ensuring
that a vision for ICT is also integrated alongside the wider holistic vision of the school. Indeed, one
challenge when it comes to school-level change can be undertaking too much and subsequently failing to
sufficiently achieve goals and causing change fatigue among teachers. Leaders’ vision is key here to
ensuring coherence across different goals.

Leaders can also play an important role in providing oversight to the evolving implementation of a digital
vision. Indeed, a school’s digital education plan is typically viewed as a ‘living’ rather than ‘static’ document.
Hence, it is to be used and worked with, shaped by ongoing, systematic reflection and adaption to meet a
school's evolving needs during an integration process. This aligns with wider literature on change
processes in schools which often set forth an iterative model that seeks to continuously monitor a new
initiative’s evolving effectiveness and facilitate its fine-tuning (Education Endowment Foundation, n.d. [18] ).
Accordingly, it may be that ICT co-ordination efforts are incorporated into school evaluation mechanisms.
How these plans are monitored and evaluated remains an area that has received limited attention in the
literature. Furthermore, it may be informed by system-level priorities and decisions. That said, leadership
teams are likely to be significant actors when it comes to both monitoring and evaluating initiatives in their
school, as well as their staff and providing them with feedback to grow. Indeed, it may also be that leaders
have a role to play in the specific appraisal of ICT co-ordination staff, which is, again, a feature where
understanding in the literature remains nascent.

This invites consideration of a final aspect of leadership that appears important: how leaders motivate their
colleagues to learn and grow as professionals. Again, while somewhat intangible beyond formal structures
of appraisal, the literature notes that leaders can also inspire change and foster teachers’ motivation in ICT
initiatives (Sosa-Díaz et al., 2022 [21] ). Hence, in this regard, more informal praise and spotlighting of
impactful work may be significant. It may also be that leaders provide more formal feedback to teachers
such as through regular formative appraisal, and here how they attend, or do not attend to digital aspects,

paragraphs.text:
may be very significant. Indeed, this may go beyond any specific school leaders with responsibility for ICT,
to impact all leaders and how they provide feedback to their staff.
Additional actors for effective ICT co-ordination

Understanding effective ICT co-ordination has primarily concentrated on the work of individual or teams of
co-ordinators, as well as their interactions with leadership teams. These can be seen as the ‘core’ of ICT
co-ordination, but the far-reaching influence of technology on schools also means that there are a range
of wider actors that also appear across the literature on co-ordination. These actors tend to operate outside
of the ‘core’ actors previously mentioned, interacting with co-ordination efforts in different ways.

Understanding these actors and their role in supporting co-ordination efforts is still nascent and may be a
valuable area of further research. The following two actors appear particularly significant.
Early adopters and champions

Studies have highlighted the potential value of particularly "enterprising teachers" (Sosa-Díaz et al.,
2022 [32] , p.9) who can help to inspire and support colleagues. While this has been discussed in relation to
co-ordinators themselves, it can be valuable to consider the wider pool of "enterprising teachers" in a
school being important allies for co-ordinators in their work. These may also be referred to as ‘early
adopters’ or ‘champions’ (Education Endowment Foundation, n.d. [18] ; Rogers, 2003 [37] ).

Such teachers can help motivate colleagues and the dissemination of important ideas, with the co-ordinator
having a degree of oversight over this and serving as a connecting node for enterprising teachers. The
endorsement by colleagues is typically important in schools for new ideas (Williams and Coles, 2007 [38] ;
Cain, 2015 [39] ). Research on school-level change (Education Endowment Foundation, n.d. [18] ), as well as
behaviour change more generally (Rogers, 2003 [37] ), has suggested that colleagues can have a powerful
influence on people. In particular, the endorsement by certain teachers may have an outsize effect on
adoption. These types of early adopters and enterprising teachers may be particularly important for
motivational effects in a school around ICT integration. Hence, there is a slight 'chicken and egg' problem
in ICT integration that a positive association has been found between teachers' use of ICT in their practice
an increase in the overall self-efficacy perception of ICT for instructional purposes (see Sosa-Díaz et al.,
2022 [32] ). This suggests that teachers need to be using ICT to believe more effectively in its value, but the
latter can be significant for driving teachers to want to use ICT in the first place. In this respect, a group of
enterprising teachers can help encourage colleagues to take small steps in a new direction that may
eventually lead to bigger, self-driven leaps by that teacher.

It can therefore be valuable to identify individuals that are already comfortable working with technology
who can demonstrate their work to colleagues, help motivate them and provide informal support. In
particular, engaging these teachers early on in co-ordination efforts to create a sense of ownership and
co-creation among teachers may be especially valuable (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ). Notably this is seemingly
feasible; as noted previously, the cluster of “highly engaged” teachers could be identified in varying
proportions across systems (Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025 [1] ). Schools and co-ordinators may seek to
invest time early on in identifying who these individuals are and supporting their role as pioneers and peer-
supports to colleagues.
Families and community stakeholders

While schools have been tasked with building students’ digital literacy and their ethical and healthy
engagement with technology, it is important to note that families and communities also play an important
role here. Indeed, this may be particularly important for supporting the equitable development of digital
literacy in a rapidly changing digital landscape (Forsström et al., 2025 [3] ). The evolving policies around
mobile-phone use or the use of Generative AI in schools are a good example of this and how collaboration

between schools and families and communities is becoming increasingly important and expected. Indeed,
there is arguably a lot of doubt and uncertainty around the role of technology in schools. In this respect, it
may be important to attend to the channels of communication and consultation between a school’s ICT co-
ordination and these other actors.

This has been, however, given limited attention in the literature. Historically, there has been some attending
to communicating with parents, though this is primarily very passive such as through the form of school
websites (León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ). Interestingly, the literature
notes some examples of more substantial engagement and work with parents. Woo and Law (2020 [22] )
found in their thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with four ICT co-ordinators that parents were
one organisational unit in a school to attend to. For instance, some co-ordinators noted running workshops
directly with parents. This is an avenue that merits further exploration. Strategic engagement with parents
may be important for fostering buy-in around a particular vision, as well as coherence in terms of how
digital tools are used between schools and homes.

adopters’ or ‘champions’ (Education Endowment Foundation, n.d. [18] ; Rogers, 2003 [37] ).
Such teachers can help motivate colleagues and the dissemination of important ideas, with the co-ordinator
having a degree of oversight over this and serving as a connecting node for enterprising teachers. The
endorsement by colleagues is typically important in schools for new ideas (Williams and Coles, 2007 [38] ;
Cain, 2015 [39] ). Research on school-level change (Education Endowment Foundation, n.d. [18] ), as well as
behaviour change more generally (Rogers, 2003 [37] ), has suggested that colleagues can have a powerful
influence on people. In particular, the endorsement by certain teachers may have an outsize effect on
adoption. These types of early adopters and enterprising teachers may be particularly important for
motivational effects in a school around ICT integration. Hence, there is a slight 'chicken and egg' problem
in ICT integration that a positive association has been found between teachers' use of ICT in their practice
an increase in the overall self-efficacy perception of ICT for instructional purposes (see Sosa-Díaz et al.,
2022 [32] ). This suggests that teachers need to be using ICT to believe more effectively in its value, but the
latter can be significant for driving teachers to want to use ICT in the first place. In this respect, a group of
enterprising teachers can help encourage colleagues to take small steps in a new direction that may
eventually lead to bigger, self-driven leaps by that teacher.
It can therefore be valuable to identify individuals that are already comfortable working with technology
who can demonstrate their work to colleagues, help motivate them and provide informal support. In
particular, engaging these teachers early on in co-ordination efforts to create a sense of ownership and
co-creation among teachers may be especially valuable (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ). Notably this is seemingly
feasible; as noted previously, the cluster of “highly engaged” teachers could be identified in varying
proportions across systems (Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025 [1] ). Schools and co-ordinators may seek to
invest time early on in identifying who these individuals are and supporting their role as pioneers and peer-
supports to colleagues.
Families and community stakeholders
While schools have been tasked with building students’ digital literacy and their ethical and healthy
engagement with technology, it is important to note that families and communities also play an important
role here. Indeed, this may be particularly important for supporting the equitable development of digital
literacy in a rapidly changing digital landscape (Forsström et al., 2025 [3] ). The evolving policies around
mobile-phone use or the use of Generative AI in schools are a good example of this and how collaboration
 39
between schools and families and communities is becoming increasingly important and expected. Indeed,
there is arguably a lot of doubt and uncertainty around the role of technology in schools. In this respect, it
may be important to attend to the channels of communication and consultation between a school’s ICT co-
ordination and these other actors.
This has been, however, given limited attention in the literature. Historically, there has been some attending
to communicating with parents, though this is primarily very passive such as through the form of school
websites (León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ). Interestingly, the literature
notes some examples of more substantial engagement and work with parents. Woo and Law (2020 [22] )
found in their thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with four ICT co-ordinators that parents were
one organisational unit in a school to attend to. For instance, some co-ordinators noted running workshops
directly with parents. This is an avenue that merits further exploration. Strategic engagement with parents
may be important for fostering buy-in around a particular vision, as well as coherence in terms of how
digital tools are used between schools and homes.

title: Beyond the school: System-level support systems and best-practice exchange mechanisms

paragraphs.text:
While ICT co-ordination is primarily concentrated on actions that occur in a school, it also has important
outwards looking features as alluded to above. A range of external actors may play a role in shaping how
co-ordination unfolds. This reflects the increasingly multi-stakeholder nature of education, with systems
relying on a greater range of actors and interconnections than was historically the case (OECD, 2025 [13] ).

This section considers some of these actors that may require particular attention when considering
approaches to ICT co-ordination. While the literature has primarily focussed on co-ordination looking
inwards, this section synthesis some of the external actors from the literature. It highlights some of the
ways that further research may also look outwards to consider some of the key connections and supports
that may be attended to in models of co-ordination.

One notable feature of several countries’ approach to ICT co-ordination is the presence of different support
systems for those responsible for ICT co-ordination. These can take different forms and vary in terms of
the degree of active, central-led support that they provide to co-ordination efforts, and the extent they rely
on more informal, ad-hoc support. They may also move fluidly between these forms of support.

It is helpful to first consider the more holistic support infrastructure. In recent years, there has been
particular attention on the type of central and more localised (e.g. municipal) support that is provided to
co-ordinators. This can be seen as a reflection of co-ordinators’ potential role straddling both more specific
local and school needs and more high-level national goals. It has been argued that a support infrastructure
may be important for sustaining school-level initiatives, as well as fostering coherent strategy across a
system (Woo, 2020 [24] ; Avidov-Ungar and Hanin-Itzak, 2019 [25] ). Indeed, a support infrastructure can help
to facilitate knowledge-exchange between schools which can both build a shared understanding of
effective digital transformation and facilitate the sharing of ways of achieving this. This may be significant
for both equity and efficiency. It means that co-ordinators are less likely to miss out on impactful
approaches, but it also means that they do not to come up with solutions from scratch to every single
common challenge and can, instead, build on others’ work and adapt it to their own local needs. Indeed,
more centralised or localised support may also have the potential to take on certain administrative functions
that demand a degree of centralised expertise (e.g. tenders, legal issues) (Desmedt, Sempels and
Pauwels, 2024 [23] ) or which can facilitate more effective purchasing power and co-ordination. This type of
support may support more efficient use of resources.

Sweden (Gustafsson, Olofsson and Bergström, 2024 [30] ). Looking across co-ordinators working in settings

Pauwels, 2024 [23] ) or which can facilitate more effective purchasing power and co-ordination. This type of

The potential influence of a local support infrastructure was thrown into stark relief by a recent study in
Sweden (Gustafsson, Olofsson and Bergström, 2024 [30] ). Looking across co-ordinators working in settings

paragraphs.text:
that had more active municipal support compared to those without, the study found that co-ordinators that
could work as part of a strong municipal support network were able to contribute to fostering more coherent,
equitable school digitalisation grounded in a joint understanding of schools’ needs and national policies.
There was also a greater emphasis on collaborative improvement of practice by co-ordinators in these
settings of municipal support, rather than co-ordinators being primarily confined to trouble-shooting
technological issues or working only with the most enthusiastic teachers. In particular, this seemed to foster
more institutional stability that went beyond relying on the individual capacities of co-ordinators, which is
important considering the aforementioned turnover of the role. While Sweden’s role of ICT co-ordinator is
in the context of a highly decentralised system and still relatively understudied, the findings of Gustafsson
et al. (2024 [30] ) highlight the potential importance of the surrounding context in shaping co-ordination efforts.

Before turning to consider more specific forms of support, there are two important high-level considerations
to attend to. Both of these may shape how policymakers develop a support infrastructure for ICT co-
ordinators. One is whether support should be more centralised at the national level or more localised, at
say the municipal level. This appears an open question and one that is shaped by the system itself and its
ways of working, as well as more practical questions such as its size and geography. It may be that there
is a need for both, seeing that challenges can be both local and national as mentioned previously. In this
respect, it may be that examining the support structure through the lens of it being nested and multi-layered
is helpful; for instance, there may be different levels of networks: one that connects co-ordinators at a local
level, and then one that connects these different localised networks at the national level.

A second high-level consideration is the extent that support structures or processes are formal or informal.
This echoes the considerations set forth with regard to the formal and informal architecture surrounding
ICT co-ordinators or teams in a school. More informal system-level support mechanisms may facilitate
better tailoring of support to specific needs. They may also allow for more responsive support or mean
more honest and authentic sharing between actors. More formal mechanisms can provide greater
orientation. Notably, this may be particularly significant in the space of digital tools where evidence
remains, as outlined, largely limited and constantly evolving. In this respect, external curation can be very
significant; curating particularly impactful best-practices can ensure that schools can work with material
that is potentially most impactful and avoids them needing to, as mentioned, ‘reinvent the wheel’ for
particular problems. This type of curation may be especially relevant for supporting say novice teachers
who may have more limited knowledge of how to align to learning goals and adapt to student needs, and
who also may need to prioritise attention elsewhere (OECD, 2025 [13] ). Indeed, more formal structures may
break down barriers and better allow the exchange of best practices. For instance, it has been argued that
technical and vocational schools are often at the forefront of digitalisation, but the connections between
these schools and others may not always be established (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ).
Overall, it seems that a support infrastructure may demand both formal and informal structures/processes.
That said, attending to the formal infrastructure early on – as with the formal structure around an ICT co-
ordinator or co-ordination team within a school – appears particularly important when seeking to establish
new ways of working, with these structures eventually being able to grow over time into a more intangible
and less formal ‘culture’ of working.

What may be some of the tangible forms of support that policymakers can leverage to support ICT co-
ordinators in their role? Some forms may include:

•
Guidance, tools and learning materials: One notable form may be the presence of centralised
resources and guidance, as in the case of the Netherlands or Andalusia (Spain). For instance, in
Andalusia (Spain) resources such as self-diagnosis tools are made available, while in the
Netherlands, the public Kennisnet Foundation has developed official guidelines on ICT
competences (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ).

•
Formal points of contact: The presence of local teacher centres to guide and advise schools has
been drawn upon in Portugal and Andalusia (Spain). These can serve as a concrete contact point

for schools that may also have expertise to help attend to particular local contextual needs. For
instance, Portugal’s “Digital Ambassadors” sit above individual schools and are an example of a
bespoke role at the local level that seeks to foster more effective in-school co-ordination.

•
Exchange networks: These can facilitate the exchange of expertise to address particular issues
and share best-practice. In some instances, these may take the form of active digital communities
that are informally organised and in others they may be more formal networks. For instance, the
Flemish Community of Belgium has both active Facebook communities and the “Digital Schools
Network” of VICLI and PXL University of Applied Sciences (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ). In Estonia,
the Association of Educational Technologists is well-established with a summer school and online
groups of exchange. Not only does it enable the sharing of ideas, but also the testing of new ideas
and serves as a sounding board for policy initiatives. More formal initiatives include professional
development programmes and regular seminars, which provide not only training but also sustained
interaction among ICT co-ordinators and wider networks of educators and policymakers. These
mechanisms help transform individual expertise into shared organisational knowledge and can
accelerate the adoption of effective digital practices in schools. Such networks may be locally
organised or operate across regions, offering structured platforms for dialogue, problem-solving
and mutual learning (Kampylis, Punie and Devine, 2015 [40] ).

•
Professional learning opportunities for co-ordinators: It may be that there is also scope for
supports that provide professional learning to ICT co-ordinators to build their capacity to effectively
fulfil their role. Some systems have platforms that facilitate professional learning for teachers (e.g.
SENECA and eAprendizaje in Andalusia [Spain] – see McGrath et al., 2024 [21] ). While these
primarily seem to target teachers more generally, these professional learning opportunities may
also be undertaken by co-ordinators to advance their knowledge. It could be that such platforms
are also leveraged by systems to offer bespoke, tailored learning opportunities for co-ordinators
on their roles.

•
Synthesising best practices: Lastly, policymakers may facilitate the formal curation and
dissemination of best practices. In general, this type of policy mechanism seems largely under-
developed, but some examples can be seen. For instance, in Wales, its inspectorate has
undertaken primary research on the use of AI in schools, including Generative AI, and made
available its findings which highlight some effective examples of AI integration (Estyn, 2025 [8] ).
While not focussed solely on the digital space, in some systems such as Ireland, its inspectorate
has undertaken work to collect and describe promising practices and programmes in its published
reports of inspected schools and broader thematic reports (OECD, 2024 [41] ). It may be that systems
already have available to them some information that could be leveraged to better synthesise and
disseminate best practices. A recent OECD policy survey found that about a third of jurisdictions
consider the use of digital resources in external school evaluations (Boeskens and Meyer, 2025 [20] ).
Slightly more see the use of digital resources included in school self-evaluations. Primarily these
types of monitoring efforts are orientated towards fostering higher standards, but they may also,
however, allow the identification of strong examples of co-ordination, which could be more widely
leveraged and disseminated.

Co-ordination is also partly shaped by interactions with external technology providers. Technical co-
ordination may demand working closely with technology providers’ support desks. Pedagogical co-
ordination may also be shaped by engagement with providers, particularly in relation to tailoring certain
tools to schools’ needs. Managing relationships with external providers may be important for helping to
align the needs of schools and teachers with what is provisioned by technology providers.

title: Matching co-ordination approaches to system contexts

paragraphs.text:
This section argues that different approaches to ICT co-ordination are likely to be more effective under
particular policy environments and cultural settings, rather than there being a single universally optimal
model (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ; Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada and León-
Jariego, 2014 [26] ; Avidov-Ungar and Hanin-Itzak, 2019 [25] ). Different approaches to ICT co-ordination have
different advantages and different potential pitfalls (Box 5.1). Building on the comparisons from the
previous section, it is useful to consider how governance arrangements, school characteristics and the
local supply of digitally competent staff can shape the feasibility and desirability of team-based versus
individual co-ordinator approaches (Woo, 2020 [24] ; OECD, 2025 [14] ).

A first key factor is the overall governance structure of the education system, particularly the degree of
centralisation versus school autonomy. In more centralised systems, such as those where national
authorities provide detailed guidance on digital strategies and infrastructure, clearly specified ICT
co-ordinator roles with common task profiles can be implemented across schools relatively consistently
(Avidov-Ungar and Hanin-Itzak, 2019 [25] ; OECD, 2025 [14] ). In more decentralised systems, such as the
Netherlands or England, where school boards or multi-academy trusts have substantial discretion,
distributed or team-based models are more common and can align well with local decision-making cultures,
but they also lead to greater variation in how ICT co-ordination is enacted (OECD, 2025 [42] ). The historic

culture of leadership in schools is also important here: contexts with traditions of distributed leadership and
collaborative decision-making may find it easier to introduce and sustain team-based ICT co-ordination,
whereas more hierarchical cultures may face greater demands when moving towards such models.

A second condition relates to school size, level and network arrangements, which together influence what
is feasible in organisational and financial terms. Smaller schools, including many in parts of Spain or rural
areas of Austria, may struggle to sustain multi-person teams and thus often rely on a single ICT
co-ordinator who combines technical, pedagogical and administrative tasks alongside teaching, which
favours individual models with carefully prioritised responsibilities (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada
and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ). Larger schools, school clusters in Portugal or networks of schools in the
Flemish Community of Belgium and the Netherlands can more readily justify specialised team-based
arrangements, including shared technical services and dedicated pedagogical leads for digital education
that operate across several sites (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ; OECD, 2025 [42] ).

A third set of considerations concerns the availability of digitally competent and data-literate staff, as well
as prevailing professional cultures. In contexts where staff with strong technical and pedagogical ICT
expertise are relatively scarce, as some studies of ICT co-ordinators in Spain suggest, it may be more
realistic to begin with a clearly mandated individual co-ordinator or a small core team and invest heavily in
their professional learning (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ). In systems
such as Singapore or the Flemish Community of Belgium, where schools participate in digital innovation
networks and benefit from a stronger supply of ICT-savvy teachers and established collaborative practices,
team-based approaches may make more effective use of existing human resources. These can distribute
co-ordination across several roles, for example combining a technical lead, pedagogical coach and data
manager in a team, that helps strengthen implementation of ICT in schools (Desmedt, Sempels and
Pauwels, 2024 [23] ; Woo, 2020 [24] ).

Country experiences illustrate how these contextual factors interact with co-ordination approaches. In the
Flemish Community of Belgium, regional guidance that defines four domains of the ICT co-ordinator role
has supported schools in formalising responsibilities, while also allowing some to evolve towards ICT
teams that share tasks across staff members (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ). In Spain,
regional regulations have established single ICT co-ordinator posts in schools, but research points to role
ambiguity and workload pressures, especially where co-ordinators juggle extensive technical and
administrative demands with limited time for pedagogical support (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada
and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ; León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ). In Portugal
and Austria, school clusters and project-based networks have provided opportunities to pool expertise and
to experiment with more team-based arrangements, while in England and the Netherlands combinations
of school-based roles and external support organisations reflect high school autonomy and diverse local
solutions (OECD, 2025 [42] ).

distributed or team-based models are more common and can align well with local decision-making cultures,
but they also lead to greater variation in how ICT co-ordination is enacted (OECD, 2025 [42] ). The historic
 43
culture of leadership in schools is also important here: contexts with traditions of distributed leadership and
collaborative decision-making may find it easier to introduce and sustain team-based ICT co-ordination,
whereas more hierarchical cultures may face greater demands when moving towards such models.
A second condition relates to school size, level and network arrangements, which together influence what
is feasible in organisational and financial terms. Smaller schools, including many in parts of Spain or rural
areas of Austria, may struggle to sustain multi-person teams and thus often rely on a single ICT
co-ordinator who combines technical, pedagogical and administrative tasks alongside teaching, which
favours individual models with carefully prioritised responsibilities (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada
and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ). Larger schools, school clusters in Portugal or networks of schools in the
Flemish Community of Belgium and the Netherlands can more readily justify specialised team-based
arrangements, including shared technical services and dedicated pedagogical leads for digital education
that operate across several sites (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ; OECD, 2025 [42] ).
A third set of considerations concerns the availability of digitally competent and data-literate staff, as well
as prevailing professional cultures. In contexts where staff with strong technical and pedagogical ICT
expertise are relatively scarce, as some studies of ICT co-ordinators in Spain suggest, it may be more
realistic to begin with a clearly mandated individual co-ordinator or a small core team and invest heavily in
their professional learning (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ). In systems
such as Singapore or the Flemish Community of Belgium, where schools participate in digital innovation
networks and benefit from a stronger supply of ICT-savvy teachers and established collaborative practices,
team-based approaches may make more effective use of existing human resources. These can distribute
co-ordination across several roles, for example combining a technical lead, pedagogical coach and data
manager in a team, that helps strengthen implementation of ICT in schools (Desmedt, Sempels and
Pauwels, 2024 [23] ; Woo, 2020 [24] ).
Country experiences illustrate how these contextual factors interact with co-ordination approaches. In the
Flemish Community of Belgium, regional guidance that defines four domains of the ICT co-ordinator role
has supported schools in formalising responsibilities, while also allowing some to evolve towards ICT
teams that share tasks across staff members (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ). In Spain,
regional regulations have established single ICT co-ordinator posts in schools, but research points to role
ambiguity and workload pressures, especially where co-ordinators juggle extensive technical and
administrative demands with limited time for pedagogical support (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada
and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ; León ‐ Jariego, Rodríguez ‐ Miranda and Pozuelos ‐ Estrada, 2019 [6] ). In Portugal
and Austria, school clusters and project-based networks have provided opportunities to pool expertise and
to experiment with more team-based arrangements, while in England and the Netherlands combinations
of school-based roles and external support organisations reflect high school autonomy and diverse local
solutions (OECD, 2025 [42] ).

title: Box 5.1. Comparing different approaches to ICT co-ordination

paragraphs.text:
Table 5.1 presents some of the advantages and disadvantages of a team-based approach relative to
that of single co-ordinator. The success of a team-based approach appears to hinge heavily on effective
implementation. System and school leaders are important here in ensuring clear, well-defined task
assignment and matching to profiles.

There is though always a degree of ‘unknown’ in team-based approaches as the collaborative nature
depends partly on how individuals can work together, which may not be totally predictable. While efforts
to support development of collaborative and communication skills can be put in place, individual
characteristics will also always have some influence here in shaping the effectiveness of the approach.

Similarly, cutting across approaches is the question of resources and what may, or may not, be feasible
with regard to organising ICT co-ordination in schools.

title: Austria

paragraphs.text:
Austria’s education system is highly centralised, with the Federal Ministry for Education overseeing all
education policies. In 2017, Austria launched the Digital School 4.0 Plan, part of the wider Digital Austria
2050 Strategic Action Plan. This initiative aims to modernise teaching and learning through unified digital
infrastructure, enhanced teacher training and strengthened digital competences (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ).
This was followed by the “Master Plan for Digitalization” as a strategy paper for the entire school sector
and the 8-point plan for digital education in 2020 with specific implementation measures.

By 2017–2018, nearly 95% of pupils at ISCED level 3 were enrolled in schools with an ICT co-ordinator
(European Commission, 2019 [43] ). ICT co-ordinators are usually teachers who assume additional ICT-
related responsibilities alongside their normal teaching load, such as maintaining hardware and software,
assisting colleagues and students, and providing in-school training. This role is mainly operational, with
limited participation in strategic planning or leadership.

More recently, ICT co-ordination has evolved towards a team-based approach, where small teams of three
to six teachers share responsibilities for technical maintenance, pedagogical support, and the delivery of
in-school digital training, with arrangements varying by school size and local needs. The eEducation
Austria network reinforces this collaborative model by linking schools through experts that exchange
practices, co-develop digital materials, and support professional development (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ). In
addition, schools can access public platforms such as eEducation, Eduthek or edutube to find teaching
resources and collaboration. Schools demonstrating outstanding commitment to digitalisation receive a
seal of approval.

However, despite efforts toward team-based approaches and stronger peer learning, some challenges
remain. For instance, ICT co-ordination is most often carried out on top of regular teaching duties, adding
1 to 11 extra hours per week and over 70% of co-ordinators report insufficient compensation, which
discourages sustained engagement in digital integration (Swertz and Graf, 2020 [44] ). This highlights the
importance of clearly defined job profiles, as well as appropriate incentives (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ).

Estonia has a long history of extensive digitalisation efforts in education (e.g. ‘Tiger Leap’ of 1997). There
are high levels of digital literacy among the teaching profession – e.g. 74.1% teachers reported that ICT
skills for teaching were included in their professional development (OECD average 60.4%), and some 95%
reported using digital solutions in the classroom (OECD, 2020 [45] ). Nevertheless, co-ordination remains

paragraphs.text:
important and relevant, with teachers reporting a desire for more preparation in the space of ICT use in
the classroom (OECD, 2020 [45] ).

Estonia has a team-based approach to ICT co-ordination in schools, with responsibilities distributed among
three profiles (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ):

•
The IT manager (technical role including user management, hardware and software infrastructure,
including servers and automation programmes).

•
The educational technologist (pedagogical role focussing on mapping staff digital competences,
co-ordinating professional training and developing digital learning strategy). This position is
typically filled by an ICT teacher with a specialised master’s in educational technology. This has
been an obligatory role in schools since 2005.

•
The computer science teacher (teaches courses in the field of computer science – a compulsory
subject in Estonia – and manages associated computer room).

There is flexibility within this approach, however. The school system is decentralised, and this allows
schools autonomy to adapt ICT co-ordination to individual needs while being supported at the same time
by a well-established infrastructure of supports. Hence, roles may be part- or full-time depending on school
resources and sometimes shared across sites (e.g. rural areas). That said, the distinct mandates of roles
ensure a balance between technical, pedagogical, and subject-specific expertise.

As mentioned, co-ordination efforts are supported by a well-established infrastructure of support. This
includes a robust policy framework and a well-developed professional network infrastructure (OECD,
2020 [45] ). A particularly influential body is the Association of Educational Technologists, a network that
facilitates the sharing of best practices among those engaged in ICT co-ordination (McGrath et al.,
2024 [32] ). It includes, bringing together key stakeholders to exchange good practices and test new ideas,
maintaining online communities for exchange and delivering a summer school for ongoing learning. It also
serves as an important consultative body for policymakers.
