title: Flemish Community of Belgium

paragraphs.text:
In recent years, the Flemish Community of Belgium has developed a team-based model to ICT co-
ordination in schools to improve efficiency and address growing technological and pedagogical demands.
Historically, ICT co-ordinators have been solely responsible for ICT-related tasks within their schools,
focussing mainly on technical work rather than using digital tools to enhance learning. Before this model,
they faced numerous challenges, including cybersecurity concerns, supporting distance learning practices,
maintaining network and server infrastructure, ensuring data security, and developing potential automation
of certain tasks (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ).

To address these issues, the Flemish Community of Belgium developed a team-oriented ICT co-ordination
approach, in collaboration with the European Commission and funded by the European Union Technical
Support Instrument. This model is built around a collaborative structure designed to balance pedagogical,
technical, and management expertise. The ICT team is designed to be flexible and its composition is not
strictly prescribed to ensure that the available skills or expertise are sufficiently leveraged. This naturally
includes designated co-ordinators (e.g. members of the teaching staff who may serve as a pedagogical
co-ordinator or someone specialised in technical ICT tasks functions serving as technical co-ordinator) and
members of school management, but where relevant it may also include other teachers, administrative
staff, parents and students.

Together, they form the school’s “ICT policy team”. This team-oriented approach is organised around four
main areas of responsibility (policy and vision, technical operations, teaching and learning, and
administration), with tasks assigned according to expertise and clearly defined mandates to ensure
transparency in decision-making. Depending on the school’s size, the model can operate at the level of an

individual school or across a community of schools. Its implementation is anchored in guiding documents,
including an articulated ICT policy plan and a pedagogical vision. Following a recent policy development,
an ICT policy will become mandatory, rather than recommend as previously, for all Flemish schools and
educational institutions as of 1 September 2026, whereas prior to this date, such plans were only
recommended. Nevertheless, despite these mechanisms, the ICT co-ordinator role remains debated, with
concerns about imbalances between workload, remuneration and the status of the position (Desmedt,
Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ).

The Flemish Community of Belgium benefits from a well-established ICT co-ordination infrastructure,
supported by earmarked funding, extended to all educational levels. Schools receive ICT hours
(government-funded resources allocated, according to student enrolment and specific needs). Schools can
also allocate additional resources at their own discretion, such as assigning ICT responsibilities to
teachers, dedicating administrative time or contracting external support.

Finally, to strengthen the efficiency of the team-based approach, different forms of support have emerged,
with differing degrees of formality. This includes informal peer-learning networks, such as active digital
communities (e.g. Facebook groups), as well as more formal networks like the “Digital Schools Network”
of VICLI and PXL University of Applied Sciences (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ). In addition, a more formal
continuous professional development programme (so-called “bootcamps”) focussing on the development
of ICT teams has recently been introduced. These programs enable schools to participate in online learning
activities with live or online group interactions with other participating schools. Such learning bootcamps
offer a valuable opportunity to consolidate the outcomes of ICT team initiatives (Vlaanderen, 2026 [46] ).

title: Norway

paragraphs.text:
Norway is among the countries with the most advanced digitalisation of compulsory education, following
the introduction of digital skills as a core competency in the national curriculum in 2006 (Letnes, 2025 [7] ).
One-to-one device coverage is now widespread, with all students in lower and upper secondary education
receiving personal digital devices provided by school owners (Tømte et al., 2019 [47] ).

Recently, attention has shifted from infrastructure towards teachers’ professional and organisational
capacity. While digitalisation has been strongly promoted at the system level, its pedagogical integration
depends heavily on local organisational capacity and school leadership (Tømte and Wollscheid, 2024 [48] ).
The concept of teacher’s professional digital competence (PDC) was introduced in 2013, in response to
the need for a more pedagogically grounded understanding of technology in education. It underscores the
integration of digital tools in subject-specific, ethical, and pedagogical practice (Letnes, 2025 [7] ).

The Norwegian model is characterised by a distributed and multi-level organisation of responsibilities, in
which the ICT co-ordinator function varies considerably across municipalities and schools. Norway has
357 municipalities of varying size, and there are large amounts of autonomy in how they approach co-
ordination to meet their different organisational and administrative capacities. It is thus hard to generalise
about approaches to ICT co-ordination, but some research studies offer a window onto some of the ways
that co-ordination is approached:

•
Tømte and Wollscheid (2024 [48] ) examined co-ordination in one larger municipal context. They
noted a two-level division straddling the municipal and the school level being used. At the municipal
level, central co-ordinators organised training programs, visited schools to run workshops, and
facilitated network meetings for local ICT co-ordinators, thereby supporting capacity-building and
co-ordination across schools. At the school level, localised ICT co-ordination was most often
carried out by teachers who combined teaching with additional responsibilities related to
digitalisation, usually within small teams (typically three to four people). ICT co-ordinators often
played an important role in fostering teachers’ digital competence, organising in-house training,

paragraphs.text:
modelling classroom uses of technology, and encouraging the sharing of best practices among
peers.

•
Letnes (2025 [7] ) recently provided a detailed case study account of one ICT co-ordinator in a
primary school setting. Letnes noted that implementation of PDC within a school can be
challenging, in particular when it comes to working across multiple teachers and consider teachers’
collective development of practice. Letnes argued that there may be a disconnect between policy
intentions and how these are practically translated into a school’s day-to-day organisation.

Moreover, secondary analysis of data from ICILS 2023 (“International Computer and Information Literacy
Study”) suggests that ICT co-ordination in Norway is often a responsibility distributed among dedicated co-
ordinators, staff with combined technical and pedagogical roles and principals or other school leaders
(Rohatgi et al., 2025 [49] ). While these findings are not based on a large sample size and should be
approached with caution – especially considering the decentralised approach to co-ordination mentioned
above – they suggest that ICT co-ordination is not always a standalone professional role but also combined
with other responsibilities. The study also reiterates the important message above that having the digital
equipment is no longer enough to make sure that it is used effectively, but success depends more on a
balance between technical resources, professional skills, and a clear vision of personalised teaching and
collaboration between teachers.

Indeed, despite robust infrastructure and strong policy support, researchers have highlighted that the
Norwegian model continues to face several challenges related to ICT co-ordination and leadership. It has
been argued that at the organisational level, the fragmentation of responsibilities among teachers further
constrains the coherence and depth of pedagogical integration across schools (Tømte et al., 2019 [47] ). In
practice, ICT co-ordinators are still expected to handle technical tasks with pedagogical support, which
creates workload pressures and often leads to unclear role boundaries. In addition, compensation and
recognition vary considerably across schools and districts; some ICT co-ordinators receive additional pay,
but others are compensated through reduced teaching loads or through time formally allocated within their
schedules (Gerick, Eickelmann and Bos, 2017 [50] ).

title: Portugal

paragraphs.text:
Following the COVID-19 pandemic, Portugal has sought to further digitalisation in schools and the
education system, in line with key legislation such as the Digital Development Action Plan (PADDE)
(Wastiau, Looney and Laanpere, 2024 [51] ). These efforts are strongly supported at the local and regional
levels, complementing a broader national strategy to advance digitalisation and considering three main
dimensions: leadership and governance, professional development, and teaching and learning practices.
A key pillar of this is the development of school digital development plans. In 2024, 98% of schools had
submitted a digital development plan (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ).

Approaches to ICT co-ordination are variable. Some institutions rely on the historic model of individual ICT
co-ordinators. Others have moved towards more collective structures that blend school-level expertise with
other local supports. In particular, in recent years there has been growing interest in more team-based
approaches for the development of the digital school plans. The “Digital Development Teams” in schools
are designed to foster collaboration and bring together subject expertise and leadership skills. Designed
as “a multidisciplinary team of teachers responsible for defining and implementing a vision for the school's
digital development” (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ), these teams follow a structured, multi-step and multi-
stakeholder approach:

•
Step 1: The diagnostic phase (analyse of tools such as SELFIE self-assessment tool, the
Portuguese Check-In tool and the school’s past performance in digitalisation).

•
Step 2: The Digital Development Team defines key objectives and priorities tailored to school
needs.

•
Step 3: The medium- to long-term action plan is formulated.

•
Step 4: Communication of these plans to all relevant stakeholders (including the school community
and Ministry).

•
Step 5: Monitoring and evaluation.

This cyclical process establishes a strong feedback loop among the “Digital Development Team”, the
central Directorate-General for Education and the immediate school community. A potential key actor here
is the presence of “Digital Ambassadors”. “Digital Ambassadors” operate under the auspices of the
Directorate-General for Education and serve as a support to multiple schools at a local level. In particular,
they provide support to co-ordinators and play a crucial role in facilitating the implementation of digital
transition plans. Their work is supported through ministry funding, and in some cases, through allocated
teaching hours (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ; OECD, 2024 [11] ).

This model demonstrates how locally driven systems can operate effectively through interconnected
networks, ensuring that schools receive both autonomy and assistance in their process of digital
transformation. It relies on internal and collaborative reflection, with the goal of promoting innovative and
inclusive learning environments.

In this context, school principals play a particularly important strategic role in ensuring the development
and implementation of the PADDE. Given that the digital transition extends beyond the acquisition of
equipment and also involve organisational, pedagogical and cultural change, principals are responsible for
integrating the digital dimension into the school’s Educational Project, defining priorities based on the
school’s digital diagnosis, and ensuring coherence between the PADDE and other instruments of school
autonomy. Furthermore, the involvement of school principals contributes to making the policy plan realistic,
contextualised and achievable. In particular, principals are in charge of appointing and monitoring the
Digital Development Team, promoting the participation of the broader educational community, validating
goals, indicators and timelines, and ensuring co-ordination between pedagogical, administrative and
technological areas.

More broadly, the Portuguese action plan on digitalisation also provides funding for the professional
development of teacher educators to better prepare teachers for digitalisation. Additional initiatives further
reinforce this effort, such as the “Training for Digital Teaching” pilot involving 700 schools and the creation
of a Centre for Digital Innovation offering training and digital materials through an online platform (McGrath
et al., 2024 [32] ).

title: Singapore

paragraphs.text:
ICT co-ordination in Singapore schools contributes to the goals of Singapore’s “Transforming Education
through Technology Masterplan 2030” (EdTech Masterplan 2030). The Masterplan seeks to harness the
potential of technology, including AI, to transform teaching and learning. Singapore adopts a team-based
approach to ICT co-ordination where School Leaders and Heads of Departments work closely together,
leading their respective teams to tap on ICT for effective teaching and learning and more efficient
administrative processes.

Singapore has dedicated considerable energy into integrating ICT within its school system, and enabling
this through continuous professional learning. In particular, the SkillsFuture for Educators (SFEd) initiative,
launched in 2020, serves as a roadmap to strengthen teachers’ competencies across six priority areas,
including ‘e-pedagogy’. It defines four progressive levels of practice to help teachers benchmark and
advance their use of digital tools for more active and personalised forms of learning. This systemic and
structured approach reflects Singapore’s focus on aligning teacher professional growth with strategic
priorities.

advance their use of digital tools for more active and personalised forms of learning. This systemic and
structured approach reflects Singapore’s focus on aligning teacher professional growth with strategic
priorities.

paragraphs.text:
At the school level, Singapore’s ICT co-ordination is structured on clearly defined roles that combine
pedagogical leadership, strategic administration and technological know-how. This team-based approach
ensures that both pedagogical and technical aspects are considered in order to achieve effective and
sustainable use of digital technologies.
Each school typically has:

•
A Head of Department (HOD) for ICT , who leads the pedagogical and strategic use of digital
resources for teaching and learning, drives curriculum integration of ICT with other department
heads, and partners with the School Staff Developer to strengthen teachers’ digital competencies.

•
An ICT Manager or Associate , who supports the effective adoption of digital tools across the
school. Working closely with the HOD ICT and school leadership, the ICT Manager/ ICT Associate
manages ICT systems, cybersecurity practices, asset and procurement processes, and the
implementation of initiatives in alignment to MOE’s broader digital transformation efforts.

Each school also typically has an ICT committee led by the Head of Department for ICT and comprises
teacher representatives across subject departments. The key function of this committee is to drive and
facilitate ICT integration at the subject and department level. Teachers who are more proficient in the use
and integration of ICT can be called to take up school-based roles of ICT Mentors or ICT Champions, who
guide their colleagues in using e-Pedagogy and ICT tools.

Teams are supported by clear national co-ordination. The Ministry of Education (MOE) oversees ICT in
education through two key divisions:

•
The Educational Technology Division drives the application of technology to support and
enhance teaching and learning. This is through (i) providing thought leadership for effective
application and development of educational technology, (ii) building capacity of school leaders, key
personnel, and teachers in the use of EdTech, especially through e-Pedagogy, and (iii) producing
digital learning content to support educational goals.

•
The Digital Excellence and Products Division (DXD) drives MOE’s digital transformation by
harnessing technology to elevate teaching, learning and operations. Adopting a product-led and
user-centric approach, DXD goes beyond traditional IT support to design and deliver reliable, high-
quality digital products and platforms. Through close collaboration with stakeholders, DXD
continually improves digital experiences for schools, educators, students, parents and MOE
officers, focussing on meaningful impact, continuous improvement, and sustainable digital
innovation.

The two divisions work closely together to ensure educationally sound ICT use and strategic integration
with MOE’s digitalisation plan. Both divisions co-ordinate across curriculum divisions and the Academy of
Singapore Teachers to ensure ICT integration in the national curriculum, support schools’ pedagogical use
of ICT, and facilitate teacher capacity building.

Given the increasing pervasiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Singapore’s co-ordination of ICT use
consists of central deployment of GenAI and digital tools to schools through the Singapore Student
Learning Space and the Personalised Digital Learning Programme. Clear guidelines on AI use through the
AI in Education (AIEd) Framework and Generative AI Guides support teachers’ responsible use of AI tools
in line with the principles of agency, inclusivity, fairness, and safety (SLS, 2025 [52] ; SLS, 2025 [53] ).

Finally, Singapore’s approach is reinforced by a strong culture of collaboration and professional learning.
Results from PISA 2022 show that nearly all students (98.6%) attend schools where teachers have
scheduled collaboration time using digital devices (OECD, 2025 [54] ). School Leaders and teachers continue
to strengthen their use of ICT including AI through participation in Professional Learning Communities and
collaborative inquiry projects to share practices, experiment with new tools, and reflect on their pedagogical
impact in the spirit that teaching is a team sport.

title: Autonomous Community of Andalusia (Spain)

paragraphs.text:
Spain, and specifically the Autonomous Community of Andalusia, has a long history of encouraging ICT
co-ordination in schools (Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ). The Spanish
education system is decentralised. Typically, the national government defines overall framework policies,
and the autonomous communities handle most day-to-day policymaking and administer the great majority
of funding (OECD, 2020 [55] ).

While there is no national regulation about the presence of an ICT co-ordinator in schools, current
education legislation (e.g. the 2020 “LOMLOE” [“Organic Law for the Amendment of the Organic Law of
Education”]) and both regional and national education policies promote the incorporation of support roles
related to ICT in schools to foster the integration of technology into pedagogy and the development of
digital competence. Hence, there is no explicit obligation in the core legislation to appoint an ICT co-
ordinator, but it is common in practice for schools at all educational levels to have staff members
responsible for, or functions dedicated to, ICT co-ordination.

The region of Andalusia has been an area of particular attention for researchers, with the ICT co-ordinator
role first introduced in Andalusia in 2003. After the COVID-19 pandemic – which exposed some
unevenness around ICT in schooling – the position of a co-ordinator was redefined as the “Co-ordinator
for the Digital Transformation in Education”, reflecting broader responsibilities. This shift aligned with
national education reforms prioritising school digitalisation, one of the main objectives of the “Digital Spain
2025” strategy and reflects a move away from technical troubleshooting toward strategic pedagogical
leadership (Junta de Andalucía, 2025 [56] ). The governance structure that supports this role reflects Spain’s
highly decentralised education system, in which the central government establishes the basic regulatory
framework while the Autonomous Communities hold primary responsibility for implementation,
organisation and resource allocation. More recently, there has been the establishment of Andalusia’s
Digital Action Plan (“Plan de Actuación Digital” or PAD), a framework that aims to develop digital
competence among students, teachers, and educational institutions, as part of a broader strategy aligned
with European digital education policies (Junta de Andalucía, 2025 [56] ).

The approach in Andalusia relies on a single ICT co-ordinator in each school, whose work role spans three
mains’ areas (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ; Rodríguez-Miranda, Pozuelos-Estrada and León-Jariego, 2014 [26] ):

•
Organisation and management of the school (e.g. hardware procurement)

•
Teaching and learning (e.g. pedagogical guidance, content development)

•
Internal and external communication (e.g. managing the intranet and website)

The balance of these responsibilities depends on the school’s size, type, and budget. In some cases,
technical tasks are outsourced and managed via the “Agencia Digital de Andalucía”, so co-ordinators can
focus more on pedagogical support (Junta de Andalucía, 2025 [56] ). Co-ordinators have dedicated hours for
their role and work closely with school leaders, local training centres and other teachers. A particularly key
responsibility is leading the school’s “School Digital Plan”.

As alluded to above, there are different available supports for co-ordinators in Andalusia – and schools in
general – to foster effective digitalisation. These include:

•
Teacher centres which offer guidance to schools, in particular on their digital plans through an
annual review process. For example, the CEP (“Centro de Profesorado”) network provides
localised training and annual reviews of Digital Plans (Junta de Andalucía, 2025 [56] ).

•
Platforms like Séneca and eAprendizaje, which help to enable peer learning and the exchange of
best practices and resources (Junta de Andalucía, 2025 [56] ).

title: Netherlands

paragraphs.text:
The Netherlands is a highly digitalised country, marked by strong connectivity and high levels of pre-
existing digital competences. A range of legislation demonstrates a clear commitment to supporting
digitalisation in schools. For instance, the “Dutch Digital Strategy 2021” identifies “digital skills and
inclusion” as one of its four central priorities, underlining the government’s commitment to enhance
digitalisation within schools (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ). At the same time, the Dutch education system is
characterised by a high degree of decentralisation and school autonomy, resulting in diverse approaches
to the implementation and management of digitalisation.

Within this context, the Netherlands has developed a distinctive model of ICT co-ordination built around
the role of “i-coaches”. This model focusses on the pedagogical dimension of digital transformation, with
some technical co-ordination functions in schools outsourced to private providers.

The i-coaches aim to guide teachers and school teams in integrating digital technologies into everyday
teaching and learning. The division of their roles are defined by a competency model, and they are
expected to play a range of different roles (Desmedt, Sempels and Pauwels, 2024 [23] ):

•
Trainer (delivers workshops and professional learning session).

•
Coach (encourages and inspires colleagues).

•
Adviser (provides guidance and communicates effectively with staff).

•
Educational guide (ensures that technology use aligns with didactic principles).

•
Change guide (supports the management of innovation processes).

•
Technovator (identifies and promotes new educational technologies).

The role of i-coaches is supported by the public organisation Kennisnet. Since 2001, Kennisnet has been
central in driving ICT development across the Dutch education sector. Kennisnet contributes to the
effective and safe use of ICT in education. As a guide and expert, Kennisnet ensures that school boards
in primary and secondary education, as well as sector councils and the Dutch Ministry of Education can
make well-informed decisions. In addition, Kennisnet develops and provides numerous services and
facilities within the national public ICT infrastructure. Finally, Kennisnet ensures that the education sector
has better insight into digital processes by providing clarity and guidance on the design, architecture and
the use of open standards in the ICT infrastructure. Its guidance includes a range of important topics; digital
infrastructure, information security and privacy, digital literacy, and the use of digital learning resources
(OECD, 2025 [42] ). Its initiatives include the development of the Computer Emergency Response Team for
primary and secondary education, which advises school boards on responding rapidly to cybersecurity
incidents and monitors and disseminates information about threats, as well as the Digital Safe Education
programme, which supports schools in ensuring a digitally secure learning environment. Kennisnet
collaborates with the sector councils, SIVON, and the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science (OCW)

on the Information Security and Privacy Framework. ( Normenkader IBP voor het onderwijs - Normenkader
informatiebeveiliging en privacy voor het onderwijs ). Kennisnet also focusses on the themes of AI,
autonomy, and public governance grounded in public values.

However, despite the existing support provided by i-coaches, there are relatively few public sources of
direct assistance for individual schools beyond private education consultancies and private providers, that
design and deliver continuing professional learning (OECD, 2025 [42] ). Kennisnet facilitates two networks
for i-coaches and ICT co-ordinators at the school-board level to promote public collaboration. The ministry
and inspectorate do not currently have a legal mandate or effective mechanism to regulate or evaluate the
quality of the CPL they provide (OECD, 2025 [42] ).

Beyond these supports, Kennisnet has also developed official guidelines on ICT competences for
educators, expanding the focus beyond digital skills to include broader capabilities such as change
management and navigating institutional demands (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ). To ensure continuous
improvement, the organisation monitors schools’ progress once every two years through its “Education
Digitalisation Monitor ( Monitor Digitalisering Onderwijs 2025: kloof tussen beleid en praktijk - Kennisnet )”.

central in driving ICT development across the Dutch education sector. Kennisnet contributes to the
effective and safe use of ICT in education. As a guide and expert, Kennisnet ensures that school boards
in primary and secondary education, as well as sector councils and the Dutch Ministry of Education can
make well-informed decisions. In addition, Kennisnet develops and provides numerous services and
facilities within the national public ICT infrastructure. Finally, Kennisnet ensures that the education sector
has better insight into digital processes by providing clarity and guidance on the design, architecture and
the use of open standards in the ICT infrastructure. Its guidance includes a range of important topics; digital
infrastructure, information security and privacy, digital literacy, and the use of digital learning resources
(OECD, 2025 [42] ). Its initiatives include the development of the Computer Emergency Response Team for
primary and secondary education, which advises school boards on responding rapidly to cybersecurity
incidents and monitors and disseminates information about threats, as well as the Digital Safe Education
programme, which supports schools in ensuring a digitally secure learning environment. Kennisnet
collaborates with the sector councils, SIVON, and the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science (OCW)
 53
on the Information Security and Privacy Framework. ( Normenkader IBP voor het onderwijs - Normenkader
informatiebeveiliging en privacy voor het onderwijs ). Kennisnet also focusses on the themes of AI,
autonomy, and public governance grounded in public values.
However, despite the existing support provided by i-coaches, there are relatively few public sources of
direct assistance for individual schools beyond private education consultancies and private providers, that
design and deliver continuing professional learning (OECD, 2025 [42] ). Kennisnet facilitates two networks
for i-coaches and ICT co-ordinators at the school-board level to promote public collaboration. The ministry
and inspectorate do not currently have a legal mandate or effective mechanism to regulate or evaluate the
quality of the CPL they provide (OECD, 2025 [42] ).
Beyond these supports, Kennisnet has also developed official guidelines on ICT competences for
educators, expanding the focus beyond digital skills to include broader capabilities such as change
management and navigating institutional demands (McGrath et al., 2024 [32] ). To ensure continuous
improvement, the organisation monitors schools’ progress once every two years through its “Education
Digitalisation Monitor ( Monitor Digitalisering Onderwijs 2025: kloof tussen beleid en praktijk - Kennisnet )”.

title: Korea

paragraphs.text:
In Korea, the digitisation of schools is characterised by a highly centralised framework led by the national
government. Current policy, notably the “AI for All: Strategy for Cultivating Artificial Intelligence Talent”
(announced in 2025), prioritises a personalised digital transition by shifting from a ‘one-size-fits-all’
textbook model toward a more flexible ecosystem of “AI Educational Materials”. This shift encompasses a
diverse range of digital platforms and tools, providing schools with administrative and financial autonomy
to select the specific resources that best suit their needs. It is also underpinned by infrastructure support
to ensure this transition is supported by universal devices.

In this context, ICT co-ordination is primarily driven by a combination of centralised institutional support
and more localised peer collaboration. One key actor is the Korea Education and Research Information
Service (KERIS). This agency acts as a central hub, managing cloud-based infrastructure that was
previously managed by regional offices (Seo, 2023 [58] ). At the school level, while there is no full-time,
specialised ICT co-ordinator role in Korea, the “Head of Information Department” (a teacher with
administrative responsibilities) effectively performs this role within schools. There is also a strong reliance
on collaboration with colleagues, with studies showing that more than half of Korean teachers (57.4%) rely
on their colleagues for technical assistance (Pang et al., 2015 [59] ). To further alleviate the technical burden
on teachers, the government has deployed “Digital Tutors” in selected schools to provide hands-on support
during classes, allowing teachers to focus on pedagogy rather than technical issues. However, it is
important to note that this initiative is currently implemented in selected schools with dedicated budgets,
rather than being a universal provision across all schools.

The government has also established regional EdTech hubs to bridge the gap between industry and
classrooms, fostering collaborative network between education authorities, local governments, and
operating organisations (Seo, 2023 [58] ). Professional development is further supported by “Jeeshik
Samter”, a voluntary knowledge-sharing platform launched in 2020. This platform facilitates peer learning
through real-time video lectures and the dissemination of effective digital teaching practices (Seo, 2023 [58] ).
In parallel, teachers and schools have received training to develop knowledge, skills and digital tools
necessary to better personalise students’ learning, in collaboration with KERIS (OECD, 2025 [60] ). These
efforts reflect a strategic focus on empowering individual teachers to lead ICT integration within their
respective classrooms.

Despite Korea’s highly developed digital infrastructure, several challenges persist. The Ministry of
Education has identified the need for improved communication, greater transparency and continued
professional learning opportunities for teachers to address technical support gaps (OECD, 2025 [60] ).

paragraphs.text:
Furthermore, addressing concerns related to digital safety and data privacy remains particularly important,
hence, Korea has taken steps to strengthen governance frameworks, notably through the introduction of
the Ethical Principles of AI in Education (OECD, 2025 [60] ). A second challenge concerns securing broad
teacher and school engagement with pedagogical innovation. Indeed, most measures under the “Digital
Transformation of Education Initiative” are voluntary, which may limit widespread adoption. To address
this, Korea has pursued two main strategies: incentivising and recognising innovative teaching practices
through reward and recognition programmes and building capacity through peer-learning and knowledge-
sharing initiatives (OECD, 2025 [60] ). More broadly, some stakeholders emphasise that digitalisation must
avoid an overly “technology-centric” approach to educational reform (Jeong, 2020 [61] ).

title: 7 Conclusion

paragraphs.text:
This Working Paper has provided an overview of the literature on how the use of digital tools can be co-
ordinated in schools. It noted that the importance of clear, coherent co-ordination is becoming increasingly
important. Research points to the fact that digital tools can have significant impact on student outcomes.
However, the use of digital tools in classrooms requires thoughtful judgement by teachers. Support to
teachers is therefore essential, ranging from more formal capacity-building in the form of professional
learning and curation of learning resources, to the informal troubleshooting of specific classroom
challenges when they arise.

Support to teachers must also be coupled with providing the relevant digital infrastructure for teachers to
work with. The digital transformation in schools is also a physical one, shaped by specific digital
technologies that must be selected, established and maintained. Indeed, digital technologies are now a
key means of interacting and working together in a school. They fulfill important administrative purposes,
and, in this respect, digitalisation may enhance student learning indirectly. Increasing efficiency in how
teachers work in a school may free up time for teachers to focus on what really matters to student learning.
In this respect, co-ordinating the digital transformation in schools is not only about what happens in
classrooms, but also in the different offices of a school and their communication channels.

All the while, the landscape of what is possible in technology is changing. This demands a degree of
responsiveness in terms of tracking the changing evidence on technologies and their affordances, as well
as their potential risks. Without clear co-ordination of digital tools in schools, and across schools, there is
the risk of certain classrooms being left behind and digital divides emerging. The ever-evolving nature of
technology makes effective co-ordination ever more important, if also more challenging.

The working paper highlighted that co-ordination can be considered as constituting four broad areas of
focus: pedagogical, technical, policy and vision, and administrative. These reflect the broad reach of
technology in schools. Within each of these, several key tasks were identified. As the paper noted, how
these tasks are fulfilled can vary. In some systems, single ICT co-ordinators have undertaken most of the
responsibility for completing these tasks. There are, however, signs of more team-based approaches
having potential value due to the range of tasks that co-ordination demands today. These teams hinge
upon the clear assignment of tasks to the most appropriate individual, clear decision-making processes,
and established formal and informal structures for interaction.

The research is still nascent in terms of exploring all of the actors that are potentially relevant in shaping
ICT co-ordination, but what seems increasingly clear is that effective co-ordination must ensure that a core
group of individuals are able to work efficiently and meaningfully with a range of internal and external
actors. This has implications for policymakers in designing the relevant support structures and incentives
that can enable this type of co-ordination. It also places great responsibility on school leaders too who
emerge as key actors in the literature as localised catalysts for ICT co-ordination efforts. The paper
presented how different systems are approaching these challenges, highlighting that there is no one way
to implement effective co-ordination.

One of the cross-cutting challenges in ICT co-ordination is that it is, quite simply, a relatively new need and
feature of education systems. Moreover, its importance has been amplified in recent years with the advent

paragraphs.text: An EU approach to online child safety

text: An EU approach to online child safety

title: 1. Introduction

paragraphs.text:
The digital world is a gateway to knowledge, an opportunity for connection and creativity .
But platforms’ business models, designed to maximise the time spent online, result in a massive
scale of online engagement and may exploit the vulnerabilities of children. According to a 2026
Eurobarometer, teenagers spend on average 4.5 hours online on school days, rising to 6.1 hours
on weekend days 1 .

The available evidence shows that the earlier children go online, the more time they are likely
to spend on screens. Those who started using social media before the age of 10 report 7.5 hours
of weekend day screen time, compared to 5.7 hours among those who started after age 14. This
amplifies pressure on youth mental health, which has never been more at risk . One in
three teenagers feel stressed or socially excluded and affected by concentration problems. One
in four children currently encounters harmful and distressing content online, ranging from
violence, and hate speech, to body pressure and misinformation. One in four also experience
online sexual solicitation at some point before age 18, including unwanted pressured sexual
interactions and forms of grooming 2 . While any child may be affected, vulnerable children are
disproportionately at risk and girls and boys experience different kinds of risks.

In addition, as confirmed by the results of the OECD's Programme for International Student
Assessment (PISA) for 2025, digital distraction is identified as a root cause of falling
educational performance among our children . Digital distraction impacts young people’s
learning and is a key factor for declining basic skills in the EU. The over-consumption of social
media and excessive screen time lead in particular to deficiencies in evaluating information,
making connections across multiple sources and thinking critically.

The development of problematic AI-generated content, such as deepfakes or dangerous
advice given by AI chatbots or AI companions, is further exacerbating the issue . Pressure
to share intimate pictures affects one in ten teenagers, representing millions of young people
across Europe. This is not merely passive exposure and does not remain confined to the screen.
Such content shapes, encourages and rewards risky behaviour, from harming others to self-
harm, including eating disorders to reckless behaviour performed and filmed to seek attention
and validation, with in some cases fatal consequences.

The Union already has strong foundations to protect minors online . The Digital Services
Act (DSA) requires online platforms to keep minors safe when considering the core design
choices of their services. The EU regulatory framework includes also comprehensive
safeguards for children online when using streaming services, online games, online retailers,
and AI products. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) provides specific rules and
safeguards regarding the use of personal data, including children’s. EU consumer protection
law, including the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD), protects minors as
vulnerable consumers.

Enforcing this legislation has been a key Commission priority . Under the DSA, for instance,
the Commission took enforcement action against ByteDance and Meta over addictive design
of their flagship online platforms TikTok, Facebook and Instagram, respectively, and over
inadequate age assurance on Facebook and Instagram. The Commission has also taken
enforcement action against X over Grok’s generation and dissemination of child sexual abuse
material. Through the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network, the Commission and
national authorities have been addressing harmful practices including in online games and e-

paragraphs.text:
commerce 3 . Data Protection Authorities have also taken action against Meta, TikTok, X and
others regarding the misuse of children’s personal data.

However existing rules do not suffice . The current EU legislative framework does not specify
a minimum age for access to platforms and services with age inappropriate or risky features
and content. There is also no outright ban on common problematic features, such as endless
scrolling, excess notifications, or harmful recommender systems. Moreover, the existing Union
framework does not provide sufficiently strong harmonisation and detail on addressing
addictive design features for digital products and services accessible to minors. It also lacks
legal certainty regarding age verification systems and legal responsibility of tech companies
for the design of their services.

Following the announcement in the 2025 State of the Union address, a Special Panel was
tasked with advising the Commission President on the development of a European approach to
keep children safe online. The Special Panel involved various stakeholder groups and heard
experts from different background, both from the Union and from partner countries. Its
deliberations resulted in the report of the Co-Chairs of the Special Panel, setting out their
findings and key recommendations 4 .

Alongside, child safety online has been acknowledged as a global challenge requiring close
cooperation among partners. In the United States, the recent Meta settlement shows that service
providers now realise that they are increasingly regarded, both legally and societally, as
responsible for the safety of children to whom they provide services 5 . Within the EU, many
Member States are considering different legislative initiatives to protect minors online, notably
by setting out a minimum age to access certain services 6 . Recent developments have however
clearly demonstrated the legal complexity surrounding the issue , alongside the need for a
targeted and proportionate approach and for protecting fundamental rights 7 .

Against this background, decisive, comprehensive and urgent action at Union level is the
most appropriate way forward to tackle effectively and swiftly the scale and gravity of the
risks encountered by children online. It represents the effective response to unequivocal calls
from the European Council, co-legislators and key stakeholders advocating for the need of a
common European approach to protect all children equally throughout the Union, as they
navigate online. It will allow Europe to restrict, once and for all, tech companies’ extensive and
damaging access to European children, so that they can live life free from algorithms. Because
‘Europe believes children should be raised by their parents, not by algorithms’.

commitments to improve its practices. Moreover, CPC coordinated actions are ongoing against Temu and Shein
for breaches of consumer law relating to dark patterns, fake discounts, and other unfair commercial practices.

addictive design features for digital products and services accessible to minors. It also lacks
legal certainty regarding age verification systems and legal responsibility of tech companies
for the design of their services.
Following the announcement in the 2025 State of the Union address, a Special Panel was
tasked with advising the Commission President on the development of a European approach to
keep children safe online. The Special Panel involved various stakeholder groups and heard
experts from different background, both from the Union and from partner countries. Its
deliberations resulted in the report of the Co-Chairs of the Special Panel, setting out their
findings and key recommendations 4 .
Alongside, child safety online has been acknowledged as a global challenge requiring close
cooperation among partners. In the United States, the recent Meta settlement shows that service
providers now realise that they are increasingly regarded, both legally and societally, as
responsible for the safety of children to whom they provide services 5 . Within the EU, many
Member States are considering different legislative initiatives to protect minors online, notably
by setting out a minimum age to access certain services 6 . Recent developments have however
clearly demonstrated the legal complexity surrounding the issue , alongside the need for a
targeted and proportionate approach and for protecting fundamental rights 7 .
Against this background, decisive, comprehensive and urgent action at Union level is the
most appropriate way forward to tackle effectively and swiftly the scale and gravity of the
risks encountered by children online. It represents the effective response to unequivocal calls
from the European Council, co-legislators and key stakeholders advocating for the need of a
common European approach to protect all children equally throughout the Union, as they
navigate online. It will allow Europe to restrict, once and for all, tech companies’ extensive and
damaging access to European children, so that they can live life free from algorithms. Because
‘Europe believes children should be raised by their parents, not by algorithms’.

for breaches of consumer law relating to dark patterns, fake discounts, and other unfair commercial practices.

title: 2. Towards a comprehensive and ambitious European approach: the EU KIDS Act

paragraphs.text:
The Union’s approach should allow minors to benefit from the huge potential of digital
services, while protecting them from abuse and exploitation. It needs to limit the access of
tech companies to our children, and not the other way around . It must stress that the key
responsibility to design safe online spaces rests with the digital service providers. It must
respect the evolving maturity of children as they grow up, and the role of their guardians,
without unduly shifting responsibility to them. The Union’s approach should therefore be
comprehensive, collective, age-appropriate and based on the actual risks children face online.
It should be grounded on children’s rights as fundamental rights, in line with the Charter of
Fundamental Rights of the EU, taking the best interests of the child as the primary
consideration.

The EU KIDS Act adopted with this Communication puts forward a single, EU-wide set of
rules providing an equal level of protection for all children throughout the Union, alongside
a set of tools for parents and guardians 8 . The proposal will reduce the risk of fragmentation
across Member States and provide clear legal certainty to EU businesses as they navigate the
Single Market.

The proposal will apply to “Social Media+” – the group of services that pose the greatest
risk to minors. These are the social media services, video-sharing platforms and online games
which pose specific design risks for minors, as well as AI chatbots and AI companions – as
virtual tools that can give mental health and personal development advice to minors. It will not
target services that are designed and operated for education or by public authorities, nor will it
apply to industrial AI or AI office products. The proposal will comprise a combined approach
of (i) an EU-wide minimum age and (ii) safe design requirements .

title: 2.1 The EU-wide minimum age for social media

paragraphs.text:
Access of children to platforms remains a key issue and whether they can have their own
personal account makes a huge difference in terms of risks. With this in mind, the proposal
prohibits social media platforms from accessing children under 13, and sets an EU-wide
minimum age for minors to open an account of their own at the age of 15 while ensuring a
gradual approach. In particular:

Children aged 0 and below 3 should not have access to any screen. At this age, children are
mainly exposed to relational risks as passive users of digital media. These risks often arise
when parents and guardians replace direct interaction with screen use to soothe or distract
young children, potentially affecting children’s attention span, language, and vision
development as well as socio-emotional growth. Parents and guardians should therefore
prioritise face-to-face interactions, limit their own time on social media while caring for
children and avoid exposing their children to screens.

Children aged 3 and below 13 should not be exposed to social media. However, providers of
video-sharing platforms can offer child-friendly services, e.g. educational material or age-
appropriate entertainment, which guardians may allow their children to watch in a supervised
environment. For that purpose, the platforms need to offer parents or guardians an easy-to-use
tool to restrict the use of the adult’s account to such child-friendly services, when it is passed
on to children, and limit the child’s exposure to one hour per day. This approach is in line with
the Recommendations from the Co-Chairs of the Special panel and allows children to get

For children aged 13 and below 15, parents or guardians may set up mini accounts for social

on social media and video-sharing platforms, without the need for parental approval, while
ensuring that this still only gives them access to an environment that is safe by design. During
this period, the role of parents and guardians still remains essential.

title: 2.2 Safe design

paragraphs.text:
In addition to the measures outlined above, the EU KIDS Act obliges all services in scope to
be designed safely by following strict rules and principles. This will ensure a safe experience
that is age-appropriate. These are in particular:

• No addictive design features , such as infinite scrolling, artificial notifications, or certain
reward features.

• Regulated recommender systems such as options to choose, tune and control
recommended content, avoid rabbit hole effects and go beyond engagement-based signals.

• Safe account settings to keep the content private, disable risky settings by default, and
unambiguously inform minors.

• No unwanted contacts form other users . Unknown users cannot initiate direct contact
outside of approved connections, explicit permission will be needed for being added to
groups, easy and anonymous blocking.
• Enable children to easily report harmful content and access support tools quickly .
• Offer effective and age-appropriate parental control tools .

These rules and principles will be complemented by tailored commitments for online games,
AI chatbots and companions, offering a co-regulatory approach based on industry-led self-
regulation. Software application stores would also be subject to requirements, building on
current self-regulatory best practices. They would apply consistent age ratings and make apps,
such as online games, inaccessible to minors below the rated age.

title: 2.3 Age verification

paragraphs.text:
The proposal also regulates privacy-preserving and accessible age verification systems and
how they function.

The EU KIDS Act will oblige providers of social media services and video-sharing platforms
to perform age verification when a user opens a new account . This would be done by relying
on the EU age verification tool or other solutions provided by public authorities that offer an
equivalent level of accuracy, reliability, robustness, privacy, security, non-discrimination and
non-intrusiveness. Existing accounts would be subject to proportionate checks rather than

blanket, retrospective age verification. This would be the case for instance if an account has
been already created many years prior or combined with a credit card linked to the account’s
holder. For online games specifically, obligatory age recommendation will be required for
every game, with strict enforcement through age verification in a software application store
before the game can be downloaded.

title: 2.4 Enforcement

paragraphs.text:
To ensure effective protection for children, strict enforcement is critical. The EU KIDS Act
builds on the existing enforcement architecture from the DSA and the AI Act. The burden of
proof to demonstrate compliance with new rules lies with the operators. This is why very large
online platforms will be obliged to submit a compliance plan to an independent auditor that has
to thoroughly assess the new service, feature or functionality. The Commission can request the
provider to propose corrective measures if the Commission considers, based on the auditor’s
report, that the compliance plan contains any shortcoming. The Act also introduces a
supervisory fee to effectively fund and support the Commission’s EU-wide enforcement and
supervision work. Within the enforcement structure, priority will be given to complaints
related to minors .

As technology moves rapidly, the proposal foresees a review clause to cater for the possible
need to update the regulatory framework.

title: 3.1. Complementary EU regulatory measures

paragraphs.text:
The EU KIDS Act will set out specific rules for those digital services, the use of which pose
the highest risk to minors’ safety and development. It focuses on a gradual access approach and
on ensuring that certain design features are safe by design. At the same time, we need to ensure
that minors’ safety is ensured when it comes to all services and products that children can
encounter online, and that commercial practices that reach them do not pose risks to their health
or safety.

The upcoming Digital Fairness Act (DFA) and the revision of the Consumer Protection
Cooperation Regulation are a key opportunity to embed the protection of children and
teenagers at the heart of EU consumer law. The DFA will update horizontal consumer
protection rules against harmful commercial practices online that also affect children as young
consumers such as manipulative business-to-consumer digital practices, unfair pricing
techniques, problematic influencer marketing and issues with digital contracts and
subscriptions. The Commission will also revise the Consumer Protection Cooperation
Regulation to ensure stronger enforcement for the benefit of all, with a focus on minors,
building on and complementing the enforcement under the EU KIDS Act. In preparing the
revised Regulation, the Commission will consider ways to improve enforcement coordination
between national consumer authorities in cross-border situations, and centralise investigation
and enforcement powers at EU level in specific cases.

In addition, the Commission will propose a revision of the Audiovisual Media Services
Directive . It will specify the categories of harmful content that video sharing platforms must
protect minors from and clarify the applicability of EU audiovisual rules to influencers as
providers of content.

Beyond the development of an appropriate regulatory framework and its effective enforcement,
the Union response needs to rely on a range of support measures, such as those outlined below.

title: 3.2 Empowering children and young people through education

paragraphs.text:
First, education is key to fostering the development of every child , equipping minors with
adequate knowledge to better understand the online environment and enabling them to discern
between appropriate and risky behaviours, including online. With this in mind, it is essential
that young people are equipped with the skills they need to safely and responsibly engage with
‘Social Media+’, including in the context of accelerated use of AI.

Against this background, the Commission will adopt an Education package to support schools
in their efforts to promote digital and AI skills, raise awareness and build resilience among
minors including through the preparation of teachers and school leaders on the impact of
"Social Media+" on mental health and cognitive development. In this context, psychological
support as well as comprehensive age-appropriate education are key.

The forthcoming Education package will further mainstream AI literacy education , including
through the EU-OECD AI literacy framework for primary and secondary education , and
will support schools in developing strategies to foster the digital wellbeing of children, focusing
on their safety and empowerment. It will also address the supply of safe interoperable European
digital education infrastructure and pedagogically sound education content, and help reduce
Europe’s strategic dependencies in educational technology.

The EU co-funded Safer Internet Centres already provide effective, trusted help to keep
children safe online. Their national presence, wide reach and specialised expertise, make the
network a valuable partner for Member States in developing and implementing effective
national strategies for a safer and better digital environment for children. Building on this work,
the Commission plans to provide tailored guidance on the new rules for different groups,
including children, guardians, educators, schools, and regulators. This will include webinars,
early detection of harm, managing age-appropriate access, and using AI chatbots and
companions safely. Member States should build on this work and strengthen it in the national,
regional and local context.

As concerns financing, the Commission already funds research on child safety online under
Horizon Europe . The work programme for 2026 includes the impact of the use of digital tools
outside school and for communication on educational outcomes and mental health, with
relevant projects starting in 2027. In addition, the Commission can identify emerging research
funding priorities , as well as opportunities to support safe services and child-centred
innovation with direct private and public-sector investment.

In parallel, action should be undertaken to ensure children spend time in the offline world .
Through Erasmus+, the Commission supports offline spaces and activities, as they are crucial
for the development of children, as they help promote healthy engagement and offer
alternatives to screen use. It therefore encourages Member States to expand access to affordable
sports, arts, youth clubs, libraries, and community spaces. EU Member States and regions
should make full use of available national and EU funding, with a view to provide appropriate
infrastructure for teachers, parents, and children.

These efforts should be part of a broader, strong collective commitment at both Union and
national level to mobilise all available resources for education, awareness raising and
exchange of best practices with a view to strengthening prevention, support and protection
mechanisms for children in the digital environment in an integrated approach to child

protection. In this context, swift transposition and implementation of the Product Liability
Directive will allow victims of defective products, including digital products, to claim
compensation under uniform conditions throughout the EU.

title: 3.3 Broader EU support measures

paragraphs.text:
Besides education and media literacy, a number of further EU complementary measures are
key to address the protection of children online. These include a comprehensive approach to
health, especially mental health, and better cooperation and coordination of those involved in
addressing online risks and crimes against children.

In 2023, the Commission had already adopted a Communication on a comprehensive approach
to mental health, including 20 flagship initiatives and almost EUR 1.3 billion in funding
opportunities. The initiative put a greater focus on inclusiveness and supporting vulnerable
groups, such as children and young people. The Commission is now developing, jointly with
UNICEF, a prevention toolkit which will help policy-makers to better support the mental and
physical health of children. The toolkit will be launched at the occasion of the World Mental
Health Day in October 2026. The toolkit will also address challenges in relation to the impact
of digitalisation on children’s mental health. In addition, the Commission is cooperating with
the World Health Organization on capacity-building in mental health systems which also
address digital determinants of youth mental health.

Children can also be victims of crime . Where children are affected by criminal offences
online, as victims, perpetrators, or both, the EU procedural criminal law acquis applies, in
particular the Victims’ Rights Directive and the 2016 procedural safeguards Directive. When it
comes to crime prevention, the substantive EU criminal law acquis is the applicable
framework, including most notably the Child Sexual Abuse Directive.

Crimes affecting children online range from hate crime, trafficking in human beings, abuse and
sexual exploitation to recruitment into organized crime and violent extremism or terrorism. EU
and national authorities enforcing different legislation will keep cooperating and sharing
information and data promptly, to allow for the highest level of protection of minors. The
upcoming Action plan to protect children from crime will seek to provide a coherent and
comprehensive response to the various risks faced by children in relation to crime, both online
and offline. It will aim at minimising children’s exposure to crime and at strengthening the
capacity of law enforcement and other competent authorities to investigate and prosecute
crimes affecting children. It will focus on supporting children in their journeys through the
national criminal justice schemes. With the child-centered approach, the rights and best
interest of the child will be at the core of all initiatives.

title: 3.4 International Cooperation

paragraphs.text:
In line with the EU International Digital Strategy, the EU has so far worked with Australia,
Brazil, Canada, Singapore, the United Kingdom and Japan to protect children online, shaped
the G7 Common Set of Principles regarding minors online 9 . It has further contributed to
discussions at multilateral level, including the United Nations 10 . Strengthening cooperation
with our international partners remains a priority to effectively protect minors online. The
introduction, via the EU KIDS Act, of an approach to mitigating the impact of artificial

9 Subsequently endorsed by Leaders from Brazil, Egypt, Kenya, India and South Korea.
10 G7 Common Set of Principles defining a safer and more secure digital space for minors.

intelligence on children via chatbots and companions strengthens the EU’s right-based and
risk-based approach to AI , which is of interest to many partners around the world. In general,
a single approach to protecting children online across the EU will make this international
cooperation more effective, by providing a strong reference point to engage with partners to
achieve the objectives of this initiative.

introduction, via the EU KIDS Act, of an approach to mitigating the impact of artificial

intelligence on children via chatbots and companions strengthens the EU’s right-based and
risk-based approach to AI , which is of interest to many partners around the world. In general,
a single approach to protecting children online across the EU will make this international
cooperation more effective, by providing a strong reference point to engage with partners to
achieve the objectives of this initiative.

title: 3.5 Monitoring

paragraphs.text:
It is important to continuously analyse the development of digital services for minors, their
impact on minors, and the effects of the initiatives taken within the Union. The Commission
will regularly take stock of progress with the support of stakeholders, including youth and
children rights organisations, children, and parents’ associations. It will monitor the impact and
effectiveness of the package of measures linked to this Communication.

This monitoring will track the effects and possible need to adjust the minimum age
framework , to establish a structured, regular data collection system to understand the lived
online experience of minors across the EU. This framework will be grounded on child
participation, notably through the EU Children’s Participation Platform under the EU Strategy
on the rights of the child and BIK+ (Better Internet for Kids+). It will draw on research, work
under the DSA and by the EU Centre for Algorithmic Transparency, which tracks how child
safety online, emerging technologies and usage patterns evolve.

The monitoring will focus in particular on impacts on youth’s mental health . It will also
capture the positive dimensions of children’s online experiences, including whether and to what
extent minors feel empowered and safe online, and how their screen time is distributed across
different activities.

title: 4. Conclusions and next steps

paragraphs.text:
This Communication sets out a framework built on a clear conviction: technology companies
bear the primary responsibility for making their products safe. Parents, not algorithms,
should be raising Europe’s children .

We must build a digital world where our children can grow up free and secure , protected by
the values that Europe stands for. Europe needs to be the best place to grow up in, and the best
place to grow old in. That is the standard against which this response should be judged.

The Special Panel has delivered the evidence. It is now for the Union’s institutions, together
with Member States, industry, civil society, schools and families to deliver the change that
children and parents across Europe are asking for – a world designed with their well-being
in mind.

title: The Challenge

paragraphs.text:
Learning levels remain low across low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Seven in ten children in
these contexts cannot read a simple text by the end of primary school, rising to nearly nine in ten in
Sub-Saharan Africa. The scale and persistence of these gaps, combined with limited instructional capa
city, have intensified interest in approaches that can operate with speed, cost efficiency, and scale,
particularly digital education technology (EdTech). Yet, despite years of investment and a proliferation of
digital tools and platforms, foundational learning outcomes remain deeply inadequate for millions of
children. Practitioners and policy makers need more focused answers that move beyond the functional
capabilities of EdTech and instead clarify which EdTech-enabled interventions improve teaching and
learning and how.

This evidence synthesis and guidance note seeks to answer that question. It draws on 23 experimental
and quasi-experimental studies and 155 implementation-focused studies published since 2016, specifically
examining EdTech interventions tested with Grade 1–3 learners and their teachers in LMIC contexts. In
doing so, it offers policy makers and practitioners something the existing literature often lacks, a struc
tured, operationally relevant framework for making smarter EdTech decisions with teaching and learning
outcomes at its center. It focuses on early primary grades (1–3) because they are the critical period in
which foundational literacy and numeracy skills are first built and early instructional gaps begin to widen.

title: The Approach

paragraphs.text:
What distinguishes this synthesis and policy guidance note is its organizing lens: the instructional core .
Rather than cataloging EdTech tools by type or platform, this synthesis is structured around the interac
tions that drive learning, that is, the interaction between teachers, learners, and instructional content that
directly shape classroom instruction and student learning. EdTech tools and programs are evaluated
based on how well they strengthen those interactions across four domains: (1) teacher support, (2)
learner support, (3) content development and delivery, and (4) immediate instructional support. This
framing is designed to be actionable for teams working across diverse country contexts, helping practitio
ners and policy makers move from ‘what technology should we use?’ to ‘what instructional problem are
we trying to solve, and does this tool solve it?’

title: Key Findings

paragraphs.text:
Across the evidence reviewed, effective EdTech tools improved foundational learning not by introducing
technology alone but by addressing concrete instructional bottlenecks that commonly constrain delivery
in LMICs. These include uneven instructional support, limited opportunities for structured practice and
feedback, slow content production, and weak visibility into instructional implementation. Artificial
intelligence (AI) tools extended these functions by providing on-demand guidance, automating assess
ments, and accelerating content adaptation. The sections below summarize the recurring design features
and mechanisms associated with these effects.

title: 4 | How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries

paragraphs.text: How effective EdTech supports teachers

Effective teacher-facing EdTech converts instructional support from a one-off training event into a more
continuous process of learning, reinforcement, and classroom use. The strongest models expand access to
structured professional development where repeated in-person training is difficult to sustain; strengthen
engagement by shifting teacher learning from passive exposure to active participation; reinforce instruc
tional practices over time through prompts, lesson guides, coaching, and peer exchange; and embed
support directly into lesson preparation and delivery through classroom-ready tools. The effect is a
meaningful reduction in the burden on teachers to translate training into practice on their own.
How effective EdTech supports learners

Effective learner-facing EdTech improves learning by increasing access to curriculum-aligned content,
creating more opportunities for repeated and individualized practice, sustaining engagement through
interactive and multisensory learning, and delivering more consistent instruction where teaching capacity
is weak or uneven. Digital tools, such as e-readers, short message service (SMS)-, and interactive voice
response (IVR)-based lessons, interactive software, tablet apps, phonics games, reading-while-listening
tools, and structured digital lesson models are most effective when they fit existing instructional time and
do not depend on unrealistic levels of connectivity, supervision, or device access.
How effective EdTech supports content and instructional support systems

Effective content-facing EdTech makes foundational learning materials more adaptable, easier to revise,
and more reliable to distribute. AI-assisted drafting, translation tools, and open educational resource
platforms can shorten production cycles and support localization across languages and contexts. Digital
ordering, barcode tracking, and offline digital libraries can improve the availability of materials where
print delivery systems are weak. For instructional support systems, EdTech is most useful when it makes
performance and participation data easier for teachers and schools to interpret and use in practice.
How AI enhances EdTech functions across the instructional core

While the evidence base remains nascent, AI can add value when it helps education systems perform
familiar instructional functions with greater speed, responsiveness, or reach. Examples include drafting
content, automating oral reading scoring, and enabling more adaptive learner feedback. In these roles, AI
mainly extends existing EdTech functions rather than creating entirely new ones, although this may shift
over time. Its practical value depends on pedagogical fit, language quality, governance, and cost.
What is needed for effective implementation

The synthesis also surfaces several critical conditions that help ensure EdTech is implemented successful
ly. At the user level , sustained use depends on ease of use, structured onboarding, ongoing support, and
visible instructional value. At the school level , uptake is stronger when tools are aligned with existing
routines, curriculum pacing, and leadership expectations, and when coaching, peer support, or follow-up
structures are in place. At the system level , implementation depends on delivery models that match real
infrastructure conditions and account for the full costs of devices, data, maintenance, training, support,
and, where relevant, AI-related licensing and oversight. Some barriers can be reduced through design and
implementation. Others, such as weak infrastructure, maintenance systems, and data governance, require
system-level action.

title: Policy Recommendations

paragraphs.text:
The evidence synthesized in this guidance note suggests that EdTech should be viewed as an investment in
instructional and delivery methods, not a stand-alone digital solution. Effective tools and programs add
value by strengthening core instructional processes and functioning reliably under real delivery conditions,
not by introducing new technology. Seven operationally grounded recommendations for policy makers and
practitioners follow from this evidence:

1. Start with the instructional problem, not the technology . EdTech is most useful when it addresses a
specific barrier in foundational learning delivery, such as weak teacher support, limited learner practice,
poor material delivery, or weak feedback loops. Technology is a means, not the objective.

2. Prioritize instructional fit over technological novelty . Across the evidence reviewed in this note, the
strongest tools align with the curriculum, fit classroom routines, and provide usable support to teachers
and learners. This suggests that technology works best when it strengthens an existing instructional
approach rather than trying to compensate for its absence.

3. Design for real conditions from the start. Choices about connectivity, devices, power, content format,
and user support should reflect actual infrastructure and implementation conditions, especially in rural
and lower-capacity settings. Over the longer term, investment in infrastructure remains important to
expand the range and reliability of EdTech options. In the meantime, where readiness is limited, offline
and low-bandwidth design should be treated as a central design choice rather than a fallback.

4. Account for the full cost of ownership. Sustainability assessments must include recurrent costs
alongside initial investments. Interventions that are affordable to launch but not to maintain are unlikely
to deliver lasting impact. Costing decisions should therefore consider continuity, not just rollout.

5. Use scalability as a design filter from the outset . Pilots can generate useful evidence, but their implica
tions depend on whether core functions can be sustained under routine conditions with realistic
staffing, infrastructure, and financing.

6. Consider both the practical risks and the potential of AI applications . AI tools should be evaluated not
only on their potential but also on safety, data governance implications, language accuracy, and the
realistic capacity of users and systems to manage them responsibly.

7. Build equity into design, not as an add-on . Interventions that depend on resources or conditions
unavailable to the most disadvantaged learners risk widening, rather than closing, the gaps they are
meant to address.

chosen for instructional purposes, designed for real-world conditions, and implemented with sustained
support. Together, they inform decisions on the design, adoption, and scaling of EdTech for foundational
learning in LMIC school contexts. Readers can use the key findings to assess instructional fit, the imple
mentation section to identify the delivery conditions required for sustained use, and the implications to
guide adoption and scaling decisions. The note also distinguishes between where the evidence is strong
and where caution is warranted, particularly for AI-enabled tools and large-scale deployment.
