title: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE

paragraphs.text:
Foundational learning skills, such as literacy and numeracy, are the basic competencies children need to
acquire in the early years of schooling , as they form the building blocks for future and lifelong learning
(World Bank 2025). A strong mastery of foundational learning skills in the early grades enables children
to progress more successfully through school and into adulthood. In contrast, early disadvantages tend to
compound over time, often widening the gap between children with access to effective learning environ
ments and those without (Cain and Oakhill 2011; Wood et al. 2020). These findings underscore the need
to ensure all children acquire foundational learning skills as a prerequisite for success in school and
beyond. Yet school systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) continue to face two persistent
challenges in achieving this goal. First, children’s foundational learning levels remain low. Seven in ten
Grade 3 students in these regions cannot read a simple text with comprehension; in Sub-Saharan Africa,
the rate rises to nearly nine in ten (World Bank et al. 2022). Second, despite growing policy commitment,
many countries lack the capacity to deliver essential instructional support on a large scale. Instructional
subsystems include the core elements of an education system that shape what and how students learn,
such as curriculum design, teaching and learning materials, classroom assessments, teacher preparation,
and ongoing instructional support. These components are often underdeveloped and of low quality
(Crouch 2020). The magnitude and complexity of these gaps make it essential to identify solutions that
can operate, if possible, at speed, at low cost, and at scale. This guidance note examines whether and how
digital education technology (EdTech) helps advance these goals in LMICs.

EdTech refers to the use of digital or technology-enabled tools in the education sector to enhance
teaching, learning, and broader system functions (Norman 2023). The use of EdTech expanded rapidly
during the COVID-19 pandemic. As schools closed, governments and development partners turned to
alternative delivery channels, such as radio, television, mobile phones, and online platforms, resulting in a
surge of technology-enabled instruction worldwide, including in LMIC schools (Rodriguez et al. 2021).
While still relatively limited in scale, more recently, artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tools have begun to
shape EdTech applications globally, including in several LMICs such as Kenya, Peru, and the Philippines
(Penprase 2025). Amid this rapid growth, emerging evidence suggests that when designed and imple
mented effectively, EdTech can enhance student engagement, improve learning outcomes, support
teacher performance, increase access to high-quality instructional materials, and contribute to overall
system efficiency (Haleem et al. 2022; Piper and Dubeck 2024). Yet there is limited consolidated informa
tion on which types of EdTech interventions are effective, for which learners and teachers, and under
what conditions in LMIC contexts (Escueta et al. 2017), with even less clarity for foundational learning
education (Norman 2023). This gap makes it difficult for governments and education practitioners to plan
or prioritize digitally enabled foundational learning reforms.

This guidance note addresses that gap by bringing together the available evidence on EdTech for founda
tional learning in LMICs. It identifies the types of tools that strengthen foundational learning outcomes
and instruction and clarifies the conditions under which they are most likely to work. The note focuses on
early primary grades because this is the critical period in which foundational learning skills are first built
and early instructional gaps begin to widen. While EdTech can be integrated across various layers of an
education system, this note focuses on technologies that strengthen the instructional core, which
emphasizes the interactions among (a) teachers, (b) students, and (c) content (City et al. 2009). It also
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 7

considers instructional support systems that reinforce this core by providing feedback loops, analytics,
and monitoring tools that help teachers plan, deliver, and adjust instruction based on evidence of student
learning. Examples include student assessment platforms that inform teaching and real-time feedback
tools that support responsive instruction. While foundational learning outcomes are shaped by conditions
across homes, schools, and the wider education system, this note focuses on classroom processes and
environments that most directly influence learning. It therefore excludes system-level applications such as
education management information systems, payroll and human resource platforms, and online tertiary
education for teacher candidates. 1 The analysis prioritizes EdTech tools that strengthen the instructional
core and its immediate support systems, while avoiding device-driven approaches that lack pedagogical
integration. Additionally, since the note aims to inform concrete policy and program choices, the analysis
draws on experimental evidence where available and uses relevant nonexperimental studies to highlight
implementation requirements.

This guidance note extends prior evidence syntheses on EdTech in LMICs in four ways. First, it focuses on
foundational learning in the early primary years, a level rarely disaggregated in earlier reviews (for
example, Hennessy et al. 2022; Popova et al. 2016; Quota et al. 2022b). Second, it evaluates EdTech for
pedagogical soundness alongside its technological functions. Many EdTech initiatives fail to improve
learning when pedagogical foundations are weak or absent (Cardim et al. 2023). This guidance note links
technology capabilities with instructional design features that strengthen early-grade teaching and
learning. Third, it examines the contexts in which interventions succeed by identifying implementation
enablers and barriers in LMIC school settings, recognizing that replicability and sustainability depend on
these conditions as much as on the EdTech tools themselves. Finally, it complements digital frameworks
that emphasize governance and system management (for example, Rajasekaran et al. 2024) by focusing
on classroom interactions between teachers, learners, and content that directly shape learning outcomes.
The following questions guide this analysis. The first two review empirical evidence on what has worked
and why. Building on those insights, the next two questions explore policy considerations and areas
where further learning could inform future action.

• What EdTech interventions have effectively strengthened the instructional core and its support
systems for foundational learning in LMICs?
• Under what conditions have these interventions succeeded or faced challenges?
• What policy and implementation strategies might support their adoption, scale, and sustainability?
• What evidence gaps remain on using EdTech to improve foundational learning in LMICs?

The remainder of this guidance note is organized into three parts. First, it presents the analytic
frameworks and methods used to identify, select, and synthesize the EdTech evidence. Second, it summa
rizes key findings from the literature and highlights case examples of how EdTech has supported founda
tional learning across diverse contexts. Third, it sets out policy, practice, and research recommendations
to guide the effective integration of EdTech into foundational learning initiatives in LMICs. Together, these
sections provide governments, World Bank teams, and partners with clear guidance on which EdTech
approaches to consider, when they are appropriate, for what purposes, and how to implement them
effectively across varied settings.

title: Instructional Core: Teacher, Student, and Content

paragraphs.text:
The integration of EdTech, such as computer-assisted reading programs and adaptive learning applications,
has improved early literacy and numeracy across diverse settings (Dorris et al. 2024). Positive effects have
been reported among children with learning difficulties (Hurwitz and Vanacore 2023), with poor attention
(Deault et al. 2009), and from economically disadvantaged backgrounds (Comaskey et al. 2009), demon
strating EdTech’s potential to support varied student populations despite individual or environmental
challenges. Yet similar efforts have not always produced comparable results in LMICs. A review of various
EdTech initiatives finds that providing technology alone rarely improves student outcomes; factors such as
poor pedagogical integration, weak software design, limited user digital skills, and inadequate implementa
tion often limit the impact (Escueta et al. 2017). A critical factor shaping EdTech’s impact, as these findings
allude to and as others (Cardim et al. 2023) have also asserted, is how meaningfully it integrates and
supports interactions among teachers, students, and content within the instructional core in the classroom
(City et al. 2009). In line with this perspective, studies have identified some defining qualities of effective
teacher development, instructional practices, student learning, and curriculum design that EdTech interven
tions can incorporate to strengthen these interactions.

Effective teacher professional development (TPD) shares several core features across various contexts,
including a clear focus on curricular goals and content knowledge, active learning, peer collaboration,
ongoing support, teacher agency, and contextual and pedagogical relevance. High-quality TPD maintains a
clear instructional focus aligned with curriculum goals and subject knowledge; promotes active learning
through modeling, practice, and feedback; and fosters peer collaboration through structured dialogue, joint
planning, and collective reflection (Avalos 2011; Darling-Hammond et al. 2017; Garet et al. 2001; Popova et
al. 2016). Ongoing support, such as expert coaching and feedback sustained over time, enables teachers to
apply and adapt trained strategies in practice (Basma and Savage 2018; Popova et al. 2016). Strong
programs also affirm teachers’ agency and professionalism, positioning them as active participants in
shaping instruction (Avalos 2011; Basma and Savage 2018). Evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa further
highlights the importance of contextual relevance, with effective TPD grounded in classroom realities and
delivered through local curricula, materials, and facilitators (Popova et al. 2016).

Effective student learning is shaped by multiple influences across students’ developmental ecology, from
the home environment to broader societal structures (Bronfenbrenner 1979). Within this broader context,
instructional practices represent a critical area where teachers and schools can make a direct impact
through clear objectives, active learning, modeling, and guided practice, as well as formative assessment,
timely feedback, and social-emotional support. Syntheses of over 800 meta-analyses suggest that strong
learning environments are characterized by explicit objectives and clear success criteria, enabling students
to understand their goals and monitor their progress (Hattie 2010). Active, constructivist approaches, such
as doing, discussing, and reflecting, promote deeper understanding, particularly when supported by
modeling and guided practice (Darling-Hammond et al. 2015; Hattie 2010). Frequent formative assessment
and timely feedback help learners understand their progress and adjust their learning strategies accordingly
(Black and Wiliam 2010; Hattie 2010). Social and emotional supports further strengthen learning by enhanc
ing students’ motivation, self-regulation, and sense of belonging (Darling-Hammond et al. 2020).
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 9

Compl ementing these instructional practices, an effective curriculum also plays a critical role. In LMIC
schools, materials tied to curriculum can also serve as de facto teacher support, offering instructional
routines and pedagogical practices. Key features of high-quality curricula include learning progressions,
real-world relevance, authentic problem-solving, collaborative engagement with challenging content,
higher-order thinking, and cultural relevance. Curricula structured around clear learning progressions help
guide instruction and student development over time and ensure that critical subskills in literacy and core
domains of math are adequately covered. Real-world relevance and authentic problem-solving connect
learning to meaningful contexts, making content more engaging and applicable (OECD 2018). Opportuni
ties for structured collaboration and sustained engagement with challenging content promote deeper
understanding and higher-order thinking (Marzano et al. 2001; OECD 2018). Culturally responsive curricu
la further enhance inclusion by drawing on students’ backgrounds and lived experiences to build rele
vance and connection (Gay 2018). The elements of the instructional core, together with the qualities of
effective support that strengthen it, form the analytic framework for this review of EdTech interventions
for foundational learning in LMICs. Specifically, our review examines how existing EdTech interventions
align with the instructional core and its evidence-based strategies, their effectiveness, and the contextual
factors shaping their implementation. The diagram below visualizes the instructional core and its adjacent
instructional support systems.

title: Core Capabilities of Technology

paragraphs.text:
Digital technology possesses several capabilities that distinguish it from traditional instructional materials,
such as printed resources, chalkboards, and physical manipulatives. These capabilities include connecti
vity, interactivity, multimedia, and data processing (Huang 2001; Quota et al. 2022b) as well as transmis
sion and storage (Huang 2001). Across these capabilities, technology can support forms of engagement,
communication, and instructional delivery that static resources may not always afford. At the same time,
these capabilities do not create instructional value on their own. Their relevance depends on the specific
teaching or learning problem being addressed, the non-digital alternatives already available, and the
conditions under which the tool must operate. Understanding these capabilities, therefore, helps identify
not only what technology can do but also when it offers a meaningful advantage over non-digital
approaches and what constraints may limit that advantage.

Connectivity enables information sharing across time and distance, allowing teachers and students to
access content, communicate, and collaborate beyond the classroom (Quota et al. 2022b; Trucano 2016).
For example, internet-enabled devices can support virtual coaching, online professional learning commu
nities, and real-time access to digital learning materials. Low-bandwidth tools, such as short message
service (SMS) or radio broadcasts also rely on connectivity to deliver instructions and maintain engage
ment in remote settings (Quota et al. 2022a). Compared with print-based reminders or in-person follow-
up alone, connectivity can extend support more quickly and at lower cost, but its value depends on
reliable networks, electricity, affordable data, and device access.

Interactivity describes technology’s ability to engage users in active participation rather than passive
consumption (Laurillard 2013). Interactive tools can prompt reflection, reinforce learning through practice,
and provide immediate feedback. Examples include simulations that illustrate instructional methods,
embedded quizzes within learning modules, and collaborative digital workspaces where teachers and
students apply concepts together (Quota et al. 2022a). Compared with static materials, interactivity can
provide more guided practice and immediate response, but only when tools are easy to use and do not
impose excessive technical or cognitive demands.

Multimedia refers to the presentation of information through multiple formats, including text, audio,
video, and graphics (Mayer 2010). This capacity makes it possible to illustrate complex concepts and
adapt resources to diverse learning needs. For example, video demonstrations can show instructional
practices, while audio resources can help present literacy and numeracy content in different languages.
Compared with print-only materials, multimedia is especially useful when modeling, pronunciation, or
worked examples matter, though its value is lower where hardware, power, or classroom conditions
cannot support regular audiovisual use.

Data processing reflects the capacity of digital tools to collect, store, and analyze information about
engagement, participation, and learning progress (Long and Siemens 2011). For teachers, this can include
tracking completion of professional development modules or monitoring classroom use of new practices.
For students, data processing can generate reports on learning progress and inform targeted support. In
both cases, the ability to analyze usage and outcomes helps strengthen accountability and guide conti
nuous improvement (Quota et al. 2022b). Compared with paper-based records, data processing can
speed up aggregation and make patterns easier to detect, but it adds value only when the data are
accurate, interpretable, and linked to actions users can take.
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 11

Transmission and storage are basic digital capabilities that enable technology to retain and deliver
content across time and settings (Huang 2001). These functions enable devices to store preloaded
materials, such as lesson plans, scripts, or digital readers, so they remain accessible even when connecti
vity or real-time updates are unavailable. This makes transmission and storage especially relevant in
low-resource environments where other capabilities may be limited. Compared with print distribution,
these functions can make content easier to update, duplicate, and preserve, although they still depend on
functioning devices, charging, and maintenance.

As AI becomes embedded in EdTech products, systems may need to evaluate the AI model itself along
side the educational intervention. This shift reinforces the importance of structured evaluation approaches
that rely on clearly defined tasks and transparent scoring criteria. Elements, like clear instructions,
easy-to-understand scoring, and tests of usability outside of controlled settings as described in the
AI-for-Education benchmarks (AI-for-Education.org), provide one structured way to assess whether an AI
model is reliable. Our evidence review applies a similar principle by examining how core technology
capabilities are operationalized into specific intervention features and how these features support and
strengthen the instructional core in diverse LMIC schools for foundational learning programs. As these
tools increasingly collect and generate user-level information, systems also need to consider data hosting,
access, retention, privacy, and security, especially for digital assessments, dashboards, adaptive systems,
and AI-enabled tools.

text:
Digital technology possesses several capabilities that distinguish it from traditional instructional materials,
such as printed resources, chalkboards, and physical manipulatives. These capabilities include connecti
vity, interactivity, multimedia, and data processing (Huang 2001; Quota et al. 2022b) as well as transmis
sion and storage (Huang 2001). Across these capabilities, technology can support forms of engagement,
communication, and instructional delivery that static resources may not always afford. At the same time,
these capabilities do not create instructional value on their own. Their relevance depends on the specific
teaching or learning problem being addressed, the non-digital alternatives already available, and the
conditions under which the tool must operate. Understanding these capabilities, therefore, helps identify
not only what technology can do but also when it offers a meaningful advantage over non-digital
approaches and what constraints may limit that advantage.
Connectivity enables information sharing across time and distance, allowing teachers and students to
access content, communicate, and collaborate beyond the classroom (Quota et al. 2022b; Trucano 2016).
For example, internet-enabled devices can support virtual coaching, online professional learning commu
nities, and real-time access to digital learning materials. Low-bandwidth tools, such as short message
service (SMS) or radio broadcasts also rely on connectivity to deliver instructions and maintain engage
ment in remote settings (Quota et al. 2022a). Compared with print-based reminders or in-person follow-
up alone, connectivity can extend support more quickly and at lower cost, but its value depends on
reliable networks, electricity, affordable data, and device access.
Interactivity describes technology’s ability to engage users in active participation rather than passive
consumption (Laurillard 2013). Interactive tools can prompt reflection, reinforce learning through practice,
and provide immediate feedback. Examples include simulations that illustrate instructional methods,
embedded quizzes within learning modules, and collaborative digital workspaces where teachers and
students apply concepts together (Quota et al. 2022a). Compared with static materials, interactivity can
provide more guided practice and immediate response, but only when tools are easy to use and do not
impose excessive technical or cognitive demands.
Multimedia refers to the presentation of information through multiple formats, including text, audio,
video, and graphics (Mayer 2010). This capacity makes it possible to illustrate complex concepts and
adapt resources to diverse learning needs. For example, video demonstrations can show instructional
practices, while audio resources can help present literacy and numeracy content in different languages.
Compared with print-only materials, multimedia is especially useful when modeling, pronunciation, or
worked examples matter, though its value is lower where hardware, power, or classroom conditions
cannot support regular audiovisual use.
Data processing reflects the capacity of digital tools to collect, store, and analyze information about
engagement, participation, and learning progress (Long and Siemens 2011). For teachers, this can include
tracking completion of professional development modules or monitoring classroom use of new practices.
For students, data processing can generate reports on learning progress and inform targeted support. In
both cases, the ability to analyze usage and outcomes helps strengthen accountability and guide conti
nuous improvement (Quota et al. 2022b). Compared with paper-based records, data processing can
speed up aggregation and make patterns easier to detect, but it adds value only when the data are
accurate, interpretable, and linked to actions users can take.

Transmission and storage are basic digital capabilities that enable technology to retain and deliver
content across time and settings (Huang 2001). These functions enable devices to store preloaded
materials, such as lesson plans, scripts, or digital readers, so they remain accessible even when connecti
vity or real-time updates are unavailable. This makes transmission and storage especially relevant in
low-resource environments where other capabilities may be limited. Compared with print distribution,
these functions can make content easier to update, duplicate, and preserve, although they still depend on
functioning devices, charging, and maintenance.
As AI becomes embedded in EdTech products, systems may need to evaluate the AI model itself along
side the educational intervention. This shift reinforces the importance of structured evaluation approaches
that rely on clearly defined tasks and transparent scoring criteria. Elements, like clear instructions,
easy-to-understand scoring, and tests of usability outside of controlled settings as described in the
AI-for-Education benchmarks (AI-for-Education.org), provide one structured way to assess whether an AI
model is reliable. Our evidence review applies a similar principle by examining how core technology
capabilities are operationalized into specific intervention features and how these features support and
strengthen the instructional core in diverse LMIC schools for foundational learning programs. As these
tools increasingly collect and generate user-level information, systems also need to consider data hosting,
access, retention, privacy, and security, especially for digital assessments, dashboards, adaptive systems,
and AI-enabled tools.

title: METHODS

paragraphs.text:
This guidance note draws on a rapid evidence review of published research and expert consultations with
LMIC-based EdTech professionals to combine established evidence with emerging applications that have
not yet been formally evaluated, particularly AI-empowered tools.

title: Rapid Evidence Review

paragraphs.text:
This review of published research followed the Cochrane Rapid Reviews Methods Group’s guidance, which
adapts systematic review methods to support timely decision-making (Garritty et al. 2021). This approach
streamlines select steps while maintaining rigor and involves five stages: (a) defining research questions
and a search strategy; (b) structured evidence searches; (c) screening for relevance; (d) removing
duplicates; and (e) prioritizing studies by evidence type.

title: Step 1 - Defining the research questions and search strategy

paragraphs.text:
The research began with a scoping exercise to define the research questions, eligibility criteria, and search
terms. Eligibility covered four dimensions: location, population, purpose, and intervention. The focus was
on LMICs, teachers and learners in early primary grades, and EdTech used to support foundational
learning. Search terms covered regions and country names, target users, EdTech delivery formats and
devices, and instructional purposes such as teacher development, learner support, curriculum materials,
assessment, analytics, and lesson planning. These terms were refined iteratively by drawing additional
keywords from relevant titles, abstracts, and keyword fields until new searches produced little additional
material.

title: Step 2 - Structured evidence searches

paragraphs.text:
Search terms were applied across six academic and sector-relevant databases selected for their relevance
to education research and development studies. These included ERIC, JSTOR, EBSCO, Web of Science,
PubMed, and Scopus. Each database was searched using combinations of terms across four eligibility
dimensions (location, population, purpose, and intervention), using Boolean operators and phrase
matching where applicable. Recognizing that EdTech evolves rapidly and that many interventions may not
be documented in peer-reviewed journals, the search was also extended to include gray literature. This
included technical reports, policy briefs, and web-based descriptions of EdTech programs.

title: Steps 3, 4, and 5 - Screening for relevance, duplicates, and prioritization

paragraphs.text:
Results were screened through title/abstract review followed by targeted full-text review. Studies were
included if they were published in 2016 or later, focused on early-grade teachers or learners in LMICs,
examined EdTech related to the instructional core or its immediate supports, and addressed foundational
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 13

learning outcomes. Experimental and quasi-experimental studies with measurable outcomes were
prioritized, while also retaining qualitative and descriptive studies that clarified implementation or user
experience. Duplicates were removed during database compilation and again during full-text review. The
final sample included 97 studies on teacher support, including 7 with effectiveness evidence; 72 on
learner support, including 16 effectiveness studies; 7 on curriculum content development and delivery,
with no effectiveness evidence; and 2 on instructional support systems, with no effectiveness evidence.
The thinner evidence base in the latter two domains likely reflects the diffuse and embedded nature of
their effects. This guidance note prioritizes causal evidence where available, while also using selected
non-causal studies to examine design features, technological capabilities, and likely mechanisms.

title: Expert Consultations

paragraphs.text:
To complement the literature, semi-structured consultations were conducted with six EdTech professio
nals and researchers working across the following LMICs: Ghana, Kenya, Pakistan, Peru, and Senegal. The
consultations aimed to identify emerging AI applications for foundational learning that have not yet been
evaluated or published in peer-reviewed journals. Participants were selected for their experience with
foundational learning initiatives and early AI or related EdTech tools. Conducted virtually between April
and November 2025, the consultations explored the AI tools being used, the problems they aimed to
address, and the contextual factors shaping early adoption. Responses were anonymized and synthesized
alongside the literature. Several experts also pointed us to relevant prototypes, technical briefs, and
small-scale studies, which we reviewed when useful. These consultations do not provide experimental
evidence, and some of the tools discussed do not fully meet the review’s inclusion criteria. Still, because
published evidence on AI for foundational learning in LMICs remains limited, we included selected
early-stage pilots when they offered useful insight into current applications, design features, implementa
tion challenges, and preliminary outcomes.

title: Evidence Synthesis

paragraphs.text:
The evidence is organized into four domains aligned with the analytic framework: teacher support, learner
support, content development and delivery, and instructional support systems. Within each domain,
findings are grouped from empirical studies and expert consultations. From the literature, information on
the EdTech tools used was extracted, including their instructional purpose, technological capabilities,
pedagogical features, reported outcomes, and implementation factors relevant to adoption, scale, and
sustained use. The consultations added complementary insights into emerging AI applications, including
the problems these tools aimed to solve, how they were adapted to local contexts, and the lessons
emerging from implementation.

title: FINDINGS

paragraphs.text:
This section analyzes recent EdTech interventions to examine what improves foundational learning in
LMICs, for whom, through what mechanisms, and at what cost, where data allow. Drawing on experimental
and descriptive studies, the evidence is organized into four functional domains aligned with persistent
instructional challenges: (1) teacher support , (2) learner support , (3) content development and delivery ,
and (4) instructional enabling systems . Within each domain, findings are grouped by the role EdTech
played (for example, expanding TPD access and reinforcing practice), its core design features, the techno
logy capabilities used, the pedagogical traits embedded, and the outcomes achieved. Contextual factors
that influenced implementation were also examined.

title: EdTech for Teacher Support

paragraphs.text:
Table 1 summarizes the key features, functions, and observed outcomes of the seven EdTech interventions
identified through our systematic literature review. All seven improved teacher performance in foundatio
nal literacy and numeracy, and most also strengthened student learning. Their approaches differed in how
they applied technological capabilities, how teachers engaged with the tools or content, and the role each
model played within the broader TPD process. Across studies, the interventions sat within pedagogical
approaches grounded in well-established traits of effective TPD: alignment with curriculum, contextual
relevance, active learning supported through modeling and feedback, peer collaboration, sustained
support through coaching, and structured opportunities for professional reflection (Avalos 2011;
Darling-Hammond et al. 2015; Popova et al. 2016). Each intervention drew on one or more digital capabili
ties, including connectivity for remote access and communication, interactivity for reciprocal engage
ment, multimedia for varied content formats, data processing for automated tracking of use or perfor
mance, and offline storage for functionality without internet access (Huang 2001; Quota et al. 2022a).

To interpret how these interventions contributed to impact, the evidence was organized into four functio
nal categories that reflect persistent challenges in TPD across LMICs: (a) expanding access to structured,
curriculum-aligned training; (b) enhancing engagement with training content; (c) reinforcing the use of
trained teaching strategies; and (d) supporting instructional delivery through digital resources. Several
teacher-facing EdTech tools also involve curriculum development and delivery, such as preloaded lesson
plans, structured training modules, and system-level functions like remote coaching, monitoring, or digital
dashboards. These dimensions are further discussed in the sections on EdTech relevant to curriculum and
instructional support systems.

title: Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
A randomized evaluation in South Africa tested an offline tablet-based teacher training model for
underserved schools (Cilliers et al. 2022). Teachers in Grades 1–3 received tablets loaded with curricu
lum-aligned lesson plans and asynchronous training modules, supported by remote coaching through
phone calls, follow-ups, and WhatsApp peer exchange. Compared with identical content delivered
through in-person coaching to a business-as-usual control group, the virtual model cost less and impro
ved writing instruction and learners’ oral language proficiency. However, the in-person model produced
broader gains, including guided reading practices, fluency, and comprehension. These findings suggest
that offline digital tools paired with light-touch remote support can improve instruction at lower cost and
greater scale, though more intensive in-person support may produce stronger effects (see appendix 2 for
further details).

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
Supporting evidence from nonexperimental studies reinforces the relevance and feasibility of access-
oriented digital TPD models. The Teacher Education in Sub-Saharan Africa initiative developed locally
adapted resources that informed a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) used by teachers in both formal
systems and displacement settings (Kennedy and Laurillard 2019; Stutchbury et al. 2025; Wambugu
2018). Similar MOOC-based TPD programs have expanded into Southeast Asia and Latin America (Kim et
al. 2023; Mabuan et al. 2018; Sok and Bennett 2025). Other systems encourage teachers to use global
platforms like Khan Academy , Coursera , and Wikiversity to build subject-matter expertise, with embedded
modeling of instructional explanations (Evans 2021). In Nigeria, e-learning platforms are increasingly
integrated into open and distance learning programs for preservice teacher trainees, signaling rising
demand for flexible digital formats even at the entry stage of the profession (Olaniran et al. 2017).

title: The Challenge: Low Engagement and Weak Instructional Alignment in Training

paragraphs.text:
In many LMICs, teachers often lack mastery of the content they are expected to teach (Bold et al. 2017a).
Even when training is available, traditional TPD programs tend to be infrequent, top-down, and discon
nected from daily instructional realities, limiting their impact on teacher learning and uptake of new
practices (Bold et al. 2017a; Lee et al. 2020; Popova et al. 2016). Emerging EdTech tools address these
gaps by making training more interactive, modular, and instructionally relevant (Evans 2021), which are
features that promote active learning, contextualized application, and sustained engagement (Avalos
2011; Darling-Hammond et al. 2015; Popova et al. 2016). Two digital TPD interventions in our review
embedded engagement-enhancing design features.

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
Additional insights from nonexperimental studies illustrate how EdTech can be designed to strengthen
teacher engagement with training content. In Ghana, the Internet Backpack initiative used solar-powered
routers and micro-servers to deliver preloaded TPD videos to rural schools, enabling repeated, self-paced
engagement and moderated discussion forums (Appiah-Okyere 2024). In Papua New Guinea, locally
produced videos featuring ‘teachers like us’ were seen as more relatable and easier to internalize than
externally developed content (Simoncini et al. 2020). In South Africa, digital literacy courseware was
paired with in-school professional learning communities, facilitating structured peer dialogue and
collaborative problem-solving (Oakley et al. 2023). Across these contexts, EdTech models strengthened
engagement by promoting relevance, interactivity, peer support, and repetition, features that conventio
nal workshop-based training often lacks (Bold et al. 2017a).

title: The Challenge: Weak Transfer of Trained Strategies into Classroom Practice

paragraphs.text:
TPD programs often introduce new instructional strategies but do not always equip teachers to apply
them consistently in classrooms (Bold et al. 2017a). Sustained instructional change requires reinforcement
through modeling, feedback, repetition, or peer reflection (Avalos 2011; Basma and Savage 2018; Popova
et al. 2022). In underresourced schools, where managing daily routines is already demanding, teachers
often revert to familiar methods without ongoing support (Lee et al. 2020). Evidence from multiple
settings shows that sustained support, like expert mentoring or coaching, can improve teaching quality,
often outperforming one-off training delivered at centralized locations (Cilliers et al. 2019). A growing set
of EdTech tools supports this reinforcement function by helping teachers revisit and refine practices over
time through digital prompts, coaching, peer groups, or asynchronous engagement (Evans 2021).

title: Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
A randomized trial in Kenya found that weekly two-way SMS prompts, paired with structured early
reading training and scripted lessons, helped reinforce instructional routines at very low cost and were
associated with stronger teaching practices and learner gains in foundational reading skills (Jukes et al.
2017). In South Africa, a randomized evaluation showed that virtual coaching delivered through phone
calls, text messages, and tablet-based lesson resources improved lesson adherence, phonics routines, and
learner reading outcomes compared with a business-as-usual control, at slightly lower cost than in-person
coaching (Kotze et al. 2019). Together, these studies suggest that light-touch digital follow-up can help
sustain trained pedagogy in classrooms when tied to structured materials, regular prompts, and ongoing
instructional support (see appendix 2 for details).

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
Beyond the two randomized trials, a growing set of EdTech models use lightweight, low-cost tools to
reinforce instructional routines through peer collaboration and reflection. For instance, in Jordan’s Zaatari
refugee camp, WhatsApp groups enabled teachers to reflect on classroom implementation and
troubleshoot challenges collaboratively (Motteram et al. 2020). A similar initiative in Kenya’s Kakuma
refugee camp combined in-person workshops with mobile mentoring and virtual peer coaching. Teachers
received phones, data, and airtime, which allowed them to access online resources, receive real-time
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 19

support from global mentors, and share classroom practices through photos and videos (Mendenhall et
al. 2018). These tools supported both pedagogical reflection and peer-based knowledge exchange in
environments where formal TPD systems were difficult to sustain. Comparable approaches have been
documented in other settings. In South Africa, peer-led WhatsApp groups helped teachers stay focused
on instructional strategies introduced during digital literacy training and promoted accountability among
peers (Moodley 2019). In India, a mobile app supporting teacher communities of practice included
structured prompts and weekly reflection tasks aligned with formal TPD content, offering a low-cost
reinforcement mechanism (Thirumalai and Sarangapani 2023). In Ghana and Indonesia, WhatsApp and
Facebook groups served as informal professional learning spaces where teachers revisited training
content, exchanged tips, and adapted instructional routines to fit their classroom contexts (Krismanto et
al. 2024; Kwaah 2024). Although these emerging platforms have not yet been formally evaluated for
effectiveness, they illustrate how EdTech facilitates sustained pedagogical change by creating repeated,
peer-supported opportunities to revisit and apply training content, whether structured or informal,
expert-led or peer-driven, even in settings where formal systems are limited.

title: The Challenge: Limited In-Class Instructional Support and Resources

paragraphs.text:
Teachers in LMICs deliver daily lessons with minimal access to high-quality instructional tools or in-class
guidance (Bold et al. 2017a; Lee et al. 2021). Without embedded resources, even well-trained teachers may
struggle to apply instructional strategies or respond to diverse learning needs (Lee et al. 2021). EdTech
tools integrated into lesson delivery, such as audio-described videos, preloaded teaching content, and
assessment apps, provide just-in-time pedagogical support (Carter et al. 2024; Hansson et al. 2018;
Wormnæs and Sellæg 2013). Multiple EdTech interventions that were reviewed show how such tools, when
aligned with curriculum and classroom realities, can enhance instructional delivery and student learning.

title: Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
A growing body of experimental evidence shows that curriculum-aligned digital tools can strengthen
classroom instruction when they provide teachers with lesson-ready guidance and fit daily teaching
conditions. In Zambia, a structured package of preloaded tablets, projectors, scripted lesson plans, and
audiovisual guides improved teachers’ use of structured pedagogy and raised learner outcomes in literacy
and math (De Hoop et al. 2024). In Kenya, the offline ABRA platform supported lesson planning, grou
ping, and data-informed instruction through interactive literacy activities, teacher guides, and perfor
mance tracking, leading to gains in decoding, word recognition, and fluency (Abrami et al. 2016). In
Angola, the ProFuturo multimedia package combined teacher laptops, student tablets, projectors, and
offline curriculum content to support lesson delivery, monitoring, and adaptation, improving teacher
practices and learner engagement (Cardim et al. 2023). Together, these studies suggest that class
room-embedded EdTech can improve instructional delivery when it gives teachers usable, curriculum-lin
ked support during the act of teaching rather than relying on training alone (see appendix 2 for further
details).

title: Emerging AI Use Cases for Teacher Support

paragraphs.text:
Recent AI applications for teacher support extend several of the same functions described in the prece
ding sections, but through more responsive and often more individualized forms of assistance. Across
emerging use cases, AI is being used to provide on-demand instructional guidance, support lesson and
assessment preparation, generate differentiated materials, and deliver more targeted feedback on
classroom practice. These applications suggest that AI may help reduce some of the time, expertise, and
coordination constraints that limit teacher support in many LMIC systems. At the same time, the evidence
base remains thinner than for more established teacher-facing EdTech models. The examples below are
therefore included to illustrate emerging directions in practice. They should not be interpreted as equiva
lent in evidentiary strength to the rigorously evaluated interventions synthesized in the main review.
AI-Enabled On-Demand Teacher Training and Support in Sierra Leone 2

TheTeacher.AI is a WhatsApp-based chatbot that provides teachers with on-demand instructio
nal support, including help understanding curriculum content, planning lessons, and managing
classrooms (Choi et al. 2024). It uses GPT-3.5 with a contextual layer that guides the model to
give explanations and examples aligned with the low-resource realities of Sierra Leonean
classrooms, rather than generic responses. This design prevents the chatbot from suggesting
activities that rely on projectors, laptops, internet research, or other unavailable resources. Also,
because the tool operates through WhatsApp, it requires minimal data and functions reliably
even under poor network conditions. Early usage patterns from 193 teachers across 122 schools
indicate that the tool is most useful for clarifying curriculum content and planning daily lessons,
with additional applications in writing support and behavior management. Although no
learning outcomes were measured, the pilot suggests that teachers can effectively integrate AI
assistance into their preparation with minimal training on how to prompt it. Its use of existing
phones, very low data requirements, simple conversational prompts, and responses tailored to
low-resource classrooms made the tool more workable in LMICs. Nonetheless, implementation
still faced constraints in connectivity, device charging, and digital confidence, and teachers
noted the need for an offline mode. The high cost of running large language models relative to
local income also limits sustained use without subsidized access.

Differentiated Instruction via AI-Created Leveled Lessons and Materials in Mali 3

A foundational learning initiative in Mali tested whether generative AI could expand the supply
of leveled materials needed for differentiated instruction (Sidibe et al. 2025). The team trained
Claude on Mali’s curriculum, competency frameworks, and lesson templates to generate
first-draft lessons, practice tasks, and assessment items for learners at different proficiency
levels in several national languages. This process, customized specifically for Mali, enabled the
production of nearly 300 leveled lessons within one year, a volume that would have been
difficult to achieve through manual development. It also yielded curriculum-aligned tasks that
fit existing instructional sequences and could be used immediately for remediation. All AI-gene

guarantee pedagogical quality and cultural relevance.

title: Key Takeaways for Effective EdTech Tools for Teacher Support

paragraphs.text:
The evidence reviewed in this section, across experimental and observational studies, shows that effective
TPD EdTech in LMICs is defined by how well it addresses persistent instructional challenges through
purposeful design and integration. Across access-expanding, engagement-enhancing, and classroom-em
bedded models, several cross-cutting strategies emerge.

First, EdTech expands access to structured, curriculum-aligned TPD in low-resource or remote contexts
when delivery models are tailored to connectivity conditions . In low-connectivity settings, such as those
in South Africa, offline tools with preloaded content have reached teachers in remote schools, supporting
alignment with national literacy curricula. In higher-connectivity environments, online platforms such as
MOOCs and open courses can offer more flexible content access, especially for teachers seeking to
strengthen subject knowledge. AI-supported tools add a related access function by giving teachers
on-demand clarification of curriculum content or by helping draft lesson materials, as shown in Sierra
Leone. Across these models, technology adds value mostly by reducing the distance, time, and staffing
constraints that often limit teachers’ access to support. It allows aligned content, explanations, and
examples to reach teachers more consistently than workshop-only models, especially where repeated
in-person delivery is difficult to sustain.

title: 22 | How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries

paragraphs.text:
Second, EdTech enhances teacher engagement when relevant content is paired with features that
promote active learning, reflection, and participation . Interactive platforms such as ABRA or Canvas-
based courses support deeper learning in connected settings. In lower-connectivity environments,
engagement can be sustained through the use of offline materials supplemented by remote coaching or
peer-to-peer exchange. AI tools also contributed to engagement by enabling teachers to ask specific
questions and receive contextually appropriate explanations or draft materials that they adapted for use.
The mechanism here is not digitization itself but the shift from passive exposure to more active forms of
participation. Digital tools can make teacher learning more engaging by enabling repeated interaction
with content, immediate response, self-paced review, and more regular opportunities for reflection or
exchange than one-off workshops usually provide. In all cases, effective digital tools embed these
engagement features in ways that connect directly to classroom realities so that the time teachers spend
in digital environments reinforces rather than distracts from instructional practice.

Third, EdTech reinforces new instructional practices by providing repeated prompts and structured
opportunities for follow-up . Tools that combine structured pedagogy with ongoing prompts, whether
through SMS, virtual coaching, or peer discussion forums, help sustain teacher focus and promote
instructional change. These reinforcement mechanisms are most effective when they operate within
regular school routines and remain closely tied to curriculum expectations, particularly in resource-limited
classrooms where ongoing support is scarce. Here, technology adds value by extending support beyond
the initial training event. Rather than relying on teachers to remember and independently apply new prac
tices, digital prompts, coaching touchpoints, and peer exchanges help keep key routines visible, timely,
and easier to revisit during implementation.

Finally, EdTech strengthens teaching when tools are embedded directly into lesson delivery . Tools such
as scripted lesson guides, audio prompts, and multimedia resources provide real-time scaffolds that help
teachers introduce new content, maintain pacing, and respond to student needs. In systems with limited
supervision, these tools often serve as de facto coaching. AI-supported planning and content-generation
tools in Indonesia and Mali complemented these instructional aids by reducing preparation burdens and
expanding the supply of leveled or draft materials for classroom use. When aligned with national curricula
and responsive to classroom constraints, these tools improve coherence in instruction across classrooms.
Their value lies in reducing the burden on teachers to translate training into practice on their own. By
carrying lesson structure, modeled routines, or draft materials into the act of teaching, these tools make
effective practice easier to enact more consistently, especially where teachers have limited preparation
time or weak access to ongoing instructional support.

Together, these insights suggest that effective EdTech is not a digital substitute for print materials or
in-person workshops, which still dominate TPD systems in LMICs (Bold et al. 2017). Instead, it serves as a
support mechanism grounded in pedagogical soundness, defined as the purposeful integration of
curriculum-aligned content, modeled strategies, opportunities for practice, and support for classroom
application. Its contribution is strongest when digital features solve specific delivery problems that
non-digital approaches struggle to address consistently, such as maintaining follow-up across distance,
providing reusable models of practice, or reducing the workload involved in preparation, adaptation, and
ongoing reinforcement.

title: EdTech for Learner Support

paragraphs.text:
Table 2 summarizes the key features, functions, and observed outcomes of the 14 student-facing EdTech
interventions that were found to be effective. All interventions improved literacy, numeracy, or both,
though impact and cost-effectiveness varied. The models reflected essential features of effective learning:
curriculum alignment, structured practice, active and motivational engagement, and scaffolding to
support progression toward mastery (Black and Wiliam 2010; Darling-Hammond et al. 2015, 2022; Hattie
2010). Each also leveraged digital capabilities, such as connectivity, interactivity, multimedia, data
processing, and offline storage, consistent with those applied in teacher-focused EdTech solutions. The
evidence is organized into four functional categories observed in learner-focused EdTech tools: (a) expan
ding learner access to curriculum-aligned content where books and materials are scarce; (b) providing
structured practice to build mastery of foundational subskills; (c) sustaining learner engagement through
active and multisensory approaches; and (d) substituting or augmenting formal instruction in contexts
where school or teacher capacity is limited. It is noteworthy that while each intervention is illustrated by
its most evident feature, several integrate more than one function.

title: The Challenge: Uneven Access to Core Curriculum and Reading Materials

paragraphs.text:
Across LMIC primary schools, the average pupil-to-textbook ratio is 3.5:1, leaving nearly four students to
share a single book, far from conducive to effective learning (World Bank 2022). Inefficiencies in supply
chains, high printing costs, and weak distribution systems compound the challenge. Even when materials
are produced, they frequently fail to reach classrooms or homes in sufficient quantities (Lee et al. 2024).
Four EdTech models from our review helped address these issues through e-readers, SMS story segments,
and interactive audio lessons in schools and homes, even where connectivity and infrastructure are
limited. Each is described in greater detail below.

title: Experimental Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
Across four experimental studies, technology-supported literacy interventions improved early reading
when they expanded access to structured practice through accessible devices. In Kenya, e-readers added
to the PRIMR program improved English and Kiswahili oral reading fluency by 0.17–0.26 SD and increased
the share of learners meeting fluency benchmarks by about 12 percentage points, though the model was
much more expensive than teacher- or supervisor-facing tablets (Piper et al. 2016). Another Kenyan trial
found that M-Shule, an adaptive SMS platform, raised Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) reading
scores by 0.46 SD among Grade 1–3 learners (Jordan et al. 2025). Results from Zambia and Bangladesh
point in the same direction. In Zambia, an SMS program that sent stories and questions to caregivers
improved children’s reading outcomes, including oral reading fluency and word recognition (Ome and
Menendez 2022). In Bangladesh, a feature phone-based IVR program delivered large gains in literacy and
numeracy during school closures, while an added leadership module showed no effect (Wang et al. 2023).
Overall, the evidence suggests that low-cost tools such as SMS and IVR can improve foundational learning
at scale when they deliver structured content through technologies that households already use (see
appendix 2 for details).

title: The Challenge: Limited Opportunities for Structured, Feedback-Rich Learner Practice During Instruction

paragraphs.text:
Classroom instruction in LMICs relies frequently on whole-class teaching with minimal time for individual
student practice or remedial support (Lee et al. 2020; Sakata et al. 2022). Large class sizes, scarce
materials, and teacher training traditions that emphasize authoritative delivery reinforce this approach
(Sakata et al. 2022). While whole-class instruction may be suitable for some instances, balancing it with
individualized attention is also important. This is because heavy reliance on whole-class, teacher-centric
instruction diverges from how children develop foundational reading and math skills, which require
repeated and scaffolded practice to build fluency in decoding, spelling, and basic number operations that
support later comprehension and problem-solving (Fuson et al. 2015; NRP 2000). Three EdTech tools in
our review directly addressed this gap by providing repeated, feedback-rich exercises that build automa
ticity in decoding, spelling, and basic number operations with demonstrated effectiveness.

title: Experimental Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
Across Kenya, Malawi, and India, experimental studies show that EdTech can improve foundational literacy
when it delivers structured practice with feedback and aligns with classroom learning. In Kenya, ABRA, a
multimedia literacy program used in school computer labs, improved passage comprehension and
listening comprehension and raised performance on national exams (Abrami et al. 2016). In Malawi,
tablet-based onebillion apps produced clear gains in early reading skills, including letter naming, syllable
reading, word and nonword reading, passage fluency, and comprehension, while also supporting stronger
math outcomes (Pitchford et al. 2019). Evidence from India suggests a narrower but still important role
for EdTech. Across three trials, GraphoLearn consistently improved letter-sound knowledge and, when
paired with structured phonics instruction, also strengthened nonword reading and spelling (Bora et al.
2024; Patel et al. 2018, 2022). However, effects rarely transferred to broader literacy outcomes such as
fluency, vocabulary, or comprehension, especially when the game operated separately from regular
instruction. Taken together, the studies suggest that EdTech is most effective when it reinforces core
teaching rather than functioning as a stand-alone tool (see appendix 2 for details).

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
While not causal, dozens of studies corroborate experimental evidence that EdTech helps create struc
tured opportunities for practicing and mastering foundational learning skills. In Kenya, the Emergent
Literacy in Mathematics software offered step-by-step mathematics tasks and improved Grade 1 numeracy
outcomes (Lysenko et al. 2022). In Pakistan and Bangladesh, the Footsteps2Brilliance platform delivered
individualized early literacy games aligned with national curricula, resulting in significant gains in Early
Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA) measured literacy (Pynnönen et al. 2022). In Morocco, the TaRL-BOT
system used AI-based speech recognition to provide instant, individualized feedback on early-grade
reading fluency (Bachiri et al. 2024). Game-based tools reinforced subskills through engaging repetition:
GraphoGame improved letter-sound recognition and spelling in Zambia (Nshimbi et al. 2020), and a
multimedia adventure game boosted numeracy skills in Indonesia (Rohendi 2019). Specialized and

adaptive applications further extend this repertoire. A mobile app for preschool children with dyslexia in
Pakistan repeated tracing and writing tasks until mastery, enhancing handwriting performance (Tariq and
Latif 2016). Low-connectivity tools also provided structured practice where the internet was limited: An
IVR phone system in Côte d’Ivoire supported home-based French phonological awareness through
structured call-in lessons (Chatterjee et al. 2020). Together, these interventions suggest that EdTech can
offer sustained, feedback-driven practice in LMIC settings, helping learners build fluency in foundational

title: The Challenge: Limited Variety in Classroom Learning Experiences

paragraphs.text:
Beyond limiting practice, traditional teacher-led instruction in LMIC schools restricts how actively students
engage with lessons (Sakata et al. 2022). Evidence is rich that children build stronger skills when they
read, listen, and interact with content in ways that capture attention and deepen processing (Guthrie and
Wigfield 2000; Hattie 2010). Three EdTech tools from our review embed active and varied engagement in
learning through synchronized reading and listening, interactive vocabulary practice, and multisensory
textbook lessons, with evidence of improved outcomes.

title: Experimental Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
Additional experimental evidence from Uganda and South Africa points to more targeted benefits from
relatively simple digital reading tools. In Uganda, SiMBi, a tablet-based reading-while-listening app,
produced modest but significant gains in Grade 3 reading fluency compared with silent print reading,
suggesting that synchronized audio–text support can strengthen fluency even with brief daily use
(Friedland et al. 2017). In South Africa, an interactive isiXhosa e-book improved Grade 1 learners’ receptive
vocabulary, expressive sentence use, and depth of word knowledge, with gains sustained over time (Klop
et al. 2018). Together, these studies suggest that even short, supplemental EdTech interventions can
improve specific literacy skills when they provide structured exposure to text, audio, and guided practice
(see appendix 2 for details).

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
Supporting evidence from nonexperimental studies further illustrates how EdTech can foster active and
sustained learner engagement through diverse formats. In Jordan, iPads loaded with interactive math
applications created multisensory lessons that students described as more enjoyable and motivating
compared to traditional methods (Al-Mashaqbeh 2016). In Ecuador, an augmented reality system with
motion sensors enabled children to interact with virtual math objects through natural gestures, providing
a playful, kinesthetic approach that captured attention and encouraged participation (Lozada-Yánez et al.
2019). Other models tested under different themes also highlight engagement features: Gamified literacy
and numeracy platforms, such as GraphoGame in Zambia (Nshimbi et al. 2020) and Footsteps2Brilliance
in Pakistan and Bangladesh (Pynnönen et al. 2022), were designed to sustain motivation through play,
while interactive radio instruction in Nigeria kept learners actively responding to characters and prompts
during lessons (Gever et al. 2024). Overall, these cases suggest that embedding motivational design,
whether through multisensory input, interactivity, or game mechanics, offers practical ways to sustain
learner engagement in settings where classroom instruction is often rote and teacher centric.

Student E-Readers within Structured Pedagogy in Kenya (Piper et al. 2016)

E-readers loaded with 100+ digital books (textbooks and storybooks) were provided to Grade 2 learners as part of a structured
pedagogy program (Primary Math and Reading, PRIMR). Learners used them daily during school hours as part of regular lessons
alongside print books, while teachers continued with regular PRIMR lesson delivery. Teacher and supervisor tablet arms were

PRACTICE
Computer-Assisted Reading Game (GraphoLearn Rime) in India (Bora et al. 2024; Patel et al. 2018, 2022)

Offline computer-assisted reading game teaching English letter-sound links, word-part (rime-unit) patterns, and word recognition
through interactive visual and auditory tasks with repeated practice and instant feedback. Students played 15–30 minutes per day
over 5–8 weeks on tablets with headphones. Early pilots (2018, 2022) delivered GraphoLearn as a stand-alone pull-out activity,
supervised by a researcher and not aligned with classroom instruction. The refined version (2024) integrated GraphoLearn with
structured classroom phonics, with teachers reinforcing content through explanations, modeling, and feedback. Control groups
played a math game to equalize screen time. *Cost not reported. Samples for the 2024 study: 1 school and 60 students. Samples
for the 2018 study: 1 school and 31 students. Samples for the 2022 study: 1 school and 136 students in total.

title: The Challenge: Lack of Structured Foundational Learning Instruction Even Among Enrolled Learners

paragraphs.text:
In many LMIC schools, millions of children face a dual challenge: Those enrolled in school often receive too
little structured, effective instruction to build foundational skills, while many others have no access to
formal schooling at all. Where schools exist, large classes, scarce materials, and limited teacher training
constrain what teachers can deliver (Bold et al. 2017a, 2017b). Even well-intentioned teachers frequently
lack the content knowledge, pedagogical support, or tools to teach diverse groups effectively (Lee et al.
2020). Instructional time is often lost to repetition, unproductive routines, or lessons pitched at levels
misaligned with students’ abilities (Bold et al. 2017b). In other settings, particularly in remote or conflict-af
fected areas, children remain out of school with no functioning classrooms or trained teachers available
(Ferráns et al. 2021). Three EdTech models in our review respond to these structural and instructional gaps
by substituting or supplementing traditional schooling with technology-delivered, scripted lessons. Each
provides structured content when teachers are unavailable or underprepared, or when schools do not exist
at all, through offline digital substitution, broadcast substitution, and self-directed tablet learning.

title: Experimental Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
Further experimental evidence shows that technology can improve foundational learning when it is
embedded in structured delivery models, though effects vary sharply by design and cost. In Zambia,
eSchool 360 used offline scripted lessons, tablets, and projectors in community schools and produced
meaningful gains in reading, math, vocabulary, and test performance, especially in the randomized
evaluation, suggesting that technology can help compensate for weak instructional capacity when paired
with facilitation, training, and supervision (De Hoop et al. 2024; Schling and Winters 2018). In Ghana,
MGCubed used satellite-transmitted lessons to improve math and literacy in rural schools, but its high
infrastructure costs made it less cost-effective than simpler non-EdTech alternatives (Johnston and Ksoll
2022). In Tanzania, KitkitTM School, a tablet-based self-learning program, improved early numeracy skills in
a small rural trial, especially in number discrimination, addition, and subtraction (Lee and Choi 2020).
Together, these studies suggest that technology can raise learning in low-resource settings, but its value
depends heavily on delivery model, instructional integration, and cost (see appendix 2 for details).

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
Additional nonexperimental evidence highlights broader trends in how EdTech substitutes for or supple
ments classroom instruction in LMICs when teaching is absent, disrupted, or insufficient. In Sudan,
E-Learning Sudan (ELS) provided out-of-school children with the full primary mathematics curriculum
through a self-paced digital game, serving as a stand-alone substitute for formal schooling (Stubbé et al.
2016). In Belize, national radio broadcasts replaced classroom lessons during COVID-19 closures, giving
remote learners continued access to teacher-recorded instruction without internet (Kirshner 2020). In
South Africa, the Bridges to the Future Initiative (BFI) complemented classroom teaching with compu
ter-based literacy sessions in multiple local languages, reinforcing skills such as phonemic awareness and
comprehension (Castillo and Wagner 2019). Interactive radio instruction improved literacy skills among
out-of-school children living in refugee camps in Nigeria (Gever et al. 2024). While not causal, these
studies underscore that EdTech can partially step into the role of the teacher where traditional delivery
falls short.

title: Emerging AI Use Cases for Learner Support

paragraphs.text:
Similar to the trend seen for teacher support, AI applications increasingly target direct learner support.
These emerging use cases deliver individualized tutoring, multisensory reading scaffolds, and adaptive
practice. Delivery models range from whole-class projection to independent, offline local servers, reflec
ting different approaches to acute infrastructure constraints. While some platforms demonstrate robust
experimental impacts on learning outcomes, others remain early-stage pilots testing new delivery
mechanisms. The examples below illustrate how AI expands differentiated learning when integrated
strategically into existing school environments.
AI-Enhanced Personalized Adaptive Learning with Mindspark in India 4

Mindspark is a personalized digital learning platform that strengthens foundational learning by
diagnosing each learner’s level and adjusting tasks accordingly (Mona Foundation 2025). Its
earlier adaptive version showed meaningful effects in a randomized trial in India. Students with
access to the program scored 0.39–60 SD higher in reading and math compared to their peers
over 4.5 months (Muralidharan et al. 2019). The program has recently integrated generative AI
to expand its capacity for differentiation in low-resource settings. The AI-enabled system
generates leveled questions, explanations, writing feedback, and voice-supported reading
practice, while the adaptive engine continues to tailor tasks to each learner’s pace and needs.
These features provide teachers with ready-made, differentiated materials, reducing the burden
of producing individualized practice. The platform is used in government schools and provides
real-time dashboards to guide grouping and targeted support. While the new AI components
have not yet been experimentally evaluated, early implementation suggests that they facilitate
content localization and leveled practice and reduce dependence on large coaching teams,
provided that reliable devices and connectivity are ensured (Mona Foundation 2025).

A randomized trial in India evaluated the AI-powered RTM platform with 33,000 primary
students, including third graders, who had limited exposure to English outside of school
(Srinivasan and Murthy 2021). RTM digitized government-prescribed textbooks and read them

paragraphs.text:
aloud while highlighting words, showing pronunciation cues, and linking vocabulary to images,
providing learners with consistent multisensory input. Regular in-class teachers, after brief
training, used RTM during regular English or ICT periods about three times per week ( ≈ 75
sessions annually), projecting from a single shared computer. In its initial version, RTM delivered
whole-class cues, such as highlighting, audio, and images, without providing individualized
feedback or adaptive correction. The platform worked directly with official textbooks; no new
materials were introduced. Control schools continued with business-as-usual instruction. After
one year, RTM students outperformed controls by 20–40 percent in letter recognition, word
recognition, vocabulary, and comprehension, with gains across all proficiency levels. A two-year
follow-up showed sustained improvements of 21–22 percent. These results suggest that
large-scale, AI-enabled multisensory tools can enhance literacy outcomes within existing
systems in low-resource contexts, although further testing is needed to assess the added value
of adaptive, individualized features before scaling.
Experimental Evidence from AI Tutoring with Teacher Guidance in Nigeria

A randomized evaluation in Edo State, Nigeria, tested whether generative AI could expand
individualized learning opportunities under teacher supervision in a low-resource public school
context (De Simone et al. 2025). The intervention involved first-year senior secondary students
and was designed to address persistent learning gaps in English. Students participated in two
90-minute after-school sessions per week in school computer labs, working in pairs on curricu
lum-aligned English grammar and writing tasks using Microsoft Copilot, powered by GPT-4 at
the time. Teachers introduced lesson topics, guided students’ use of structured prompts,
monitored AI-student interactions, and facilitated reflection activities, positioning the AI as a
complement to instruction rather than a substitute for teacher support. The randomized
controlled trial found statistically significant gains of 0.23 SD in English and 0.31 SD in a
combined assessment of English, digital skills, and AI knowledge. This suggests that AI can
support language learning when it is embedded in structured, teacher-mediated practice that
gives learners more opportunities to write, revise, and receive responsive feedback than regular
classroom instruction alone.

A clear pattern across these learner-facing applications is that AI’s effectiveness requires its adaptation to
local infrastructure and integration with teacher-led instruction. Regardless of the delivery model, systems
need to prevent essential hardware bottlenecks to enable student access. Furthermore, the examples
show that AI tools do not replace educators. Rather, they function best as active complements to instruc
tion, requiring teacher mediation to translate automated feedback and adaptive practice into measurable
learning gains.
