title: Supporting Instructional Delivery through Digital Resources

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Preloaded Digital Tools in Zambia

A randomized evaluation in Zambia tested a structured EdTech package designed to support
daily instruction in rural community schools, including Grade 3 classrooms (De Hoop et al.
2024). Teachers received solar-powered tablets and projectors preloaded with curricu
lum-aligned materials: scripted lesson plans, audiovisual teaching guides, and student
workbooks in local languages. Tablets provided daily lesson prompts and instructional cues,
while projectors displayed modeled routines and core concepts to the whole class. These tools
aimed to help teachers introduce new content, pace phonics and math lessons, and manage
group activities more effectively. Weekly in-person coaching sessions reinforced tool use and
addressed classroom-level challenges. Compared to a business-as-usual control group,
intervention teachers demonstrated stronger use of structured pedagogy, including more
participatory methods (0.21 SD). Their students achieved significantly higher outcomes in
literacy, including letter decoding, fluency, reading comprehension (0.40 SD), and vocabulary
knowledge (0.25 SD), and early math skills such as number recognition and computation (0.21
SD). These results suggest that curriculum-embedded EdTech tools can enhance instructional
quality and learning outcomes when paired with modest in-person support.
Experimental Evidence from Offline Courseware and Instructional Tools in Kenya

A randomized evaluation in Kenya examined the use of ABRACADABRA (ABRA) , an offline digi
tal literacy tool integrated into Grade 1 classrooms (Abrami et al. 2016). Teachers received iBook
laptops preloaded with the ABRA software, which included 32 interactive reading activities and
narrated digital stories designed to improve phonics, fluency, and comprehension. The platform
also featured a teacher module with scripted lesson plans, printable teaching aids, demonstra
tion videos, a performance dashboard for tracking student progress, and a wiki-based peer
community. Teachers used the tools to plan lessons, deliver modeled instruction, group
students by ability, and adjust content pacing based on learner performance. The program
operated entirely offline, enabling consistent classroom use without reliance on internet
connectivity. Compared to business-as-usual classrooms, teachers in the intervention group
demonstrated stronger use of ABRA in planning and grouping, improved literacy content
knowledge, and more frequent use of student data to inform instruction. Students in ABRA
classrooms achieved significantly greater gains in letter decoding (0.29 SD), word recognition
(0.23 SD), and reading fluency (0.21 SD). These findings highlight how well-structured digital
courseware, paired with teacher-facing supports, can strengthen instructional delivery and
improve early literacy outcomes in resource-constrained environments.
Experimental Evidence from Multimedia Classroom Packages in Angola

A randomized evaluation in Angola assessed the ProFuturo program, which equipped class
rooms with a multimedia digital package to support daily instruction (Cardim et al. 2023). Each
classroom received student tablets, a teacher laptop, and a projector preloaded with offline
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 61

content across subjects. Lesson materials included interactive multimedia resources aligned with
the national curriculum. Teachers used the projector to present new concepts and model
instructional routines to the whole class. Students used tablets for independent exploration and
practice, while teachers accessed performance dashboards on laptops to monitor engagement
and identify learners who needed support. The system also included authoring tools that allowed
teachers to modify lesson pacing and tasks based on classroom needs, all without requiring
internet access. Compared to standard instruction, teachers using ProFuturo tools more
frequently (0.79 SD), prepared lessons more often (0.11 SD), allocated more time to instruction
(0.05 SD), and monitored student learning more consistently (0.07 SD). Student outcomes also
improved: learners reported spending more time reading (0.23 SD), having greater interest in
mathematics (0.20 SD), and experiencing stronger peer collaboration (0.21 SD). These results
show that comprehensive, classroom-based EdTech packages can enhance teacher practice and
student engagement when tools are well integrated and instructionally aligned.

title: Expanding Learner Access to Instructional Content

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Student E-Readers in Kenya

A randomized trial in Kenya tested three ICT-based add-ons to a structured pedagogy program
(PRIMR), involving 1,580 Grade 2 learners across 80 schools in Kisumu County (Piper et al.
2016). The base program already provided teacher training, structured lesson plans, pupil
books, and coaching by government instructional supervisors, known as teacher advisory
center (TAC) tutors. The main student-facing intervention supplied e-readers loaded with over
100 digital books, giving learners daily access to textbooks and storybooks otherwise unavai
lable. Two other models provided tablets to teachers (with lesson plans, grouping tools, and
quizzes) and to TAC tutors (with digitized observation tools and guides). All three ICT models
produced significant reading gains compared to 20 control schools ( ≈ 400 learners) receiving
regular instruction. In the student e-reader arm, English and Kiswahili oral reading fluency
improved (0.17–0.26 SD), and the share of learners meeting national fluency benchmarks
increased by about 12 percentage points. Costs varied sharply: TAC tutor tablets added US$0.10
per student, teacher tablets US$3 per student, and student e-readers US$40 per student. These
findings show that direct student access to digital books can improve reading outcomes in
low-resource settings, though relative cost-effectiveness depends on whether technology is
placed in the hands of students, teachers, or instructional supervisors.

A randomized trial in Kenya tested the M-Shule platform, which delivered adapted Tusome
literacy lessons via SMS to Grade 1–3 learners (Jordan et al. 2025). The intervention was
implemented as a supplemental learning tool alongside regular schooling after COVID-19
reopening, with learners engaging from home or the community. Learners received short
lessons and quizzes by text message, and their answers were automatically logged and scored
by the system. Based on performance, the platform advanced learners to harder content or
repeated easier review material, ensuring progression and remedial support without teacher
grading. The platform functioned without internet or smartphones, and parents received
supportive reminders. Content was offered in English and Kiswahili as grade-level booster

reopening, with learners engaging from home or the community. Learners received short
lessons and quizzes by text message, and their answers were automatically logged and scored
by the system. Based on performance, the platform advanced learners to harder content or
repeated easier review material, ensuring progression and remedial support without teacher
grading. The platform functioned without internet or smartphones, and parents received
supportive reminders. Content was offered in English and Kiswahili as grade-level booster

A randomized trial in Zambia’s Eastern Province tested Makhalidwe Athu (‘our culture’ in
Chinyanja), an SMS-based program, designed to improve reading among Grade 2–3 learners
(Ome and Menendez 2022). Over nine months, caregivers received short story segments via
basic mobile phones, broken into 160-character messages with comprehension questions. They
were expected to read these with their children three times per week, supported by SMS
reminders and monthly facilitator meetings. Voice messages were also offered but were more
costly and less central. The intervention required only basic phones, parental engagement, and
minimal facilitation, with no internet or school-based resources, while classroom instruction
continued as usual. Treatment learners were compared to control peers in similar schools who
did not receive SMS content. Results showed significant improvements in literacy: Treated
children improved 0.19 SD on a composite reading index, 0.28 SD in oral reading fluency (3.35

also read more frequently at home, both alone and with caregivers, though attitudes toward

accounting for about 15 percent of costs. These findings show that SMS-based story delivery,
paired with caregiver engagement, can improve foundational literacy cost-effectively in

Experimental Evidence from Low-Tech Remote Learning in Bangladesh

A three-arm cluster-randomized trial in rural Bangladesh evaluated a feature phone-based
remote learning intervention for primary-age children during COVID-19 school closures (Wang
et al. 2023). The program used IVR technology to deliver 60 prerecorded audio lessons in
Bangla, English, and numeracy. Lessons followed an interactive audio instruction format that
prompted learners to answer questions and complete exercises. Families accessed lessons
through a toll-free number at any time, with caregivers facilitating learning using simple
guidebooks and alphabet sheets. A subset of children also received 15 leadership lessons. To
encourage participation, the program offered small weekly prizes (mobile airtime worth about
US$3, roughly 250 Bangladeshi taka) to 15 randomly selected quiz winners. The trial involved
1,763 children ages 5–10 across 90 villages, randomly assigned to two treatment groups or a
control group. After 15 weeks, children in treatment villages scored 0.60–0.63 SD higher than
controls. Literacy improved by ~0.55 SD, with significant gains in Bangla and English letter
recognition, word reading, and sentence comprehension. Numeracy improved by ~0.53–0.54
SD, including number identification, basic addition and subtraction, and simple problem-sol
ving. Oral vocabulary also increased (0.25 SD). The leadership module produced no measurable
impact on leadership or socioemotional skills, and effects on grit, growth mindset, and empathy
were null. The findings show that a low-cost IVR platform can substantially improve foundatio
nal literacy and numeracy in low-resource settings where high-tech options are not feasible.

title: Supporting Repeated, Individualized Practice for Skill Mastery

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Multimedia Interactive Literacy Software in Kenya

A randomized trial in Kenya tested ABRA , a free web-based literacy software designed to
strengthen early reading skills (Abrami et al. 2016). ABRA provided 32 interactive multimedia
activities on alphabetics, fluency, comprehension, and writing, supported by story texts and
student-generated narratives. Students used ABRA in weekly 90-minute computer lab sessions
during regular English classes, with low-performing learners receiving additional remedial
access. Because the software required internet connectivity, implementation depended on
school computer labs with online access, though offline print worksheets and teacher iBooks
were also available to support lesson preparation. To support implementation, teachers
received a three-day training, digital lesson plans, and ongoing online coaching, with the
software providing embedded tutorials and progress reporting tools. After 13 weeks, ABRA
students showed significant literacy gains in passage comprehension (0.32 SD) and listening
comprehension (0.54 SD). They also outperformed peers on national exams in English, math,
science, and social studies.
Experimental Evidence from Interactive Learning Apps in Malawi

A study in Malawi evaluated the impact of two interactive tablet applications from the onebil
lion © suite on early mathematics and reading, using randomized controlled trials with primary
learners in Grades 1–3 (Pitchford et al. 2019). The apps presented a structured sequence of
topics through game-like activities, guided by a virtual teacher who provided instructions in
Chichewa. Features included interactive practice, immediate feedback, quizzes, and motivatio
nal rewards. Learners used tablets with headphones individually in school-based learning
centers during school hours, supported by facilitators who managed logistics but did not
provide instruction. The math trial included 256 Grade 1–2 students who used the app for an
average of nine hours over 14 months, compared to their peers who received only regular
classroom instruction. Students using the app achieved moderate gains in number identifica
tion, number discrimination, addition, subtraction, and pattern recognition ( η p2 ≈ 0.04–0.06).
Crucially, the intervention prevented the gender disparities in math observed in control schools,
where boys typically outperformed girls. The reading trial involved 360 Grade 1–3 students who
used a literacy app for 60 minutes daily across 14 weeks (up to 70 hours). Compared to
controls, treatment learners achieved medium-to-large improvements ( η p2 ≈ 0.05–0.09) in
letter naming, syllable reading, word and nonword reading, passage fluency, and comprehen
sion. However, girls continued to outperform boys, suggesting that preexisting gender gaps in
reading persisted. These findings indicate that interactive tablet apps enhance foundational
math and reading skills in low-resource classrooms, with a stronger potential to equalize gender
outcomes in mathematics than in reading.

such as vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension did not improve beyond phonics instruction

spelling skills. However, the small samples (30, 136, and 54 students), short exposure periods,
researcher-supervised implementation, and nonstandardized measures limit generalizability.

title: Fostering Active and Sustained Learner Engagement

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from a Reading-While-Listening App in Uganda

A randomized trial in rural Uganda tested SiMBi , a tablet-based reading-while-listening app,
with Grade 3 students (Friedland et al. 2017). SiMBi paired children’s books in PDF with audio
narration, allowing students to follow the text while listening through headphones. The app
incorporated effective learning strategies by combining visual and auditory input, as well as
modeling fluent reading, although it lacked interactive feedback. Students used the tablets for
10 minutes daily over 30 days as a supplemental activity alongside regular classroom instruc
tion. This group was compared to a control group that read the same passages silently in print
for the same duration, while both groups continued regular classroom instruction. After one
month, SiMBi students made modest but statistically significant gains in reading fluency, rising
from 40.8 to 43.3 words correct per minute compared to 35.3 to 36.8 in the control group (an
advantage of about one additional word per minute on average). Although based on a small-
scale pilot with 46 students, the trial provides early but causal evidence that short, low-inten
sity use of synchronized audio–text tools can improve fluency more than silent print reading,
even in low-resource settings with limited prior exposure to technology.

development among isiXhosa-speaking Grade 1 learners (Klop et al. 2018). Delivered on
Android tablets, the e-book combined a story with text-to-speech isiXhosa narration, illustra
tions, and quizzes with immediate feedback. Fifteen Tier 2 target words (nouns, verbs, adjec

title: Substituting or Augmenting Classroom Instruction

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Technology-Delivered Instruction in Rural Zambia

Two evaluations in rural Zambia tested the eSchool 360 program, a computer-assisted instruc
tion (CAI) model implemented by Impact Network in community schools (De Hoop et al. 2024;
Schling and Winters 2018). Zambia’s community schools are typically staffed by untrained local
teachers with limited materials, which limits instructional quality. eSchool 360 substituted
teacher-led instruction with offline digital scripts and projected lessons, while retaining
teachers as facilitators. Schools were equipped with solar power, projectors, and tablets
preloaded with the national curriculum. Facilitators guided students through daily scripted
lessons and received regular training and supervision, with additional measures including class
size limits, attendance monitoring, and community involvement through Parent-Teacher
Associations.

The first evaluation (Schling and Winters 2018) used a quasi-experimental design with 571
Grade 1–2 learners across 15 schools: 5 eSchools , 5 untreated community schools, and 5
government schools staffed by trained teachers. After 18 months, eSchool learners achieved
similar gains to government school peers in number recognition (+15 percentage points) and
nonword decoding (+3 points), despite starting behind at baseline. Learners in untreated
community schools did not catch up. No impacts were observed on broader literacy, numeracy,
or grade progression. Beyond learning outcomes, the program also increased enrollment (+7.5
percentage points) and attendance (+0.36 days per week). These catch-up gains were achieved
at about US$3 per learner monthly, roughly one-third the cost of government schools. Yet, the
findings remain indicative rather than definitive because of the small sample, nonrandom
school selection, and a difference-in-differences design that only partly addresses bias.

A subsequent cluster-randomized trial with 1,865 Grade 1 learners across 63 schools (De
Hoop et al. 2024) found larger and more robust gains after 14 months: +0.40 SD in reading
(EGRA composite including print knowledge, letter-sound knowledge, nonword decoding,
reading fluency, and comprehension), +0.21 SD in math (Early Grade Math Assessment, EGMA,
composite including rational counting, number recognition, quantity discrimination, and pattern
completion), +0.25 SD in oral vocabulary, and +0.15 SD on the Zambian Achievement Test.
Treatment-on-the-treated effects were even higher, with reading gains above 0.60 SD.
Together, these studies indicate that embedding technology into a structured pedagogy
package with trained facilitators and community ownership can raise foundational skills in
highly resource-constrained settings, though longer-term cost-effectiveness and sustainability
require further study.

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Satellite-Transmitted Instruction in Ghana

A cluster-randomized trial in Ghana tested MGCubed , a satellite-based program delivering daily
English and math lessons to students in Grades 2–5 in 70 rural primary schools (Johnston and
Ksoll 2022). Expert ‘studio teachers’ in Accra broadcast live to 10–12 classrooms, while in-class
teachers acted as facilitators, operating equipment, managing classrooms, grading work, and
supporting students when broadcasts failed. In the second year, facilitators grouped students
by ability in English to provide targeted support. The program required substantial infrastruc
ture, including solar power, video equipment, and training and stipends for facilitators. The
satellite lessons were fully integrated into regular school hours, replacing part of teacher-led
instruction. Compared to control schools (n = 77) with regular teacher-led lessons, MGCubed
produced math gains of 0.20–0.21 SD after one year and 0.26–0.27 SD after two years. Literacy
effects emerged more slowly, with a 0.33 SD improvement on the EGRA composite by Year 2,
very large for letter naming and decoding, modest for oral fluency, and none for comprehen
sion. Gains were consistent across teachers and districts, and math improvements persisted one
year later. Costs were high. About 30 percent of total two-year expenses went to upfront
infrastructure (studios, equipment, solar power, and satellite links). Even with a 7–8-year
lifespan to spread these costs, the program delivered only ≈ 0.12 SD of learning gain per US$100
per student. This was well below the return from non-EdTech approaches, such as structured
teacher training, which cost about US$10–11 per student per year and delivered ≈ 0.36 SD of
learning gain per US$100 (Duflo et al. 2020). This means that while satellite instruction can
improve foundational learning in rural schools, it is only financially viable if infrastructure is
shared across more learners and services.
Experimental Evidence from a Tablet-based Self-learning Suite in Tanzania

A randomized trial in rural Tanzania evaluated Kitkit TM School, a self-directed tablet learning
suite combining interactive activities, digital books, videos, and tools for independent use
among Grade 1 students (Lee and Choi 2020). The program included nine curriculum-aligned
modules on number recognition, comparison, and basic operations, with gamification features
such as progress tracking and rewards to encourage daily practice. Children used tablets with
headphones in a dedicated classroom. A local assistant managed devices but provided no
instructions. The app operated offline with periodic data uploads. The intervention group (n =
30) replaced regular math lessons with daily 20-minute sessions over 46 days. The control
group (n = 31) continued with standard math classes. After the intervention, learners in the
treatment group showed significant gains in number identification, quantity discrimination,
addition, subtraction, and missing-number tasks, with greater improvements than controls in
number discrimination (0.58 SD), addition (0.78 SD), and subtraction (0.75 SD). Students could
identify numbers up to 100, compare magnitudes, and perform simple operations; however,
regrouping and complex missing-number tasks remained challenging. These findings show that
a short, game-based intervention can improve early numeracy in low-resource classrooms, even

school with 61 children) limits generalizability.

text:
Experimental Evidence from Satellite-Transmitted Instruction in Ghana
A cluster-randomized trial in Ghana tested MGCubed , a satellite-based program delivering daily
English and math lessons to students in Grades 2–5 in 70 rural primary schools (Johnston and
Ksoll 2022). Expert ‘studio teachers’ in Accra broadcast live to 10–12 classrooms, while in-class
teachers acted as facilitators, operating equipment, managing classrooms, grading work, and
supporting students when broadcasts failed. In the second year, facilitators grouped students
by ability in English to provide targeted support. The program required substantial infrastruc
ture, including solar power, video equipment, and training and stipends for facilitators. The
satellite lessons were fully integrated into regular school hours, replacing part of teacher-led
instruction. Compared to control schools (n = 77) with regular teacher-led lessons, MGCubed
produced math gains of 0.20–0.21 SD after one year and 0.26–0.27 SD after two years. Literacy
effects emerged more slowly, with a 0.33 SD improvement on the EGRA composite by Year 2,
very large for letter naming and decoding, modest for oral fluency, and none for comprehen
sion. Gains were consistent across teachers and districts, and math improvements persisted one
year later. Costs were high. About 30 percent of total two-year expenses went to upfront
infrastructure (studios, equipment, solar power, and satellite links). Even with a 7–8-year
lifespan to spread these costs, the program delivered only ≈ 0.12 SD of learning gain per US$100
per student. This was well below the return from non-EdTech approaches, such as structured
teacher training, which cost about US$10–11 per student per year and delivered ≈ 0.36 SD of
learning gain per US$100 (Duflo et al. 2020). This means that while satellite instruction can
improve foundational learning in rural schools, it is only financially viable if infrastructure is
shared across more learners and services.
Experimental Evidence from a Tablet-based Self-learning Suite in Tanzania
A randomized trial in rural Tanzania evaluated Kitkit TM School, a self-directed tablet learning
suite combining interactive activities, digital books, videos, and tools for independent use
among Grade 1 students (Lee and Choi 2020). The program included nine curriculum-aligned
modules on number recognition, comparison, and basic operations, with gamification features
such as progress tracking and rewards to encourage daily practice. Children used tablets with
headphones in a dedicated classroom. A local assistant managed devices but provided no
instructions. The app operated offline with periodic data uploads. The intervention group (n =
30) replaced regular math lessons with daily 20-minute sessions over 46 days. The control
group (n = 31) continued with standard math classes. After the intervention, learners in the
treatment group showed significant gains in number identification, quantity discrimination,
addition, subtraction, and missing-number tasks, with greater improvements than controls in
number discrimination (0.58 SD), addition (0.78 SD), and subtraction (0.75 SD). Students could
identify numbers up to 100, compare magnitudes, and perform simple operations; however,
regrouping and complex missing-number tasks remained challenging. These findings show that
a short, game-based intervention can improve early numeracy in low-resource classrooms, even
for children with limited prior exposure to technology. However, the study’s scope (one rural
school with 61 children) limits generalizability.

title: Expanding Learner Access to Instructional Content

paragraphs.text: Open Educational Resources for Content Creation, Localization, and Updates

Three studies show how OER function as structured mechanisms for generating, adapting, and
sharing instructional content at a low cost in LMIC contexts (Arinto et al. 2017; Oates and
Hashimi 2016; Tlili et al. 2022). For instance, a multi-region review of OER adoption (Arinto et al.
2017) finds that open licensing supports a digital ecosystem where users can revise, remix, and
share educational materials. Open licenses allow curriculum developers and teachers to update
content and add context-specific examples without copyright constraints. These permissions
lower legal and financial barriers to creating instructional resources, helping keep materials
aligned with evolving curricula. Another review study (Tlili et al. 2022) highlights that OER
adoption in Africa is driving the development of digital books in African languages. These
initiatives typically use digital-first production models that create, store, and share materials in
formats that can be easily adapted or printed. The African Storybook Initiative is one such
example. Its openly licensed storybooks can be downloaded, translated, adapted, and printed
for classroom use. Teachers often revise them collaboratively to reflect local languages and
cultural references, making foundational learning content more contextually responsive.
Evidence from Afghanistan points to similar benefits. The Darakht-e Danesh Library uses a
multilingual content management system that allows contributors to adapt materials into Dari,
Pashto, and English languages (Oates and Hashimi 2016). The platform also includes tools for
refining terminology, examples, and imagery to match local contexts, expanding teachers’ and
learners’ access to locally relevant resources in settings with acute shortages of aligned
instructional materials.

title: Distributing, Storing, and Managing Teaching and Learning Materials

paragraphs.text: Digital Textbook Tracking Platforms in Cambodia and Other Locations

TnT systems replace paper-based textbook ordering with a simple digital workflow that works
on basic phones (Bun et al. 2024; Read 2017). Some systems allow schools to directly request
books through SMS, IVR, or short mobile forms while others still use centrally managed data.
Shipments carry barcodes, and school directors or community members confirm receipt
digitally. TnT models have been used or piloted in various locations, including Cambodia,
Afghanistan, Malawi, Nigeria, Niger, Nepal, and India, with designs adapted for basic phones
and limited connectivity (Bun et al. 2024; Khan 2020). Evidence from Cambodia (Bun et al.
2024; Khan 2020) shows three main benefits: (a) faster processing as hundreds of schools
submitted requests within two weeks instead of several months under paper-based procedures,
(b) i mproved accuracy as delivery records show that more than 90 percent of requested books
arrived on time and in the correct quantities, and (c) greater visibility as time-stamped logs
highlight where procurement or transportation delays occur, allowing ministries to intervene
early. Although not experimental studies, these findings illustrate how lightweight digital
workflows can improve transparency in the distribution chain and reduce the administrative
burden on school leaders.

title: 68 | How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries

paragraphs.text: Offline Digital Libraries Using Raspberry Pi Servers in Indonesia

A low-cost digital library model tested in Indonesia uses a Raspberry Pi microcomputer as a
local server for preloaded books (Wiguna et al. 2024). The device broadcasts its own Wi-Fi
signal, which learners can join using basic smartphones. There is no internet connection; the
system creates a closed network, allowing users to browse and download materials from local
storage. The model offers several advantages. It operates at very low power and can be
powered by solar or battery sources. Content can be updated simply by replacing the SD card,
without needing to download new content. This reduces reliance on connectivity for ongoing
maintenance. As of January 2024, the full setup (one server and five client devices) costs about
US$904. Field monitoring reported that the deployed library contained more than 7,000 items,
including children’s storybooks used in village reading houses. Visits by children to these
reading houses increased after installation, and parents reported perceived improvements in
their children’s reading skills. While these are not directly measured learning outcomes, the
model expands access to literacy materials in places where printed texts and reliable internet
are scarce.

title: Emerging AI Use Cases for Curriculum Development and Delivery

paragraphs.text: AI-Enabled Drafting, Editing, Illustration, Translation, and Production Planning

A review of 12 published, mostly qualitative studies on the African publishing industry reports
that AI tools are beginning to support multiple stages of textbook and storybook production
(Salani and Tapfuma 2025). While not all reviewed sources focus on foundational learning
materials, the workflows they describe remain relevant. The tools support four areas: drafting
and editing, illustration, translation, and production planning. In drafting and editing , tools such
as Grammarly, GPT-based drafting systems, and AI-assisted plagiarism detectors (for example,
GPTZero and AI Text Classifier) support grammar correction, readability checks, fact-checking,
and early copyediting, which helps small editorial teams manage high workloads. In illustration
and design , publishers have begun to experiment with generative image models, similar to
Midjourney, to create early artwork that designers later refine to ensure cultural accuracy,
thereby helping address shortages of illustrators and slow visual production cycles. In transla
tion , multilingual machine translation engines are tested to produce first-round drafts in African
languages using back-translation and reconstruction techniques, thereby reducing the early
stages of translation in multilingual systems that often face lengthy timelines and high costs.
Some publishers are also beginning to test data analytics tools for production planning,
although applications to textbook demand forecasting are still limited. Similar experimentation
is underway in Senegal, where a 2025 workshop applied generative AI to book creation and
produced 18 original titles in five days, confirming that AI can speed up production when paired
with strong editorial oversight and culturally grounded design (Diop and Teel 2025).

title: Edtech for Instructional Support Systems

paragraphs.text: AI-powered Offline Speech Recognition Tool in Morocco 6

A TaRL program in Morocco piloted an AI-powered automatic speech recognition tool to
automate early-grade oral reading assessment (Bachiri et al. 2024). The tool, known as TaRL-
BOT , integrates Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) into Moodle and allows students in
Grades 1–3 to record short reading passages through a simple web interface. Learners comple
ted the tasks individually on tablets or school computers. The tool stored each reading sample,
transcription, and score within Moodle’s database and identified the highest level reached
across letter, word, sentence, paragraph, and story tasks. Teachers and supervisory teams
accessed these records to confirm skill levels and monitor progress across TaRL groups.
TaRL-BOT operated offline for classroom use and synced data when connectivity was available.
Pilot evidence showed that TaRL-BOT -generated scores were mostly consistent with human
scoring benchmarks used in TaRL. Teachers viewed automated scoring as helpful for reducing
assessment workload and providing structured records for grouping and progress monitoring.
AI-powered Oral Reading Assessment Tool in India 7

Vaachan Samiksha (meaning ‘reading assessment’ in Hindi) is an AI-enabled oral reading
fluency tool that automates timing, scoring, and reporting for early-grade literacy (Wadhwani
AI 2025). Similar to TaRL-BOT , it replaces manual oral reading fluency checks with quick,
objective assessments and records results with verified school locations that cannot be altered
after submission. Since July 2023, the tool has been deployed across nearly 30,000 public
schools in Gujarat, supporting about 120,000 teachers and more than 2.5 million learners. The
state integrated the tool into its existing digital systems so teachers can access it through
familiar channels, which has eased adoption. According to developers, the automation enables
teachers to conduct brief fluency checks with small groups each day, and the immediate
feedback helps them track progress and identify learners who need targeted support. Students
appear more engaged because they receive instant results. While the current version requires
internet connectivity, the offline version is under development.

title: 1. Introduction

paragraphs.text:
We are currently in the midst of a period of rapid and uneven change driven by major commercial
investments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), a sharp rise in the use of AI and its increasing inte-
gration into virtually every aspect of daily life – all of which represent significant opportunities
as well as risks for work, education and society.

Major shifts are taking place in the labour market (Greenan et al., 2025). We are seeing a rising
use of AI in the workplace, whether intended/desired or not, as well as changes in the type and
number of vacancies, the nature and content of work and the way in which work is organised
within organisations. In this exploratory study, we examine how developments in AI are affecting
the labour market and what implications this has for the design and agility of curricula in
educational institutions in the Netherlands.

We cannot yet fully grasp the current and future impact of AI, nor what these developments
will mean for work, education and society in the long term. Economic, demographic, geo
political and other technological developments also have an impact on the labour market.
There is, however, a growing awareness and sense of urgency to take a stance, respond to
developments in AI and find answers to the questions raised by the uncertain future that
lies ahead.

AI-GO!, a framework for AI literacy in education
AI-GO! is a framework for AI literacy in education in the Netherlands that has been
designed by Npuls. Work is underway to develop digital, AI and data literacy for
learners and students.

This also presents a major challenge for tertiary education in the Netherlands: how to ade-
quately prepare all these current and upcoming professionals for a future in which AI plays a
prominent role. And the rapid pace of AI developments is, if anything, only intensifying that
challenge. After all, how do you ensure that curricula are future-proof and suitable to prepare
students for careers that are subject to rapid change – or may not even exist yet? And what
impact does AI have on society (and vice versa)?

title: Reading guide

paragraphs.text:
In Chapter 2 , we begin by introducing and clarifying the key concepts used in this exploratory
study: Artificial Intelligence (AI), curriculum and the labour market.

In this exploratory study, we seek to find answers to questions relating to the interplay between
developments in AI, the changes we are seeing – caused or accelerated by AI – in the labour
market, and how tertiary education in the Netherlands can respond to these developments
in its curricula. The aim is to inspire educational institutions and provide them with guidance
on how to future-proof their curricula and transition towards AI-ready study programmes.
Pag. 9

In Chapter 3 , we explore how AI is affecting the labour market and what effects we are seeing
as a result. Topics covered in this chapter include changes in work processes, roles and
productivity, and how skills and occupational profiles are evolving.
Pag. 15

We have sought to answer these questions through a review of the literature, interviews,
discussions with experts and extensive input from the community. A key insight from this
exploratory study, nonetheless, is that there are more questions than we can answer in a
single, concise report. We therefore view this document primarily as a valuable starting point.
It draws together different perspectives and highlights just how vast and complex the
challenge we face is.

Chapter 4 subsequently describes how the education sector and the labour market can
prepare for the impact of AI. In this chapter, we outline the frameworks we use to shape our
education, explain how we can effectively prepare students for the changing labour market
and emphasise the importance of systematically monitoring developments.
Pag. 27

This exploratory study focuses primarily on the impact of AI on the labour market and the
related implications for education. At the same time, AI also offers opportunities to improve
educational processes. AI can be used to enhance curriculum processes, for example by
gaining a better understanding of developments in the labour market, ensuring consistency
in language and structure across different documents and providing insight into the accessi-
bility of the curriculum.

Chapter 5 examines how curricula can be designed or redesigned and kept up to date
against the backdrop of rapid technological change, including the impact of AI. It describes
the process of responsive curriculum development and curriculum management, with a focus
on curriculum awareness, stakeholder engagement and the importance of a shared vision.
Pag. 37

It is essential to distinguish between these two perspectives: on the one hand, AI as a devel-
opment that is transforming the labour market and thus placing new demands on education;
and on the other hand, AI as a tool that can help educational institutions improve their
curriculum development.

Chapter 6 examines the process of change within educational institutions. It explores how
they can integrate AI responsibly and future-proof themselves through gradual institutional
change, adaptive governance and a focus on the human factor (teaching staff, students and
support staff).

For those who want to get started straight away, Chapter 7 contains a summary and sugges-
tions on how to proceed.
Pag. 53

In both cases, this requires decisive action and clear choices, with AI- and data-driven
strategies structurally integrated into how educational institutions operate. How successfully
we address this issue depends largely on collaboration and connection with all stakeholders.
It is only by working in partnership with the professional field and the government – and by
pooling knowledge, data and expertise within a community – that we can make progress.
This calls for ambition, as well as accepting that we do not yet know all the answers and cannot
predict everything.

If you have any additions or good practices to share after reading
this exploratory study, please let us know at info@npuls.nl and the
Npuls communitysite AI & Data.

Npuls. Moving education.

title: 2. What do we mean by AI, curricula and labour market ?

paragraphs.text:
Npuls
Education that is ready for the future. Tertiary educational institutions in the Netherlands
work together in National Growth Fund programme Npuls so that learners can learn
without barriers and receive continuously high-quality education.

Before discussing the possible impact of AI on our curricula and labour market, it is important
to first explain these concepts. We do so in this chapter.

What is Artificial Intelligence?
Many different terms are used to describe AI, and this can sometimes be confusing. When
talking about AI, many people tend to associate it mainly with chatbots, but AI is much broader
than that.

An AI system is a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives,
infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions,
content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual
environments. (OECD, 2024)

Under the Npuls umbrella, we work together to build a wealth of knowledge and insights
that we share in our knowledge base. An overview of practical documents relevant to
this memorandum is provided below:
• Exploratory study: Assessment, examination and AI
• Exploratory study: AI and equity
• Exploratory study: AI Act in brief: an introduction to and explanation regarding the
AI Act
• Exploratory study: Npuls Initial Memorandum (Startnota): State of AI (2023)
• Frameworks: AI-GO Framework: an overview of what AI literacy is and how we can
promote it in tertiary education
• Frameworks: Reference Framework 2.0: Responsible use of education data and AI
• Practice: Learning Analytics Magazines (I, II, III): Inspiration and practitioner stories
on how to get started with learning analytics in education.
• Practice: Smarter education with AI magazine: information and inspiration for
education professionals
• Tool: Guide to collaborating on continuous delivery of AI in EdTech
• Tool: Center for Teaching & Learning (CTL) Starter kit

More broadly speaking, there are different AI systems that work with different types of data
(e.g. audio, text, video, signals), use different types of learning architectures and produce
different types of output (e.g. predictions, content generation, etc.). We have also seen progress
recently in the field of physical AI, where AI systems are combined with hardware to create
robots. There are also agentic AI systems that operate within the context of digital worlds.

In this exploratory study, we are essentially discussing AI in the broadest sense of the term,
since we are interested in the impact that AI has on the labour market and, consequently, on
our education and curriculum. We also talk about technological developments, for although
AI is not the only technological driver of these developments, it does have a significant impact
on them.

What do we mean by curriculum?
The term curriculum is often defined as a plan for learning (Taba, 1962). It is in the simplicity
of this definition that we find the challenge, as the learning plan can be designed at different
levels and in various manifestations. Thijs and Van den Akker (2009) distinguish between five

The quality of the curriculum is determined by its internal and external consistency (Kessels,

in relation to one another.

What do we mean by labour market?
Generally speaking, the labour market is described as an imaginary market where the supply
and demand for labour meet. In this market, employment and unemployment are measured,
analysed and forecast – for example by Statistics Netherlands (CBS) and the Research Centre
for Education and the Labour Market (ROA) – for both the short and long term. Many analyses
also treat the labour market as a collection of occupations or occupational groups, with different
job levels within those groups.

title: AI LABOUR MARKET

paragraphs.text:
There is no such thing as the labour market. When we talk about the impact of AI on the labour
market in this exploratory study, we are seeking to identify the influence AI will have on the future
employment conditions which our students will be facing. In doing so, we examine both the
effects we observe on overall employment and changes in work processes and specific tasks
within occupations, as well as the resulting implications for skills, job requirements and study
programmes.

What is the correlation between curriculum, AI and labour market?
Over the years, there has been considerable focus on curriculum design. Three key factors
play a central role in curriculum development: the stakeholders involved in the process, views
on what constitutes a good curriculum and developments in society and the subject area.
Figure 2 The reciprocal influence between labour market, curriculum and AI.

We see this dynamic reflected in the correlation between curriculum, AI and the labour market.
This is not just about views on the curriculum; opinions about AI are also significant factors.
Reciprocal influence is often at play, for example as a result of new developments in AI.
Developments in AI are affecting not only the labour market but also the expertise required
of future professionals. The curriculum is the foundation for preparing these professionals for
their future careers. Educational offerings – as well as professional attitudes and opinions – play
a part in shaping how future professionals will enter the labour market. From this perspective,
the curriculum influences how , when and for what purpose AI is used, and how ethically and
critically future professionals will use the technology. Figure 2 illustrates this reciprocal influence.

title: 3. The impact of AI on the labour market

paragraphs.text:
Chapter overview
There are various ways of approaching AI in relation to the labour market. A macro-
critical view warns of a growing divide between capital and labour due to automation,
whereas a micro-optimistic perspective highlights opportunities for productivity
growth, provided that technology is implemented and applied effectively.

There is no such thing as the labour market. AI’s impact on the labour market is
gradual and varies significantly by sector, organisation and profession.

The main way AI is changing work is through job tasks. Occupations do not usually
disappear entirely, but roles shift as AI replaces some tasks, supports others and
creates new ones. We see this playing out in a decline in junior roles and internships,
among other things.

AI is changing the demand for skills. Transversal skills like critical thinking, problem-
solving and communication are becoming increasingly important, with digital skills
and AI literacy becoming core competencies.

The impact of AI depends to a large extent on organisational, policy and adoption
decisions. Investing in training, ethical frameworks and a culture of lifelong learning
is critical to making responsible use of the opportunities offered by AI.

AI is shaping our labour market and society. An article in the trade journal Economisch
Statistische Berichten (Economic Statistical Reports, Groenewegen et al., 2026) from January
2026 notes that employment in occupations prone to automation by generative AI – particu-
larly those centred on language, data and routine tasks, such as business and administrative
roles – fell by 13%. In the Future of Jobs Report 2025 by the World Economic Forum (WEF), it
is predicted that only one-third of all work will be carried out entirely by humans by 2030, due
in part to the use of AI and robotics.

Npuls. Moving education.
15

The economic debate: macro-critical versus micro-optimistic
To understand the impact of AI on the labour market, we can consider two influential economic
perspectives that are shaping the current debate.

Macro-critical view
(Acemoglu, 2024)

Micro-optimistic view
(Brynjolfsson, 2023, 2025)

At the same time, recent research shows that the labour market is not collapsing but adapting:
the jobs most affected by automation are also those undergoing the most augmentation, with
AI playing a supporting role (Sigelman et al., 2026). While the role itself will not disappear, the
nature of the work will change as a result of AI assistance. Furthermore, the use of AI may
increase demand for some existing occupations and lead to the emergence of new ones,
for example in the fields of data analysis, cybersecurity, AI development and AI governance
(Verduijn et al., 2025).

Most experts therefore describe this as a gradual process, with certain tasks shifting and
new forms of human-AI collaboration emerging. The Insight Report, published in 2026 by the
WEF in collaboration with the McKinsey Health Institute, emphasises the importance of
investing in human brain capital, as it is precisely the collaboration between humans and
machines – and how they reinforce each other’s skills – that is becoming increasingly significant
(WEF, 2026).

By contrast, this approach emphasises the
significant productivity gains achieved in
the workplace. Experiments showed that
average productivity increased by 14%
(15% in the 2025 study), with peaks of up to
35% among less experienced employees
(Brynjolfsson et al., 2023; 2025). In this view,
AI is seen as an “augmentation technology”
that helps to boost the performance of
employees, particularly those with lower
levels of education.

We cannot make any definitive statements about the impact of AI on the labour market,
simply because we do not know if and to what extent changes can be attributed to AI, or how
predictions unfold and play out in the workplace and in society. Furthermore, we see that the
changes in the labour market attributed to AI vary significantly by occupational group and
nature of the work. Bearing that in mind, we will in this chapter look at a number of implications
that are relevant to this theme.

This view cautions against placing too
much emphasis on automation and the
replacement of human tasks. The author
predicts modest macroeconomic growth
(a maximum of 0.71% growth in total factor
productivity over ten years) and fears that AI
will primarily widen the gap between capital
and labour (Acemoglu, 2024). For education,
the takeaway is that we must avoid prepa-
ring students for roles that AI can perform
“adequately” but that devalue human worth
– hence Acemoglu’s call for innovation to
be directed in a desirable way (Acemoglu,
2024).

Brynjolfsson’s research highlights the
potential for inclusive growth in the work-
place, as those with lower levels of educa-
tion benefit disproportionately more from
the use of AI, while Acemoglu’s perspective
serves as a reminder of the need to continue
investing in human capital.

Changing work processes and tasks
Developments in AI are changing the way in which work processes and related tasks are
carried out. Technology generally automates only part of the work-related tasks, not an
entire job (SER, 2025). This picture has not changed significantly since the emergence of
generative AI in late 2022. Many studies show that while occupations are not disappearing,
there is a redistribution of tasks driven by the use of AI. AI’s impact on the level of tasks and
subtasks manifests itself through three mechanisms (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2019):

Npuls. Moving education.
17

Substitution
( displacement effect)

Complementarity
( productivity effect )

Creation of new jobs
( reinstatement effect )

learning in the workplace, harnessing talent more effectively and developing modern organi-
sations with an innovative structure built around collaboration, trust and engagement. Acemo-
glu (2024), like Pot (2024), posits that the influence of technology on the organisation of work,
and consequently on the quality of work, is a matter of choice for employers.

AI creates new and more
complex tasks that need to
be carried out by humans
(e.g. verifying or curating AI
output, prompt engineer-
ing or providing personal
guidance, for which there is
more time as administrative
tasks are eliminated).

AI speeds up the perfor-
mance of a task or makes it
more efficient, which in turn
makes people more produc-
tive. Humans remain “in the
loop”, but perform better
(e.g. teaching staff using AI
to create personalised les-
son plans more quickly).

Research into the impact of AI on the quality of work shows that there are consistently two
sides to the coin. On the one hand, the use of AI can automate routine or administrative tasks.
This frees up time for other, potentially more meaningful, tasks. On the flip side, this often
leads to an increase in workload, as the tasks that require greater cognitive effort still need to
be done, while natural periods of rest – such as those experienced when performing routine
tasks – disappear. AI can increase employees’ autonomy by providing practical support or feed-
back. But AI can also limit this autonomy by prescribing and monitoring tasks in detail, for
example in the context of algorithmic management (Van der Torre et al., 2025; p. 9). According
to Acemoglu et al., when there is no balance between job displacement and the creation of
new tasks and automation dominates on a structural level, this constitutes “bad technology”
– technology that displaces work without creating enough new, valuable activities.

AI takes over tasks entire-
ly. In earlier automation
processes, this involved
physical routine tasks (e.g.
assembly line work). In the
context of AI, this refers
to routine cognitive tasks ;
activities that are frequently
repeated, follow a set of
fixed steps and require little
creativity or deep thinking
(e.g. writing meeting min-
utes, basic programming
work, translation).

We find the same three-pronged approach in education, according to a 2025 publication by the
Dutch Education Lab for AI ( Nationaal Onderwijslab AI , NOLAI). This refers to replacing, supple-
menting and enhancing the tasks of teaching staff through the use of AI (NOLAI, 2025; p. 15).

Mathijssen et al. (2025) propose that, in addition to impact assessments on specific appli-
cations of AI within sectors, quantitative research should also be carried out into the impact
of AI on the quality of work, as this can contribute to the development and adaptation of
legislation and regulations.

“Without AI and automation, we won’t cut it in the labour market.
There aren’t enough people to keep doing work the way we’ve done in
the past. The challenge is figuring out how to use AI in a way that makes
work easier, more enjoyable and more human – and ensures that humans
and technology can enhance each other’s strengths.”

Marian Thunnissen,
Professor of Talent Development and Talent Management

This shift in tasks impacts equity in the workplace. New tasks created by AI could either reduce
inequity or, conversely, increase it. Recent studies show, among other things, that the use of AI
enables employees to carry out certain tasks that do not directly correlate with their level of ed-
ucation (Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond, 2023). At the same time, we are seeing that employees
who mainly carry out knowledge-based work are at risk of having fewer opportunities, despite
their level of education. The impact on job security for those with a theoretical education is
particularly evident among younger employees in entry-level roles, as they have relatively more
theoretical knowledge and less tacit knowledge (knowledge gained through experience),
making them more vulnerable to being replaced by AI (Brynjolfsson, Chandar & Chen, 2025).
Take for example an administrative assistant who has had practical training. This employee
can perform more complex tasks thanks to AI, whereas a new entrant with a theoretical
background has fewer opportunities because AI can replace their “book knowledge”.

AI adoption and productivity gains
Productivity gains are often cited as one of the potential benefits AI could bring to the
labour market. Indeed, we see many examples of AI being used to speed up work and boost
productivity. Yet research shows that, despite the rising use of digital technologies over the
past twenty years, labour productivity has barely increased (Statistics Netherlands, CBS,
2024a; 2024b). Businesses also indicate that AI has had little impact on employment and

The impact of AI on the quality of work
According to Pot (2020), the current debate on skills still focuses overly on education and
professionals’ individual responsibility for their skills and long-term employability. Pot calls for
broadening the debate to include the organisation and quality of work. Consider, for example,

Npuls. Moving education.
19

productivity over the past three years – more than 80% have not seen any noticeable effect.
However, they do expect changes in the coming years: AI is projected to increase productivity
by 1.4% and output by 0.8%, while reducing employment by 0.7% (Yotzov et al., 2026).

The low adoption rate may indicate that the need to use AI varies significantly by sector and
type of work. Although AI is often presented as a so-called general-purpose technology,
current adoption patterns show that, in practice, the value of AI lies mainly in specific appli-
cations and tasks. As such, it is not necessarily a solution for all sectors or processes.

Productivity gains from AI still appear to depend largely on the extent and speed of adoption
in the workplace and on employees’ AI literacy (Verduijn et al., 2025). This means that businesses
looking to boost productivity should not only invest in AI, but primarily in rethinking the business
and work processes. Investing in AI literacy of employees is an essential condition to bring about
this change in processes.

At the same time, the capabilities of AI are expanding, with costs falling. Models are becoming
smaller and more efficient, making them easier to integrate into phones, laptops and business
software. Substantial investments and fierce international competition are accelerating the
development of autonomous (agentic) AI applications. Physical AI, such as robots and smart
systems, is also becoming cheaper and easier to program. Given this technological acceleration,
it is likely that AI adoption will continue to grow.

“We’re currently seeing a lot of restructuring in the financial
sector under the guise of AI. You could certainly question that,
as we’re also seeing that rising costs and economic uncertainty

AI adoption is still lagging behind in many companies. Large companies use AI technology more
often than smaller companies. There is virtually no sector in the Netherlands where AI is
currently used to a considerable extent, with the exception of the education and information
sectors, as well as the communication sector – which also includes media companies. Lack
of experience is by far the main reason for this in businesses of all sizes and across all sectors
(CBS, 2024a; 2024b). Many employers are also reluctant to allow the use of AI, due in part to
uncertainty about privacy, security and legal frameworks.
are putting pressure on businesses. It would appear that some
companies would rather call it ‘AI development’
than ‘cost-cutting’.”

Frank Eskes,
labour market adviser for the UWV (Employee Insurance Agency)

The Netherlands is investing in AI
Advances in AI are progressing rapidly thanks to more powerful and smaller models,
making AI more affordable and suitable for a wider range of applications. Many initi-
atives are underway in the Netherlands to build a strong position on AI that focuses
concurrently on innovation, public values and digital autonomy. The AI Coalition for
the Netherlands (AIC4NL) is calling for significant public and private investment in
AI (at least €5 billion over five years) and for a European strategy based on FairTech .
Invest NL emphasises that the Netherlands should not focus on frontier models but
on its own strengths, such as energy-efficient, green AI and new AI services .

Employment agencies for digital employees
Digital employees – AI agents that perform tasks independently and are available 24/7
– are making inroads into the workplace. In addition to tech companies that develop
bespoke AI agents, there are firms that market themselves as “employment agencies”
for digital employees, offering a solution to labour shortages and cost reduction. For
a fixed monthly fee, they provide digital employees to assist with specific tasks like
customer service, appointment scheduling or lead generation. For businesses, this
lowers the barrier to adopting AI, but it also introduces cybersecurity risks and trans-
forms the working environment: collaborating with digital colleagues is becoming less
of a choice and more of a given. If working with AI continues to become an increasingly
common component of day-to-day work, new skills, responsibilities and (social) divisions
of labour in the workplace will also become a necessity.

Policy initiatives like the national AI Delta Plan and the Action agenda AI & Data focus
on building a strong AI ecosystem through increased AI adoption, talent development
and national projects. Concerns are growing about dependence on large tech com-
panies from the US and China. Digital sovereignty is therefore being prioritised, with
the aim of bringing more elements of the digital infrastructure under European control.
A clear example of this is the development of AI factories in Europe , including that of
a Dutch AI factory in collaboration with SURF, TNO and AIC4NL, based on public values
such as sustainability, transparency and collaboration.

Npuls. Moving education.
21

experience are dwindling (see the pr-eDict dashboard, p. 26 (Dutch Expertise Centre for IT &
Digitalisation, n.d.)).

Impact on skills and competencies
AI is not only changing the kinds of skills required, but also changing how existing skills are used:
with AI assistance, these skills are developed further – and sometimes undermined – and
applied in new work contexts. It is not so much about learning new skills and competencies
as it is about combining human skills (such as critical information literacy, communication
skills and problem-solving skills) with AI in a smart way. In this context, AI primarily plays a role
in complementing and enriching tasks (NOLAI, 2025; OECD, 2025).

That said, we must be careful not to attribute changes in junior roles and internships directly
to AI. During times when the labour market is contracting, entry-level roles are often the first
to be affected, as mid-level and senior roles are usually held by employees on permanent
contracts. And while AI can exacerbate this trend, it is not the sole cause of changes in the
number of junior roles and internships available.

Cognitive, social and ethical skills – such as critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving
– are becoming increasingly important and provide a secure foundation in a changing world.
Ongoing technological developments mean that the ability to learn and adapt has also become
essential. There is also a growing need to develop digital skills. With AI tools becoming increas-
ingly common in the workplace, digital skills – including AI literacy – are fast becoming essential
(WEF, 2025).

Growing need for Lifelong Learning (LLL)
AI is increasing the need and demand for retraining and upskilling. On top of that, there are
still many uncertainties regarding the future development, application and impact of AI.
Professional development and adoption of a learning mindset across all sectors of society
are therefore crucial, as is development-oriented monitoring to support that development.
We must continue to learn, assess and respond to these developments. According to the SER
(SER, 2025), it is therefore essential that all groups in society – young people, older people,
those in work and those not in work – have access to suitable education and development
opportunities.

Finally, the importance of hybrid skills – which combine subject knowledge with AI skills – is
growing. Information technology is becoming ever more important across all sectors of our
economy. This means that the need for digital professionals is growing in almost all sectors,
while at the same time the demand for digital skills is increasing in virtually all roles.

Continuing education is more urgent than ever to enhance employees’ adaptability, better
align supply and demand in the labour market and harness underutilised labour potential. In
the coming years, there will be a particular need for broad-based upskilling, possibly followed
later by retraining in occupations that are disappearing.

National labour market policy
The impact of AI on work and the labour market is high on the national policy agenda. Several
Dutch government departments, including the Ministries of Social Affairs and Employment
(SZW), of Education, Culture and Science (OCW) and of Economic Affairs (EZ), are working
together on a coordinated approach as part of the Dutch Digitalisation Strategy ( Nederlandse
Digitaliseringsstrategie , NDS). This policy focuses on future-proofing work and prevent-
ing inequity. Particular attention is paid to AI literacy, training and upskilling, monitoring the
impact on the labour market and establishing social agreements. Employers and educational
institutions play a key role in implementing these policy objectives. Furthermore, the Dutch
Social and Economic Council (SER) emphasises that it is not only technology, but above all
organisational structure, a culture of learning, employee participation and the quality of work
that are decisive in making responsible use of the opportunities afforded by AI.

Continuing education and development is not something that comes naturally to everyone.
There are clear differences in the degree of participation in continuing education between,
on the one hand, people who have completed vocational, higher professional or university
education and, on the other, people without a basic qualification. We also see that flex workers
generally receive less training than those with permanent contracts, and that SMEs offer
fewer development opportunities than large companies (Verduijn et al., 2025). Investment
in training has fallen (-8%), and confidence in training as the primary route to literacy has
declined (-14%). Smaller employers, in particular, lack incentives to invest in their employees’
general knowledge and skills (SER, 2025). Sector and business activities are key factors in
determining the use of AI. Small businesses are lagging behind due to a lack of capacity,
while larger businesses have more possibilities. This lag stems from a combination of unfamil-
iarity with the possibilities, reluctance due to financial uncertainty and inability due to a lack
of knowledge and data. It seems that SMEs currently have a greater need for – and stand to
benefit more from – support in developing their vision and strategy regarding AI (Vankan et
al., 2025).

Difficulties for new entrants
Considerable attention is being paid to the impact of AI on the labour market for new entrants.
AI systems are increasingly capable of performing routine and support tasks, which is changing
the nature of work and leading to a decline in the number of junior roles and internships in some
sectors. These are typically the tasks that new entrants and interns start with. This creates a
paradox: new entrants need work experience to get a job, but the opportunities to gain that

Npuls. Moving education.
23

industry – and in specialist business services. Examples include interpreters/translators,
writers and authors (Tomlinson et al., 2025).

Investing in a culture of Lifelong Learning (LLL) is a shared responsibility of the government,
the education sector and the business community. This calls for the joint development of
flexible and relevant course offerings and ensuring that these are accessible through targeted
funding and incentivising policies.

But at the same time, these figures are also causing confusion. If we take a closer look at the
IT sector, we see a decline in the number of vacancies for digital occupations on the one hand,
while new or other data- and AI-related occupations and job titles also top the lists of the occu-
pations expected to grow the fastest (Dutch Centre of Expertise for Digitalisation and IT, n.d.).

Connection between education & labour market
Student intake and graduation figures and demand for entry-level roles in 2024

The human factor
Implementing AI in the labour market has both positive and negative aspects, which depend
on multiple factors and vary across occupations. Given the pace of change, with all of us
guinea pigs for the new reality, we need to routinely check that AI systems are aligned with
our values and are doing what they are supposed to do. Timely detection and monitoring are
important in this regard (Eriksson et al., 2025).
