title: The Challenge: Limited Opportunities for Structured, Feedback-Rich Learner Practice During Instruction

paragraphs.text:
Classroom instruction in LMICs relies frequently on whole-class teaching with minimal time for individual
student practice or remedial support (Lee et al. 2020; Sakata et al. 2022). Large class sizes, scarce
materials, and teacher training traditions that emphasize authoritative delivery reinforce this approach
(Sakata et al. 2022). While whole-class instruction may be suitable for some instances, balancing it with
individualized attention is also important. This is because heavy reliance on whole-class, teacher-centric
instruction diverges from how children develop foundational reading and math skills, which require
repeated and scaffolded practice to build fluency in decoding, spelling, and basic number operations that
support later comprehension and problem-solving (Fuson et al. 2015; NRP 2000). Three EdTech tools in
our review directly addressed this gap by providing repeated, feedback-rich exercises that build automa
ticity in decoding, spelling, and basic number operations with demonstrated effectiveness.

paragraphs.text:
Across Kenya, Malawi, and India, experimental studies show that EdTech can improve foundational literacy
when it delivers structured practice with feedback and aligns with classroom learning. In Kenya, ABRA, a
multimedia literacy program used in school computer labs, improved passage comprehension and
listening comprehension and raised performance on national exams (Abrami et al. 2016). In Malawi,
tablet-based onebillion apps produced clear gains in early reading skills, including letter naming, syllable
reading, word and nonword reading, passage fluency, and comprehension, while also supporting stronger
math outcomes (Pitchford et al. 2019). Evidence from India suggests a narrower but still important role
for EdTech. Across three trials, GraphoLearn consistently improved letter-sound knowledge and, when
paired with structured phonics instruction, also strengthened nonword reading and spelling (Bora et al.
2024; Patel et al. 2018, 2022). However, effects rarely transferred to broader literacy outcomes such as
fluency, vocabulary, or comprehension, especially when the game operated separately from regular
instruction. Taken together, the studies suggest that EdTech is most effective when it reinforces core
teaching rather than functioning as a stand-alone tool (see appendix 2 for details).

text:
Across Kenya, Malawi, and India, experimental studies show that EdTech can improve foundational literacy
when it delivers structured practice with feedback and aligns with classroom learning. In Kenya, ABRA, a
multimedia literacy program used in school computer labs, improved passage comprehension and
listening comprehension and raised performance on national exams (Abrami et al. 2016). In Malawi,
tablet-based onebillion apps produced clear gains in early reading skills, including letter naming, syllable
reading, word and nonword reading, passage fluency, and comprehension, while also supporting stronger
math outcomes (Pitchford et al. 2019). Evidence from India suggests a narrower but still important role
for EdTech. Across three trials, GraphoLearn consistently improved letter-sound knowledge and, when
paired with structured phonics instruction, also strengthened nonword reading and spelling (Bora et al.
2024; Patel et al. 2018, 2022). However, effects rarely transferred to broader literacy outcomes such as
fluency, vocabulary, or comprehension, especially when the game operated separately from regular
instruction. Taken together, the studies suggest that EdTech is most effective when it reinforces core
teaching rather than functioning as a stand-alone tool (see appendix 2 for details).

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
While not causal, dozens of studies corroborate experimental evidence that EdTech helps create struc
tured opportunities for practicing and mastering foundational learning skills. In Kenya, the Emergent
Literacy in Mathematics software offered step-by-step mathematics tasks and improved Grade 1 numeracy
outcomes (Lysenko et al. 2022). In Pakistan and Bangladesh, the Footsteps2Brilliance platform delivered
individualized early literacy games aligned with national curricula, resulting in significant gains in Early
Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA) measured literacy (Pynnönen et al. 2022). In Morocco, the TaRL-BOT
system used AI-based speech recognition to provide instant, individualized feedback on early-grade
reading fluency (Bachiri et al. 2024). Game-based tools reinforced subskills through engaging repetition:
GraphoGame improved letter-sound recognition and spelling in Zambia (Nshimbi et al. 2020), and a
multimedia adventure game boosted numeracy skills in Indonesia (Rohendi 2019). Specialized and
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 25

adaptive applications further extend this repertoire. A mobile app for preschool children with dyslexia in
Pakistan repeated tracing and writing tasks until mastery, enhancing handwriting performance (Tariq and
Latif 2016). Low-connectivity tools also provided structured practice where the internet was limited: An
IVR phone system in Côte d’Ivoire supported home-based French phonological awareness through
structured call-in lessons (Chatterjee et al. 2020). Together, these interventions suggest that EdTech can
offer sustained, feedback-driven practice in LMIC settings, helping learners build fluency in foundational
learning skills.

title: The Challenge: Limited Variety in Classroom Learning Experiences

paragraphs.text:
Beyond limiting practice, traditional teacher-led instruction in LMIC schools restricts how actively students
engage with lessons (Sakata et al. 2022). Evidence is rich that children build stronger skills when they
read, listen, and interact with content in ways that capture attention and deepen processing (Guthrie and
Wigfield 2000; Hattie 2010). Three EdTech tools from our review embed active and varied engagement in
learning through synchronized reading and listening, interactive vocabulary practice, and multisensory
textbook lessons, with evidence of improved outcomes.

title: Experimental Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
Additional experimental evidence from Uganda and South Africa points to more targeted benefits from
relatively simple digital reading tools. In Uganda, SiMBi, a tablet-based reading-while-listening app,
produced modest but significant gains in Grade 3 reading fluency compared with silent print reading,
suggesting that synchronized audio–text support can strengthen fluency even with brief daily use
(Friedland et al. 2017). In South Africa, an interactive isiXhosa e-book improved Grade 1 learners’ receptive
vocabulary, expressive sentence use, and depth of word knowledge, with gains sustained over time (Klop
et al. 2018). Together, these studies suggest that even short, supplemental EdTech interventions can
improve specific literacy skills when they provide structured exposure to text, audio, and guided practice
(see appendix 2 for details).

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
Supporting evidence from nonexperimental studies further illustrates how EdTech can foster active and
sustained learner engagement through diverse formats. In Jordan, iPads loaded with interactive math
applications created multisensory lessons that students described as more enjoyable and motivating
compared to traditional methods (Al-Mashaqbeh 2016). In Ecuador, an augmented reality system with
motion sensors enabled children to interact with virtual math objects through natural gestures, providing
a playful, kinesthetic approach that captured attention and encouraged participation (Lozada-Yánez et al.
2019). Other models tested under different themes also highlight engagement features: Gamified literacy
and numeracy platforms, such as GraphoGame in Zambia (Nshimbi et al. 2020) and Footsteps2Brilliance
in Pakistan and Bangladesh (Pynnönen et al. 2022), were designed to sustain motivation through play,
while interactive radio instruction in Nigeria kept learners actively responding to characters and prompts
during lessons (Gever et al. 2024). Overall, these cases suggest that embedding motivational design,
whether through multisensory input, interactivity, or game mechanics, offers practical ways to sustain
learner engagement in settings where classroom instruction is often rote and teacher centric.

ACCESS
Student E-Readers within Structured Pedagogy in Kenya (Piper et al. 2016)

E-readers loaded with 100+ digital books (textbooks and storybooks) were provided to Grade 2 learners as part of a structured
pedagogy program (Primary Math and Reading, PRIMR). Learners used them daily during school hours as part of regular lessons
alongside print books, while teachers continued with regular PRIMR lesson delivery. Teacher and supervisor tablet arms were
also tested, providing digital lesson tools and observation guides. The intervention required devices, charging facilities, and
training for teachers/supervisors. This model was compared to business-as-usual classrooms without the structured pedagogy
program. * Cost: About US$40 for student e-readers (US$0.10 per pupil for supervisor tablets; US$3 for teacher tablets). Samples:

Computer-Assisted Reading Game (GraphoLearn Rime) in India (Bora et al. 2024; Patel et al. 2018, 2022)

Offline computer-assisted reading game teaching English letter-sound links, word-part (rime-unit) patterns, and word recognition
through interactive visual and auditory tasks with repeated practice and instant feedback. Students played 15–30 minutes per day
over 5–8 weeks on tablets with headphones. Early pilots (2018, 2022) delivered GraphoLearn as a stand-alone pull-out activity,
supervised by a researcher and not aligned with classroom instruction. The refined version (2024) integrated GraphoLearn with
structured classroom phonics, with teachers reinforcing content through explanations, modeling, and feedback. Control groups
played a math game to equalize screen time. *Cost not reported. Samples for the 2024 study: 1 school and 60 students. Samples
for the 2018 study: 1 school and 31 students. Samples for the 2022 study: 1 school and 136 students in total.

title: The Challenge: Lack of Structured Foundational Learning Instruction Even Among Enrolled Learners

paragraphs.text:
In many LMIC schools, millions of children face a dual challenge: Those enrolled in school often receive too
little structured, effective instruction to build foundational skills, while many others have no access to
formal schooling at all. Where schools exist, large classes, scarce materials, and limited teacher training
constrain what teachers can deliver (Bold et al. 2017a, 2017b). Even well-intentioned teachers frequently
lack the content knowledge, pedagogical support, or tools to teach diverse groups effectively (Lee et al.
2020). Instructional time is often lost to repetition, unproductive routines, or lessons pitched at levels
misaligned with students’ abilities (Bold et al. 2017b). In other settings, particularly in remote or conflict-af
fected areas, children remain out of school with no functioning classrooms or trained teachers available
(Ferráns et al. 2021). Three EdTech models in our review respond to these structural and instructional gaps
by substituting or supplementing traditional schooling with technology-delivered, scripted lessons. Each
provides structured content when teachers are unavailable or underprepared, or when schools do not exist
at all, through offline digital substitution, broadcast substitution, and self-directed tablet learning.

title: Experimental Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
Further experimental evidence shows that technology can improve foundational learning when it is
embedded in structured delivery models, though effects vary sharply by design and cost. In Zambia,
eSchool 360 used offline scripted lessons, tablets, and projectors in community schools and produced
meaningful gains in reading, math, vocabulary, and test performance, especially in the randomized
evaluation, suggesting that technology can help compensate for weak instructional capacity when paired
with facilitation, training, and supervision (De Hoop et al. 2024; Schling and Winters 2018). In Ghana,
MGCubed used satellite-transmitted lessons to improve math and literacy in rural schools, but its high
infrastructure costs made it less cost-effective than simpler non-EdTech alternatives (Johnston and Ksoll
2022). In Tanzania, KitkitTM School, a tablet-based self-learning program, improved early numeracy skills in
a small rural trial, especially in number discrimination, addition, and subtraction (Lee and Choi 2020).
Together, these studies suggest that technology can raise learning in low-resource settings, but its value
depends heavily on delivery model, instructional integration, and cost (see appendix 2 for details).

title: Broader Patterns Across LMICs

paragraphs.text:
Additional nonexperimental evidence highlights broader trends in how EdTech substitutes for or supple
ments classroom instruction in LMICs when teaching is absent, disrupted, or insufficient. In Sudan,
E-Learning Sudan (ELS) provided out-of-school children with the full primary mathematics curriculum
through a self-paced digital game, serving as a stand-alone substitute for formal schooling (Stubbé et al.
2016). In Belize, national radio broadcasts replaced classroom lessons during COVID-19 closures, giving
remote learners continued access to teacher-recorded instruction without internet (Kirshner 2020). In
South Africa, the Bridges to the Future Initiative (BFI) complemented classroom teaching with compu
ter-based literacy sessions in multiple local languages, reinforcing skills such as phonemic awareness and
comprehension (Castillo and Wagner 2019). Interactive radio instruction improved literacy skills among
out-of-school children living in refugee camps in Nigeria (Gever et al. 2024). While not causal, these
studies underscore that EdTech can partially step into the role of the teacher where traditional delivery
falls short.

title: Emerging AI Use Cases for Learner Support

paragraphs.text:
Similar to the trend seen for teacher support, AI applications increasingly target direct learner support.
These emerging use cases deliver individualized tutoring, multisensory reading scaffolds, and adaptive
practice. Delivery models range from whole-class projection to independent, offline local servers, reflec
ting different approaches to acute infrastructure constraints. While some platforms demonstrate robust
experimental impacts on learning outcomes, others remain early-stage pilots testing new delivery
mechanisms. The examples below illustrate how AI expands differentiated learning when integrated
strategically into existing school environments.
AI-Enhanced Personalized Adaptive Learning with Mindspark in India 4

Mindspark is a personalized digital learning platform that strengthens foundational learning by
diagnosing each learner’s level and adjusting tasks accordingly (Mona Foundation 2025). Its
earlier adaptive version showed meaningful effects in a randomized trial in India. Students with
access to the program scored 0.39–60 SD higher in reading and math compared to their peers
over 4.5 months (Muralidharan et al. 2019). The program has recently integrated generative AI
to expand its capacity for differentiation in low-resource settings. The AI-enabled system
generates leveled questions, explanations, writing feedback, and voice-supported reading
practice, while the adaptive engine continues to tailor tasks to each learner’s pace and needs.
These features provide teachers with ready-made, differentiated materials, reducing the burden
of producing individualized practice. The platform is used in government schools and provides
real-time dashboards to guide grouping and targeted support. While the new AI components
have not yet been experimentally evaluated, early implementation suggests that they facilitate
content localization and leveled practice and reduce dependence on large coaching teams,
provided that reliable devices and connectivity are ensured (Mona Foundation 2025).

A randomized trial in India evaluated the AI-powered RTM platform with 33,000 primary
students, including third graders, who had limited exposure to English outside of school
(Srinivasan and Murthy 2021). RTM digitized government-prescribed textbooks and read them

paragraphs.text:
aloud while highlighting words, showing pronunciation cues, and linking vocabulary to images,
providing learners with consistent multisensory input. Regular in-class teachers, after brief
training, used RTM during regular English or ICT periods about three times per week ( ≈ 75
sessions annually), projecting from a single shared computer. In its initial version, RTM delivered
whole-class cues, such as highlighting, audio, and images, without providing individualized
feedback or adaptive correction. The platform worked directly with official textbooks; no new
materials were introduced. Control schools continued with business-as-usual instruction. After
one year, RTM students outperformed controls by 20–40 percent in letter recognition, word
recognition, vocabulary, and comprehension, with gains across all proficiency levels. A two-year
follow-up showed sustained improvements of 21–22 percent. These results suggest that
large-scale, AI-enabled multisensory tools can enhance literacy outcomes within existing
systems in low-resource contexts, although further testing is needed to assess the added value
of adaptive, individualized features before scaling.
Experimental Evidence from AI Tutoring with Teacher Guidance in Nigeria

A randomized evaluation in Edo State, Nigeria, tested whether generative AI could expand
individualized learning opportunities under teacher supervision in a low-resource public school
context (De Simone et al. 2025). The intervention involved first-year senior secondary students
and was designed to address persistent learning gaps in English. Students participated in two
90-minute after-school sessions per week in school computer labs, working in pairs on curricu
lum-aligned English grammar and writing tasks using Microsoft Copilot, powered by GPT-4 at
the time. Teachers introduced lesson topics, guided students’ use of structured prompts,
monitored AI-student interactions, and facilitated reflection activities, positioning the AI as a
complement to instruction rather than a substitute for teacher support. The randomized
controlled trial found statistically significant gains of 0.23 SD in English and 0.31 SD in a
combined assessment of English, digital skills, and AI knowledge. This suggests that AI can
support language learning when it is embedded in structured, teacher-mediated practice that
gives learners more opportunities to write, revise, and receive responsive feedback than regular
classroom instruction alone.

A clear pattern across these learner-facing applications is that AI’s effectiveness requires its adaptation to
local infrastructure and integration with teacher-led instruction. Regardless of the delivery model, systems
need to prevent essential hardware bottlenecks to enable student access. Furthermore, the examples
show that AI tools do not replace educators. Rather, they function best as active complements to instruc
tion, requiring teacher mediation to translate automated feedback and adaptive practice into measurable
learning gains.

title: Key Takeaways for Effective EdTech Models for Learner Support

paragraphs.text:
The evidence in this section, drawn from randomized trials and observational studies of apps, multimedia
tools, and remote platforms, shows that learner-facing EdTech in LMICs enhances foundational skills when
built on six essential principles: curriculum alignment, adaptive pathways, sequenced and scaffolded
practice, engaging input, interactive feedback, and offline accessibility. Across these principles, effective
tools added value by helping learners access, practice, and consolidate foundational skills in ways that
were often difficult to sustain through standard classroom instruction alone.

First, EdTech tools are effective when explicitly aligned with the curriculum and skills learners are
expected to master. Curriculum alignment ensures that digital activities reinforce the same competencies
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 33

targeted in classrooms and assessments rather than functioning as parallel or disconnected exercises.
Effective models, such as onebillion in Malawi or e-readers integrated into Kenya’s PRIMR program, linked
content directly to national standards. This alignment made the tools relevant for learners, embedded in
classroom instruction, and tied to measurable progress on grade-level skills. By contrast, early
GraphoLearn pilots in India showed limited transfer: Students improved on in-game phonics tasks, but
these gains did not extend to oral or paper-based school assessments when the tool was not tightly
connected to classroom instruction, underscoring the importance of curricular integration. AI-enabled
tools such as RTM and Mindspark ’s AI-enhanced version follow the same principle by working with official
textbooks and competency frameworks rather than introducing unrelated content. In this respect, digital
tools add value when they make it easier to distribute, reuse, and standardize aligned content across
classrooms that may otherwise rely on scarce books, uneven materials, or teacher-created adaptations of
varying quality.

Second, EdTech tools are effective when they adapt instruction to learners’ performance through
personalized pathways . Evidence from cognitive science highlights that progress accelerates when tasks
are pitched at the right level of challenge (Vygotsky 1978). Effective models embedded this adaptivity
directly into their design. Some used simple branching logic, as in SMS- or IVR-based platforms that
adjusted lessons or review tasks based on quiz responses. Others apply more structured progression
rules, such as GraphoLearn ’s requirement that learners reach specific performance thresholds before
advancing or onebillion ’s sequenced game levels that unlock as learners master core skills. AI-enabled
systems extend this adaptive function. RTM uses AI to process text and support learners across proficien
cy levels, while TaRL-BOT uses speech recognition to adjust feedback on reading fluency, and Mindspark ’s
newer AI components generate leveled questions and explanations linked to learners’ current perfor
mance. Whether low-tech or AI-driven, these digital tools help learners progress more effectively when
tasks match their current level of understanding. Their value lies in making this adjustment more conti
nuous and manageable than whole-class teaching typically allows, especially where one teacher is
responsible for many learners at very different levels.

Third, EdTech tools are effective when they use sequenced and scaffolded practice that requires
learners to master subskills before progressing. Research in early reading and mathematics shows that
fluency develops through cumulative sequences, introducing skills in small steps and reinforcing them
until mastery is reached (Fuson et al. 2015; NRP 2000). Effective models built this directly into their
design. GraphoLearn required mastery of phonics units before advancement, Kitkit TM sequenced numeracy
tasks from number recognition to operations, and ABRA combined sequenced activities with tutorials that
modeled and guided attempts. Adaptive and AI-enabled tools build on this logic. Mindspark sequences
items by difficulty within learning progressions and uses its AI features to generate leveled questions and
practice tasks aligned with those sequences, while TaRL-BOT provides repeated, structured opportunities
to practice reading aloud until fluency improves. These designs promote mastery before progression and
scaffold skill acquisition, ultimately building stronger foundations for later comprehension and
problem-solving. Here, digital tools add value by helping organize practice in cumulative steps and by
ensuring that learners do not move on before consolidating prerequisite skills, something that is often
difficult to manage consistently in large, resource-constrained classrooms.

Fourth, EdTech tools are effective when they sustain engagement through multisensory and motivatio
nal features. Children’s attention and persistence increase when instruction engages multiple senses and
makes practice rewarding (Guthrie and Wigfield 2000; Hattie 2010). Effective models layer visual,
auditory, and interactive cues, such as synchronized audio–text in SiMBi or animated stories with
embedded quizzes in interactive e-books, to make abstract skills more concrete and memorable. Others

classroom instruction, and tied to measurable progress on grade-level skills. By contrast, early
GraphoLearn pilots in India showed limited transfer: Students improved on in-game phonics tasks, but
these gains did not extend to oral or paper-based school assessments when the tool was not tightly
connected to classroom instruction, underscoring the importance of curricular integration. AI-enabled
tools such as RTM and Mindspark ’s AI-enhanced version follow the same principle by working with official
textbooks and competency frameworks rather than introducing unrelated content. In this respect, digital
tools add value when they make it easier to distribute, reuse, and standardize aligned content across
classrooms that may otherwise rely on scarce books, uneven materials, or teacher-created adaptations of
varying quality.
Second, EdTech tools are effective when they adapt instruction to learners’ performance through
personalized pathways . Evidence from cognitive science highlights that progress accelerates when tasks
are pitched at the right level of challenge (Vygotsky 1978). Effective models embedded this adaptivity
directly into their design. Some used simple branching logic, as in SMS- or IVR-based platforms that
adjusted lessons or review tasks based on quiz responses. Others apply more structured progression
rules, such as GraphoLearn ’s requirement that learners reach specific performance thresholds before
advancing or onebillion ’s sequenced game levels that unlock as learners master core skills. AI-enabled
systems extend this adaptive function. RTM uses AI to process text and support learners across proficien
cy levels, while TaRL-BOT uses speech recognition to adjust feedback on reading fluency, and Mindspark ’s
newer AI components generate leveled questions and explanations linked to learners’ current perfor
mance. Whether low-tech or AI-driven, these digital tools help learners progress more effectively when
tasks match their current level of understanding. Their value lies in making this adjustment more conti
nuous and manageable than whole-class teaching typically allows, especially where one teacher is
responsible for many learners at very different levels.
Third, EdTech tools are effective when they use sequenced and scaffolded practice that requires
learners to master subskills before progressing. Research in early reading and mathematics shows that
fluency develops through cumulative sequences, introducing skills in small steps and reinforcing them
until mastery is reached (Fuson et al. 2015; NRP 2000). Effective models built this directly into their
design. GraphoLearn required mastery of phonics units before advancement, Kitkit TM sequenced numeracy
tasks from number recognition to operations, and ABRA combined sequenced activities with tutorials that
modeled and guided attempts. Adaptive and AI-enabled tools build on this logic. Mindspark sequences
items by difficulty within learning progressions and uses its AI features to generate leveled questions and
practice tasks aligned with those sequences, while TaRL-BOT provides repeated, structured opportunities
to practice reading aloud until fluency improves. These designs promote mastery before progression and
scaffold skill acquisition, ultimately building stronger foundations for later comprehension and
problem-solving. Here, digital tools add value by helping organize practice in cumulative steps and by
ensuring that learners do not move on before consolidating prerequisite skills, something that is often
difficult to manage consistently in large, resource-constrained classrooms.
Fourth, EdTech tools are effective when they sustain engagement through multisensory and motivatio
nal features. Children’s attention and persistence increase when instruction engages multiple senses and
makes practice rewarding (Guthrie and Wigfield 2000; Hattie 2010). Effective models layer visual,
auditory, and interactive cues, such as synchronized audio–text in SiMBi or animated stories with
embedded quizzes in interactive e-books, to make abstract skills more concrete and memorable. Others

title: 34 | How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries

paragraphs.text:
embedded motivational features like progress indicators, certificates, or game-like challenges, as in
onebillion ’s reading and math apps. By combining multisensory input with motivational design, these
tools reduced disengagement in resource-constrained classrooms where teacher-led instruction often
relied on rote repetition. Their contribution is especially visible where conventional instruction offers
limited variation, few opportunities for active participation, and little individualized encouragement to
persist with difficult subskills.

Fifth, EdTech tools are effective when they embed interactive feedback loops that promptly guide
progress and correct errors. Timely, specific feedback consolidates memory and steers learners toward
accurate skill use (Hattie 2010). Several tools in the review incorporated automatic scoring and feedback
that adjusted practice in real time. M-Shule auto-scored quizzes and adapted subsequent SMS lessons,
and onebillion’s apps and ABRA provided immediate responses to learner inputs. AI-enhanced tools
further enhance this feedback function in some cases. Morocco’s TaRL-BOT used speech recognition to
correct reading fluency immediately, and Mindspark ’s AI layer generated explanations and hints that
respond to learners’ specific errors. These feedback loops are promising when they focus on targeted
foundational skills and help learners understand how to correct mistakes. In settings where teachers
cannot feasibly review every learner response in real time, this kind of immediate correction can make
practice more productive and prevent repeated rehearsal of errors.

Finally, EdTech tools are effective when flexibly designed for offline functionality and lightweight
delivery. Many LMIC contexts continually face intermittent connectivity, high data costs, or unreliable
electricity. Successful models preloaded content onto devices (for example, onebillion , Kitkit TM, and PRIMR
e-readers), delivered lessons through SMS or IVR on basic phones, or ran fully offline with periodic data
uploads. The offline AI Tutor in Guatemala shows that even large language models can operate in such
environments when hosted locally on school servers and accessed through shared workstations, avoiding
dependence on continuous internet connectivity. While this pilot has not yet reported learning impacts, it
demonstrates the technical feasibility of providing AI-powered tutoring in rural schools without cloud
access. By minimizing technological barriers, these designs extended reach to learners most at risk of
exclusion.

Across these design principles, a central insight emerges: Learner-facing EdTech is most effective when it
supports core learning processes that are otherwise hard to deliver consistently in many LMIC classrooms,
including access to aligned content, practice at the right level, structured progression, timely feedback,
and sustained engagement. Within this broader landscape, AI expands design options for personalization,
feedback, and access. When tools meet these conditions, they operate as core supports for foundational
learning rather than as peripheral enrichment. But their value, like that of other EdTech tools, depends on
whether they strengthen these instructional processes under real delivery conditions rather than simply
adding another layer of technology.

title: Edtech for Curricular Support

paragraphs.text:
LMIC book supply chains often experience fragmented book policies, slow production cycles, high
production costs, shortages of editorial staff, and unreliable delivery of printed materials. These
constraints are especially acute in multilingual systems, where each update requires parallel translation
and adaptation across several languages (ADEA 2019; Fredriksen and Brar 2015). Addressing these
system gaps would require a sequence of interdependent tasks, including developing high-quality source
materials, localizing them across multiple languages, producing them at scale, and ensuring they reach
schools in the correct quantities . EdTech tools, described in Table 3 , support these tasks at the speed
required for effective foundational learning . These tools form two broad functional categories: (a) tools
that support content creation, localization, and regular updates to curriculum materials and (b) tools that
strengthen the distribution, storage, and management of books and other printed resources . Table 3
summarizes the primary features of each tool.

paragraphs.text:
EdTech tools in this category address bottlenecks related to content creation by accelerating early

costs. In varied forms, they converge on the same goal: ensuring teachers and learners receive timely,
coherent, and culturally relevant materials aligned with grade-level expectations.

title: Evidence on Relevant EdTech Solutions

paragraphs.text:
Three studies show that OER enable low-cost creation, adaptation, and sharing of instructional materials
in LMICs (Arinto et al. 2017; Oates and Hashimi 2016; Tlili et al. 2022). Open licenses let teachers and
curriculum developers revise, remix, and update materials without copyright barriers, which helps keep
content aligned with changing curricula. In Africa, OER initiatives have supported digital books in local
languages, including the African Storybook Initiative, whose openly licensed storybooks can be trans
lated, adapted, and printed for classroom use. In Afghanistan, the Darakht-e Danesh Library uses a
multilingual content system that allows contributors to adapt materials into Dari, Pashto, and English
while refining terminology, examples, and imagery for local relevance. Together, these studies show that
OER support scalable content creation and localization in contexts with limited access to aligned instruc
tional materials (see appendix 2 for details).

recordkeeping, stock management, and verification processes. These breakdowns limit learners’ exposure

barcode tracking, and digital confirmation of delivery. Evidence from Cambodia suggests that these

title: Emerging AI Use Cases for Curriculum Development and Delivery

paragraphs.text:
A review of 12 mostly qualitative studies finds that AI tools are beginning to support several stages of
publishing in Africa, including drafting and editing, illustration, translation, and production planning
(Salani and Tapfuma 2025). Tools such as Grammarly and GPT-based systems help with grammar correc
tion, readability checks, fact-checking, and early copyediting, while generative image tools support draft
illustrations that designers later refine for cultural accuracy. Machine translation tools are also being
tested to produce first-round drafts in African languages, which may reduce time and cost in multilingual
publishing systems. Evidence from a 2025 workshop in Senegal points in the same direction: Participants
used generative AI to create 18 original titles in five days, suggesting that AI can speed up content
production when paired with strong editorial oversight and culturally grounded design (Diop and Teel
2025) (see appendix 2 for details).

title: Key Takeaways for Effective EdTech for Curriculum

paragraphs.text:
The curriculum-facing tools reviewed reveal three design lessons about how EdTech can strengthen
foundational learning materials systems: (a) digital-first workflows that enable rapid drafting and iterative
updates, (b) built-in supports for systematic localization into local languages and contexts, and (c)
tracking and storage features that improve visibility and reliability in distribution. Across these functions,
the value of EdTech lies in making core material-development and delivery processes faster, more
adaptable, and more reliable than fully manual systems often allow.

First, tools supporting digital-first and iterative workflows make content development more efficient
and responsive. Across cases, digital and AI-supported production tools reduced dependence on long
manual cycles by accelerating early drafting, editing, illustration, and translation. AI-assisted drafting and
editing compressed the earliest phases of content development, while OER ecosystems provided editable
source files that curriculum teams could reorganize or adapt without restarting full print processes. This
design approach allows small teams to complete recurring tasks more quickly and at lower cost, keeping
materials aligned with curriculum reforms and instructional expectations.

Second, tools with structured mechanisms for localization make materials more instructionally usable.
Whether through AI-assisted translation, digital-first production, or open licensing, effective tools made
adaptation routine rather than exceptional. They provided accessible ways for curriculum teams and
teachers to adjust terminology, cultural references, and language versions so materials reflected learners’
environments. This design feature is especially important in multilingual foundational learning systems
and for learners with disabilities, where timely access to aligned, readable, and usable formats often
determines whether instruction can be delivered as intended. When localization and accessibility are
embedded in the workflow, adapted materials are more likely to reach classrooms in forms that teachers
and learners can use. In this respect, EdTech adds value by making adaptation easier to repeat, modify,

title: Edtech for Instructional Support Systems

paragraphs.text:
The Challenge: Limited Availability of Timely, Instructionally Useful Data to Inform Teaching,
Supervision, or Course Correction

Most LMIC systems lack reliable ways to track what learners can do between infrequent summative
assessments, which would reinforce the instructional core by providing feedback loops that help teachers
adjust their instruction. Recent evidence from Africa suggests that digital tools can help address this gap
(Prinsloo and Kaliisa 2022). The models reviewed in this section provide illustrative examples of what these
tools are and how they work in practice, including (a) AI-enabled oral reading assessments, (b) assess
ments built into digital activities, (c) usage logs that capture student engagement, and (d) dashboards that
compile these student data for teacher or supervisory review. Table 4 provides a summary.

(Prinsloo and Kaliisa 2022). The models reviewed in this section provide illustrative examples of what these
tools are and how they work in practice, including (a) AI-enabled oral reading assessments, (b) assess
ments built into digital activities, (c) usage logs that capture student engagement, and (d) dashboards that
compile these student data for teacher or supervisory review. Table 4 provides a summary.

title: ﻿ Embedding Digital Assessments into Learning Activities

paragraphs.text:
Several tools generate foundational learning data through assessments embedded directly in learning
activities. These checks run during regular use and produce frequent, low-stakes information without
separate testing sessions. This model appears across ABRA , GraphoLearn , the onebillion apps, and
ProFuturo . For instance, ABRA (Abrami et al. 2016) embeds short assessments in its literacy activities and
summarizes student performance in phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, and comprehension. These
summaries enable teachers to monitor student progress over time. GraphoLearn (Bora et al. 2024) uses
similar embedded checks within a phonics-based reading environment. Each activity captures subskill
data such as letter-sound knowledge and word recognition. Numeracy tools use similar features. The
onebillion apps in Malawi (Pitchford et al. 2019) include short end-of-topic quizzes that verify student
mastery before they advance, while ProFuturo ’s modules in Angola (Cardim et al. 2023) include brief
checks that generate immediate feedback for teachers to review when tracking individual and class-level
progress. Across platforms, embedded checks give teachers frequent, curriculum-aligned evidence of
how children are progressing. They also reduce the burden of stand-alone assessments and generate
digital records that can support lesson planning and follow-up.

title: ﻿ Monitoring Engagement and Learning Dosage

paragraphs.text:
Some tools generate foundational skill data through simple usage logs to record how often learners show
up, how they interact, what they attempt, how long they stay, and how usage patterns reflect engage
ment, besides mastery. This approach works in low-connectivity settings and provides basic indicators of
engagement and progression. For instance, M-Shule in Kenya (Jordan et al. 2025) records SMS responses,
quiz attempts, and subtopic completion to show which learners are engaging with the content and how
frequently they interact with each lesson. An IVR model in Bangladesh (Wang et al. 2023) logs atten
dance and responses to short audio quizzes, allowing programs to track which caregiver-child pairs
access each lesson and how often. Kitkit School (Lee and Choi 2020) stores local play-log data showing
how often children complete math activities and how these patterns relate to performance. Makhalidwe
Athu in Zambia (Ome and Menendez 2022) offers a lighter-touch approach through self-reported reading
frequency, which still gives project teams a sense of regular engagement with reading tasks.

title: ﻿ Synthesizing Data for Instructional Decision-Making

paragraphs.text:
Several tools introduced in earlier sections organize digital traces from assessments, activities, and usage
logs into simple dashboards that provide teachers, school leaders, or supervisory teams with a clearer
view of learner progress. These dashboards compile performance indicators captured during routine
digital use and present them in formats that support quick review and follow-up. Morocco’s TaRL-BOT , an
AI-based oral reading tool, presents accuracy and fluency profiles that enable teachers to identify learners
who need targeted reading practice. M-Shule uses quiz performance to determine when learners progress
to the next unit, and its log data helps supervisors track participation across schools. ABRA and ProFuturo
summarize activity-level performance and highlight which skills learners have mastered and where
additional support is needed. These summaries help teachers adjust grouping, pacing, or practice
activities without additional data entry or manual scoring. These developments show that well-designed
dashboards can give teachers and supervisory teams a practical way to access performance trends, timely
alerts, and clear summaries so they can respond quickly to emerging learning needs.

title: ﻿ Emerging AI Use Cases for Automating Foundational Skill Assessment

paragraphs.text:
Evaluating oral reading fluency traditionally requires significant one-on-one teacher time, creating a
bottleneck for continuous progress monitoring. Emerging use cases deploy automatic speech recognition
to record, score, and track student reading independently. These platforms aim to reduce assessment
workloads and standardize data collection across school systems. The examples below illustrate these
tools in practice. While they demonstrate operational viability and rapid scale, their causal impact on
downstream learning outcomes remains untested. Two recent examples suggest that AI-enabled oral
reading assessment tools can reduce teacher workload and strengthen progress monitoring in early-
grade literacy. In Morocco, TaRL-BOT uses offline speech recognition within Moodle to score learners’
reading tasks and generate structured records that teachers and supervisors can use for grouping and
tracking progress; pilot results found that its scores were broadly consistent with human benchmarks
(Bachiri et al. 2024). In India, Vaachan Samiksha automates oral reading fluency checks at a large scale
within Gujarat’s public school system, enabling faster scoring, immediate feedback, and easier identifica
tion of learners who need support, though it currently depends on internet connectivity (Wadhwani AI
2025). Together, these cases suggest that AI can make foundational literacy assessment more efficient
and actionable when integrated into existing instructional systems (see appendix 2 for details).

title: ﻿ Key Takeaways for Effective EdTech for Instructional Support

paragraphs.text:
The tools reviewed in this section highlight several design features that make digital assessment and
monitoring models workable in low-resource environments. Three design lessons emerge across AI-en
abled and more traditional EdTech-based tools: (a) integrating instruction-aligned checks directly into
learning routines, (b) using lightweight data-capture channels suited to low-connectivity settings, and (c)
converting digital traces into simple, actionable dashboards. Across these functions, different technologies
add value in different ways: Lighter tools such as SMS, IVR, and offline logs make it feasible to capture
basic learner participation and performance under weak infrastructure conditions, while richer digital and
AI-enabled tools can process more complex responses, automate scoring, and support faster feedback.

Second, instructional support tools work effectively when they use data-capture methods designed for
low-connectivity environments. SMS- and IVR-based systems, as in M-Shule and Bangladesh’s audio
lessons and locally stored gameplay logs in Kitkit School, illustrate how lightweight channels can operate
consistently without broadband. These features allow schools to collect participation and performance
data even in settings where connectivity is sporadic, extending visibility into learning patterns over time.
This is where lighter technologies have a clear advantage: They make routine data capture feasible where
more connected systems would be too fragile or costly, even if they generate narrower information than
richer adaptive platforms.

Finally, simple reporting formats and well-structured dashboards make digital traces actionable for
teachers and supervisory teams. Dashboards that present a small set of performance indicators, such as
reading accuracy, key subskills, or activity completion, can help educators interpret performance data
quickly and identify learners needing additional support. When paired with prompts for grouping, pacing,
or targeted practice, these design features ensure that data lead to concrete instructional adjustments
rather than remaining only informational. Their value lies in translating learner traces into signals that
teachers or supervisors can use. This function becomes more important as systems adopt more connec
ted, adaptive, or AI-enabled tools, and it depends on clear arrangements for data quality, hosting, access,
privacy, and security.

title: Implementation Enablers and Barriers

paragraphs.text:
Effective EdTech models described in this guidance note show that pedagogical soundness is central to
their design. Effective tools align with what is known about how children develop foundational learning
skills, how teachers build and refine the instructional practices supportive of that development, and what
an effective curriculum requires. Their success in practice also depends on the conditions into which they
are introduced and how users interact with them. Across teacher-facing, learner-facing, curriculum, and
instructional support system tools, the evidence reveals shared enablers and barriers, with distinct
nuances in each category. These implementation conditions operate across three interrelated levels of the
education system: micro, meso, and macro. The micro level refers to individual actors, including learners,
teachers, and learning facilitators, and the immediate environments in which they use EdTech tools. The
meso level refers to organizational and institutional settings, such as classrooms, schools, and other
learning facilities, where collective routines and support structures influence implementation. The macro
level refers to system-wide infrastructure, governance, and policy environments, including electricity,
internet access, data costs, and device maintenance, that enable or constrain sustained EdTech use. These
factors can either facilitate or hinder EdTech integration, depending on how they are addressed. This
section synthesizes cross-cutting and category-specific conditions at each level. In some cases, challen
ges arose from the absence of enabling conditions. Rather than restating those gaps, we highlight distinct
constraints that have not been discussed earlier. Table 5 summarizes the main implementation enablers
and barriers across the micro, meso, and macro levels of the education system. Additionally, while all
factors are relevant to both conventional and AI-enabled EdTech, those marked with an asterisk (*)
hold particular importance for the use of AI-enabled tools .

title: Enablers

paragraphs.text: Familiar devices and interfaces*

Implementation was smoother when EdTech, including emerging AI tools, used devices and
platforms already familiar to users, such as mobile phones, WhatsApp, or basic tablets. This
familiarity reduced onboarding time and lowered barriers to initial uptake, particularly in
settings with limited digital literacy (Appiah-Okyere 2024; Cardim et al. 2023; Jukes et al. 2017).
In Sierra Leone, theTeacher.AI benefited from its WhatsApp-based interface, which allowed
teachers to access AI-generated support without navigating new software environments (Choi
et al. 2024). In India, Vaachan Samiksha was deployed through digital systems that teachers
already used, which supported adoption at scale (Wadhwani AI 2025). Programs in Kenya
showed similar results when a complex learning management system was replaced with
WhatsApp, leading to faster teacher responses and more consistent use (Head et al. 2023).
Learners showed the same tendency; children adapted quickly to interactive e-books when
already familiar with tablets, while first-time users of tablet-based math tools required facilita
tor supervision to manage devices and remain focused (Klop et al. 2018; Lee and Choi 2020).
Simple, easy-to-read reporting formats also supported implementation. Dashboards that
summarized progress in clear, low-burden displays made it easier for teachers to interpret
digital traces, including AI-generated assessments such as automated oral reading scores, and
to act on them during lessons (Abrami et al. 2016; Bachiri et al. 2024; Cardim et al. 2023).
Onboarding support*

Programs that embedded onboarding supports, such as multimedia tutorials, orientation
sessions, or dedicated walkthroughs, helped teachers navigate new technologies and imple
ment them as intended, while ongoing technical support was important (Abrami et al. 2016;
Cilliers et al. 2022; Uribe-Banda et al. 2023). Learners also benefited when onboarding was
scaffolded by adults: In Zambia, the Makhalidwe Athu project trained parents to share SMS
stories at home, while Bangladesh’s IVR program included household visits to prepare caregiv
ers as facilitators (Ome and Menendez 2022; Wang et al. 2023). In school-based settings,
facilitators supervised children’s initial use of digital tools, such as interactive e-books in South
Africa and tablet-based math games in Tanzania, ensuring that learners could manage devices
and engage with the content effectively (Klop et al. 2018; Lee and Choi 2020). As tools incorpo
rated AI capabilities, onboarding needs expanded. Effective implementation required prepara
tion that went beyond general digital literacy, with training focused on foundational AI literacy
skills such as constructing and refining prompts, since basic device familiarity was insufficient
(Leba et al. 2025). The onboarding for theTeacher.AI in Sierra Leone illustrated this shift.
Teachers participated in guided practice sessions on asking questions, adjusting prompts, and
posing instructional scenarios to elicit contextually appropriate responses, as many initially
interacted with the tool as if it were a standard search engine (Choi et al. 2024).
User buy-in*

Sustained participation depended on whether users perceived clear value. Teacher motivation
and perceived instructional benefit influenced continued engagement; implementation was
more consistent when teachers experienced tangible improvements in their practice or student
learning and had opportunities to reflect, adapt, and apply new strategies in ways that felt

routine prompts or in-lesson cues helped teachers sustain new instructional practices. Regular

In Sierra Leone, theTeacher.AI benefited from its WhatsApp-based interface, which allowed
teachers to access AI-generated support without navigating new software environments (Choi

already used, which supported adoption at scale (Wadhwani AI 2025). Programs in Kenya
showed similar results when a complex learning management system was replaced with
WhatsApp, leading to faster teacher responses and more consistent use (Head et al. 2023).

already familiar with tablets, while first-time users of tablet-based math tools required facilita

posing instructional scenarios to elicit contextually appropriate responses, as many initially
interacted with the tool as if it were a standard search engine (Choi et al. 2024).

title: Barriers

paragraphs.text: Low digital literacy levels*

Implementation was frequently constrained when EdTech tools demanded unfamiliar digital
skills, disrupted established routines, or lacked perceived instructional relevance. Across various
settings, teachers and learners struggled when tools demanded skills beyond their prior
experience. For instance, in Kenya, 12 percent of the 75 teachers in the ABRA -Integrated Online
TPD program reported that they did not know how to navigate the provided tablets, and 28
percent had difficulty troubleshooting devices when they froze mid-lesson (Uribe-Banda et al.
2023). Similar frustrations were observed in Ghana, where teachers found multistep logins and
app switching to be impractical without direct support (Head et al. 2023). Learners also lost
instructional time when initial sessions were consumed by learning basic device navigation, as
in Uganda’s audiobook intervention and Tanzania’s Kitkit TM math program (Friedland et al. 2017;
Lee and Choi 2020).

prompts (Choi et al. 2024). In Senegal, artists who worked only with hand-drawn methods and
lacked the required digital skills were unable to join an AI-supported book creation workshop,
narrowing the pool of contributors (Diop and Teel 2025) and potentially reinforcing existing
skill-based inequities in the book industry in LMICs (ADEA 2019). While targeted onboarding
and prompt-focused training eased some barriers, the findings point to a broader need to
strengthen digital and AI literacy if systems were to maximize the benefits of EdTech.
Entrenched practices and weak persistence

Even when technology was available, teachers sometimes reverted to traditional routines that
sidelined digital content when instructional habits and classroom formats were not easily
adaptable to new tools. In Kenya, laptops preloaded with literacy software were used only
superficially in classrooms that remained centered on whole-class delivery, limiting exposure to
interactive reading activities (Abrami et al. 2016). Similar patterns were noted in India, where
GraphoLearn was introduced as a supplement but not integrated into classroom phonics
instruction (Bora et al. 2024). Additionally, without sustained motivation or external reinforce
ment, initial uptake often gave way to attrition. In Kenya, many learners enrolled in the
SMS-based M-Shule platform disengaged after a short period (Jordan 2023). In Bangladesh,
participation in an IVR program declined steadily over 15 weeks, particularly after schools
partially reopened (Wang et al. 2023).
Linguistic misalignment

In Kenya, some teachers found English-accented voice-overs in the ABRA training modules
difficult to follow (Uribe-Banda et al. 2023). In Uganda, children struggled with unfamiliar
English words in audiobook passages (Friedland et al. 2017). In India, GraphoLearn ’s reliance on
English-only content limited learning transfer where classroom teaching occurred in Hindi (Bora
et al. 2024). Although often observed at the classroom level, these mismatches reflected design
decisions that failed to account for local language dynamics.

title: Enablers

paragraphs.text: Teacher collaboration

Implementation of EdTech tools or EdTech-based TPD was often stronger when embedded in
daily school routines that enabled teachers to learn from and support one another over time
(Graham et al. 2021). This involved fostering a collective responsibility for EdTech use among
teachers and reinforcing it with structured routines like regular coaching and peer support
beyond initial onboarding (Cilliers et al. 2022; De Hoop et al. 2020). Peer interaction, whether in
person, through online discussion forums, or via WhatsApp groups, gave teachers space to
exchange strategies, solve problems, and sustain motivation (Appiah-Okyere 2024; Head et al.
2023). In Kenya, for example, teachers in an online course reported that group work and peer
communication were ‘very motivating’ and increased their confidence (Head et al. 2023). Peer
facilitators and mentors also bridged the gap between training and daily classroom practice. In
Zambia, for instance, a school-based professional development program was facilitated by a
peer teacher whose role was pivotal in establishing discussion norms and helping colleagues
reflect on their practice (Hennessy et al. 2016). Similarly, in another program for teachers in
Sub-Saharan Africa, facilitators were trained to organize institutional study groups, and
How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries | 47

graduates later became mentors supporting local peer groups (Stutchbury et al. 2025). These
practices emphasize that collaborative structures help institutionalize EdTech as part of
teachers’ professional culture rather than an external add-on.
Leadership engagement

School leaders played a crucial role in sustaining EdTech use. In South Africa, school manage
ment teams received tailored orientation to encourage ongoing teacher support, and virtual
coaches regularly checked in with them to reinforce accountability and encouragement (Cilliers
et al. 2022). These efforts ensured that leaders actively supported and monitored technology
use, rather than leaving the responsibility to teachers alone. When leadership promoted shared
ownership, teachers were more likely to see the tools as part of their professional environment
rather than as external demands (Johnston and Ksoll 2022).
Accountability and incentives

Programs reinforced consistent use by linking participation to clear expectations and monito
ring systems. For teachers, supervision and mentoring created visible accountability. In Zambia,
a school-based program designated a peer teacher as facilitator, whose role was pivotal in
setting discussion norms (Hennessy et al. 2016). In Kenya, lab staff supported teachers during
computer sessions and provided pedagogical feedback, ensuring learners engaged effectively
with the software (Abrami et al. 2016). Other programs combined monitoring with explicit
incentives. In Kenya’s Health and Literacy Intervention (HALI), teachers received weekly mobile
phone credit for responding to instructional text messages (Jukes et al. 2017). In Zambia, the
GraphoGame TM Teacher Training Service required weekly submission of student game logs;
teachers who complied received completion certificates (STS 2017). These mechanisms
sustained use by making technology expected, visible, and rewarded.
Alignment with existing programs and workflows*

Sustainability improved when EdTech, including AI-enabled models, was aligned with estab
lished school curricula, routines, and instructional programs. Tools were purposefully designed
to support national literacy goals, structured pedagogy practices, and curriculum pacing, ensur
ing coherence with school instruction (Abrami et al. 2016; Bora et al. 2024; Piper et al. 2016;
Sidibe et al. 2025; Uribe-Banda et al. 2023). In Kenya, the ABRA software was designed to
match national English language requirements by grade (Abrami et al. 2016). In India, large-
scale initiatives, such as RightToRead , embedded software directly into official timetables and
teacher-led lessons under the principle of ‘minimum change and sustainability’, which
enhanced adoption and continuity (Srinivasan and Murthy 2021). This need for contextual
relevance and alignment is especially important for AI-enabled models. Recent AI initiatives
show the value of grounding systems in national curriculum structures. RTM in India, an
AI-enabled multisensory reading platform, layers audio, visual cues, and images onto govern
ment textbooks and is used during regular English lessons, requiring minimal deviation from
routine (Srinivasan and Murthy 2021). In Mali, generative AI was trained on Mali’s curriculum,
competency frameworks, and national language lesson templates to ensure that outputs
aligned with local instructional expectations (Sidibe et al. 2025). Similarly, AI-driven book
production in Senegal integrated new tools into existing publishing workflows. Writers and illus
trators followed familiar drafting, illustration, and revision processes, while AI tools were added
into these established routines, enabling AI components to complement rather than replace
standard book production processes (Diop and Teel 2025). Overall, these cases demonstrate
that aligning EdTech, whether conventional or AI-enabled, with established routines, programs,

and workflows is crucial for ensuring local adoption and potentially achieving long-term
sustainability at scale.
Opening licensing

Open li censing is an important enabler of curriculum- and instructional support tools. It made it
easier for curriculum teams and implementing partners to adapt digital materials to local
languages and instructional needs. In LMICs, projects often faced delays when materials were
locked or subject to restrictive copyright, which prevented translation, contextual adjustments,
or updates to examples and visuals; these constraints reduced relevance and slowed alignment
with national curriculum priorities (ADEA 2019; Fredriksen and Brar 2015). When files were
openly licensed or provided in editable formats, teams could adapt terminology, examples, and
imagery to reflect local contexts without lengthy approval processes (Arinto et al. 2017; Oates
and Hashimi 2016; Tlili et al. 2022). These permissions supported routine localization and made
ongoing updates possible as curriculum requirements evolved.

title: Barriers

paragraphs.text: Weak monitoring

Inconsistent monitoring and follow-up were a common challenge in supporting regular EdTech
use across multiple programs, whether offline tablet-based training, digital resource provision,
or remote coaching (Cilliers et al. 2019; De Hoop et al. 2024; Kotze et al. 2019). In South Africa,
for instance, tablet usage among teachers in a virtual coaching model declined over time,
peaking only during assessment weeks, suggesting that engagement was driven by external
compliance, and without it, consistent use was not sustained (Cilliers et al. 2022).
Logistical and environmental constraints

Learner-focused studies also highlighted logistical barriers that reduced exposure time. In
Kenya, busing students to off-site computer labs led to time loss and limited practice (Abrami
et al. 2016). In Malawi and Zambia, hardware shortages, scheduling challenges, and large class
sizes restricted the ability to provide individualized or small-group support (Bora et al. 2024;
Pitchford et al. 2019).
In-school facilitation and relational support in remote formats

While trusted peer facilitators helped bridge training and daily classroom practice in some
settings, not all schools had access to such in-house support, particularly in rural areas, where
teacher capacity tends to be lower. In rural Ghana, for example, teachers participating in an
online TPD program delivered via the Internet Backpack reported challenges in forming strong
in-school scaffolding structures. Facilitator support varied widely; some school-based facilita
tors lacked the expertise to provide meaningful instructional guidance while teachers were
completing the program (Appiah-Okyere 2024). Additionally, in virtual coaching models,
teachers reported that support was often one-directional, with limited personalization or
classroom-specific guidance, an issue that may have been compounded by the reduced
relational connection in remote formats (Cilliers et al. 2019; Kotze et al. 2019). Similar issues
arose in learner-focused programs: In Ghana’s MGCubed initiative, classroom facilitators were
observed off task about 40 percent of the time, undermining the effectiveness of satel
lite-transmitted lessons. This challenge was often compounded by limited or inconsistent
support from school leadership, which further weakened school-wide coordination and
oversight (Haßler 2020; Hennessy et al. 2016).

title: BOX 1. WHY DOES DIGITAL PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE INFLUENCE EDTECH VIABILITY AT SCALE?

paragraphs.text:
Digital public infrastructure (DPI) provides the shared digital building blocks that allow services to
function across entire systems, replacing isolated platforms (Bandura et al. 2023; OECD 2024a).
These building blocks typically include digital identity, payment rails, and data-exchange frameworks.
Together, they allow institutions to verify users, move resources, and share information across
platforms using common standards (Clark et al. 2025; ITU 2025).

In education, EdTech tools rarely remain stand-alone products. Scaling these tools requires mecha
nisms to identify learners and teachers, transfer records across platforms, verify credentials, and
exchange data between vendors and ministries. Without these shared foundations, public systems
risk dependence on fragmented, closed systems (Ingram et al. 2022; ITU 2025). Consequently, EdTech
models require varying levels of DPI. Lighter tools, such as SMS nudges, IVR lessons, preloaded
tablets, and offline libraries, function with minimal shared infrastructure. Connected tools, including
digital assessments, adaptive platforms, and AI applications, depend on secure hosting, interoperable
data systems, authentication, and institutional governance (ITU 2025; OECD 2024a). A tool may
succeed in an isolated pilot but fail at scale if the broader system lacks these operational functions.

Building identity, payments, and data exchange as shared public goods reduces fragmentation,
lowers long-term costs, and mitigates vendor lock-in (GovTech Intelligence Hub 2024; ITU 2025).
Experiences from countries such as Estonia and India suggest that shared digital architecture can

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) provides the shared digital building blocks that allow services to
function across entire systems, replacing isolated platforms (Bandura et al. 2023; OECD 2024a).
These building blocks typically include digital identity, payment rails, and data-exchange frameworks.
Together, they allow institutions to verify users, move resources, and share information across
platforms using common standards (Clark et al. 2025; ITU 2025).
In education, EdTech tools rarely remain stand-alone products. Scaling these tools requires mecha
nisms to identify learners and teachers, transfer records across platforms, verify credentials, and
exchange data between vendors and ministries. Without these shared foundations, public systems
risk dependence on fragmented, closed systems (Ingram et al. 2022; ITU 2025). Consequently, EdTech
models require varying levels of DPI. Lighter tools, such as SMS nudges, IVR lessons, preloaded
tablets, and offline libraries, function with minimal shared infrastructure. Connected tools, including
digital assessments, adaptive platforms, and AI applications, depend on secure hosting, interoperable
data systems, authentication, and institutional governance (ITU 2025; OECD 2024a). A tool may
succeed in an isolated pilot but fail at scale if the broader system lacks these operational functions.

lowers long-term costs, and mitigates vendor lock-in (GovTech Intelligence Hub 2024; ITU 2025).

title: Enablers

paragraphs.text: Interim infrastructure substitutes*

Adaptive design and interim infrastructure substitutes were central to effective EdTech and AI
implementation. Limited electricity access, weak internet connectivity, and unreliable devices
constrained use across nearly all LMIC settings, especially in rural schools. Programs that
anticipated these constraints and built solutions into their design were far more likely to reach
underserved schools and sustain regular use. Tools that offered offline functionality, preloaded
content, or solar-powered devices created workable substitutes for absent infrastructure and
allowed teachers and learners to engage with digital resources even when core systems were
missing (Appiah-Okyere 2024; Cardim et al. 2023; Cilliers et al. 2019; De Hoop et al. 2024).

entirely without internet access and required no subscription fees, directly addressing the dual
barriers of connectivity and cost (Arrow Electronics 2025; Gutwein 2025). Other programs

interim solutions can reduce immediate access barriers. Interim solutions bypass immediate

hardware and local servers. Systems thus need to build shared digital foundations to manage
how tools, users, and data interact across the education sector over the long term (see Box 1 for
more information).
Affordability

While imperative, infrastructure adaptations had cost implications. In South Africa, the virtual
coaching model cost less per teacher annually (US$2,168) than the on-site model (US$2,750),
but additional implementation expenses offset expected savings. These included tablet
provision (through a seven-year depreciation schedule), software hosting (5 percent of total
costs), an extra day of training, and dedicated technology support. This means implementation
planning must account not only for delivery modality but also for ongoing infrastructure,
personnel, and maintenance needs. Affordability at the user level also influenced implementa
tion. Even when hardware was available, high data costs could restrict access and engagement.
Programs that reduced or covered recurring data expenses, whether by relying on free plat
forms like ABRA and Facebook (Abrami et al. 2016; Krismanto et al. 2024; Kwaah 2024) or
providing data stipends (Jukes et al. 2017), lowered participation barriers.
Partnerships

Finally, system partnerships and monitoring structures helped sustain local successes and
support scale-up. In many cases, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), implementation
partners, and telecom providers played central roles in designing, delivering, and troubleshoo
ting EdTech initiatives, while governments retained oversight, approval, or eventual scale-up
responsibility (Srinivasan and Murthy 2021). Monitoring and reporting systems, such as school
visits, call-ins, and server log analysis, enabled fidelity checks and iterative improvements
(Jordan 2023; Srinivasan and Murthy 2021). While role arrangements vary across partnerships,
government ownership of day-to-day implementation frequently remains limited in EdTech
initiatives (UNICEF 2022). This pattern underscores the importance of clear partnership struc
tures and monitoring mechanisms as essential enablers for sustained EdTech implementation.
Data governance

Many digital tools collect and process learner-level data, including quiz responses in M-Shule ,
activity completion and gameplay logs in Kitkit School and onebillion , oral reading scores in
TaRL-BOT and Vaachan Samiksha , and progression through tasks or skill levels in GraphoLearn
and adaptive platforms such as Mindspark . These data can support more responsive instruc
tion, but they also require clear rules for storage, access, retention, privacy, and security.
International guidance (UNICEF Innocenti 2025) now treats these issues as central to
responsible EdTech governance, especially for tools that continuously collect, store, or process
children’s data. At a minimum, systems should specify where data are hosted, who can access
learner-level rather than aggregated data, how long records are kept, what security protections
apply, and what oversight governs vendors or platforms that process education data. Without
these conditions, systems may collect useful instructional data but still struggle to manage
them responsibly and sustain their use at scale.

title: BOX 2. BALANCING THE PROMISE AND RISKS OF AI IN FOUNDATIONAL LEARNING

paragraphs.text:
AI and connected technologies can support foundational learning, but they also raise developmental,
pedagogical, and rights-based concerns. Over-automating decoding or calculation can reduce the
practice children need to build independent literacy and numeracy skills, while excessive screen time
can increase cognitive fatigue and weaken sustained attention, especially among younger learners
(Deckker and Sumanasekara 2025; OECD 2023; UNESCO 2023). These risks mean AI use in education
should be treated as a policy choice, not an inevitable solution. Systems need to define where AI
adds clear pedagogical value and where human-led, relational, or culturally grounded approaches
remain more appropriate (EdTech Hub and World Bank 2026).

Evidence from Malawi, Uruguay, and India suggests that safeguards work best when they are built
into instructional design rather than added later. Effective models use digital tools as structured
supplements, maintain teacher control over pacing and task assignment, and embed technology
within blended routines rather than allowing it to dominate instruction (Muralidharan et al. 2019;
Perera and Aboal 2019; Pitchford et al. 2019). At the same time, AI’s reliance on learner-level data
raises major privacy, governance, and equity concerns. Ministries therefore need procurement and
regulatory rules that govern data hosting, access, retention, and commercial use, while also requiring
localized testing for bias, pedagogical fit, and performance across underrepresented groups such as
rural learners and speakers of nondominant languages (EdTech Hub and World Bank 2026; OECD
2024b; UNICEF 2025). Beyond system-level safeguards, children also need age-appropriate digital
and AI literacy so they can engage with technology critically and safely.

title: Barriers

paragraphs.text: Infrastructure gaps and malfunctioning devices*

Several constraints at the macro system level reflect the absence or partial fulfillment of the
enabling conditions discussed earlier, such as reliable infrastructure, device availability, and cost
mitigation. Where this support was missing, implementation of EdTech-based TPD became
difficult to sustain, particularly in underserved or rural areas. In other cases, however,
constraints emerged even when basic infrastructure was nominally present but failed to
function as intended. For instance, devices were sometimes available but frequently malfunc
tioned, lacked maintenance support, or could not be used effectively due to missing accesso
ries such as headphones or chargers (Abrami et al. 2016; Uribe-Banda et al. 2023). Platforms
designed for offline use still required periodic connectivity for updates or coordination, which
remained out of reach in areas with persistent power outages or unreliable networks (STS
2017). These subtler constraints limited the practical usability of EdTech tools even where they
were technically in place.

initiative were found to be the least cost-effective design, with costs per child far exceeding
alternatives (Piper et al. 2016). Although device costs have likely declined since this early study,
hardware affordability remains a salient concern for system-level adoption and scale. Some

Overall, these constraints indicate that system-wide readiness is crucial for the effective use of

is unreliable or access is costly.

AI-Specific Challenges: Gaps in Content Accuracy and Pedagogical Suitability
AI-enabled tools introduced several cross-cutting challenges related to the accuracy of outputs, the
degree of localization achievable with existing models, and the extent to which recommendations
aligned with pedagogical needs. In Mali, for example, the use of Claude to generate structured
lessons exposed persistent accuracy issues; the drafts required extensive human editing due to AI
hallucination, particularly when producing content in national languages with limited training data
(Sidibe et al. 2025). Localization challenges also emerged in Senegal’s AI-supported book produc
tion workshop, where prompts had to be written in French for the model to function effectively,
reducing local nuance and generating images that reflected global rather than Senegalese cultural
patterns (Diop and Teel 2025).

Concerns about pedagogical fit appeared across settings. In Indonesia, AI-generated recommen
dations often failed to match local instructional traditions, community values, or learners’ needs
(Leba et al. 2025). Facilitators in Senegal’s AI-supported book creation training also flagged unsafe
or unsuitable outputs, including images that showed risky scenarios such as a child riding a horse
without a saddle; these required removal or correction before use (Diop and Teel 2025). Beyond
content errors, Indonesia’s TPD pilot further showed that heavy reliance on AI tools could weaken
teacher autonomy and contribute to emotional and behavioral disengagement (Leba et al. 2025).
These issues highlight the need for careful human oversight, strong local grounding, and thorough
review processes to ensure that AI enhances, rather than distorts, instructional practice.
