title: For Policy

paragraphs.text:
The evidence synthesized in this guidance note points to a set of higher-level decisions that could guide
policy and program design, particularly when governments and partners are considering whether, when,
and how EdTech can strengthen foundational learning.

text:
The evidence synthesized in this guidance note points to a set of higher-level decisions that could guide
policy and program design, particularly when governments and partners are considering whether, when,
and how EdTech can strengthen foundational learning.

title: 1. Start with the instructional problem, not the technology.

paragraphs.text:
Throughout this guidance note, we show that foundational learning systems in LMICs face persistent
constraints in the instructional core. Teachers often lack support to model and practice effective methods;
learners experience uneven opportunities for guided practice, feedback, and differentiation; and schools
struggle with irregular access to aligned materials, protected instructional time, and reliable ways to
monitor progress. The interventions that demonstrated value addressed these barriers by strengthening
instructional routines under real system constraints, not by adding parallel digital tasks. The relevant
policy question, therefore, is not whether a tool is innovative, but whether it addresses a defined instruc
tional problem in ways that improve teaching and learning in context.

policy question, therefore, is not whether a tool is innovative, but whether it addresses a defined instruc
tional problem in ways that improve teaching and learning in context.

title: 2. Prioritize instructional fit over novelty.

paragraphs.text:
The strongest tools align with the curriculum, fit classroom routines, and provide usable support for
teachers and learners. Across teacher-, learner-, curriculum-, and assessment-facing interventions,
technology added value when it helped model target skills, scaffold practice, support differentiation,
extend learning time, or guide instructional decisions in ways that reinforced established pedagogical
goals. These effects depended on how technology and pedagogy worked together, not on digital features
alone. Technology should therefore be judged by whether it strengthens an existing instructional
approach, not by novelty or technical sophistication in itself.

title: 3. Design based on real-world LMIC school conditions from the start.

paragraphs.text:
Across teacher-, learner-, curriculum-, and assessment-facing initiatives, EdTech was effective when
teachers and learners could use it within their existing routines. Choices about connectivity, devices,
power, content format, and user support should reflect actual infrastructure and implementation condi
tions, especially in rural and lower-capacity settings. Tools were more likely to be used consistently when
they fit naturally within existing routines, required minimal navigation, reduced operational friction, and
functioned reliably despite limited connectivity, shared devices, or irregular electricity. Where readiness is
limited, offline and low-bandwidth design should be treated as a central design choice, not a fallback.
Operational usability is a core design requirement because even instructionally sound tools lose value
when delivery conditions make regular use difficult.

title: 4. Account for the full cost of ownership.

paragraphs.text:
Many reviewed interventions suggest that recurring expenditures, especially for data, maintenance,
hosting, and support, become more constraining over time than the initial hardware purchase. Although
cost evidence remains uneven, the available studies show substantial variation across models and make
clear that affordability shapes continuity as much as technical reliability. Tools that depend on paid data
plans, frequent top-ups, or costly maintenance are harder to sustain, even when their instructional design
is strong. Costing decisions should therefore focus on continuity, not just rollout, and should account for
the full set of recurring requirements that shape long-term use.

Cost data are reported inconsistently, but available figures suggest broad reference ranges where
assumptions are explicit. Teacher-facing models ranged from about US$2 to US$70 per student per year,
depending on delivery format and hardware inclusion. Learner-facing models also varied widely, from
roughly US$20 to US$36 per learner across SMS, IVR, and shared-device approaches, with some
device-intensive models costing more. AI-enabled models introduced additional costs; in Guatemala, for
example, an offline AI Tutor required dedicated labs averaging US$30,000 per site, excluding mainte
nance (Arrow Electronics 2025). These figures are not inflation adjusted and should be treated as refe
rence points, not benchmarks. Country-specific costing remains essential. Readers seeking practical tools
to assess these conditions can consult appendix 1, which groups selected system readiness resources by
use case, including infrastructure and connectivity planning, affordability and scale, DPI, AI governance,
and language and inclusion.

title: 5. Use scalability as a design filter from the outset.

paragraphs.text:
Small pilots can generate useful evidence, but their implications depend on whether core functions can be
sustained under routine conditions with realistic staffing, infrastructure, and financing. The evidence
shows that effective implementation depends on readiness across system levels. At the micro level,
teachers, learners, and facilitators need the skills, time, and confidence to use tools without added
burden. At the meso level, schools need routines, leadership engagement, and shared responsibility that
make EdTech part of everyday practice. At the macro level, systems need workable infrastructure,
affordable access, and enabling policies. Scalability should therefore be treated as a design question from
the beginning, not as a later aspiration once pilots appear promising.

title: 6. Assess AI-enabled models in terms of both instructional promise and practical risk.

paragraphs.text:
AI tools can extend existing EdTech functions, but their relevance depends on model quality, language
accuracy, governance arrangements, user capacity, ongoing cost, and the system’s ability to manage
associated safeguards and risks. Their value should be judged by whether they improve instructional
usefulness under local constraints without introducing risks that systems cannot manage.

title: 7. Build equity into design, not as an add-on.

paragraphs.text:
Electricity and connectivity constraints were often most binding in rural areas. At the same time, several
interventions show that EdTech can support meaningful gains in remote settings when delivery conditions
are stable or when tools are designed for offline or low-bandwidth use. Rural constraints should not be
treated as a reason to avoid EdTech, but as a reason to choose models that can operate reliably within
those conditions. This requires careful attention to delivery feasibility, including electricity, connectivity,
offline functionality, recurring costs, and maintenance beyond district centers. When these conditions are
addressed, EdTech can expand access and support more equitable learning opportunities across settings.

text:
Electricity and connectivity constraints were often most binding in rural areas. At the same time, several
interventions show that EdTech can support meaningful gains in remote settings when delivery conditions
are stable or when tools are designed for offline or low-bandwidth use. Rural constraints should not be
treated as a reason to avoid EdTech, but as a reason to choose models that can operate reliably within
those conditions. This requires careful attention to delivery feasibility, including electricity, connectivity,
offline functionality, recurring costs, and maintenance beyond district centers. When these conditions are
addressed, EdTech can expand access and support more equitable learning opportunities across settings.

title: 1. Strengthen the causal evidence base, especially for foundational learning.

paragraphs.text:
Despite a large number of EdTech pilots globally, only a small subset uses designs that allow clear
attribution of effects, and even fewer examine foundational literacy and numeracy directly. As a result,
many tools promoted as scalable solutions for foundational learning still rest on inconclusive evidence.
Research priorities should therefore include generating more replicable causal evidence, particularly for
tools intended for wider adoption.

title: 2. Move beyond pilot conditions to test whether effects hold at scale.

paragraphs.text:
Several high-quality studies reviewed here were implemented in narrow geographic areas, short time
frames, or with substantial implementation support. These conditions still protected internal validity but
limited generalizability of findings. Because large-scale deployment environments differ substantially
from pilot contexts, further research is needed to determine whether instructional gains persist when
programs expand to more diverse schools, systems, and implementation conditions. Strong pilot findings
should therefore be treated as promising but not as definitive evidence of scalability.

title: 3. Track sustainability over time, not only short-term effects.

paragraphs.text:
Very few available studies track how EdTech performs beyond the first year of implementation. Evidence
on device durability, maintenance cycles, teacher attrition, platform updates, or the stability of instructio
nal gains is scarce. This makes it difficult to judge long-term viability or return on investment. Future
research should therefore collect multiyear evidence on usage, costs, and learning outcomes so that
policy makers can assess whether tools remain effective and affordable once initial support declines.

title: 4. Improve the quality and comparability of cost evidence.

paragraphs.text:
Cost evidence remains fragmented and inconsistently reported. Many studies do not report cost data at
all, and those that do often omit key assumptions, per-learner conversions, or full accounting of recurrent
costs such as data, electricity, maintenance, and replacement. This limits the ability to judge affordability,
which is a primary determinant of sustained use. Future studies should apply more standardized costing
approaches and report cost, cost-effectiveness, and affordability metrics transparently so results can be
interpreted and compared across settings.

title: 5. Treat evidence on AI-enabled tools as preliminary and validation-focused.

paragraphs.text:
Although interest in AI-enabled tools for foundational learning is growing, the evidence base is still
limited. Most AI applications reviewed, including oral reading assessments, teacher-support chatbots, and
AI-assisted content generation, are in early stages and demonstrate feasibility rather than validated
effectiveness. Important gaps remain in language accuracy, cultural and curricular alignment, implications
for workload, and data governance in low-resource settings. Research on AI-enabled tools should
therefore focus first on validation, accuracy, safeguarding, and delivery feasibility before moving toward
larger-scale claims.

title: 6. Invest in comparative research that shows what travels across contexts.

paragraphs.text:
Most studies evaluate a single EdTech model in one setting. Few compare delivery modalities under
similar conditions or examine how design features perform across different infrastructure environments,
languages, or curriculum structures. This limits what the field can say about transferability. Future
research should more often test plausible alternatives side by side, document performance under real
delivery constraints, and identify which design features remain effective across contexts.

title: 7. Make equity a core research question, not a secondary one.

paragraphs.text:
While rural delivery constraints are well documented, evidence on how EdTech affects other equity
dimensions is limited. Few evaluations examine impacts by gender, disability, linguistic background, or
baseline performance, and subgroup analyses are often absent or underpowered. This weakens unders
tanding of who benefits, who is excluded, and under what conditions EdTech narrows or widens dispari
ties. Future research should therefore build equity into study design from the outset by specifying
equity-related hypotheses, collecting relevant subgroup data, and ensuring adequate power to assess
differential effects rigorously.

title: CONCLUSION

paragraphs.text:
This guidance note synthesizes the available evidence on how EdTech can support foundational learning
in LMIC contexts. Across teacher support, learner support, curriculum, and instructional support systems,
the evidence points to a consistent conclusion: EdTech adds value when it strengthens the instructional
core by clarifying expectations, supporting consistent practice, expanding access to materials and
training, and generating actionable information that teachers and systems can use. Its effectiveness
depends less on technological sophistication than on instructional fit, delivery feasibility, and sustained
use under real system constraints.

Importantly, this document does not take any stance for or against EdTech or AI-enabled education
interventions. Rather, its purpose is to synthesize evidence and translate that evidence into practical
guidance for decision-makers responsible for designing, adopting, and scaling foundational learning
interventions. Where credible evidence exists, it is highlighted; where evidence is limited or uneven,
caution is emphasized. The recommendations reflect what the current evidence supports rather than aspi
rational claims about technology’s potential. At the same time, decisions about EdTech, particularly AI-en
abled tools, inevitably intersect with broader sociopolitical, economic, environmental, and ethical conside
rations. Issues such as data privacy, equity, labor implications, cost structures, environmental
sustainability, language politics, and governance shape how these tools are perceived, adopted, and
sustained. While these dimensions have important implications for policy and practice, they fall outside
the scope of this guidance note, which is deliberately focused on instructional effectiveness and imple
mentation feasibility. Emerging AI applications show promise in expanding access to instructional
support, accelerating content development, and providing responsive assistance to teachers and learners
in resource-constrained settings. However, they also introduce new risks related to reliability, bias, cost,
accountability, and long-term dependence on proprietary systems. These trade-offs underscore the need
for careful design, transparent evaluation, and strong public sector stewardship as AI becomes more
embedded in education systems.

Ultimately, this guidance note positions EdTech, including AI, as a means rather than an end. Its value lies
in whether it strengthens teaching and learning at scale, under realistic conditions, and in ways that
systems can sustain. Future work will need to integrate instructional evidence with broader policy debates
to ensure that technology adoption in education is not only effective but also responsible, equitable, and
aligned with public goals.

title: Expanding Access to TPD Opportunities

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Offline Tablets + Remote Coaching in South Africa

A randomized evaluation in South Africa tested a tablet-based teacher training intervention
designed to operate entirely offline and reach underserved schools (Cilliers et al. 2022).
Teachers in Grades 1–3 received tablets preloaded with electronic lesson plans aligned with the
national English literacy curriculum and structured asynchronous training modules. These
modules included video modeling, phonics sound clips, and interactive quizzes. To supplement
the self-paced content, teachers participated in remote coaching through termly phone calls,
biweekly follow-ups, and peer interaction via WhatsApp. These support mechanisms enabled
teachers to exchange classroom photos and teaching reflections with coaches and peers,
helping reinforce the use of digital materials. On average, teachers spent 13 hours engaging
with the tablet content and received 10 coaching calls per term. This virtual model was
compared to in-person coaching with identical content and a business-as-usual control group.
Training frequency, curriculum alignment, and materials were held constant across arms. The
virtual model cost US$2,168 per teacher per year (or US$52 per student), compared to
US$2,750 per teacher (or US$66 per student) for the in-person model. Teachers in the virtual
model improved the implementation of writing instruction, and students showed modest gains
in oral language proficiency (0.12 SD). The in-person coaching model produced effects on
additional outcomes, including guided reading practices and student fluency and comprehen
sion. These results suggest that offline digital tools, paired with light-touch remote support, can
improve teacher and student performance at lower cost and on a larger scale, though intensive
in-person support may still yield broader gains.

title: Enhancing Engagement with Training Content

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Interactive and Blended TPD Courses in Kenya

A randomized evaluation in Kenya tested a 12-week digital TPD course integrating ABRA into
an online platform for early literacy instruction (Uribe-Banda et al. 2023). Unlike offline models
that deliver preloaded content, such as the tablet-based TPD module in South Africa (Cilliers et
al. 2022), this course was designed as a comprehensive digital training experience. Delivered
through the Canvas learning management system, the course included narrated instructional
videos, interactive ABRA activities, weekly quizzes, written reflections, and moderated online
discussion forums. Teachers accessed the content asynchronously via smartphones or compu
ters. A blended version of the course combined the digital training with biweekly in-person
coaching sessions to support classroom application. Both the online-only and blended groups
showed similar improvements in lesson planning and confidence with teaching literacy,
including word reading, fluency, comprehension, and writing. The online-only group demons
trated greater gains in literacy knowledge. These findings suggest that when digital training is
well designed and grounded in instructional practice, it can foster meaningful teacher learning
even without in-person support. However, blended models may offer additional scaffolding to
support applications in the classroom.

Offline Content Paired with Remote Coaching and Peer Exchange in South Africa

As described in the earlier section on offline tablet-based teacher training in South Africa, a
lower-tech intervention in South Africa delivered multimedia TPD content offline via preloaded
tablets (Cilliers et al. 2019). While the core modules lacked interactive components, the
program embedded engagement-enhancing features through remote coaching and WhatsApp
groups. Teachers used these platforms to share photos and videos, receive reminders, and
exchange ideas with peers and coaches. These structured interpersonal supports simulated
observation and reflection. Although teacher and learner outcomes were stronger in the
in-person coaching arm, the virtual group also showed improvement in writing instruction and
oral language skills. This suggests that even when core content is static, engagement can be
reinforced through carefully designed support mechanisms.

title: Reinforcing the Use of Trained Teaching Strategies

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from SMS Prompts in Kenya

A randomized trial in Kenya examined how low-cost SMS messages could reinforce a newly
introduced pedagogy for early reading (Jukes et al. 2017). Implemented in Grades 1 and 2 over
two school years, the program included a three-day in-person training on core reading strate
gies, including print awareness, letter-sound recognition, phonics, and shared reading, paired
with scripted lesson plans aligned to the national curriculum. During implementation, teachers
received two-way SMS messages weekly, containing pedagogical tips, reminders, and motiva
tional prompts. Teachers could respond, and selected replies were shared to encourage peer
interaction. Participation was incentivized through small weekly mobile credits. Teachers
responded to 87 percent of messages. The full program costs US$273 per school annually, or
US$2.41 per student, with SMS accounting for less than 10 percent of the total costs. Compared
to a control group that received no structured training or support, teachers in the intervention
group demonstrated significantly stronger instructional practices, including increased time on
phonics, print-based activities, and reading instruction, with large effect sizes ranging from 0.57
to 1.15 SD. Students in the intervention schools also outperformed those in the control group on
key early reading skills, including letter-sound knowledge, nonword decoding, and fluency, with
effect sizes between 0.43 and 0.64 SD. Though the evaluation did not isolate the specific
contribution of the SMS messages, teacher feedback indicated that these weekly prompts
reinforced lesson routines and helped maintain instructional focus. These findings show that
pairing structured pedagogy with mobile-based reinforcement can improve instruction quality
and learning outcomes through a low-cost, familiar, and scalable form of EdTech.

title: Supporting Instructional Delivery through Digital Resources

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Preloaded Digital Tools in Zambia

A randomized evaluation in Zambia tested a structured EdTech package designed to support

title: Expanding Learner Access to Instructional Content

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Student E-Readers in Kenya

A randomized trial in Kenya tested three ICT-based add-ons to a structured pedagogy program
(PRIMR), involving 1,580 Grade 2 learners across 80 schools in Kisumu County (Piper et al.
2016). The base program already provided teacher training, structured lesson plans, pupil
books, and coaching by government instructional supervisors, known as teacher advisory
center (TAC) tutors. The main student-facing intervention supplied e-readers loaded with over
100 digital books, giving learners daily access to textbooks and storybooks otherwise unavai
lable. Two other models provided tablets to teachers (with lesson plans, grouping tools, and
quizzes) and to TAC tutors (with digitized observation tools and guides). All three ICT models
produced significant reading gains compared to 20 control schools ( ≈ 400 learners) receiving
regular instruction. In the student e-reader arm, English and Kiswahili oral reading fluency
improved (0.17–0.26 SD), and the share of learners meeting national fluency benchmarks
increased by about 12 percentage points. Costs varied sharply: TAC tutor tablets added US$0.10
per student, teacher tablets US$3 per student, and student e-readers US$40 per student. These
findings show that direct student access to digital books can improve reading outcomes in
low-resource settings, though relative cost-effectiveness depends on whether technology is
placed in the hands of students, teachers, or instructional supervisors.
Experimental Evidence from SMS-Based Literacy Lessons in Kenya

A randomized trial in Kenya tested the M-Shule platform, which delivered adapted Tusome
literacy lessons via SMS to Grade 1–3 learners (Jordan et al. 2025). The intervention was
implemented as a supplemental learning tool alongside regular schooling after COVID-19
reopening, with learners engaging from home or the community. Learners received short
lessons and quizzes by text message, and their answers were automatically logged and scored
by the system. Based on performance, the platform advanced learners to harder content or
repeated easier review material, ensuring progression and remedial support without teacher
grading. The platform functioned without internet or smartphones, and parents received
supportive reminders. Content was offered in English and Kiswahili as grade-level booster

and control groups, with server log data from 800 additional users. Treatment learners received

Experimental Evidence from SMS-Based Reading Support in Zambia

A randomized trial in Zambia’s Eastern Province tested Makhalidwe Athu (‘our culture’ in
Chinyanja), an SMS-based program, designed to improve reading among Grade 2–3 learners
(Ome and Menendez 2022). Over nine months, caregivers received short story segments via
basic mobile phones, broken into 160-character messages with comprehension questions. They
were expected to read these with their children three times per week, supported by SMS
reminders and monthly facilitator meetings. Voice messages were also offered but were more
costly and less central. The intervention required only basic phones, parental engagement, and
minimal facilitation, with no internet or school-based resources, while classroom instruction
continued as usual. Treatment learners were compared to control peers in similar schools who
did not receive SMS content. Results showed significant improvements in literacy: Treated
children improved 0.19 SD on a composite reading index, 0.28 SD in oral reading fluency (3.35
additional words per minute), and 0.10 SD in word recognition compared to their peers. They
also read more frequently at home, both alone and with caregivers, though attitudes toward
reading were unchanged. The program cost US$20–22 per child, with SMS transmission
accounting for about 15 percent of costs. These findings show that SMS-based story delivery,
paired with caregiver engagement, can improve foundational literacy cost-effectively in
low-resource contexts, though reach is constrained to households with phones.
Experimental Evidence from Low-Tech Remote Learning in Bangladesh

A three-arm cluster-randomized trial in rural Bangladesh evaluated a feature phone-based
remote learning intervention for primary-age children during COVID-19 school closures (Wang
et al. 2023). The program used IVR technology to deliver 60 prerecorded audio lessons in
Bangla, English, and numeracy. Lessons followed an interactive audio instruction format that
prompted learners to answer questions and complete exercises. Families accessed lessons
through a toll-free number at any time, with caregivers facilitating learning using simple
guidebooks and alphabet sheets. A subset of children also received 15 leadership lessons. To
encourage participation, the program offered small weekly prizes (mobile airtime worth about
US$3, roughly 250 Bangladeshi taka) to 15 randomly selected quiz winners. The trial involved
1,763 children ages 5–10 across 90 villages, randomly assigned to two treatment groups or a
control group. After 15 weeks, children in treatment villages scored 0.60–0.63 SD higher than
controls. Literacy improved by ~0.55 SD, with significant gains in Bangla and English letter
recognition, word reading, and sentence comprehension. Numeracy improved by ~0.53–0.54
SD, including number identification, basic addition and subtraction, and simple problem-sol
ving. Oral vocabulary also increased (0.25 SD). The leadership module produced no measurable
impact on leadership or socioemotional skills, and effects on grit, growth mindset, and empathy
were null. The findings show that a low-cost IVR platform can substantially improve foundatio
nal literacy and numeracy in low-resource settings where high-tech options are not feasible.

title: Supporting Repeated, Individualized Practice for Skill Mastery

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Multimedia Interactive Literacy Software in Kenya

A randomized trial in Kenya tested ABRA , a free web-based literacy software designed to
strengthen early reading skills (Abrami et al. 2016). ABRA provided 32 interactive multimedia
activities on alphabetics, fluency, comprehension, and writing, supported by story texts and
student-generated narratives. Students used ABRA in weekly 90-minute computer lab sessions
during regular English classes, with low-performing learners receiving additional remedial
access. Because the software required internet connectivity, implementation depended on
school computer labs with online access, though offline print worksheets and teacher iBooks
were also available to support lesson preparation. To support implementation, teachers
received a three-day training, digital lesson plans, and ongoing online coaching, with the
software providing embedded tutorials and progress reporting tools. After 13 weeks, ABRA
students showed significant literacy gains in passage comprehension (0.32 SD) and listening
comprehension (0.54 SD). They also outperformed peers on national exams in English, math,
science, and social studies.
Experimental Evidence from Interactive Learning Apps in Malawi

A study in Malawi evaluated the impact of two interactive tablet applications from the onebil
lion © suite on early mathematics and reading, using randomized controlled trials with primary
learners in Grades 1–3 (Pitchford et al. 2019). The apps presented a structured sequence of
topics through game-like activities, guided by a virtual teacher who provided instructions in
Chichewa. Features included interactive practice, immediate feedback, quizzes, and motivatio
nal rewards. Learners used tablets with headphones individually in school-based learning
centers during school hours, supported by facilitators who managed logistics but did not
provide instruction. The math trial included 256 Grade 1–2 students who used the app for an
average of nine hours over 14 months, compared to their peers who received only regular
classroom instruction. Students using the app achieved moderate gains in number identifica
tion, number discrimination, addition, subtraction, and pattern recognition ( η p2 ≈ 0.04–0.06).
Crucially, the intervention prevented the gender disparities in math observed in control schools,
where boys typically outperformed girls. The reading trial involved 360 Grade 1–3 students who
used a literacy app for 60 minutes daily across 14 weeks (up to 70 hours). Compared to
controls, treatment learners achieved medium-to-large improvements ( η p2 ≈ 0.05–0.09) in
letter naming, syllable reading, word and nonword reading, passage fluency, and comprehen
sion. However, girls continued to outperform boys, suggesting that preexisting gender gaps in
reading persisted. These findings indicate that interactive tablet apps enhance foundational
math and reading skills in low-resource classrooms, with a stronger potential to equalize gender
outcomes in mathematics than in reading.

alone. Across all three trials, GraphoLearn consistently strengthened specific decoding and

title: Fostering Active and Sustained Learner Engagement

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from a Reading-While-Listening App in Uganda

A randomized trial in rural Uganda tested SiMBi , a tablet-based reading-while-listening app,
with Grade 3 students (Friedland et al. 2017). SiMBi paired children’s books in PDF with audio
narration, allowing students to follow the text while listening through headphones. The app
incorporated effective learning strategies by combining visual and auditory input, as well as
modeling fluent reading, although it lacked interactive feedback. Students used the tablets for
10 minutes daily over 30 days as a supplemental activity alongside regular classroom instruc
tion. This group was compared to a control group that read the same passages silently in print
for the same duration, while both groups continued regular classroom instruction. After one
month, SiMBi students made modest but statistically significant gains in reading fluency, rising
from 40.8 to 43.3 words correct per minute compared to 35.3 to 36.8 in the control group (an
advantage of about one additional word per minute on average). Although based on a small-
scale pilot with 46 students, the trial provides early but causal evidence that short, low-inten
sity use of synchronized audio–text tools can improve fluency more than silent print reading,
even in low-resource settings with limited prior exposure to technology.
Experimental Evidence from an Interactive E-Book in South Africa

A randomized trial in rural South Africa tested an interactive e-book to support vocabulary
development among isiXhosa-speaking Grade 1 learners (Klop et al. 2018). Delivered on
Android tablets, the e-book combined a story with text-to-speech isiXhosa narration, illustra
tions, and quizzes with immediate feedback. Fifteen Tier 2 target words (nouns, verbs, adjec

meaning and promoted deeper processing. The intervention was delivered in groups of 3–4

with headphones while a researcher supervised, and sessions were conducted during school

intervention can enhance vocabulary learning and retention among learners in overcrowded,

Experimental Evidence from a Reading-While-Listening App in Uganda
A randomized trial in rural Uganda tested SiMBi , a tablet-based reading-while-listening app,
with Grade 3 students (Friedland et al. 2017). SiMBi paired children’s books in PDF with audio
narration, allowing students to follow the text while listening through headphones. The app
incorporated effective learning strategies by combining visual and auditory input, as well as
modeling fluent reading, although it lacked interactive feedback. Students used the tablets for
10 minutes daily over 30 days as a supplemental activity alongside regular classroom instruc
tion. This group was compared to a control group that read the same passages silently in print
for the same duration, while both groups continued regular classroom instruction. After one
month, SiMBi students made modest but statistically significant gains in reading fluency, rising
from 40.8 to 43.3 words correct per minute compared to 35.3 to 36.8 in the control group (an
advantage of about one additional word per minute on average). Although based on a small-
scale pilot with 46 students, the trial provides early but causal evidence that short, low-inten
sity use of synchronized audio–text tools can improve fluency more than silent print reading,
even in low-resource settings with limited prior exposure to technology.

A randomized trial in rural South Africa tested an interactive e-book to support vocabulary
development among isiXhosa-speaking Grade 1 learners (Klop et al. 2018). Delivered on
Android tablets, the e-book combined a story with text-to-speech isiXhosa narration, illustra
tions, and quizzes with immediate feedback. Fifteen Tier 2 target words (nouns, verbs, adjec

meaning and promoted deeper processing. The intervention was delivered in groups of 3–4
children for 20 minutes, three times per week over two weeks. Learners worked individually
with headphones while a researcher supervised, and sessions were conducted during school
hours as a supplemental pull-out activity. The control group continued regular classroom
activities before later receiving the same e-book. Eight weeks later, treatment learners showed
significant gains in receptive vocabulary, expressive sentence use, and in-depth definitions, and
retained these gains. The delayed control group also improved after receiving the intervention,

title: Substituting or Augmenting Classroom Instruction

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Technology-Delivered Instruction in Rural Zambia

Two evaluations in rural Zambia tested the eSchool 360 program, a computer-assisted instruc
tion (CAI) model implemented by Impact Network in community schools (De Hoop et al. 2024;
Schling and Winters 2018). Zambia’s community schools are typically staffed by untrained local
teachers with limited materials, which limits instructional quality. eSchool 360 substituted
teacher-led instruction with offline digital scripts and projected lessons, while retaining
teachers as facilitators. Schools were equipped with solar power, projectors, and tablets
preloaded with the national curriculum. Facilitators guided students through daily scripted
lessons and received regular training and supervision, with additional measures including class
size limits, attendance monitoring, and community involvement through Parent-Teacher
Associations.

The first evaluation (Schling and Winters 2018) used a quasi-experimental design with 571
Grade 1–2 learners across 15 schools: 5 eSchools , 5 untreated community schools, and 5
government schools staffed by trained teachers. After 18 months, eSchool learners achieved
similar gains to government school peers in number recognition (+15 percentage points) and
nonword decoding (+3 points), despite starting behind at baseline. Learners in untreated
community schools did not catch up. No impacts were observed on broader literacy, numeracy,
or grade progression. Beyond learning outcomes, the program also increased enrollment (+7.5
percentage points) and attendance (+0.36 days per week). These catch-up gains were achieved
at about US$3 per learner monthly, roughly one-third the cost of government schools. Yet, the
findings remain indicative rather than definitive because of the small sample, nonrandom
school selection, and a difference-in-differences design that only partly addresses bias.

A subsequent cluster-randomized trial with 1,865 Grade 1 learners across 63 schools (De
Hoop et al. 2024) found larger and more robust gains after 14 months: +0.40 SD in reading
(EGRA composite including print knowledge, letter-sound knowledge, nonword decoding,
reading fluency, and comprehension), +0.21 SD in math (Early Grade Math Assessment, EGMA,
composite including rational counting, number recognition, quantity discrimination, and pattern
completion), +0.25 SD in oral vocabulary, and +0.15 SD on the Zambian Achievement Test.
Treatment-on-the-treated effects were even higher, with reading gains above 0.60 SD.
Together, these studies indicate that embedding technology into a structured pedagogy
package with trained facilitators and community ownership can raise foundational skills in
highly resource-constrained settings, though longer-term cost-effectiveness and sustainability
require further study.

title: 66 | How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries

paragraphs.text: Experimental Evidence from Satellite-Transmitted Instruction in Ghana

A cluster-randomized trial in Ghana tested MGCubed , a satellite-based program delivering daily
English and math lessons to students in Grades 2–5 in 70 rural primary schools (Johnston and
Ksoll 2022). Expert ‘studio teachers’ in Accra broadcast live to 10–12 classrooms, while in-class
teachers acted as facilitators, operating equipment, managing classrooms, grading work, and
supporting students when broadcasts failed. In the second year, facilitators grouped students
by ability in English to provide targeted support. The program required substantial infrastruc
ture, including solar power, video equipment, and training and stipends for facilitators. The
satellite lessons were fully integrated into regular school hours, replacing part of teacher-led
instruction. Compared to control schools (n = 77) with regular teacher-led lessons, MGCubed
produced math gains of 0.20–0.21 SD after one year and 0.26–0.27 SD after two years. Literacy
effects emerged more slowly, with a 0.33 SD improvement on the EGRA composite by Year 2,
very large for letter naming and decoding, modest for oral fluency, and none for comprehen
sion. Gains were consistent across teachers and districts, and math improvements persisted one
year later. Costs were high. About 30 percent of total two-year expenses went to upfront
infrastructure (studios, equipment, solar power, and satellite links). Even with a 7–8-year
lifespan to spread these costs, the program delivered only ≈ 0.12 SD of learning gain per US$100
per student. This was well below the return from non-EdTech approaches, such as structured
teacher training, which cost about US$10–11 per student per year and delivered ≈ 0.36 SD of
learning gain per US$100 (Duflo et al. 2020). This means that while satellite instruction can
improve foundational learning in rural schools, it is only financially viable if infrastructure is
shared across more learners and services.
Experimental Evidence from a Tablet-based Self-learning Suite in Tanzania

A randomized trial in rural Tanzania evaluated Kitkit TM School, a self-directed tablet learning
suite combining interactive activities, digital books, videos, and tools for independent use
among Grade 1 students (Lee and Choi 2020). The program included nine curriculum-aligned
modules on number recognition, comparison, and basic operations, with gamification features
such as progress tracking and rewards to encourage daily practice. Children used tablets with
headphones in a dedicated classroom. A local assistant managed devices but provided no
instructions. The app operated offline with periodic data uploads. The intervention group (n =
30) replaced regular math lessons with daily 20-minute sessions over 46 days. The control
group (n = 31) continued with standard math classes. After the intervention, learners in the
treatment group showed significant gains in number identification, quantity discrimination,
addition, subtraction, and missing-number tasks, with greater improvements than controls in
number discrimination (0.58 SD), addition (0.78 SD), and subtraction (0.75 SD). Students could
identify numbers up to 100, compare magnitudes, and perform simple operations; however,
regrouping and complex missing-number tasks remained challenging. These findings show that
a short, game-based intervention can improve early numeracy in low-resource classrooms, even
for children with limited prior exposure to technology. However, the study’s scope (one rural
school with 61 children) limits generalizability.

title: Expanding Learner Access to Instructional Content

paragraphs.text: Open Educational Resources for Content Creation, Localization, and Updates

Three studies show how OER function as structured mechanisms for generating, adapting, and
sharing instructional content at a low cost in LMIC contexts (Arinto et al. 2017; Oates and
Hashimi 2016; Tlili et al. 2022). For instance, a multi-region review of OER adoption (Arinto et al.
2017) finds that open licensing supports a digital ecosystem where users can revise, remix, and
share educational materials. Open licenses allow curriculum developers and teachers to update
content and add context-specific examples without copyright constraints. These permissions
lower legal and financial barriers to creating instructional resources, helping keep materials
aligned with evolving curricula. Another review study (Tlili et al. 2022) highlights that OER
adoption in Africa is driving the development of digital books in African languages. These
initiatives typically use digital-first production models that create, store, and share materials in
formats that can be easily adapted or printed. The African Storybook Initiative is one such
example. Its openly licensed storybooks can be downloaded, translated, adapted, and printed
for classroom use. Teachers often revise them collaboratively to reflect local languages and
cultural references, making foundational learning content more contextually responsive.
Evidence from Afghanistan points to similar benefits. The Darakht-e Danesh Library uses a
multilingual content management system that allows contributors to adapt materials into Dari,
Pashto, and English languages (Oates and Hashimi 2016). The platform also includes tools for
refining terminology, examples, and imagery to match local contexts, expanding teachers’ and
learners’ access to locally relevant resources in settings with acute shortages of aligned
instructional materials.

title: Distributing, Storing, and Managing Teaching and Learning Materials

paragraphs.text: Digital Textbook Tracking Platforms in Cambodia and Other Locations

TnT systems replace paper-based textbook ordering with a simple digital workflow that works
on basic phones (Bun et al. 2024; Read 2017). Some systems allow schools to directly request
books through SMS, IVR, or short mobile forms while others still use centrally managed data.
Shipments carry barcodes, and school directors or community members confirm receipt
digitally. TnT models have been used or piloted in various locations, including Cambodia,
Afghanistan, Malawi, Nigeria, Niger, Nepal, and India, with designs adapted for basic phones
and limited connectivity (Bun et al. 2024; Khan 2020). Evidence from Cambodia (Bun et al.
2024; Khan 2020) shows three main benefits: (a) faster processing as hundreds of schools
submitted requests within two weeks instead of several months under paper-based procedures,
(b) i mproved accuracy as delivery records show that more than 90 percent of requested books
arrived on time and in the correct quantities, and (c) greater visibility as time-stamped logs
highlight where procurement or transportation delays occur, allowing ministries to intervene
early. Although not experimental studies, these findings illustrate how lightweight digital
workflows can improve transparency in the distribution chain and reduce the administrative
burden on school leaders.

title: 68 | How To Integrate Edtech Into Foundational Learning In Low- And Middle-Income Countries

paragraphs.text: Offline Digital Libraries Using Raspberry Pi Servers in Indonesia

A low-cost digital library model tested in Indonesia uses a Raspberry Pi microcomputer as a
local server for preloaded books (Wiguna et al. 2024). The device broadcasts its own Wi-Fi
signal, which learners can join using basic smartphones. There is no internet connection; the
system creates a closed network, allowing users to browse and download materials from local
storage. The model offers several advantages. It operates at very low power and can be
powered by solar or battery sources. Content can be updated simply by replacing the SD card,
without needing to download new content. This reduces reliance on connectivity for ongoing
maintenance. As of January 2024, the full setup (one server and five client devices) costs about
US$904. Field monitoring reported that the deployed library contained more than 7,000 items,
including children’s storybooks used in village reading houses. Visits by children to these
reading houses increased after installation, and parents reported perceived improvements in
their children’s reading skills. While these are not directly measured learning outcomes, the
model expands access to literacy materials in places where printed texts and reliable internet
are scarce.

title: Emerging AI Use Cases for Curriculum Development and Delivery

paragraphs.text: AI-Enabled Drafting, Editing, Illustration, Translation, and Production Planning

A review of 12 published, mostly qualitative studies on the African publishing industry reports
that AI tools are beginning to support multiple stages of textbook and storybook production
(Salani and Tapfuma 2025). While not all reviewed sources focus on foundational learning
materials, the workflows they describe remain relevant. The tools support four areas: drafting
and editing, illustration, translation, and production planning. In drafting and editing , tools such
as Grammarly, GPT-based drafting systems, and AI-assisted plagiarism detectors (for example,
GPTZero and AI Text Classifier) support grammar correction, readability checks, fact-checking,
and early copyediting, which helps small editorial teams manage high workloads. In illustration
and design , publishers have begun to experiment with generative image models, similar to
Midjourney, to create early artwork that designers later refine to ensure cultural accuracy,
thereby helping address shortages of illustrators and slow visual production cycles. In transla
tion , multilingual machine translation engines are tested to produce first-round drafts in African
languages using back-translation and reconstruction techniques, thereby reducing the early
stages of translation in multilingual systems that often face lengthy timelines and high costs.
Some publishers are also beginning to test data analytics tools for production planning,
although applications to textbook demand forecasting are still limited. Similar experimentation
is underway in Senegal, where a 2025 workshop applied generative AI to book creation and
produced 18 original titles in five days, confirming that AI can speed up production when paired
with strong editorial oversight and culturally grounded design (Diop and Teel 2025).

title: Edtech for Instructional Support Systems

paragraphs.text: AI-powered Offline Speech Recognition Tool in Morocco 6

A TaRL program in Morocco piloted an AI-powered automatic speech recognition tool to
automate early-grade oral reading assessment (Bachiri et al. 2024). The tool, known as TaRL-
BOT , integrates Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) into Moodle and allows students in
Grades 1–3 to record short reading passages through a simple web interface. Learners comple
ted the tasks individually on tablets or school computers. The tool stored each reading sample,
transcription, and score within Moodle’s database and identified the highest level reached
across letter, word, sentence, paragraph, and story tasks. Teachers and supervisory teams
accessed these records to confirm skill levels and monitor progress across TaRL groups.
TaRL-BOT operated offline for classroom use and synced data when connectivity was available.
Pilot evidence showed that TaRL-BOT -generated scores were mostly consistent with human
scoring benchmarks used in TaRL. Teachers viewed automated scoring as helpful for reducing
assessment workload and providing structured records for grouping and progress monitoring.
AI-powered Oral Reading Assessment Tool in India 7

Vaachan Samiksha (meaning ‘reading assessment’ in Hindi) is an AI-enabled oral reading
fluency tool that automates timing, scoring, and reporting for early-grade literacy (Wadhwani
AI 2025). Similar to TaRL-BOT , it replaces manual oral reading fluency checks with quick,
objective assessments and records results with verified school locations that cannot be altered
after submission. Since July 2023, the tool has been deployed across nearly 30,000 public
schools in Gujarat, supporting about 120,000 teachers and more than 2.5 million learners. The
state integrated the tool into its existing digital systems so teachers can access it through
familiar channels, which has eased adoption. According to developers, the automation enables
teachers to conduct brief fluency checks with small groups each day, and the immediate
feedback helps them track progress and identify learners who need targeted support. Students
appear more engaged because they receive instant results. While the current version requires
internet connectivity, the offline version is under development.

title: EU AI Act

paragraphs.text: Implementation Guide

text:
Implementation Guide
1

title: 1.1 The Artificial Intelligence Act

paragraphs.text:
1.
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying
down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU)
No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and
Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (the Artificial Intelligence Act) 1 entered
into force on 1 August 2024. The Regulation aims to improve the functioning of the internal market
and to promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring
a high level of protection of health, safety and the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of
Fundamental Rights of the European Union, including democracy, the rule of law and
environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union.

2.
The Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) follows a risk-based approach. It prohibits a limited number
of AI practices, lays down requirements and obligations in respect of AI systems classified as high-
risk, establishes transparency obligations for certain AI systems irrespective of their risk
classification, and sets out a dedicated regime for general-purpose AI models. Chapter III of the AI
Act is built upon the EU's New Legislative Framework (NLF) set out in Regulation (EC) No 765/2008
and Decision No 768/2008/EC 2 , applying the familiar logic of essential requirements, conformity
assessment, CE marking and market surveillance to high-risk AI systems. Chapters II, IV and V, by
contrast, do not follow that logic and should not be interpreted by analogy with it.

title: 1.2 Purpose of the guidance

paragraphs.text:
5.
Article 96(1) of the AI Act requires the Commission to develop guidelines on the practical
implementation of the Regulation. That provision sets out the minimum aspects that such
guidelines should address. These include: (i) the application of the requirements and obligations
referred to in Articles 8 to 15 and in Article 25; (ii) the prohibited practices referred to in Article 5;
(iii) the practical implementation of the provisions related to substantial modification; (iv) the
practical implementation of the transparency obligations laid down in Article 50; (v) detailed
information on the relationship of the AI Act with the Union harmonisation legislation listed in
Annex I as well as with other relevant Union law, including as regards consistency in their
enforcement; and (vi) the application of the definition of an AI system as set out in Article 3(1).

implementation of the Regulation. That provision sets out the minimum aspects that such
guidelines should address. These include: (i) the application of the requirements and obligations
referred to in Articles 8 to 15 and in Article 25; (ii) the prohibited practices referred to in Article 5;
(iii) the practical implementation of the provisions related to substantial modification; (iv) the
practical implementation of the transparency obligations laid down in Article 50; (v) detailed
information on the relationship of the AI Act with the Union harmonisation legislation listed in

enforcement; and (vi) the application of the definition of an AI system as set out in Article 3(1).

title: 3 Established by Article 65 of the AI Act.

paragraphs.text:
6.
Article 96(2) requires the Commission, when issuing such guidelines, to pay particular attention to
the needs of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including start-ups, of local public
authorities and of the sectors most likely to be affected by the AI Act. This is complemented by
Article 62, which requires Member States and the Commission to take a number of specific
measures for providers and deployers that are SMEs, including priority access to regulatory
sandboxes, dedicated awareness-raising and information activities, and simplified technical
documentation.

7.
The Commission has already published guidelines on the definition of an artificial intelligence
system and guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices 4 , as well as guidelines on the
scope of the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, accompanied by the General-
Purpose AI Code of Practice and by the template for the public summary of training content 5 . The
present guidance complements those documents; it does not replace them and should be read
together with them.

8.
This guidance is intended to help operators comply with the AI Act and to support the activities of
market surveillance authorities, notifying authorities and notified bodies, with a view to ensuring
the harmonised enforcement of the AI Act across the Union. This guidance is not intended to cover
the AI Act in its entire scope, but rather to provide clarifications on the rationale of certain key
provisions and on how they could be implemented in practice. This guidance concerns the AI Act
and is not applicable to other EU laws.

9.
Stakeholders were extensively consulted in the preparation of this guidance, including through the
advisory forum referred to in Article 67, the European Artificial Intelligence Board, and a public
consultation held between 9 February and 20 March 2026.

10.
This guidance is not binding on operators or other actors subject to the AI Act. An authoritative
interpretation of the AI Act may only be given by the Court of Justice of the European Union.
Nevertheless, these guidelines set out the Commission's interpretation of the AI Act, with a view to
supporting compliance and contributing to the effective implementation of the Regulation.
Furthermore, the guidance contains a number of examples to illustrate the application of specific
provisions. However, these examples are not intended to replace a case-by-case assessment, which
will always be necessary to account for the specifics of each individual case.

11.
In line with Article 96, the Commission may consider issuing further guidance, including guidance

title: 2.1 Placing on the market and putting into service

paragraphs.text:
12.
Article 2(1) sets out the personal and territorial scope of the AI Act. It applies, among others, to
providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems, or placing general-purpose AI
models on the market, in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or
located in the Union or in a third country; to deployers of AI systems that have their place of
establishment or are located within the Union; to providers and deployers of AI systems that have
their place of establishment or are located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI
system is used in the Union; and to importers, distributors, product manufacturers and authorised
representatives.

13.
Article 3(9) defines 'placing on the market' as the first making available of an AI system or a general-
purpose AI model on the Union market. Article 3(10) defines 'making available on the market' as
the supply of an AI system or a general-purpose AI model for distribution or use on the Union
market in the course of a commercial activity, whether in return for payment or free of charge.
Article 3(11) defines 'putting into service' as the supply of an AI system for first use directly to the
deployer or for own use in the Union for its intended purpose.

14.
Unlike most Union harmonisation legislation built on the NLF, the AI Act attaches obligations not
only to the placing on the market of an AI system but also to its putting into service. A provider that
develops an AI system and uses it exclusively for its own purposes within the Union puts that system
into service and is subject to the obligations of a provider, even though the system is never supplied
to any third party. In such cases, the same legal person is both provider and deployer, and is subject
to both sets of obligations.

Example 1: A bank develops in-house an AI system intended to be used to evaluate the
creditworthiness of natural persons, and uses it exclusively within its own organisation. The bank
has put a high-risk AI system into service under its own name. It is therefore the provider of that
system for the purposes of the AI Act, and is subject to the obligations laid down in Article 16, as
well as to the deployer obligations laid down in Article 26.

15.
The latest edition of the 'Blue Guide on the implementation of EU product rules' 6 provides guidance
facilitating the understanding of the EU product rules and their uniform application across the
different sectoral legal frameworks aligned to the NLF. The Blue Guide indicates that the concepts
of 'placing on the market' and of 'making available' are to be understood as referring to each
individual product, not to a type of product, and whether it was manufactured as an individual unit
or in series (Section 2.3).
6 Commission notice – The 'Blue Guide' on the implementation of EU product rules 2022 (Text with EEA relevance) 2022/C 247/01, OJ C 247, 29.6.2022, pp. 1–152.
Figure 3 — Placing on the market and putting into service

16.
However, given the nature of AI systems, which are typically intangible, further guidance is useful
on when such systems are considered to be placed on the market. Once the development phase of
the AI system is complete and the system is offered to prospective users in the Union, its provider
can be regarded as having produced multiple copies of the same AI system and as having supplied
them for distribution or use. Unlike tangible products, software is not subject to physical production
or stock limitations: each act of making the system available for download or distribution results in
a new identical copy being created for the user. As long as that version is not modified in a way that
affects compliance with the AI Act, the placing on the market is to be considered to have occurred
at the moment of the first offering for distribution or use.

17.
Therefore, an AI system should be considered to have been placed on the market when its
development phase is complete and it is first supplied for distribution or use on the Union market
in the course of a commercial activity. The provider should be considered to have placed on the
market multiple copies of the same AI system at the same time, regardless of when possession or
use of each individual copy is transferred to another natural or legal person. At the same time,
where the provider makes an AI system available in different variants that differ in their included
components, configurations or enabled functionalities, those variants cannot be regarded as
multiple copies of the same AI system and should be treated as distinct AI systems for the purposes
of placing on the market.

Example 2: On 3 August 2026, company A first supplies for distribution via its website version 1.0.0
of its AI system X. On the same day, customer 1 obtains a copy of version 1.0.0 of AI system X. On

17 August 2026, customer 2 obtains a copy of version 1.0.0 of AI system X. Both copies of version
1.0.0 of AI system X are placed on the market on 3 August 2026.

18.
Given the iterative nature of software development, it should be further clarified that subsequent
iterations of an AI system are considered as newly placed on the market where those iterations
qualify as a 'substantial modification' within the meaning of Article 3(23). Iterations that do not
qualify as substantial modifications do not require the provider to perform a new conformity
assessment procedure under Article 43(4) and therefore do not modify that system's date of
placing on the market. For more guidance on the concept of substantial modification, see Section
4.

Example 3: On 3 August 2026, company A first supplies for distribution via its website version 1.0.0
of AI system X. On 17 August 2026, company A issues an updated version 1.0.1 of AI system X that
does not constitute a substantial modification. On 30 August 2026, customer 2 obtains a copy of
version 1.0.1. Both copies are considered to be placed on the market on 3 August 2026.

19.
The AI Act is not confined to AI systems that are supplied to the user for local execution. Where an
AI system is made available exclusively through an interface operated by the provider, and is
therefore accessed rather than obtained by the user, that supply nonetheless constitutes a making
available on the market, since Article 3(10) refers to the supply of an AI system for distribution or
use. Providers of AI systems offered as a service are therefore subject to the AI Act on the same
footing as providers of systems distributed for installation. Furthermore, in accordance with Article
2(1), point (c), a provider established in a third country falls within the scope of the AI Act where
the output produced by its system is used in the Union.

title: 2.2 The notion of an AI system

paragraphs.text:
20.
Article 3(1) defines an AI system as a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying
levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or
implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions,
content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. That
definition is composed of seven elements, not all of which need to be present at all times
throughout the lifecycle of the system.

21.
The element that principally distinguishes an AI system from simpler traditional software is the
capability to infer how to generate outputs. As explained in recital 12, that notion refers to the
process of obtaining the outputs and to the capability of AI systems to derive models or algorithms,
or both, from inputs or data. Systems that are based solely on rules defined by natural persons to
automatically execute operations should not be considered AI systems, even where those rules are
numerous, complex, or produce outputs that are difficult for a human to anticipate.

Example 4: A spreadsheet application that applies a statutory formula fixed in law in order to
calculate a social benefit entitlement, where all thresholds and coefficients are set by natural
persons, does not infer how to generate its output. It is not an AI system.

Example 5: A model trained on historical maintenance records to estimate the probability that a
given machine will fail within a given period derives its output from patterns learned from data. It
infers how to generate its output and is an AI system.

Example 6: A descriptive analytics tool that computes averages, medians and standard deviations
across a dataset and presents them in a dashboard is not an AI system, even where it is described
as 'AI-powered' in the provider's promotional materials. The classification of a system depends on
its objective technical characteristics and not on the way it is marketed.

22.
The reference to 'varying levels of autonomy' indicates some degree of independence of action
from human involvement and of capability to operate without human intervention. A system that
requires a manual human input in order to generate an output may nevertheless operate with the
degree of autonomy required by the definition, provided that it is not fully and exclusively
determined by human instruction at every step.
Figure 5 — Models are components; systems are products

23.
The reference to a system that 'may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment' is expressed in
permissive terms. Self-learning behaviour, or the capacity of a system to change while in use, is
therefore not a necessary condition for a system to qualify as an AI system. Conversely, where such
adaptiveness is present, it has consequences for the provider's obligations, in particular under
Articles 9, 15 and 43(4), as further discussed in Sections 4.2 and 7.

title: 2.3 Models, computer code and AI components

paragraphs.text:
24.
The AI Act distinguishes AI models from AI systems. As explained in recital 97, AI models, including
general-purpose AI models, are essential components of AI systems but do not by themselves
constitute AI systems. AI models require the addition of further components, such as a user
interface, in order to become AI systems. Chapter V accordingly establishes a distinct set of
obligations attaching to general-purpose AI models as such, independently of any system into which
they may subsequently be integrated.

25.
It is also useful to clarify the treatment of computer code. Source code, training scripts, model
weights and datasets, where supplied as such and not as an AI system or as a general-purpose AI
model, are not themselves regulated by the AI Act. By contrast, a general-purpose AI model is
subject to Chapter V irrespective of the way in which it is placed on the market, whether through
an application programming interface, as a downloadable set of parameters, through a model
repository, or as a component of an AI system supplied by the same provider.

26.
In accordance with Article 2(8), the AI Act does not apply to any research, testing or development
activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into
service. That exclusion does not extend to testing in real world conditions 7 . Unfinished code and
intermediate model checkpoints shared during the design and development phase, for example for
7 Testing in real world conditions is governed by Articles 60 and 61, and, for the purposes of AI regulatory sandboxes, by Article 57.

testing or peer review, are therefore not considered to be placed on the market. Similarly, sample
or demonstration code provided as part of tutorials or training materials is not considered to be
placed on the market for the purposes of the AI Act.

Example 7: A research team trains a model and shares intermediate checkpoints within a closed
consortium exclusively for the purposes of evaluation, prior to any decision on release. That activity
falls within Article 2(8) and the model is not placed on the market.

Example 8: Company A licenses to company B the source code and weights of a model together with
an inference interface, for integration into company B's internal platform. Even if further adaptation
and integration by company B is required before the system can be used, company A is placing an
AI system, and potentially a general-purpose AI model, on the market. Company A is not responsible
for the compliance of company B's subsequent adaptations.

title: 2.4 Combination of hardware and AI systems

paragraphs.text:
27.
Whether an AI system forms part of a product should be determined not by how or when the
software is delivered to the user, but by whether, in light of the product's intended purpose and
reasonably foreseeable use, that software is necessary for the product to perform its intended
functions. Where a hardware product is designed to work together with a specific AI system
provided by the same provider in order to perform its functions, the hardware and that AI system
together constitute the product placed on the market, even where the software is obtained
through a separate channel.

28.
Where an AI system is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union
harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, and where that product is required to
undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, the AI system is classified as
high-risk under Article 6(1). In accordance with Article 25(3), where a product manufacturer places
on the market or puts into service a high-risk AI system together with the product under its own
name or trademark, that manufacturer is considered to be the provider of the AI system. Article
8(2) allows the provider to integrate the testing, reporting and documentation obligations of the AI
Act into the documentation and procedures already existing under that other legislation, in order
to avoid duplication.

Example 9: A robotic lawnmower is placed on the market as a product, while the obstacle-
recognition functionality that allows it to stop when a person or animal is detected is delivered
through an application supplied by the same manufacturer. Although supplied through different
channels, the mower and that functionality together constitute a single product, because the mower
cannot fulfil its intended purpose safely without it.

Example 10: A surgical robot incorporates an AI-based navigation module that constitutes a safety
component. The robot is a medical device subject to third-party conformity assessment under
Regulation (EU) 2017/745. The navigation module is therefore a high-risk AI system under Article
6(1). In accordance with Article 43(3), compliance with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 is
assessed as part of the conformity assessment procedure carried out under Regulation (EU)
2017/745, and a single EU declaration of conformity is drawn up in accordance with Article 47(1).

title: 2.5 Activities excluded from the scope of the AI Act

paragraphs.text:
29.
Article 2 excludes a number of activities from the scope of the AI Act. These include AI systems and
models placed on the market, put into service or used, with or without modification, exclusively for
military, defence or national security purposes (Article 2(3)); public authorities in third countries
and international organisations acting under international cooperation agreements for law
enforcement and judicial cooperation (Article 2(4)); AI systems and models specifically developed
and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development (Article 2(6));
research, testing and development activity prior to placing on the market or putting into service
(Article 2(8)); deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal
non-professional activity (Article 2(10)); and AI systems released under free and open-source
licences, subject to the limits set out in Article 2(12) and discussed in Section 3.

30.
As exceptions to the general scope of the Regulation, these exclusions are to be interpreted strictly.
In particular, the exclusion in Article 2(3) applies by reference to the purpose for which the system
is placed on the market, put into service or used, and not by reference to the identity of the actor
concerned. Where an AI system is developed for a military purpose but is also placed on the market
or put into service for a civilian, humanitarian, law enforcement or public security purpose, the AI
Act applies in respect of that placing on the market or putting into service.

Example 11: An individual uses a general-purpose AI chatbot to draft a letter to a friend. That
individual is acting in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity and the deployer

obligations of the AI Act do not apply to them. This has no effect on the obligations of the provider
of that chatbot, which continue to apply in full.

text:
29.
Article 2 excludes a number of activities from the scope of the AI Act. These include AI systems and
models placed on the market, put into service or used, with or without modification, exclusively for
military, defence or national security purposes (Article 2(3)); public authorities in third countries
and international organisations acting under international cooperation agreements for law
enforcement and judicial cooperation (Article 2(4)); AI systems and models specifically developed
and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development (Article 2(6));
research, testing and development activity prior to placing on the market or putting into service
(Article 2(8)); deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal
non-professional activity (Article 2(10)); and AI systems released under free and open-source
licences, subject to the limits set out in Article 2(12) and discussed in Section 3.
30.
As exceptions to the general scope of the Regulation, these exclusions are to be interpreted strictly.
In particular, the exclusion in Article 2(3) applies by reference to the purpose for which the system
is placed on the market, put into service or used, and not by reference to the identity of the actor
concerned. Where an AI system is developed for a military purpose but is also placed on the market
or put into service for a civilian, humanitarian, law enforcement or public security purpose, the AI
Act applies in respect of that placing on the market or putting into service.

individual is acting in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity and the deployer
14
obligations of the AI Act do not apply to them. This has no effect on the obligations of the provider
