national education budgets in low income and lower-middle income countries. In Sub-Saharan Africa
alone, achieving affordable universal connectivity is estimated to require US$91 billion, equivalent to 4.5
percent of regional GDP (Oughton, Amaglobeli, & Moszoro, 2023). This precondition for widespread “Big
AI” use would cost tens of billions of dollars to be financed by governments, the private sector, and donors.
While these estimates include society more broadly rather than only the education sector and will change
with time and technological advances, the magnitude of the cost makes them difficult to achieve. For
education systems, UNESCO estimates that enabling electricity, connectivity, and devices for all schools in
LICs and LMICs would require more than US$125 billion, with additional annual maintenance costs of
about US$12 billion (UNESCO, 2023). Against this backdrop, “Small AI” may enable access at lower cost,
but with highly constrained budgets, use-at-scale will require additional sources of finance.

title: 2.3.2. Innovative Financing for Infrastructure

paragraphs.text:
Innovative approaches for financing AI in education at scale are necessary. Traditional approaches to
procurement and financing fall short as education ministries shift their spending. Instead of funding
predictable capital expenditures like infrastructure and fixed operating costs for digital content and
training, they must now navigate the dynamic, token-based usage economies that characterize the age of
AI. Relying on standard approaches to budgeting and financing risks potentially bankrupting ministries or
shutting down access for schools when, for example, token usage spikes. Policymakers do not need to
invent entirely new financing mechanisms from scratch. A potential path forward can be found in adapting
funding streams such as national Universal Service Funds (USFs), which are massive financial pools
generated by a compulsory regulatory fee on domestic telecommunications revenues. M any countries
have successfully deployed USF monies to finance the infrastructure needed to connect rural and
disadvantaged schools to the internet (Trucano, 2015). By legally updating the scope of USFs, governments
can shift their focus from supporting the extension of telephony and the Internet to, for example, help to
subsidize cloud compute data and offline ‘edge’ hardware. Pairing USF capital with proven financial
instruments borrowed from the global health sector, such as front-loaded capital facilities that utilize
donor pledges to issue bonds, which raise fund the development of vaccines (Barder & Yeh, 2006); from
the climate sector, which has utilized debt-for nature swaps to support conservation efforts (Green Climate
Fund, 2024); and from results-based financing approaches increasingly common in international
development (Lee & Medina, 2019); can allow governments to systematically de-risk the unique cost
dynamics of AI deployment in education.

The table below maps how established, successful financing mechanisms can be repurposed to fund
national, scalable, and equitable educational AI infrastructure. It is important to note that, at this point in
time, these ideas remain conceptual and have not yet been tested. In some cases —such as the "compute-
for-data" swap — these concepts may prove controversial, but their inclusion here is intentionally meant
to spark innovative thinking and debate among policymakers. Ultimately, financing educational technology
only using traditional mechanisms is unlikely to be sufficient to meet the financial realities of the AI era.

Infrastructure costs remain a binding, first-order constraint to AI adoption in education for LICs and
many LMICs. Without sustained investment in electricity, connectivity, and devices, AI use will remain
limited to a small subset of schools and users, and risk deepening existing inequalities.
Infrastructure-aware design choices—including phased rollouts and selective use of lower-compute, ‘small
AI’—are therefore critical to making AI adoption feasible and fiscally sustainable.
Box 3 . Why the Costs of AI Pilots in Education are Not Good Predictors of AI Costs at Scale

The vast majority of current AI initiatives in education in low- and middle-income countries take the
form of pilot projects. These are typically small-scale, localized initiatives designed to explore how AI
tools function in challenging operating environments. While a few pilots are designed to reflect the
realities of an intervention at scale, most are heavily subsidized by corporate partners, who may donate
free API tokens or waive cloud compute fees, and international donor agencies and nonprofits, these
pilots can appear at first glance to be remarkably cheap to run. Many of these projects utilize global
Large Language Models (LLMs), though a growing number are experimenting with compact, localized
"Small AI". However, education planners must face a hard truth: The costs incurred during an AI pilot
project cannot be simply extrapolated to budget for the rollout of AI in education at scale. While some

cost components may benefit from economies of scale (e.g. bulk discounts on subscriptions to AI
chatbots), many costs may only become apparent at scale:

The Disappearance of Subsidies : A tech company may happily donate free AI access for 500 students in
a controlled trial to generate good public relations. They are unlikely to absorb the data and token costs
for 5 million students nationwide. When a project scales, the ministry transitions from a "free trial" to
the dynamic volatility of the token economy.

From Apps to Platforms : A pilot can run on a standalone app or a basic web interface. Scaling AI across
a national education system requires building secure data pipelines to connect an AI model with the
national Education Management Information System (EMIS). The costs of data integration,
cybersecurity, and cloud infrastructure are entirely absent from a small-scale pilot budget.

Equity at Scale : In a small pilot, technical support and teacher troubleshooting are often handled directly
by the partner organization's engineers or a few dedicated, highly capable project staff, conducted in
major urban centers or standard languages of instruction to minimize variables. When scaling the use
of AI, the Ministry of Education must ensure equity by funding large-scale, ongoing teacher professional
development and support, providing new infrastructure and additional technical support for rural
schools and in some cases deploying AI in minority languages and regional dialects.

Many ministries of education fund pilot edtech projects because they can't afford to do something at a
large scale for financial reasons, and they can’t afford to do nothing for political reasons, so instead they
fund something small. Ideally, these small initiatives can serve as 'pilot' projects, explicitly designed and
implemented to understand what works, and what does not, when implementing a new technology.
Such pilots can have value in supporting system readiness as well, serving as sandboxes for ministries
to develop the core institutional capacities of their personnel. Crucially, a pilot project can enable a
ministry of education to observe and understand the peculiar, variable cost dynamics of AI usage in real
time. By watching how teachers and students actually interact with the tool, and closely monitoring
associated costs, planners can gain vital insights in order to make more informed decisions before
committing to a costly, system-wide rollout.

title: 2.4. Costs of Teacher Training and AI Adoption

paragraphs.text:
Beyond basic infrastructure, teacher readiness and adoption represent a significant—and costly—
constraint to effective AI integration in education. Evidence across income levels shows that access to AI
tools does not automatically translate into sustained classroom use (World Bank, 2024; Molina et al.,
2024). Teachers’ skills, attitudes, incentives, and perceptions of risk play a central role in determining
whether AI is adopted in practice.

Teacher adoption of AI remains uneven, even in high-income contexts, with persistent concerns around
pedagogical value, safety, workload, and readiness. A Pew Research Center study (2024) finds that U.S.

teachers across pre-primary to senior secondary education hold more negative than positive attitudes
toward AI use in schools. In Latin America, self-assessments suggest that 73 percent of teachers lack the
basic digital skills required for teaching, a critical barrier to AI use (Della Nina Gambi et al., 2025). Evidence
from a forthcoming study in Peru highlights the challenge of sustained uptake: only 15 percent of teachers
who were offered free AI licenses, training on effective lesson-planning prompts, and regular
encouragement used the AI tool on a weekly basis (Lopez et al, forthcoming (b)). Privacy and safety
concerns are also a concern of policymakers (UNESCO 2025; UNICEF 2021), which further raise the cost of
adoption by requiring additional safeguards, guidance, and oversight. At the same time, teacher
engagement with AI is evolving rapidly. In a 21-country Google-Ipsos survey, 81 percent of teachers
reported using AI tools, most commonly to learn new topics, understand complex content, or save time
(Gomes, 2026).

From a cost perspective, teacher-focused AI adoption is often more affordable than student-facing
approaches, particularly in LICs and LMICs. Providing AI access to teachers typically involves fewer users
and devices than student-facing deployment, which substantially reduces upfront infrastructure needs and
recurrent costs. Focusing initial efforts on secondary and tertiary teachers can further lower costs, as these
institutions are more likely to be in urban areas with more reliable electricity, better connectivity, and
existing digital infrastructure, reducing expenditures related to connectivity, maintenance, and training.
While broader student - level access is likely to be beneficial, a teachers - first strategy offers a more fiscally
feasible starting point for systems operating under tight budget constraints.

Digital skills gaps substantially increase the cost and complexity of AI adoption. By 2030, over 230 million
jobs across Sub-Saharan Africa will require digital skills (IFC, 2020). Yet large gaps persist across all income
groups, with sharp inequalities between countries and within them. Fewer than five percent of people in
LICs have basic digital skills, compared with 21 percent in LMICs, 38 percent in UMICs, and 66 percent in
HICs. Intermediate skills show similar disparities: fewer than 15 percent of people in LMICs demonstrate
intermediate proficiency, compared with 26 percent in UMICs and 57 percent in HICs. Advanced digital
skills are scarce everywhere—about 1 in 10 people in HICs have them, while the rate falls below 1 percent
in LICs. Gaps widen for intermediate and advanced skills and are larger for women and rural populations
(World Bank, 2025). Teachers need basic digital skills to effectively use AI tools, and in addition they require
the conceptual grounding to evaluate and appropriately contextualize AI in their classrooms. This means
that effective AI - related teacher training cannot be marginal or one - off, rather it can be embedded in
initial teacher education, continuous professional development, and ongoing instructional support, which
can increase both upfront and recurrent costs. Helpfully, GenAI may reduce some digital-skills barriers
since users can interact through natural language and familiar channels like chat. Evidence from Sierra
Leone shows teachers used a WhatsApp-based AI assistant for teaching support more often than web
search, even though web search was available (Björkegren et. al., 2025). GenAI, when and where available,
may allow users to leapfrog more complex digital interfaces.

Patterns of AI adoption also reflect broader inequalities related to income and gender. As of April 2025, 24
percent of internet users in HICs reported using ChatGPT, compared with only 4.7 percent in LMICs and 0.7
percent in LICs (Liu, Huang, and Wang, 2025). Evidence also suggests differences in how AI tools are used across

contexts: in LICs, early adopters tend to be technical users, while usage in HICs includes large amounts of casual
and personal engagement (Appel et al., 2026). The same study finds that a one percent increase in GDP per
capita is associated with a 0.7 percent increase in the use of the AI tool Claude per capita. For Claude users
specifically, coursework use was highest in countries with the lowest GDP per capita, while rich countries show
the highest rates of personal use. Gender gaps are also present but evolving: looking at the growth of ChatGPT
from November 2022 through July 2025, Chatterjee et al. (2025) found that early adopters were
disproportionately male, though this gap has narrowed substantially over time, and recent user growth has
been relatively faster in LICs. Cost projections for teacher training programs on AI should account for gender
and other relevant considerations in their design.

Taken together, teacher training and adoption represent a major cost driver and risk factor for AI integration
in education. Without sustained investment in digital skills, pedagogical support, and institutional incentives
for use, AI tools are unlikely to be effectively and responsibly adopted at scale—even when infrastructure and
licenses are available. Designing cost-effective AI strategies therefore requires treating teacher adoption not as
a complementary input, but as a central component of total cost and implementation planning.

title: 2.5. Costs of AI Models: Retail Pricing and Licensing

paragraphs.text:
The cost of using retail AI models in education are shaped by many factors. Pricing schemes for the use
of frontier commercial AI chatbots in education range from individual student or teacher subscriptions to
institution - wide and system - level licenses (Annex 1). They differ in functionality, data governance, usage
caps, customization, and integration with learning management systems (LMS), with important
implications for affordability and scalability across country contexts.

In high-income systems with strong infrastructure, large-scale licensing agreements can lower per-user
costs through volume pricing. For instance, the California State University (CSU) system launched a
US$16.9 million initiative in partnership with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and others to integrate AI across
its campuses. 6 The program provides systemwide access to ChatGPT Edu and plans to develop AI tutors
and streamline student services. With benefits to 460,000 students and 63,000 faculty and staff, this
initiative demonstrates how strategic large-scale investments can support both access and functionality,
while leveraging volume agreements to manage costs (CSU; GIA). In Estonia, cost of AI deployment across
all primary and secondary schools is approximately €4 million annually, split evenly between the national
government and private partners. Estonia's flagship national AI in education initiative, called AI Leap,
provides access to AI-driven learning tools and training for over 58,000 students and 5,000 educators, with
no out-of-pocket costs to users (Education Estonia, 2025). Such initiatives are designed for systems with
mature infrastructure, strong institutional capacity, and predictable recurrent funding, and are not directly
transferable to LICs and LMICs without significant adaptation and external support. Annex 1 provides a
detailed comparison of these models. To date, reliable public data on implementation costs of AI in
education systems in middle and low-income countries are lacking.

6 The operating budget for the California State University system was US$8.5 billion for 2025-26, meaning that this
initiative cost less than two tenths of a percent of the overall budget (CSU 2025).

In LICs and LMICs, even low AI licensing fees can represent a substantial fiscal burden. Licensing costs of
only a few dollars per student per year translate into large increases relative to current per-student
education spending. Moreover, licensing costs must be financed alongside infrastructure, training, and
operational expenditures, which often dominate total cost of ownership. As a result, affordability
constraints in these contexts are less about the price of AI models alone and more about their interaction
with broader system costs.

The long-run affordability of AI in education is strongly influenced by financing and governance risks,
including vendor lock-in. Vendor lock-in can emerge when tools rely on proprietary data formats, closed
application programming interfaces (APIs), or tightly bundled cloud services that raise switching costs over
time. Market concentration among a small set of cloud and foundation-model providers also increases
exposure to price changes, usage-based fee escalation, service outages, and policy shifts that are outside
a ministry’s control. These risks are especially relevant where pilots begin with discounted or donor-
supported access and later transition to renewals and scale-up.

Mitigating these risks requires deliberate procurement and design choices. Options include prioritizing
interoperability and data portability, adopting modular system architectures, negotiating clear
renewal/price-adjustment and exit/transition clauses, and using pooled or consortium-based purchasing
where feasible. In infrastructure-constrained settings, combining cloud-based services with smaller,
task-specific models that can run locally may further reduce dependency on external providers and help
contain recurrent licensing costs over time. These considerations point to the importance of procurement
strategies and private sector engagement in managing AI - related costs.

text:
The cost of using retail AI models in education are shaped by many factors. Pricing schemes for the use
of frontier commercial AI chatbots in education range from individual student or teacher subscriptions to
institution - wide and system - level licenses (Annex 1). They differ in functionality, data governance, usage
caps, customization, and integration with learning management systems (LMS), with important
implications for affordability and scalability across country contexts.
In high-income systems with strong infrastructure, large-scale licensing agreements can lower per-user
costs through volume pricing. For instance, the California State University (CSU) system launched a
US$16.9 million initiative in partnership with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and others to integrate AI across
its campuses. 6 The program provides systemwide access to ChatGPT Edu and plans to develop AI tutors
and streamline student services. With benefits to 460,000 students and 63,000 faculty and staff, this
initiative demonstrates how strategic large-scale investments can support both access and functionality,
while leveraging volume agreements to manage costs (CSU; GIA). In Estonia, cost of AI deployment across
all primary and secondary schools is approximately €4 million annually, split evenly between the national
government and private partners. Estonia's flagship national AI in education initiative, called AI Leap,
provides access to AI-driven learning tools and training for over 58,000 students and 5,000 educators, with
no out-of-pocket costs to users (Education Estonia, 2025). Such initiatives are designed for systems with
mature infrastructure, strong institutional capacity, and predictable recurrent funding, and are not directly
transferable to LICs and LMICs without significant adaptation and external support. Annex 1 provides a
detailed comparison of these models. To date, reliable public data on implementation costs of AI in
education systems in middle and low-income countries are lacking.

initiative cost less than two tenths of a percent of the overall budget (CSU 2025).

operational expenditures, which often dominate total cost of ownership. As a result, affordability
constraints in these contexts are less about the price of AI models alone and more about their interaction
with broader system costs.

where feasible. In infrastructure-constrained settings, combining cloud-based services with smaller,

title: Box 4 . Separating the Intelligence Layer From the Application Layer

paragraphs.text:
When making procurement decisions for AI in education, separating the intelligence layer (the AI models)
from the application layer (the user interface and software) is a critically important decision. Doing so helps
‘future-proof’ procurement decisions made today and help prevent vendor lock-in. Education systems are
not stuck with one AI provider if a better, cheaper, or more ethical model comes along. If a vendor raises
its prices or goes out of business, the ministry of education still retains its core data. Even if neither of these
actions occur, ministries maintain the power to renegotiate terms of contracts, because switching models
does not require retraining staff on a different user interface. Given the rate of change and improvement
in AI, separating the intelligence from the application layer allows for easier upgrade paths to take
advantage of new AI models. Doing so can also enhance data privacy and the ability to enforce consistent
safety and bias guardrails when using AI.

Cost-effective AI adoption at scale may be difficult using only traditional public financing mechanisms.
Emerging practice shows that strategic and pooled procurement can reduce costs and risk. Approaches
such as bulk purchasing, framework agreements, and centralized or consortium-based procurement can
lower unit prices while improving alignment with system needs. For example, Portugal’s b-On online digital

library pools demand across public higher-education institutions to negotiate nationwide access to
academic digital content at substantially reduced cost.

Innovative approaches to public-private partnerships are particularly important in LICs and LMICs, given
the scale of investment required to expand digital infrastructure and access. Well - structured
partnerships can mobilize private capital and technical expertise, support connectivity and device
provision, and shift some financial and operational risks away from governments. A notable example is the
UNICEF-ITU Giga initiative, which partners with governments, telecom operators, and technology
providers to connect schools to the internet using service-based and risk-sharing models rather than large
upfront public investments. (adapted from: Digital Skills for Africa: How to Empower a Growing Workforce
for More and Better Jobs , World Bank (forthcoming).

title: 3.1. Beyond Financing: A Phased Approach to AI Adoption in Education

paragraphs.text:
Despite rapid experimentation, many countries face large gaps in infrastructure, digital skills,
institutional readiness, and financing that make immediate systemwide AI adoption unrealistic. Rather
than asking whether countries should adopt AI now, a more practical question is how they can sequence
adoption in ways that are low risk, cost effective, and aligned with capacity constraints. This section
proposes a three-phase implementation framework designed to help countries roll out AI while learning,
adapting, and minimizing fiscal and operational risk (Figure 1).

Across all phases, certain essential features are needed for AI tools to be viable in LIC and LMIC contexts.
These cross - cutting requirements include some offline functionality (even if limited), compatibility across
devices, especially mobile phones, low total cost of ownership, relevance to local languages and cultural
contexts, and built - in data privacy and safety guardrails. AI tools for both teachers and students should be
accessible through a national or government endorsed learning management system (LMS) to support
curriculum alignment, user management, and data governance, while lowering marginal costs and
enabling more efficient scaling, particularly in Phases 1 and 2.

The phased framework includes parallel investments in building teacher digital skills and pedagogical
competencies across all stages. Building teacher capacity is not limited to classroom level pedagogical
guidance; it requires systematic investment in both initial teacher education (pre - service) and continuous

professional development (in - service). This is a critical component that underpins the effective use of AI
tools at each phase.

Phase 1 prioritizes teacher augmentation as the lowest risk and most affordable entry point. This phase
focuses on tools that enhance teacher productivity, reduce administrative burden, and strengthen
instructional capacity. While Phase 1 does not eliminate infrastructure costs—teachers still require devices
and some connectivity—it avoids the significantly higher costs associated with universal student - level

deployment. By limiting the number of users and devices and leveraging existing infrastructure where
possible, Phase 1 allows systems to build familiarity with AI while managing fiscal exposure.

Phase 2 expands AI use to targeted student support, increasing infrastructure requirements but in a
selective and prioritized manner. This phase focuses on addressing specific learning gaps or teacher
shortages through targeted deployment—by grade, subject, or geography—rather than universal
coverage. Infrastructure costs therefore rise in this phase, but are incurred progressively rather than all at
once. Integration through national platforms can further help manage costs and complexity as access
expands. Prioritizing secondary school students and focusing on applications where AI outperforms
available alternatives can help guide investments.

Phase 3 represents a shift toward systemwide integration and transformation. This phase includes
embedding AI into curricula, assessment systems, student services, and administrative processes. While it
offers the greatest potential impact, it is also the most complex and risk - prone stage, contingent on prior
investments in infrastructure, human capital, governance, and data systems.

title: Figure 1. Rollout of AI in Low- and Middle-Income Education Systems Framework

paragraphs.text:
Note: Phases are indicative and may overlap.
Source: Authors’ elaboration.

Although the framework is presented sequentially, phases may overlap in practice. Completing Phase 1
before Phase 2 is appropriate in basic education systems, regardless of infrastructure strength, as it builds
teacher capacity and institutional readiness. However, Phase 3 does not need to wait for full completion
of Phases 1 and 2. In particular, system-level AI applications—such as those supporting education
management information systems (EMIS), planning and resource allocation, or early warning systems for
dropout and learning risk—can be developed in parallel, as they primarily serve administrators and do not
require universal classroom-level readiness.

The phased framework does not assume that infrastructure costs are avoided in early stages, but that
they are sequenced deliberately. By aligning investments with demonstrated demand, teacher readiness,
and emerging evidence, countries can reduce the risk of overinvestment while building the foundations
required for equitable, sustainable, and high-impact AI integration in education.

title: 3.2. Supporting Cost-Effective AI Adoption in Education

paragraphs.text:
Implementing AI in education is both very similar to earlier challenges of integrating EdTech -- and at the
same time different. It is similar in that costly infrastructure constraints limit access, and skills
upgrades and training are required for effective uptake at scale. What is notably different about AI is the
speed that has characterized its development and roll-out over a very short period of time. Today’s AI
technologies are becoming widely adopted within a period of less than a decade. This speed increases
risks in a number of obvious ways: move fast, and you might make mistakes. FOMO (fear of missing out)
is an unfortunate but real driver of many efforts around the world to quickly deploy AI in education
before knowing exactly how to do it, who benefits and who does not, the necessary enabling
environment and prerequisites for success, and what related costs are. At the same time, not doing
anything potentially risks that countries and communities already on the wrong side of the digital
divide fall further behind their peers.

Given fiscal constraints and infrastructure gaps, cost-effective AI strategies in LICs and LMICs should
prioritize approaches that minimize upfront investment, manage recurrent costs, and generate policy
relevant evidence. Rather than systemwide deployment, countries can begin with targeted applications
that address binding constraints in teaching and learning while building institutional capacity and
learning over time.
Countries can consider eight key takeaways to support cost-effective AI adoption:

a.
Teacher - facing applications are often more cost-effective than direct student - facing
interventions, particularly in early stages. Interventions that support teachers through lesson
planning, feedback, coaching, or administrative assistance can be more cost-effective, even if their
effect on learning outcomes are less direct, as they require fewer devices and users and may be
feasible even where student - level access is limited. Where tools can run on basic smartphones,
which many teachers already have, school-based electricity constraints may also be less binding.
Although the effects on learning outcomes may be less immediate than student tutoring
applications, teacher - focused tools can improve instructional quality at lower fiscal cost.

b.
AI costs should be assessed against the high fiscal costs and often low learning levels of
‘business-as-usual’ education methods. Estimates of global learning poverty –the share of 10-
year-olds who are unable to read and understand a short text– stands at 70 percent (World Bank
et al., 2022). At the same time, expanding traditional teacher - based service delivery is fiscally

demanding: in Sub - Saharan Africa alone, reaching SDG 4 would require additional annual
spending of US$6.4 billion for primary and US$38.7 billion for secondary teachers by 2030 to
finance new salaried teacher posts (UNESCO & International Task Force on Teachers for
Education 2030, 2025).
c.
To keep costs manageable when introducing AI in education, systems can maximize impact by
building on infrastructure that is already in place. Leveraging existing hardware, like shared
school devices, and utilizing current mobile networks removes the need for massive, budget-
straining capital investments in new technology. This pragmatic approach shifts the focus from
expensive hardware procurement to affordable, scalable software deployment. This approach
enables resource-constrained education systems to channel more funding toward critical areas
like teacher training and localized digital content rather than redundant infrastructure.
d.
Traditional financing models may need to be reimagined to support the deployment of AI at
scale across an education system. Ministries of education can adapt existing funding streams like
national Universal Service Funds (USFs) to help finance AI use by subsidizing cloud computing
costs and edge hardware on a national scale. AI infrastructure bonds, innovative ‘computer-for-
data’ swaps and other financing approaches borrowed from other sectors may be utilized to
expand access to AI for use in education. Public-private partnerships can combine public sector
oversight with private sector capital and technical expertise to share the financial risks of
deploying fast-evolving AI technologies.
e.
“Offline-first” and low connectivity designs can further reduce costs and expand access. AI
applications that function without connectivity and then synchronize when low-bandwidth
access becomes available can be particularly valuable in rural or underserved areas. These
models can include personalized coaching to teachers that r eview in-classroom teacher practices
and perform an analysis for immediate feedback. Similar approaches in health and agriculture
have demonstrated large efficiency gains, including evidence that support to community health
workers through LLMs was over 500 times cheaper per response (Rutunda et. al, 2026; Shah et al.
2025).
f.
Innovative procurement approaches, such as outcome-based contracting and dynamic
purchasing systems, allow ministries of education to pivot away from rigid, multi-year software
licensing models that lock them into outdated technologies. By structuring agreements around
clear learning metrics or flexible, pay-as-you-go token usage, ministries of education can mitigate
the high financial risks associated with fast-evolving AI tools. By separating the underlying AI
intelligence layer from the user-facing application layer , education ministries can avoid costly
vendor lock-in and swap out AI models as newer, cheaper, or more powerful ones emerge.
g.
“Small AI” offers a promising entry point where infrastructure and budgets are constrained.
One approach is to leverage interventions that do not require reliable, continuous internet
access. This includes the use of Small Language Models, whose performance is increasing, and
which can work offline and be hosted on personal and edge devices. While the performance of

these models is not yet comparable to those of LLMs, they are improving fast (Lelievre et al., 2025),
and they can outperform the counterfactual of often limited support for students and teachers.
When the main cost driver is servers (compute costs), countries could explore alternative
approaches to access AI capabilities through shared or regional cloud services to avoid large
capital investments.
h.
Cost - effective AI adoption depends on building—and financing—a strong evidence base. The

evidence on cost - effectiveness, scalability, and implementation of LLMs and SLMs in low and
middle income countries remains very limited. Governments and development partners should
therefore treat evidence generation as a core investment, not an afterthought. This includes
funding well - designed pilots, collecting comparable data on total cost of ownership and
outcomes, and creating feedback loops that allow systems to adapt design choices as technologies
and prices evolve. Without intentional learning agendas and sustained financing for evaluation, AI
risks either premature scaling or missed opportunities for cost - saving innovation.

The current shallow evidence base related to AI use in education across all countries, and in low- and
middle-income countries in particular, represents a critical constraint for policy and operational
decision-making. We are still in an early phase of diffusion and deployment characterized by
experimentation, iteration, and rapid improvement. Limited evidence to date should not be interpreted
as “low potential ,” but rather as a call to systematically generate evidence to inform and guide education
policymakers and planners as they make consequential decisions about the use of AI in education in their
education systems.

Building a robust evidence base is perhaps the most critical prerequisite for long-term AI planning in
education. Without it, ministries risk making blind, multi-million-dollar commitments to technologies that
may not work, cannot scale, and/or could harm both individual learners and the larger learning ecosystem
in which teaching and learning takes place. Early causal research on uses of generative AI in education
reveals a major challenge for education planners: students using AI tools often show immediate, significant
performance gains while they have active access to the technology, but when assessed independently
without AI support, the learning effects are mixed or even decline (Stanford SCALE, 2026). Importantly,
how AI is used in education might be more important than whether it is used or not. Preliminary evidence
in developing countries shows that when AI is used following the best pedagogical principles and
embedded in alignment with the curriculum and teacher support, large learning gains are possible (e.g.r
De Simone et al, 2025; Henkel et. Al. 2024). On the other hand, when AI is deployed in a way that can be
used a shortcut rather than as a pedagogically-aligned tool, it can harm learning. Without building a
rigorous, locally-relevant evidence base, a ministry might mistake temporary, AI-assisted performance
for durable, long-term learning, wasting scarce public funds in the process. A ministry cannot responsibly
budget for a national rollout of AI use in education based on the results of a small pilot project where
token usage was constrained and heavily subsidized. Building a detailed evidence base allows planners to
understand actual user behavior over time, including that of "power users" of AI who can potentially, and
quickly, drain system resources by consuming tokens at rates that are financially unsustainable. Because
existing global evidence on the impacts of AI use on educational equity and student wellness is still
remarkably thin, ministries can deliberately generate their own evidence base and be open and willing to

share with, and learn from, their peers around the world. Systematic data collection allows policymakers
to determine whether the use of AI tool is helping to narrow achievement gaps or exacerbating the digital
divide, helping to ensure that decisions to ‘scale up’ are guided by ethical guardrails and proven
pedagogical efficacy rather than speculative hype.

remarkably thin, ministries can deliberately generate their own evidence base and be open and willing to
21
share with, and learn from, their peers around the world. Systematic data collection allows policymakers
to determine whether the use of AI tool is helping to narrow achievement gaps or exacerbating the digital
divide, helping to ensure that decisions to ‘scale up’ are guided by ethical guardrails and proven
pedagogical efficacy rather than speculative hype.

title: ABSTRACT

paragraphs.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a potential accelerator of human
capital development in low- and middle-income countries, with implications
and opportunities for learning, technical skills development, and labor
market productivity. Unlike earlier education technologies, AI shifts
spending from relatively predictable purchases of hardware, software, and
connectivity toward dynamic, usage-based expenditures for inference,
cloud compute, data integration, governance, and continuous teacher
support. These costs are volatile, cumulative, and often poorly captured in
traditional education budgets. The paper develops a planning lens for
understanding AI adoption as a transition from products to services to
tokens, showing how this shift changes the fiscal risks facing ministries
of education. It highlights why pilot costs are especially misleading
predictors of system-wide affordability, as subsidies disappear, integration
requirements expand, and equity obligations become more expensive at
scale. It also examines pathways that may make AI more feasible in
resource-constrained settings.

The paper situates AI within the hard realities of infrastructure gaps, low
digital skills, constrained public education budgets, and weak evidence on
learning impacts. Its core contribution is to reframe AI in education as a
problem of cost architecture, sequencing, and institutional readiness. For
policymakers, the implication is clear: cost-effective AI adoption will depend
less on access to the latest model than on the ability to govern recurrent
costs, learn from carefully designed pilots, protect equity, and build flexible
systems that can adapt as technologies, prices, and evidence evolve.

title: Prompt Engineering for LLMs

paragraphs.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are revolutionizing the world,
promising to automate tasks and solve complex problems.
A new generation of software applications are using these
models as building blocks to unlock new potential in almost
every domain, but reliably accessing these capabilities
requires new skills. This book will teach you the art and
science of prompt engineering—the key to unlocking the
true potential of LLMs.

John Berryman is founder
of Arcturus Labs, specializing
in LLM-based application
development. He was an early
GitHub Copilot engineer, working
on chat and code completions.
John is also a search expert
and author of Relevant Search
(Manning).

Industry experts John Berryman and Albert Ziegler share how
to communicate effectively with AI, transforming your ideas
into a language model–friendly format. By learning both the
philosophical foundation and practical techniques, you’ll be
equipped with the knowledge and confidence to build the
next generation of LLM-powered applications.

Albert Ziegler is Head of AI for
the AI cybersecurity firm XBOW.
As founding engineer for GitHub
Copilot, the first successful
industry-scale LLM product, he
designed its model interaction
and prompt engineering systems.

• Understand LLM architecture and learn how
to best interact with it

• Design a complete prompt-crafting strategy
for an application

• Gather, triage, and present context elements
to make an efficient prompt

• Master specific prompt-crafting techniques like
few-shot learning, chain-of-thought prompting,
and RAG

title: Preface

paragraphs.text:
Since OpenAI introduced GPT-2 in early 2019, large language models (LLMs) have
rapidly changed our world. In 2019, if you, as a coder, had a technical question,
then you would search the internet for an answer. More often than not, there would
be no answer, leaving only the option to post on some question-and-answer (Q&A)
forum in the possibly vain hope that someone might answer you. But today, instead
of breaking your flow, you just ask an LLM assistant for direct commentary on the
code you’re working on. Moreover, you can even engage in a pairing session where
the assistant writes the code to your specifications. This is just in the field of software
engineering, and similar tectonic shifts are beginning to be felt in almost any field
that you can name.

The reason that this revolution is taking place is because the LLM is truly a revo‐
lutionary technology that makes it possible to achieve in software what formerly
could be done only through human interaction. LLMs can generate content, answer
questions, extract tabular data from natural language text, summarize text, classify
documents, translate, and (in principle) do just about anything that you can do with
text—except that LLMs will do it many orders of magnitude faster and never stop for
a break.

For entrepreneurs, this opens endless doors of opportunity in every field imaginable.
But before you can take advantage of these opportunities, you have to be prepared.
This book serves as a guide to help you understand LLMs, interact with them
through prompt engineering, and build applications that will bring value to your
users, your company, or yourself.

title: Who Is This Book For?

paragraphs.text:
This book is written for application engineers. If you build software products that
customers use, then this book is for you. If you build internal applications or
data-processing workflows, then this book is also for you. The reason that we are
being so inclusive is because we believe that the usage of LLMs will soon become
ix

ubiquitous. Even if your day-to-day work doesn’t involve prompt engineering or LLM
workflow design, your codebase will be filled with usages of LLMs, and you’ll need to
understand how to interact with them just to get your job done.

However, a subset of application engineers will be the dedicated LLM wranglers—
these are the prompt engineers . It’s their job to convert problems into a packet of
information that the LLM can understand—which we call the prompt —and then
convert the LLM completions back into results that bring value to those who use the
application. If this is your current role—or if you want this to be your role—then this
book is especially for you.

LLMs are very approachable—you speak with them in natural language. So, for this
book, you won’t be expected to know everything about machine learning. But you do
need to have a good grasp of basic engineering principles—you need to know how to
program and how to use an API. Another prerequisite for this book is the ability to
empathize, because unlike with any technology before, you need to understand how
LLMs “think” so that you can guide them to generate the content you need. This book
will show you how.

LLMs are very approachable—you speak with them in natural language. So, for this
book, you won’t be expected to know everything about machine learning. But you do
need to have a good grasp of basic engineering principles—you need to know how to
program and how to use an API. Another prerequisite for this book is the ability to
empathize, because unlike with any technology before, you need to understand how
LLMs “think” so that you can guide them to generate the content you need. This book
will show you how.

title: What You Will Learn

paragraphs.text:
The goal of this book is to equip you with all the theory, techniques, tips, and tricks
you need to master prompt engineering and build successful LLM applications.

In Part I of the book, we convey a foundational understanding of LLMs, their inner
workings, and their functionality as text completion engines. We cover the extension
of LLMs to their new role as chat engines, and we present a high-level approach to
LLM application development.

In Part II , we introduce the core techniques for prompt engineering—how to source
context information, rank its importance for the task at hand, pack the prompt
(without overloading it), and organize everything into a template that will result in
high-quality completions that elicit the answer you need.

In Part III , we move to more advanced techniques. We assemble loops, pipelines,
and workflows of LLM inference to create conversational agency and LLM-driven
workflows, and we then explain techniques for evaluating LLMs.
Throughout this book, we highlight one principle that underlies all others:

At their core, LLMs are just text completion engines that mimic the text they see
during their training.

title: CHAPTER 1 Introduction to Prompt Engineering

paragraphs.text:
ChatGPT was released in late November of 2022. By January of the following year,
the application had accumulated an estimated 100 million monthly users, making
ChatGPT the fastest-growing consumer application ever . (In comparison, TikTok
took 9 months to reach 100 million users, and Instagram took 2.5 years.) And as you
can surely attest, esteemed reader, this public acclaim is well deserved! LLMs—like
the one that backs ChatGPT—are revolutionizing the way we work. Rather than
running to Google to find answers via a traditional web search, you can easily just
ask an LLM to talk about a topic. Rather than reading Stack Overflow or rummaging
through blog posts to answer technical questions, you can ask an LLM to write you a
personalized tutorial on your exact problem space and then follow it up with a set of
questions and answers (a Q&A) about the topic. Rather than following the traditional
steps to build a programming library, you can boost your progress by pairing with
an LLM-based assistant to build the scaffolding and autocomplete your code as you
write it!

And to you, future reader, will you use LLMs in ways that we, your humble authors
from the year 2024, cannot fathom? If the current trends continue, you’ll likely have
conversations with LLMs many times during the course of a typical day—in the voice
of the IT support assistant when your cable goes out, in a friendly conversation with
the corner ATM, and, yes, even with a frustratingly realistic robo dialer. There will
be other interactions as well. LLMs will curate your news for you, summarizing the
headline stories that you’re most likely to be interested in and removing (or perhaps
adding ) biased commentary. You’ll use LLMs to assist in your communications by
writing and summarizing emails, and office and home assistants will even reach out
into the real world and interact on your behalf. In a single day, your personal AI
assistant might at one point act as a travel agent, helping you make travel plans, book
flights, and reserve hotels; and then at another point, act as a shopping assistant,
helping you find and purchase items you need.

Why are LLMs so amazing? It’s because they are magic! As futurist Arthur C. Clarke
famously stated, “Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from
magic.” We think a machine that you can have a conversation with certainly qualifies
as magic, but it’s the goal of this book to dispel this magic. We will demonstrate
that no matter how uncanny, intuitive, and humanlike LLMs sometimes seem to
be, at the core, LLMs are simply models that predict the next word in a block of
text—that’s it and nothing more! As such, LLMs are merely tools for helping users to
accomplish some task, and the way that you interact with these tools is by crafting
the prompt ― the block of text ― that they are to complete. This is what we call prompt
engineering . Through this book, we will build up a practical framework for prompt
engineering and ultimately for building LLM applications, which will be a magical
experience for your users.

This chapter sets the background for the journey you are about to take into prompt
engineering. But first, let us tell you about how we, your authors, discovered the
magic for ourselves.

title: LLMs Are Magic

paragraphs.text:
Both authors of this book were early research developers for the GitHub Copilot code
completion product. Albert was on the founding team, and John appeared on the
scene as Albert was moving on to other distant-horizon LLM research projects.
Albert first discovered the magic halfway through 2020. He puts it as follows:

Every half year or so, during our ideation meetings in the ML-on-code group, someone
would bring up the matter of code synthesis. And the answer was always the same: it
will be amazing, one day, but that day won’t come for another five years at least. It was
our cold fusion.

This was true until the first day I laid hands on an early prototype of the LLM that
would become OpenAI Codex. Then I saw that the future was now: cold fusion had
finally arrived.

It was immediately clear that this model was wholly different from the sorry stabs
at code synthesis we had known before. This model wouldn’t just have a chance of
predicting the next word ― it could generate whole statements and whole functions
from just the docstring. Functions that worked!

Before we decided what we could build with this model (spoiler: it would eventually
become GitHub’s Copilot code completion product), we wanted to quantify how good
the model really was. So, we crowdsourced a bunch of GitHub engineers and had
them come up with self-contained coding tasks. Some of the tasks were comparatively
easy ― but these were hardcore coders, and many of their tasks were also pretty
involved. A good number of the tasks were the kind a junior developer would turn
to Google for, but some would push even a senior developer to Stack Overflow. Yet, if
we gave the model a few tries, it could solve most of them.

title: Early Language Models

paragraphs.text:
Language models have actually been around for a long time. If you’re reading this
book soon after its publication, then the language model that powers the iPhone
guess-the-next-word functionality is based upon a Markov model of natural language
that was first introduced in 1948 . However, there are other more recent language
models that have more directly set the stage for the AI revolution that is now
underway.

By 2014, the most powerful language models were based on the sequence to sequence
(seq2seq) architecture introduced at Google . Seq2seq was a recurrent neural network,
which, in theory, should have been ideal for text processing because it processes one

title: Language Models: How Did We Get Here? | 5

paragraphs.text:
token at a time and recurrently updates its internal state. This allows seq2seq to
process arbitrarily long sequences of text. With specialized architectures and training,
the seq2seq architecture was capable of performing several different types of natural
language tasks: classification, entity extraction, translation, summarization, and more.
But these models had an Achilles’ heel—an information bottleneck limited their
capabilities.

The seq2seq architecture has two major components: the encoder and the decoder
(see Figure 1-3 ). Processing starts by sending the encoder a stream of tokens that are
processed one at a time. As the tokens are received, the encoder updates a hidden
state vector that accumulates information from the input sequence. When the last
token has been processed, the final value of the hidden state, called the thought
vector, is sent to the decoder. The decoder then uses the information from the
thought vector to generate output tokens. The problem, though, is that the thought
vector is fixed and finite. It often “forgets” important information from longer blocks
of text, giving the decoder little to work with—this is the information bottleneck.

token has been processed, the final value of the hidden state, called the thought
vector, is sent to the decoder. The decoder then uses the information from the
thought vector to generate output tokens. The problem, though, is that the thought
vector is fixed and finite. It often “forgets” important information from longer blocks
of text, giving the decoder little to work with—this is the information bottleneck.

A 2015 paper, “Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Trans‐
late” , introduced a new approach to addressing this bottleneck. Rather than having
the encoder supply a single thought vector, it preserved all the hidden state vectors
generated for each token encountered in the encoding process and then allowed
the decoder to “soft search” over all of the vectors. As a demonstration, the paper
showed that using soft search with an English-to-French translation model increased
translation quality significantly. This soft search technique soon came to be known as
the attention mechanism.

The attention mechanism soon gained a good deal of attention of its own in the
AI community, culminating in the 2017 Google Research paper “Attention Is All
You Need” , which introduced the transformer architecture shown in Figure 1-4 . The
transformer retained the high-level structure of its predecessor—consisting of an
encoder that received tokens as input followed by a decoder that generated output
tokens. But unlike the seq2seq model, all of the recurrent circuitry had been removed,
and the transformer instead relies completely upon the attention mechanism. The
resulting architecture was very flexible and much better at modeling training data
than seq2seq. But whereas seq2seq could process arbitrarily long sequences, the
transformer could process only a fixed, finite sequence of inputs and outputs. Since
the transformer is the direct progenitor of the GPT models, this is a limitation that we
have been pushing back against ever since.

title: GPT Enters the Scene

paragraphs.text:
The generative pre-trained transformer architecture was introduced in the 2018
paper “Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training” . The archi‐
tecture wasn’t particularly special or new. Actually, the architecture was just a trans‐
former with the encoder ripped off—it was just the decoder side. However, this
simplification led to some unexpected new possibilities that would only be fully real‐
ized in coming years. It was this generative pre-trained transformer architecture—
GPT—that would soon ignite the ongoing AI revolution.

In 2018, this wasn’t apparent. At that point in time, it was standard practice to pre-
train models with unlabeled data—for instance, scraps of text from the internet—and
then modify the architecture of the models and apply specialized fine-tuning so that
the final model would then be able to do one task very well. And so it was with the
generative pre-trained transformer architecture. The 2018 paper simply showed that
this pattern worked really well for GPTs—pre-training on unlabeled text followed by
supervised fine-tuning for a particular task led to really good models for a variety of
tasks such as classification, measuring similarities among documents, and answering
multiple-choice questions. But we should emphasize one point: after the GPT was
fine-tuned, it was only good at the single task for which it was fine-tuned.

GPT-2 was simply a scaled-up version of GPT. When it was introduced in 2019, it
was beginning to dawn upon researchers that the GPT architecture was something
special. This is clearly evidenced in the second paragraph of the OpenAI blog post
introducing GPT-2 :

Our model, called GPT-2 (a successor to GPT), was trained simply to predict the next
word in 40 GB of Internet text. Due to our concerns about malicious applications of
the technology, we are not releasing the trained model.

Wow! How can those two sentences belong next to each other? How does something
as innocuous as predicting the next word—just like an iPhone does when you write a
text message—lead to such grave concerns about misuse? If you read the correspond‐
ing academic paper, “Language Models Are Unsupervised Multitask Learners” , then
you start to find out. GPT-2 was 1.5 billion parameters, as compared with GPT’s 117
million, and was trained on 40 GB of text, as compared with GPT’s 4.5 GB. A simple
order-of-magnitude increase in model and training set size led to an unprecedented
emergent quality—instead of having to fine-tune GPT-2 for a single task, you could
apply the raw, pre-trained model to the task and often achieve better results than
state-of-the-art models that were fine-tuned specifically for the task. This included
benchmarks for understanding ambiguous pronouns, predicting missing words in
text, tagging parts of speech, and more. And despite falling behind the state of the art,
GPT-2 also fared surprisingly well on reading comprehension, summarization, trans‐
lation, and question-answering tasks, again against models fine-tuned specifically for
those tasks.

title: Language Models: How Did We Get Here? | 9

paragraphs.text:
But, why all the concern about “malicious applications” of this model? It’s because the
model had become quite good at mimicking natural text. And, as the OpenAI blog
post indicates, this capability could be used to “generate misleading news articles,
impersonate others online, automate the production of abusive or faked content to
post on social media, and automate the production of spam/phishing content.” If
anything, this possibility has only become more real and concerning today than it was
in 2019.

GPT-3 saw another order-of-magnitude increase in both model size and training
data, with a corresponding leap in capability. The 2020 paper “Language Models Are
Few-Shot Learners” showed that, given a few examples of the task you want the
model to complete, (a.k.a. “few-shot examples”), the model could faithfully reproduce
the input pattern and, as a result, perform just about any language-based task that
you could imagine—and often with remarkably high-quality results. This is when
we found out that you could modify the input—the prompt—and thereby condition
the model to perform the requisite task at hand. This was the birth of prompt
engineering.

ChatGPT, released in November 2022, was backed by GPT-3.5 ― and the rest is
history! But, it’s a history rapidly in the making (see Table 1-1 ). In March of 2023,
GPT-4 was released, and although the details were not officially revealed, that model
was rumored to be another order of magnitude larger in both model size and amount
of training data, and it was again much more capable than its predecessors. Since
then, more and more models have appeared. Some are from OpenAI while others are
from major industry players, such as Llama from Meta, Claude from Anthropic, and
Gemini from Google. We have continued to see leaps in quality, and increasingly, the
same level of quality is available in smaller and faster models. If anything, the progress
is only accelerating .

title: Prompt Engineering

paragraphs.text:
Now, we arrive at the beginning of your journey into the world of prompt engineer‐
ing. At their core, LLMs are capable of one thing—completing text. The input into
the model is called the prompt —it is a document, or block of text, that we expect
the model to complete. Prompt engineering , then, in its simplest form, is the practice
of crafting the prompt so that its completion contains the information required to
address the problem at hand.

In this book, we provide a much larger picture of prompt engineering that involves
moves well beyond a single prompt and discuss the entire LLM-based application,
where prompt construction and the interpretation of the answer are done program‐
matically. To build a quality piece of software and a quality UX, the prompt engineer
must create a pattern for iterative communication among the user, the application,
and the LLM. The user conveys their problem to the application, the application con‐
structs a pseudodocument to be sent to the LLM, the LLM completes the document,
and finally, the application parses the completion and conveys the result back to the
user or otherwise performs an action on the user’s behalf. The science and art of
prompt engineering is to make sure that this communication is structured in a way
that best translates among very different domains, the user’s problem space, and the
document space of LLMs.

Prompt engineering comes in several levels of sophistication. The most basic form
makes use of only a very thin application layer. For instance, when you engage
with ChatGPT, you’re crafting a prompt almost directly; the application is merely
wrapping the conversation thread in a special ChatML markdown. (You’ll learn more
about this in Chapter 3 .) Similarly, when GitHub Copilot was first created for code
completions, it was doing little more than passing the current file along to the model
to complete.

At the next level of sophistication, prompt engineering involves modifying and aug‐
menting the user’s input into the model. For instance, LLMs deal with text, so a tech
support hotline could transcribe a user’s speech to text and use it in the prompt sent
to the LLM. Additionally, relevant content from previous help transcripts or from
relevant support documentation could be included in the prompt. As a real-world
example, as GitHub Copilot code completions developed, we realized that the com‐
pletion quality improved considerably if we incorporated relevant snippets from the
user’s neighboring tabs. This makes sense, right? The user had the tabs open because
they were referencing information there, so it stands to reason that the model could
benefit from this information as well. Another example is the new Bing chat-based
search experience. In this instance, content from traditional search results is pulled
into the prompt. This allows the assistant to competently discuss information that
it never saw in the training data (for instance, because it referred to events that
happened after the model was trained). More importantly, this approach helps Bing

title: Prompt Engineering | 11

paragraphs.text:
reduce hallucinations, a topic we’ll revisit several times throughout the book, starting
in the next chapter.

Another aspect of prompt engineering at this level of sophistication comes when
the interactions with the LLM become stateful , meaning they maintain context and
information from prior interactions. A chat application is the quintessential example
here. With each new exchange from the user, the application must recall what hap‐
pened in previous exchanges and generate a prompt that faithfully represents the
interaction. As the conversation or history gets longer, you will have to be careful to
not overfill the prompt or include spurious content that might distract the model.
You may choose to drop the earliest exchanges or less relevant content from previous
exchanges, and you may even employ summarization to compress the content.

Yet another aspect of prompt engineering at this level of sophistication involves
giving the LLM-based application tools that allow the LLM to reach out into the real
world by making API requests to read information or to even create or modify assets
that are available on the internet. For instance, an LLM-based email application might
receive this input from a user: “Send Diane an invitation to a meeting on May 5.”
This application would use one tool to identify Diane in the user’s contacts list and
then use a calendar API to look up her availability before finally sending an email
invitation. As these models get cheaper and more powerful, just imagine the possibili‐
ties available with the APIs already at our disposal today! Prompt engineering here is
critical. How will the model know which tool to use? How will it use the tool in the
correct way? How will your application properly share the information from the tool
execution with the model? What do we do when the tool usage results in some sort of
error state? We will talk about all of this in Chapter 8 .

The final level of sophistication that we cover in this book is how to provide the
LLM application with agency—the ability to make its own decisions about how to
accomplish broad goals supplied by the user. This is clearly on the frontier of our
capabilities with LLMs, but research and practical exploration are underway. Already,
you can download AutoGPT and supply it with a goal, and it will take off on a
multistep process to gather the information it needs to accomplish the goal. Does it
always work? No. Actually, unless the goal is quite constrained, it tends to fail at the
task more often than it succeeds. But giving LLM applications some form of agency
and autonomy is still an important step toward exciting future possibilities. You’ll
read our take on this in Chapters 8 and 9 .

title: Conclusion

paragraphs.text:
As we said at the start, this chapter sets the background for the journey you are about
to take into prompt engineering. We started with a discussion of the recent history
of language models, and we highlighted why LLMs are so special and different—and
why they are fueling the AI revolution that we are all now witnessing. We then
defined the topic of this book: prompt engineering.

In particular, you should understand that this book isn’t going to be all about how to
do nitpicky wording of a single prompt to get one good completion. Sure, we’ll cover
that, and we’ll cover in detail all the things you need to do to generate high-quality
completions that serve their intended purpose. But when we say, “prompt engineer‐
ing,” we mean building the entire LLM-based application. The LLM application
serves as a transformation layer, iteratively and statefully converting real-world needs
into text that LLMs can address and then converting the data provided by the LLMs
into information and action that address those real-world needs.

Before we set off on this journey, let’s make sure we’re appropriately packed. In the
next chapter, you’ll learn how LLM text completion works from the top-level API
all the way down to low-level attention mechanisms. In the subsequent chapter, we’ll
build upon that knowledge to explain how LLMs have been expanded to handle chat
and tool usage, and you’ll see that deep down, it’s really all the same thing—text
completion. Then, with those foundational ideas in store, you’ll be ready for your
journey.

title: CHAPTER 2 Understanding LLMs

paragraphs.text:
So you want to become the LLM whisperer who unlocks the wealth of their knowl‐
edge and processing power with clever prompts? Well, to appreciate which kinds
of prompts are clever and tease the right answer from the LLM, you first need to
understand how LLMs process information ― how they think .

In this chapter, we’ll approach this problem onion style. You’ll first see LLMs from
the very outside as trained mimics of text in “What Are LLMs?” on page 16 . You’ll
learn how they split the text into bite-size chunks called tokens in “How LLMs See the
World” on page 22 , and you’ll learn about the fallout if they can’t easily accomplish
that split.

You’ll also find out how the token sequences are generated bit by bit in “One Token
at a Time” on page 29 , and you’ll learn about the different ways to choose the next
token in “Temperature and Probabilities” on page 32 . Finally, in “The Transformer
Architecture” on page 37 , you’ll delve into the very inner workings of an LLM,
understand it as a collection of minibrains that communicate through a Q&A game
called attention , and learn what that means for prompt order.

During all that, please keep in mind that this is a book about using LLMs, not
about LLMs themselves. So, there are a lot of cool technical details that we’re not
mentioning because they’re not relevant for prompt engineering. If you want matrix
multiplications and activation functions, you’ll need to turn elsewhere—the classic
reference The Illustrated Transformer is an excellent starting point for a deep dive.
But we promise you won’t need that amount of technical background if all you want
to do is write great prompts ― so let’s dive into what you do need to know.

So you want to become the LLM whisperer who unlocks the wealth of their knowl‐
edge and processing power with clever prompts? Well, to appreciate which kinds
of prompts are clever and tease the right answer from the LLM, you first need to
understand how LLMs process information ― how they think .
In this chapter, we’ll approach this problem onion style. You’ll first see LLMs from
the very outside as trained mimics of text in “What Are LLMs?” on page 16 . You’ll
learn how they split the text into bite-size chunks called tokens in “How LLMs See the
World” on page 22 , and you’ll learn about the fallout if they can’t easily accomplish
that split.
You’ll also find out how the token sequences are generated bit by bit in “One Token
at a Time” on page 29 , and you’ll learn about the different ways to choose the next
token in “Temperature and Probabilities” on page 32 . Finally, in “The Transformer
Architecture” on page 37 , you’ll delve into the very inner workings of an LLM,
understand it as a collection of minibrains that communicate through a Q&A game
called attention , and learn what that means for prompt order.
During all that, please keep in mind that this is a book about using LLMs, not
about LLMs themselves. So, there are a lot of cool technical details that we’re not
mentioning because they’re not relevant for prompt engineering. If you want matrix
multiplications and activation functions, you’ll need to turn elsewhere—the classic
reference The Illustrated Transformer is an excellent starting point for a deep dive.
But we promise you won’t need that amount of technical background if all you want
to do is write great prompts ― so let’s dive into what you do need to know.
15

title: What Are LLMs?

paragraphs.text:
At the most basic level, an LLM is a service that takes a string and returns a string:
text in, text out. The input is called the prompt , and the output is called the completion
or sometimes, the response (see Figure 2-1 ).

Figure 2-1. An LLM taking the prompt “One, Two,” and presenting the completion
“ Buckle My Shoe”

When an untrained LLM first sees the light of day, its completions will look like
a pretty random jumble of unicode symbols and bear no clear relationship to the
prompt. It needs to be trained before it’s useful. Then, the LLM won’t just answer
strings with strings but language with language.

Training takes skill, compute, and time far beyond the scope of most project groups,
so most LLM applications use off-the-shelf generalist models (known as foundation
models ) that are already trained (maybe after a bit of fine-tuning; see the sidebar).
So, we don’t expect you to train an LLM yourself ― but if you want to use an LLM,
especially programmatically, it is essential for you to understand what it has been
trained to do.

title: What Is Fine-Tuning?

paragraphs.text:
Training LLMs takes lots of data and compute, although many basic lessons, such
as the rules of English grammar, don’t differ much between the training sets. It’s
therefore common not to start completely from scratch when training an LLM but
to start with a copy of a different LLM, possibly one that’s trained on different
documents.

For example, the early versions of OpenAI Codex (an LLM for producing source code
that was developed for GitHub Copilot) were copies of an existing model (GPT-3, a
natural language LLM) that were fine-tuned with lots of source code published on
GitHub.

If you have such a model trained on dataset A and fine-tuned on dataset B, your
prompts should normally be written as if it had been trained on B outright. We’ll
delve deeper into fine-tuning in Chapter 7 .

title: 16 | Chapter 2: Understanding LLMs

paragraphs.text:
LLMs are trained using a large set of documents (again, strings) known as the training
set . The kind of documents depends on the purpose of the LLM (see Figure 2-2 for
an example). The training set is often a mixture of different training inputs such as
books, articles, conversations on platforms such as Reddit, and code on sites such as
GitHub. From the training set, the model is supposed to learn how to produce output
that looks just like the training set. Concretely, when the model receives a prompt
that is the beginning of a document from its training set, the resulting completion
should be the text that is most likely to continue the original document. In other
words, models mimic.

Figure 2-2. Composition of “The Pile” , a popular open source training set comprising a
mixture of factual prose, fictional prose, dialogues, and other internet content

So, how’s an LLM different from, say, a big search engine index full of the training
data? After all, a search engine would ace the task the LLM was trained with—given
the beginning of a document, it could find a completion for that document with
100% accuracy. And yet, having a search engine that just parrots the training set
isn’t the goal here: the LLM shouldn’t learn to recite the training set by heart but to
apply the patterns it encounters there (in particular, logical and reasoning patterns) to
complete any prompt, not just those from the training set. Mere rote memorization
is considered a defect. Both the inner architecture of the LLM (which encourages it
to abstract from concrete examples) and the training procedure (which tries to feed
it diverse, nonrepetitive data and measures success on unseen data) are supposed to
prevent this defect.

title: What Are LLMs? | 17

paragraphs.text:
That prevention sometimes fails, and instead of learning facts and patterns, the model
learns chunks of text by rote—which is known as overfitting . Large-scale overfitting
should be rare in off-the-shelf models, but it’s worth being aware of the possibility
that if an LLM seemingly solves a problem that it’s seen during training, it doesn’t
necessarily mean that the LLM will do as well when confronted with a similar
problem it hasn’t seen before.

Nevertheless, after you work with LLMs for a while, you start to develop an intuition
for how an LLM will behave based on the task it was trained on. So when you want to
know how a given prompt might be completed, don’t ask yourself how a reasonable
person would “reply” to the prompt but rather how a document that happens to start
with the prompt might continue.

Assume you have picked a document from the training set at
random. All you know about it is, it starts with the prompt. What
is the statistically most likely continuation? That’s the LLM output
you should expect.

paragraphs.text: \n
First, try unplugging the TV from the wall and plugging it back in.

Well, it depends on the training set. Let’s say the LLM was trained on a dataset of
narrative prose such as short stories, novels, magazines, and newspapers—in that
case, completion a , about reading a book, sounds rather more likely than the others.
While the sentence about the TV, followed by the question from completion b , could
well appear somewhere in the middle of a story, a story wouldn’t open with this
question without at least the starting quotation marks (“). So it’s unlikely that a model
trained on short stories would predict option b .

But throw emails and conversation transcripts into the training set, and suddenly,
option b appears very plausible. I made up both of them, though: it’s the third option
that was produced by an actual LLM (OpenAI’s text-davinci-003, which is a variant of
GPT-3), mimicking the advice and customer service conversations that abound in its
training set.

A theme is emerging here: the better you know the training data, the better the
intuition you can form about the likely output of an LLM trained on that training
data. Many commercial LLMs don’t publish their training data—choosing a good
training set is a big part of the special sauce that makes their models successful. Even
then, however, it’s usually possible to form some sensible expectations about the kind
of documents the training set consists of.

title: Human Thought Versus LLM Processing

paragraphs.text:
The LLM selects the most likely looking continuation, and this goes against some
assumptions humans make when reading text. That’s because when humans produce
text, they do so as part of a process that involves more than producing plausible-
looking text output. Let’s say you want to write a blog post about a podcast you came
across at the podcasting site Acast. You might start writing the following: In their
newest installment of `The rest is history`, they talk about the Hundred
Years’ War (listen on acast at http://. Of course you don’t know the URL
by heart, so this is the point where you stop writing and do a quick internet search.
Hopefully, you find the correct link: shows.acast.com/the-rest-is-history-podcast/epi‐
sodes/321-hundred-years-war-a-storm-of-swords. Or maybe you can’t find it, in
which case, you might go back and delete the whole bracket and replace it with
