title: Additional support

paragraphs.text:
The Department has published further advice for those working in education settings with
safeguarding responsibilities on the Prevent duty. The advice is intended to complement
the Prevent guidance and signposts to other sources of advice and support.
The Home Office has developed three e-learning modules:
• Prevent awareness e-learning offers an introduction to the Prevent duty.

• Prevent referrals e-learning supports staff to make Prevent referrals that are
robust, informed and with good intention .

• Channel awareness e-learning is aimed at staff who may be asked to contribute to
or sit on a multi-agency Channel panel.

Educate Against Hate is a government website designed to support school and college
teachers and leaders to help them safeguard their students from radicalisation and
extremism. The platform provides free information and resources to help staff identify and
address the risks, as well as build resilience to radicalisation. These resources are
regularly updated to ensure they remain relevant and practical. Resources have been
developed working closely with education professionals and civil society groups to
identify and produce high-quality materials that assist teachers in building pupils’ critical
thinking skills and resilience to extremist ideologies.

For advice specific to further education, Educate Against Hate hosts a suite of teaching
packs and accompanying guidance to meet the specific needs of students and
practitioners in further education and training settings. The Education and Training
Foundation (ETF) hosts the Prevent for FE and Training . This hosts a range of free,
sector specific resources to support further education settings to comply with the Prevent
duty. This includes the Prevent Awareness e-learning, which offers an introduction to the
duty, and the Prevent Referral e-learning, which is designed to support staff to make
robust, informed and proportionate referrals. The Education and Training Foundation
(ETF) provides online training modules for practitioners, leaders and managers, to
support staff and governors/Board members in outlining their roles and responsibilities
under the duty.

London Grid for Learning has also produced useful resources on Prevent ( Online Safety
Resource Centre - London Grid for Learning (lgfl.net).

title: Serious violence

paragraphs.text:
There are a number of indicators, which may signal children are at risk from, or are
involved in committing serious violence. These may include:
• increased absence from school or college,
• a change in friendships or relationships with older individuals or groups,
• a significant decline in educational performance,

• signs of self-harm or a significant change in wellbeing, or signs of assault or
unexplained injuries, and

• unexplained gifts or new possessions could also indicate that children have been
approached by, or are involved with, individuals associated with criminal networks
or gangs and may be at risk of criminal exploitation.
The likelihood of involvement in serious violence may be increased by factors such as:
• being male,

• having been suspended, spent time in Alternative Provision or permanently
excluded from school,
• having experienced child maltreatment,
• having been involved in offending, such as theft or robbery,
• having used drugs or alcohol in early adolescence, and
• having previously been a victim or previously perpetrated violence
A fuller list of risk factors can be found in the Home Office’s Serious Violence Strategy .

Professionals should also be aware that violence can often peak in the hours just before
or just after school, when pupils are travelling to and from school and can concentrate in
particular places. These times can be particularly risky for young people involved in
serious violence. It is important that schools and colleges try to understand where these
places are, with a view to working with partners to promote safety for children. Listening
to children and consulting with staff can help establish when and where they feel unsafe.
Working with wider partners can also help build understanding of the local context
beyond the school or college and help co-ordinate a collective safeguarding response
around the school day.

Advice for schools and colleges is provided in the Home Office’s Criminal exploitation of
children and vulnerable adults: county lines guidance. The Youth Endowment Fund

(YEF) (the “what works” centre for preventing violence) has produced practical guidance
for schools and colleges and an accompanying self-assessment tool to help introduce
evidenced practice for preventing children becoming involved in violence.

Home Office funded Violence Reduction Units (VRU) operate in the 20 police force areas
across England and Wales that have the highest volumes of serious violence, as
measured by hospital admissions for injury with a sharp object. A list of these locations
can be found here . As the strategic co-ordinators for local violence prevention, each VRU
is mandated to include at least one local education representative within their Core
Membership group, which is responsible for setting the direction for VRU activity. Schools
and educational partners within these areas are encouraged to reach out to their local
VRU, either directly or via their education Core Member, to better ingrain partnership
working to tackle serious violence across local areas and ensure a joined-up approach to
young people across the risk spectrum.

Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 introduced a new Serious Violence Duty
(Statutory Guidance ) on a range of specified authorities, such as the police, local
government, youth offending teams, health and probation services, to work
collaboratively, share data and information, and put in place plans to prevent and reduce
serious violence within their local communities. Educational authorities and prisons/youth
custody authorities are under a separate duty to co-operate with core duty holders when
asked, and there is a requirement for the partnership to consult with all such institutions
in their area.
The Duty does not replace or duplicate existing safeguarding duties.

Honour or faith-based abuse (including female genital mutilation and
forced marriage)

Honour or faith-based abuse (HBA) encompasses incidents or crimes which have been
committed to protect or defend the honour of the family and/or the community, including
female genital mutilation (FGM), forced marriage, and practices such as breast ironing.
Abuse committed in the context of preserving honour often involves a wider network of
family or community pressure and can include multiple perpetrators. It is important to be
aware of this dynamic and additional risk factors when deciding what form of
safeguarding action to take. All forms of HBA are abuse (regardless of the motivation)
and should be handled and escalated as such. Professionals in all agencies, and
individuals and groups in relevant communities, need to be alert to the possibility of a
child being at risk of HBA, or already having suffered HBA.

title: Actions

paragraphs.text:
If staff have a concern regarding a child who might be at risk of HBA or who has suffered
from HBA, they should speak to the designated safeguarding lead (or a deputy). As

appropriate, the designated safeguarding lead (or a deputy) will activate local
safeguarding procedures, using existing national and local protocols for multi-agency
liaison with the police and local authority children’s social care. Where FGM has taken
place, since 31 October 2015 there has been a mandatory reporting duty placed on
teachers 157 that requires a different approach (see below).

FGM comprises all procedures involving partial or total removal of the external female
genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs. It is illegal in the UK and a form of
child abuse with long-lasting harmful consequences.
FGM mandatory reporting duty for teachers

Section 5B of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 (as inserted by section 74 of the
Serious Crime Act 2015) places a statutory duty upon teachers , along with regulated
health and social care professionals in England and Wales, to report to the police where
they discover (either through disclosure by the victim or visual evidence) that FGM
appears to have been carried out on a girl under 18. Those failing to report such cases
may face disciplinary sanctions. It will be rare for teachers to see visual evidence, and
they should not be examining pupils or students, but the same definition of what is meant
by “to discover that an act of FGM appears to have been carried out” is used for all
professionals to whom this mandatory reporting duty applies. Information on when and
how to make a report can be found at: Mandatory reporting of female genital mutilation
procedural information.

Teachers must personally report to the police cases where they discover that an act of
FGM appears to have been carried out. 158 Unless the teacher has good reason not to,
they should still consider and discuss any such case with the school or college’s
designated safeguarding lead (or a deputy) and involve local authority children’s social
care as appropriate. The duty does not apply in relation to at risk or suspected cases (i.e.
where the teacher does not discover that an act of FGM appears to have been carried
out, either through disclosure by the victim or visual evidence) or in cases where the
woman is 18 or over. In these cases, teachers should follow local safeguarding
procedures. The following is a useful summary of the FGM mandatory reporting duty:
FGM Fact Sheet.

Further information can be found in the Multi-agency statutory guidance on female genital
mutilation and the FGM resource pack particularly section 13.

title: Forced marriage

paragraphs.text:
157 Under Section 5B(11)(a) of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003, “teacher” means, in relation to England, a
person within section 141A(1) of the Education Act 2002 (persons employed or engaged to carry out teaching work at
schools and other institutions in England).
158 Section 5B(6) of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 states teachers need not report a case to the police if they
have reason to believe that another teacher has already reported the case.

Forcing a person into a marriage is a crime in England and Wales. A forced marriage is
one entered into without the full and free consent of one or both parties and where
violence, threats or any other form of coercion is used to cause a person to enter into a
marriage. Threats can be physical or emotional and psychological. A lack of full and free
consent can be where a person does not consent or where they cannot consent (if they
have learning disabilities, for example). Nevertheless, some perpetrators use perceived
cultural practices to coerce a person into marriage. Schools and colleges can play an
important role in safeguarding children from forced marriage.

The Forced Marriage Unit (FMU) has created: Multi-agency practice guidelines: handling
cases of forced marriage (chapter 8 provides guidance on the role of schools and
colleges) and, Multi-agency statutory guidance for dealing with forced marriage, which
can both be found at The right to choose: government guidance on forced marriage -
GOV.UK (www.gov.uk) School and college staff can contact the Forced Marriage Unit if
they need advice or information: Contact: 020 7008 0151 or email fmu@fcdo.gov.uk .

In addition, since February 2023 it has also been a crime to carry out any conduct whose
purpose is to cause a child to marry before their eighteenth birthday, even if violence,
threats or another form of coercion are not used. As with the existing forced marriage
law, this applies to non-binding, unofficial ‘marriages’ as well as legal marriages.

title: Annex B: Role of the designated safeguarding lead

paragraphs.text:
Governing bodies and proprietors should ensure an appropriate senior member of staff,
from the school or college leadership team , is appointed to the role of designated
safeguarding lead. The designated safeguarding lead should take lead responsibility for
safeguarding and child protection (including online safety and understanding the filtering
and monitoring systems and processes in place). This should be explicit in the role
holder’s job description.

The designated safeguarding lead should have the appropriate status and authority
within the school or college to carry out the duties of the post. The role of the designated
safeguarding lead carries a significant level of responsibility, and they should be given
the additional time, funding, training, resources and support they need to carry out the
role effectively. Their additional responsibilities include providing advice and support to
other staff on child welfare, safeguarding and child protection matters, taking part in
strategy discussions and inter-agency meetings, and/or supporting other staff to do so,
and contributing to the assessment of children.

strategy discussions and inter-agency meetings, and/or supporting other staff to do so,
and contributing to the assessment of children.

title: Deputy designated safeguarding leads

paragraphs.text:
It is a matter for individual schools and colleges as to whether they choose to have one
or more deputy designated safeguarding leads. Any deputies should be trained to the
same standard as the designated safeguarding lead and the role should be explicit in
their job description. Whilst the activities of the designated safeguarding lead can be
delegated to appropriately trained deputies, the ultimate lead responsibility for child
protection, as set out above, remains with the designated safeguarding lead, this lead
responsibility should not be delegated.

title: Availability

paragraphs.text:
During term time the designated safeguarding lead (or a deputy) should always be
available (during school or college hours) for staff in the school or college to discuss any
safeguarding concerns. Whilst generally speaking the designated safeguarding lead (or a
deputy) would be expected to be available in person, it is a matter for individual schools
and colleges, working with the designated safeguarding lead, to define what “available”
means and whether in exceptional circumstances availability via phone and or Microsoft
Teams or other such media is acceptable. It is a matter for individual schools and
colleges and the designated safeguarding lead to arrange adequate and appropriate
cover arrangements for any out-of-hour/out of term activities.

To ensure continuity of safeguarding responsibilities, schools should implement robust
cover arrangements for periods when the DSL is unavailable due to illness, leave, or

other circumstances. Schools and colleges have the flexibility and discretion in how
these
arrangements
operate,
provided
safeguarding
responsibilities
remain
appropriately covered. It would be good practice that, whenever the DSL is unavailable,
there is a clear, reliable, and known arrangement in place so that concerns can be raised.
This could, for example, include a confidential shared mailbox or equivalent system to
ensure that safeguarding concerns are received, monitored, and acted upon without
delay.

title: Manage referrals

paragraphs.text: The designated safeguarding lead is expected to refer cases:

• of suspected abuse and neglect to the local authority children’s social care as
required and support staff who make referrals to local authority children’s social
care,

• to the Channel programme where there is a radicalisation concern as required and
support staff who make referrals to the Channel programme,

• where a person is dismissed or left due to risk/harm to a child to the Disclosure
and Barring Service as required, and

• where a crime may have been committed to the Police as required. NPCC - When
to call the police should help understand when to consider calling the police and
what to expect when working with the police.

title: Working with others

paragraphs.text: The designated safeguarding lead is expected to:
• act as a source of support, advice and expertise for all staff,
• act as a point of contact with the safeguarding partners,

• liaise with the headteacher or principal to inform him or her of issues- especially
ongoing enquiries under section 47 of the Children Act 1989 and police
investigations. This should include being aware of the requirement for children to
have an Appropriate Adult. Further information can be found in the Statutory
guidance - PACE Code C 2019 ,

• as required, liaise with the “case manager” (as per Part four) and the local
authority designated officer(s) (LADO) for child protection concerns in cases which
concern a staff member,

• liaise with staff (especially teachers, pastoral support staff, school nurses, IT
technicians, senior mental health leads and special educational needs co-

ordinators (SENCOs), or the named person with oversight for SEND in a college
and senior mental health leads) on matters of safety and safeguarding and welfare
(including online and digital safety) and when deciding whether to make a referral
by liaising with relevant agencies so that children’s needs are considered
holistically,

• liaise with the senior mental health lead and, where available, the mental health
support team, where safeguarding concerns are linked to mental health,

• promote supportive engagement with parents and/or carers in safeguarding and
promoting the welfare of children, including where families may be facing
challenging circumstances, and

• work with the headteacher and relevant strategic leads, taking lead responsibility
for promoting educational outcomes by knowing the welfare, safeguarding and
child protection issues that children in need are experiencing, or have
experienced, and identifying the impact that these issues might be having on
children’s attendance, engagement and achievement at school or college. 159 This
includes:
o ensuring that the school or college knows who its cohort of children who

have or have had a social worker are, understanding their academic
progress and attainment, and maintaining a culture of high aspirations for
this cohort, and
o supporting teaching staff to provide additional academic support or

reasonable adjustments to help children who have or have had a social
worker reach their potential, recognising that even when statutory social
care intervention has ended, there is still a lasting impact on children’s
educational outcomes.

title: Information sharing and managing the child protection file

paragraphs.text:
The designated safeguarding lead is responsible for ensuring that child protection files
are kept up to date.

Information should be kept confidential and stored securely. It is good practice to keep
concerns and referrals in a separate child protection file for each child. Safeguarding
records should be clear, factual, and distinguish between observed concerns,
professional opinion, and historic information.
Records should include:

159 We recognise that in some settings there may be a different strategic lead for promoting the educational outcomes
of children who have or have had a social worker, particularly in larger schools or colleges.
Where this is the case, it is important that the DSL works closely with the lead to provide strategic oversight for the
outcomes of these children and young people.
• a clear and comprehensive summary of the concern,

•
details of how the concern was followed up and resolved, and
• a note of any action taken, decisions reached and the outcome.

They should ensure the file is only accessed by those who need to see it and where the
file or content within is shared, this happens in line with information sharing advice set
out in Parts one and two of this guidance.

Appropriate arrangements should be in place to ensure that safeguarding information is
transferred, reviewed and actioned promptly at all transition points, including in-year
moves.

Where children leave the school or college (including in year transfers) the designated
safeguarding lead should ensure their child protection file is transferred to the new school
or college as soon as possible, and within 5 days for an in-year transfer or within the first
5 days of the start of a new term.

This should be transferred separately from the main pupil file, ensuring secure transit,
and confirmation of receipt should be obtained. Where child protection files are
transferred, the exporting school or college should include a clear, structured summary
identifying current safeguarding concerns, relevant context, and any ongoing support
needs.

Particular care should be taken to distinguish between current safeguarding concerns
and historic information, ensuring that past issues are presented with appropriate
context. For example, where a file contains extensive historical information, a concise
summary of current risk and relevant context is likely to support more effective
safeguarding than the transfer of unstructured records alone.

Receiving schools and colleges should ensure that safeguarding information is reviewed
by an appropriately trained member of staff so that key risks and needs are clearly
understood. Safeguarding information should be used to support, not disadvantage, the
child.

Where the receiving school or college considers that safeguarding information is unclear
or incomplete, it should seek clarification where necessary to support effective
safeguarding.

They should also ensure key staff such as designated safeguarding leads and special
educational needs co-ordinators (SENCOs) or the named person with oversight for
SEND in colleges, are aware as required. It will then be for the DSL to consider what
other information should be shared with other relevant staff and when this should be
shared.

Lack of information about their circumstances can impact on the child’s safety, welfare
and educational outcomes. In addition to the child protection file, the designated
safeguarding lead should also consider if it would be appropriate to share any additional
information with the new school or college in advance of a child leaving particularly where
the information would support an assessment of risk to others in the school as well as the
individual pupil to help them put in place the right support to safeguard this child and to
help the child thrive in the school or college. For example, information that would allow
the new school or college to continue supporting children who have had a social worker
and been victims of abuse, incidents that may indicate concerns about serious violence
or harmful behaviours and/or details of those who are currently receiving support through
the ‘Channel’ programme and have that support in place for when the child arrives. It
would be good practice for a conversation to take place at the appropriate and relevant
points between the designated safeguarding leads at both settings, where there are
issues or concerns to ensure information is being actively considered and acted upon.

Where the receiving school or college considers that safeguarding information is unclear
or incomplete, it should seek clarification where necessary to support effective
safeguarding.
They should also ensure key staff such as designated safeguarding leads and special
educational needs co-ordinators (SENCOs) or the named person with oversight for
SEND in colleges, are aware as required. It will then be for the DSL to consider what
other information should be shared with other relevant staff and when this should be
shared.
184
Lack of information about their circumstances can impact on the child’s safety, welfare
and educational outcomes. In addition to the child protection file, the designated
safeguarding lead should also consider if it would be appropriate to share any additional
information with the new school or college in advance of a child leaving particularly where
the information would support an assessment of risk to others in the school as well as the
individual pupil to help them put in place the right support to safeguard this child and to
help the child thrive in the school or college. For example, information that would allow
the new school or college to continue supporting children who have had a social worker
and been victims of abuse, incidents that may indicate concerns about serious violence
or harmful behaviours and/or details of those who are currently receiving support through
the ‘Channel’ programme and have that support in place for when the child arrives. It
would be good practice for a conversation to take place at the appropriate and relevant
points between the designated safeguarding leads at both settings, where there are
issues or concerns to ensure information is being actively considered and acted upon.

title: Raising awareness

paragraphs.text: The designated safeguarding lead should:

• ensure each member of staff has access to, and understands, the school or college’s
child protection policy and procedures, especially new and part-time staff,

• ensure the school or college’s child protection policy is reviewed annually (as a
minimum) and the procedures and implementation are updated and reviewed
regularly, and work with governing bodies or proprietors regarding this,

• ensure the child protection policy is available publicly and parents know that referrals
about suspected abuse or neglect may be made and the role of the school or college
in this,

• link with the safeguarding partner arrangements to make sure staff are aware of any
training opportunities and the latest local policies on local safeguarding
arrangements, and

• help promote educational outcomes by sharing information about welfare,
safeguarding and child protection issues that children who have or have had a social
worker are experiencing with teachers and school and college leadership staff.

title: Training, knowledge and skills

paragraphs.text:
The designated safeguarding lead (and any deputies) should undergo training to provide
them with the knowledge and skills required to carry out the role. This training should be
updated at least every two years. The designated safeguarding lead (and any deputies)
should also undertake Prevent awareness training. Training should provide designated

safeguarding leads (and any deputies) with a good understanding of their own role, how
to identify, understand and respond to specific needs that can increase the vulnerability
of children, as well as specific harms that can put children at risk, and the processes,
procedures and responsibilities of other agencies, particularly local authority children’s
social care, so they:

• understand the assessment process for providing family help and statutory
intervention, including local criteria for action and local authority children’s social
care referral arrangements 160 ,

• have a working knowledge of how local authorities conduct a child protection case
conference and a child protection review conference and be able to attend and
contribute to these effectively when required to do so,

• understand the importance of the role the designated safeguarding lead has in
providing information and support to local authority children social care in order to
safeguard and promote the welfare of children,

• understand the lasting impact that adversity and trauma can have, including on
children’s behaviour, mental health and wellbeing, and what is needed in
responding to this in promoting educational outcomes,

•
are alert to the specific needs of children in need, those with special educational
needs and disabilities (SEND), those with relevant health conditions and young
carers 161 ,

• understand the importance of information sharing, both within the school and
college, and with the safeguarding partners, other agencies, organisations and
practitioners,

• understand and support the school or college with regards to the requirements of
the Prevent duty and are able to provide advice and support to staff on protecting
children from the risk of radicalisation,

• are able to understand the unique risks associated with online safety and be
confident that they have the relevant knowledge and up to date capability required
to keep children safe whilst they are online at school or college,

• can recognise the additional risks that children with special educational needs and
disabilities (SEND) face online, for example, from bullying, grooming and
radicalisation and are confident they have the capability to support children with
SEND to stay safe online,

• obtain access to resources and attend any relevant or refresher training courses,
160 Full details in Chapter one of Working Together to Safeguard Children.
161 Section 17(10) Children Act 1989: those unlikely to achieve a reasonable standard of health and development
without local authority services, those whose health and development is likely to be significantly impaired without the
provision of such services, or disabled children.
and

• encourage a culture of listening to children and taking account of their wishes and
feelings, among all staff, and in any measures the school or college may put in
place to protect them.

In addition to the formal training set out above, their knowledge and skills should be
refreshed (this might be via e-bulletins, meeting other designated safeguarding leads, or
simply taking time to read and digest safeguarding developments) at regular intervals, as
required, and at least annually, to allow them to understand and keep up with any
developments relevant to their role.

title: Providing support to staff

paragraphs.text:
Training should support the designated safeguarding lead (and deputies) in developing
expertise, so they can support and advise staff and help them feel confident on welfare,
safeguarding and child protection matters. This includes specifically to:
• ensure that staff are supported during the referrals processes, and

• support staff to consider how safeguarding, welfare and educational outcomes
are linked, including to inform the provision of academic and pastoral support.

title: Understanding the views of children

paragraphs.text:
It is important that all children feel heard and understood. Therefore, designated
safeguarding leads (and deputies) should be supported in developing knowledge and
skills to:

• encourage a culture of listening to children and taking account of their wishes and
feelings, among all staff, and in any measures the school or college may put in
place to protect them, and

• understand the difficulties that children may have in approaching staff about their
circumstances and consider how to build trusted relationships which facilitate
communication.

title: Holding and sharing information

paragraphs.text:
The critical importance of recording, holding, using and sharing information effectively is
set out in Parts one, two and five of this document, and therefore the designated
safeguarding lead (and deputies) should be equipped to:
• understand the importance of information sharing, both within the school and

college, and with other schools and colleges on transfer including in-year and
between primary and secondary education, and with the safeguarding partners,
other agencies, organisations and practitioners,
• understand relevant data protection laws, and

• be able to keep detailed, accurate, secure written records of all concerns,
discussions and decisions made including the rationale for those decisions.
This should include instances where referrals were or were not made to another
agency such as LA children’s social care or the Prevent program etc.

title: Annex C: KCSIE 2026: Summary of changes

paragraphs.text:
This summary explains where we have made changes to KCSIE 2025 and our rationale
for doing so. We will publish KCSIE (final version) 2026 on 1 September 2026.

KCSIE has been revised regularly for many years, and we intend that it will continue to
be revised and improved on a regular basis. This update reflects substantive changes
that strengthen or clarify existing content, changes to multi agency working ahead of any
legislation changes in the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Bill, where appropriate the
recent Casey Audit, and adds content in relation to Violence Against Women and Girls.

This Government is clear that there are and will continue to be further learnings about
how we can better protect children in the future as we come to understand more clearly
what has gone wrong in the past and schools and colleges will continue to need to play
an incredibly important role in this.

title: 3.1. Productive engagement: when high engagement translates to learning 20
Executive summary

paragraphs.text:
Large language models (LLMs) 1 have entered European classrooms more
quickly than any educational technology before them,and outpacing the capacity
of schools to guide their use. In 2025, 63.8 % of 16–24-year-olds in the EU
reported using generative AI (GenAI), with 41 % of this age group using GenAI
for formal education (Eurostat, 2026). A survey of 12–17-year-olds across seven
European countries found that nearly half of them had used ChatGPT, half of
them at their teacher’s instruction (Vodafone Foundation, 2025). The policy
question is therefore not if LLMs should enter secondary education; they already
have. The question this report addresses is under what conditions LLMs support
learning, and under what conditions their use undermines it.

The central message of this report is that the effects LLMs have on learning
depend on their implementation, not on the technology itself. The idea that
context matters is a familiar lesson from earlier educational technologies; what is
new here is that the evidence with regard to LLMs now demonstrates this causally
– within individual studies – and shows that the downside is not merely the
absence of benefit but measurable, hidden harm. The published evidence looks
encouraging: meta-analyses report moderate-to-large positive effects on
engagement and performance. But part of this optimism is a reporting artefact,
as studies that yield positive results are more likely to be published. Once this
bias is corrected, the average effect falls to roughly one-third of its published size.
For the latest generation of tools, the effect size may be close to zero (Bartoš et
al., 2026, preprint). More importantly, this average conceals extreme
heterogeneity, conflating carefully designed pedagogical systems with unguided
chatbot access. The strongest evidence for conditionality comes from within
individual studies, where the same technology produces opposite outcomes
depending on how it is deployed. In a large randomised trial in Turkish secondary
schools, the same GPT-4 model harmed learning when it was offered as an open
chat interface, but caused no harm when deployed with pedagogical guardrails
(Bastani et al., 2025). In a Flemish trial involving 2,440 secondary school
students, a chatbot tailored to the curriculum increased module completion by
13.2 percentage points, and produced retention gains still visible two months later
(0.309 SD). Meanwhile, a generic chatbot built on the same underlying model
produced no effect at all (Polanco-Jiménez & De Witte, 2026, preprint). In a third
set of trials, which involved Chinese secondary physics students, an AI feedback
system generated the largest achievement gains in this evidence base for low-
achieving students when access was structured and compulsory, but eroded

1 Large language models (LLMs) are a subset of generative AI. They are systems trained on
very large text corpora to generate language in response to a prompt. Generative AI is the
broader category, which also includes tools that generate images, audio, or video. This
report focuses on LLMs and LLM-based applications (such as chatbots, tutoring systems,
and feedback tools). Where survey data cover generative AI as a whole, this is explicitly
indicated, as that data cannot be disaggregated by specific model types.

those same students' autonomy when access was voluntary (Dai et al., 2025).
The lesson for policymakers is direct: whether LLMs help or harm is determined
by choices about design, integration and access. These choices are made at
levels that can be reached by European policy: procurement criteria,
implementation guidance, teacher preparation and assessment rules.

This mechanism behind this sensitivity to implementation is identifiable. This
report's analytical framework, the engagement-learning nexus, locates the
answer in the gap between the engagement that LLMs produce by default, and
engagement that produces learning. Conversational fluency makes students
behaviourally active and emotionally satisfied almost automatically. But cognitive
engagement (effortful reasoning, self-explanation, monitoring one's own
understanding) is the only dimension that reliably predicts durable learning, and
it is rare. In an analysis of 34,000 real tutoring conversations between secondary
students and an AI tutor, only 1 % achieved constructive cognitive engagement,
while 68 % were passive. When conditions do not demand cognitive
engagement, an engagement paradox emerges: students in the Turkish trial who
used un-guardrailed GPT-4 outperformed controls by 48 % while the tool
remained available, but once it was removed, went on to score 17 % worse than
students who had never used AI. Moreover, students in the treatment group did
not perceive that they had learned less. Usage, satisfaction and task performance
were all high precisely where learning was weakest . This is the mode of failure
one can expect wherever LLM access is provided without pedagogical structure.

The conditions that separate productive from counterproductive use of LLMs are
identifiable and actionable. Five design principles emerge consistently from the
evidence:

● Preserve cognitive demand (hints and Socratic questioning rather than
direct answers);
● Align tools with the curriculum rather than deploying generic interfaces;

● Match the structure of access to the learner’s profile, since struggling
students require scaffolding that capable students find constraining;

● Integrate teacher mediation by design rather than as an afterthought
(qualitative evidence across five EU Member States identifies teacher
mediation as the factor that distinguishes effective implementations from
ineffective ones, and the strongest transfer result in this evidence base
came from a tool deployed under direct human supervision); and

● Assess learning without AI, since only AI-free assessment makes the
gap between assisted performance and independent capability visible.

The above principles are complementary, and imply a division of labour: content
personalisation is performed by the tool; pedagogical differentiation by the
teacher. Decisions about access, procurement and assessment are the
responsibility of schools and systems. The principle of scaffolding also carries

implications for equity: voluntary, unstructured access disproportionately harms
precisely those students it is meant to help, while the largest gains made by
structured support produces are among low achievers. Simply making tools
available is not equitable provision, and uniform access models risk widening
achievement gaps rather than narrowing them.
Six actions follow for policymakers:

1. Monitor learning, not usage. Evaluation frameworks should require
evidence of the quality of cognitive engagement and learning outcomes
assessed without AI support; usage rates and satisfaction surveys can be
high precisely when learning is weakest.

2. Procure on the basis of pedagogical design, and require evidence.
Procurement should evaluate guardrails, curriculum integration and
structured interaction modes, and educational AI tools should be required
to demonstrate positive learning outcomes, as distinct from task
performance, before they are deployed in compulsory education. No such
requirement currently exists.

3. Invest in teacher preparation at system level. Teacher mediation
distinguishes effective implementations from ineffective ones, yet three out
of four lower-secondary teachers across OECD education systems report
that they lack the knowledge or skills needed to teach using AI. This is a
matter for initial teacher education and professional development, not
individual effort.

4. Reform the methods used for assessment. AI-free transfer assessments
should function as routine, low-stakes diagnostics that make the gap
between assisted and independent performance visible to students and
teachers alike, not as punitive policing.

5. Implement with equity by design. Calibrate scaffolding to learner profiles,
and treat learner AI literacy as a precondition for autonomous-access
models rather than an optional supplement.

6. Fund the research upon which these decisions depend. Priorities include
longer-duration studies that track engagement and learning over a school
year; experimental designs that include the teacher rather than isolating
the AI-student interaction; studies in European secondary contexts, which
remain underrepresented; and the adoption of AI-free transfer and
retention as standard outcome measures, with gender-disaggregated
reporting.

LLMs are not neutral tools. Students are already using them at rates that outpace
the capacity of schools to guide their use as well as the preparedness of teachers.
The task for policymakers is to create the conditions (in terms of procurement,

teacher preparation, assessment and monitoring) under which their adoption
produces learning.

title: 1.1. Background

paragraphs.text:
The release of ChatGPT in November 2022 marked a turning point in the use of
artificial intelligence (AI) across society. Within months of its launch, ChatGPT
became the fastest-adopted technology in history, reaching 100 million users
within two months (Pazzanese, 2024). The education sector has not escaped this
phenomenon. Across the EU, 63.8 % of 16–24-year-olds reported using
generative AI (GenAI) in 2025, with 41 % of this age group using it for formal
education (Eurostat, 2025; Eurostat, 2026), a cross-country survey of 12–17-
year-olds covering seven countries 2 showed high use of GenAI among students,
with 48 % having reported using ChatGPT in 2024 (half of them having been
instructed to do so by their teachers) (Vodafone Foundation, 2025). In Estonia,
74 % of lower-secondary students and 90 % of upper-secondary students
reported using AI tools in 2024 (OECD, 2026). This rate of adoption is
unprecedented for a technology used in education, and has led to large language
models (LLMs) 3 becoming ubiquitous in under three years.

The emerging evidence on the effects that LLM has use on students is cautiously
positive, but the size of the benefit depends heavily on how these tools are
deployed. Meta-analyses of (largely short-term) experimental studies report
moderate-to-large effects on learner engagement, motivation and academic
performance (Deng et al. [2025] find a large pooled effect of Hedges’ g = 0.712 4
for academic performance). However, this early research also reveals a troubling
pattern. While LLM-based interventions generally produce positive effects on
learner engagement, the use of these tools often shifts from their intended role
as “cognitive support” to being used as shortcuts. Students may rely on GenAI to
work more efficiently or to lessen mental effort, and some use it to complete whole
assignments. Research indicates that nearly one-third (31 %) of students report
using AI to provide complete solutions to tasks rather than to support their own
reasoning, which can lead to “metacognitive laziness”, whereby students bypass
essential learning processes (OECD, 2026). However, these aggregate findings

actually being undermined). It seeks to uncover those conditions under which
high engagement with LLMs translates into genuine learning, versus those in
which it actually hinders and discourages learning.

also mask significant heterogeneity. As this report demonstrates, the effects of
LLM-based interventions critically depend on the specific tool used and its design
features. A further factor – namely, how teachers integrate these tools into their
teaching – is widely regarded as decisive. This is supported by qualitative
evidence (e.g. European Commission, Joint Research Centre et al., 2025) – even
though it is rarely captured by experimental studies, which typically isolate the AI
from the teacher. This is precisely this kind of variation (across tools, designs and
classroom use) that is concealed by headline effect sizes.
The present report therefore aims to examine this paradox (i.e. the situation in
which students appear highly engaged with LLM tools, while their learning is
actually being undermined). It seeks to uncover those conditions under which
high engagement with LLMs translates into genuine learning, versus those in
which it actually hinders and discourages learning.

title: 1.2. Objectives of the report

paragraphs.text:
This report employs an engagement-centred analytical framework, the
Engagement–Learning Nexus, as its central organising principle (see Chapter 2).
This framework examines the relationship between LLM-mediated engagement
(across three dimensions – behavioural, cognitive, and emotional), and learning
outcomes. This choice of engagement as the primary analytical lens, rather than
learning outcomes directly, reflects a need for deliberate differentiation. Where
other recent syntheses (notably the OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026)
examine what LLMs do for learning, this report asks a prior question: when does
the engagement generated by LLMs actually translate into learning, and
when does it mask the absence of genuine learning 5 ?

This distinction matters because LLM tools, through their conversational
accessibility and fluent responses, generate high levels of behavioural and
emotional engagement almost by default. The critical question is whether or not
these surface indicators are accompanied by cognitive engagement, the
dimension that predicts durable learning. This structure enables the identification
of the engagement paradox: a pattern in which students show high behavioural
and emotional engagement with LLM tools while experiencing only surface-level
cognitive engagement, ultimately impairing durable learning. Moving beyond
the simple question of “does AI help learning?” towards understanding
when, how, and for whom LLM-mediated engagement becomes productive
is the central analytical contribution of this report.

5 This question is particularly important for LLMs as, unlike earlier educational technologies, their
conversational fluency and generative capacity allow them to perform core cognitive tasks on
behalf of students. They do not limit themselves to presenting information or delivering drill-and-
practice exercises, but produce complete written arguments, solve problems, and generate
plausible explanations.
In this context, the report aims to address the following research questions:

1. How do LLM-based interventions affect the three dimensions of learner
engagement (behavioural, cognitive, emotional) in secondary education?
2. Under what conditions does LLM-mediated engagement translate into
improved learning outcomes, and when does it mask the absence of
genuine learning through cognitive offloading?
3. Through which mechanisms (such as feedback, scaffolding, content
generation and personalisation) do LLMs affect engagement and learning,
and how do these mechanisms interact?
4. What pedagogical design features (including guardrails, scaffolded
support vs. direct answers, teacher oversight) distinguish productive from
counterproductive use of LLMs?

Questions 1 and 2 are addressed primarily in Chapter 3, in which the evidence is
organised around four engagement–learning patterns (productive engagement,
the engagement paradox, disengagement, and mixed patterns). Questions 3 and
4 are addressed in Chapter 4, which synthesises the evidence into cross-cutting
design principles. Chapter 5 draws on the full evidence base to formulate
implications and policy recommendations.

title: 1.3. Scope and focus

paragraphs.text:
The report’s analysis focuses on experimental and quasi-experimental studies
that investigate LLM-based educational interventions, whether these involve
general-purpose tools such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini, or purpose-built
educational applications 6 . Experimental and quasi-experimental designs provide
the evidence for research questions 1 and 2, which explore the impact of LLM-
based interventions on engagement and their relationship to learning outcomes.
For research questions 3 and 4, which focus on mechanisms and design features,
the evidence base is expanded to include observational studies, qualitative
research and large-scale survey data, as these questions require an examination
of implementation processes that controlled experiments alone cannot capture.

The report’s primary focus is on secondary education. However, since most
experimental research on LLM-based educational interventions has been
conducted in higher education, evidence specific to secondary schools, while

6 The latter group of tools range from pedagogical models developed at scale, such as LearnLM
(Google DeepMind, 2025), to bespoke systems configured by researchers for a specific study –
e.g. chatbots tailored to the curriculum that incorporate guardrails vs. direct-answer provision
(Bastani et al., 2025; Polanco-Jimenez & De Witte, 2026). Many of the most effective purpose-
built tools in the literature are research prototypes rather than products that schools can readily
procure. The European EdTech market also remains fragmented and largely made up of micro-
enterprises (Havinga & Clary, 2024). The evidence behind individual products is also uneven –
some offer little more than a thin layer over a general-purpose model rather than pedagogically
distinctive functionality (Lindroos Cermakova et al., 2026).

growing, remains limited. Where secondary-level evidence is lacking, this report
relies on evidence from higher education. Throughout the report, where evidence
from higher education is used, this is consistently highlighted. This matters
analytically, as students in secondary education often have less advanced
metacognitive skills and self-regulation than university students (Granström &
Oppi, 2025; Singh et al., 2025). The developmental stakes are higher still:
capacities such as working memory, executive function and critical reasoning are
still maturing through adolescence, and a student who habitually delegates
cognitive work during these years risks not acquiring the cognitive architecture
on which subsequent learning depends (European Parliament & Chounta, 2026).
This suggests that higher education findings on productive engagement might be
an upper estimate of what secondary students can achieve. Conversely, findings
related to cognitive offloading and metacognitive miscalibration could
underestimate the risks for younger learners.

Outcome measures span both engagement (behavioural, cognitive and
emotional indicators) and learning outcomes (performance, retention, transfer
and higher-order thinking). This report treats as analytically central the distinction
between performance during AI use, and retention or transfer without AI – a
measurement issue that proves essential in interpretating the evidence reviewed
in Chapter 3. The report covers research published between November 2022 (the
release of ChatGPT) and early 2026, including both peer-reviewed articles and
preprints, with quality explicitly flagged.

Importantly, two framing distinctions shape the way in which the evidence in this
report should be read. Both are maintained throughout the analysis:

• Temporal. Despite the short time frame, the landscape of tools used has
changed rapidly. The general-purpose models available at the start of this
period (GPT-3.5, late 2022 to 2023) differ in capability from those available
by 2025, which include GPT-4-class models and purpose-built
pedagogical systems such as LearnLM (Google DeepMind, 2025) as well
as curriculum-tailored chatbots developed for specific educational
contexts. Treating all LLM-based interventions as equivalent would
obscure critical differences in what productive engagement can
realistically look like at each point in this trajectory.
• Types of tools. A second distinction cuts across the entire evidence base
and is maintained throughout this report: free, general-purpose access
versus purpose-built or institutionally integrated tools. General-purpose
tools (such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini) are designed for broad use
and lack an inherent pedagogical structure: any educational scaffolding
must be provided by the teacher or the student. Purpose-built tools (e.g.
LLM-based tutoring chatbots, conversational learning agents and
curriculum-aligned content generators) are designed or fine-tuned for
specific educational functions. This typically alignment with the curriculum

alignment, and incorporating guardrails against direct answer provision, as
well as structured interaction patterns. As the evidence synthesis in
chapters 3 and 4 demonstrates, this distinction is among the most
consequential moderators of engagement and learning outcomes. Where
studies involve purpose-built tools, their specific design features and the
underlying LLM model are reported. Where studies use general-purpose
tools, the version and access conditions are noted. In both cases, this
report concerns only the use of generative, LLM-based systems. It does
not cover non-generative or pre-LLM forms of educational AI (such as rule-
based intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) or adaptive learning platforms that
do not rely on LLMs), even where these are marketed as “AI tutors”.

title: 1.4. Methodology

paragraphs.text:
This report employs a targeted evidence synthesis, combining systematic search
methods with pragmatic constraints appropriate to an emerging, rapidly evolving
evidence base. This approach builds on existing meta-analyses (notably Deng et
al., 2025; Heung & Chiu, 2025; Bartoš et al., 2026) while conducting focused
primary searches for secondary education-specific experimental evidence.

The search proceeded in three stages. First, a broad systematic search was
conducted using the Elicit research platform, which identified approximately 500
sources across academic databases and preprint servers. These sources were
screened for their relevance to the report’s research questions – a step that
yielded 173 potentially relevant studies. Second, a focused review of the most
relevant sources was conducted: 69 studies were subjected to detailed screening
against the report’s inclusion criteria (target population, LLM intervention,
engagement or learning outcomes measured, student interaction with LLMs,
formal educational setting, and methodological rigour), leading to 57 being
retained for extraction. Third, this database was supplemented through snowball
sampling from the reference lists of key meta-analyses and systematic reviews,
which captured recent studies not yet indexed in standard databases, in particular
preprints and working papers.

From this combined pool, each study was analysed in depth and coded for tool
type, population, study design, engagement dimensions measured, learning
outcomes and engagement-learning pattern classification. The final analytical
corpus comprised approximately 29 primary empirical studies and six meta-
analyses or systematic reviews that directly inform the evidence synthesis in
Chapters 3 and 4. Several additional sources (systematic reviews, qualitative
studies and large-scale surveys) provide contextual framing, but are not treated
as primary evidence for causal claims. The most relevant studies are documented
in the Annex Table, which reports the tool, population, design, engagement
dimensions, learning outcomes and pattern classification for each study.

title: Limitations

paragraphs.text:
The current evidence base is subject to a number of important limitations that
shape the scope of and confidence in this report’s conclusions:

• Population coverage. As mentioned, most experimental research on
LLM-based educational interventions comes from higher education;
secondary school-specific evidence is growing, but remains limited.
European contexts 7 are underrepresented, with most randomised
controlled trials (RCTs) having been conducted in the United States,
Türkiye and Asian countries.
• Intervention duration. Studies typically employ short intervention
periods, often consisting of a single session. The meta-analytic evidence
suggests that these are the least informative: interventions lasting under
one week showed no significant effect on academic performance, whereas
all longer durations did (Deng et al., 2025). It is notable that the strongest
findings of productive engagement in this report come from longer
implementations (Polanco-Jiménez & De Witte [2026], 4 months; Zhang &
Huang [2024], 8 weeks). Whether the design principles identified in
Chapter 4 are sufficient to sustain productive engagement over extended
periods remains an open question.
• Publication bias. This factor affects the evidence base in at least two
directions. First, evidence on disengagement patterns and null findings is
likely to be underreported, as publication norms favour positive outcomes;
the fact that one of the clearest demonstrations of disengagement in this
report comes from a doctoral thesis (Kline, 2024) is illustrative. Second,
and importantly, publication bias also inflates the apparent strength of
evidence for productive engagement. Bartoš et al. (2026), in a meta-meta-
analysis of 67 meta-analyses involving 1,840 effect sizes, found that after
bias adjustment, the model-averaged effect of AI on learning was
approximately one-third of the unadjusted magnitude (SMD = 0.196, 95 %
CI: 0.000 to 0.323). This correction applies to the aggregate evidence
discussed in section 3.1.4, and should be borne in mind when interpreting
effect sizes throughout the report.
• Teacher mediation. The causal evidence presented in this report comes
almost entirely from studies whose designs isolate the AI–student
interaction: the teacher is absent from the live session, even where
teachers have shaped the intervention upstream. In Bastani et al. (2025),

7 Coverage of the European Union is thin: causal evidence comes from two Member States:
Germany (four studies) and Belgium (one). Broader EU coverage is provided by a qualitative
study of early adopters across five Member States: Finland, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg and
Spain; (European Commission, Joint Research Centre et al., 2025). Findings should therefore be
read as indicative for, rather than representative of, EU secondary education; direct causal
evidence is absent for the large majority of Member States.

for example, teachers designed the practice problems and pedagogical
guardrails but did not interact with students during use. The experimental
literature can therefore say little directly about how teachers mediate,
scaffold or constrain the use of LLMs. The evidence that does address this
is qualitative rather than experimental: a multi-country qualitative study
(European Commission, Joint Research Centre et al., 2025) identifies
teacher mediation as a key factor distinguishing effective implementations
from ineffective ones (this analysis if further developed in Chapter 4).
Thus, claims regarding the teacher’s role rest on a different, non-causal
tier of evidence than the findings on engagement and learning outcomes,
and integrating the two remains a priority for future research.

As the table above shows, the three engagement dimensions can vary
independently in LLM-mediated learning. Behavioural volume is an unreliable
indicator; emotional positivity may reflect novelty rather than learning; and
cognitive engagement is both the hardest to attain and the most impactful for
outcomes. Combining engagement level (high vs. low across dimensions) with
cognitive engagement quality (deep vs. surface-level) creates four distinct
configurations, each leading to a different learning path. This typology is designed
for specific analysis. While existing meta-analyses combine diverse interventions
into single average effect sizes, the engagement–learning relationship offers a
way to break down those averages: it allows us to explore not only whether LLM-

As the table above shows, the three engagement dimensions can vary
independently in LLM-mediated learning. Behavioural volume is an unreliable
indicator; emotional positivity may reflect novelty rather than learning; and
cognitive engagement is both the hardest to attain and the most impactful for
outcomes. Combining engagement level (high vs. low across dimensions) with
cognitive engagement quality (deep vs. surface-level) creates four distinct
configurations, each leading to a different learning path. This typology is designed
for specific analysis. While existing meta-analyses combine diverse interventions
into single average effect sizes, the engagement–learning relationship offers a
way to break down those averages: it allows us to explore not only whether LLM-
based interventions lead to engagement or learning gains on average, but also
under which engagement configurations the link between them is maintained or
fails.

title: 3.1. Productive engagement: when high engagement translates into learning

paragraphs.text:
Productive engagement, as defined in the framework that underpins this report,
requires high engagement across all three dimensions (behavioural, cognitive
and emotional) in ways that jointly support durable learning. The aggregate meta-
analytic picture appears encouraging: Heung and Chiu (2025) report medium-to-
large positive effects on all three engagement dimensions. However, this
optimism must be tempered.

First, publication bias inflates the apparent strength of these findings. Bartoš et
al. (2026, preprint) carried out a meta-meta-analysis covering the broader field of
AI in education (67 meta-analyses; 1,840 effect sizes across all outcome types).
When the authors systematically corrected for publication bias, the average effect
shrank to roughly one-third of its original size. Crucially, this overall effect was
accompanied by extreme heterogeneity between studies, meaning the true effect
for any given intervention ranges widely from large negative to large positive
outcomes. Furthermore, when isolating studies published after January 2023 (i.e.
those more likely to involve GenAI tools rather than earlier AI technologies such
as intelligent tutoring systems), the adjusted effect shrank even further
(SMD = 0.108), meaning a null aggregate effect for modern LLMs cannot be
excluded. This implies that the average across all interventions, good and bad, is
far more modest than the published literature suggests. This correction applies
throughout this section, and should be kept in mind when interpreting the results
of individual studies.

Second, as previously mentioned, these meta-analyses pool together very
different types of tools and implementations (general-purpose chatbots used
without guidance, alongside carefully designed pedagogical systems) and
present a single average effect. But this average obscures enormous variation.
When Weatherholtz et al. (2025) examined more than 34,000 real tutoring
conversations between secondary students and Khanmigo (Khan Academy’s AI
tutor), they found that only 1 % of interactions reached the level of deep cognitive
engagement that predicts learning, while 68 % were passive. The positive
average effects reported in the meta-analyses are likely to be driven by a
minority of well-designed implementations, rather than reflecting what
happens when students simply gain access to an LLM.

title: 3.1.1. Behavioural engagement

paragraphs.text:
Positive behavioural engagement, measured through participation rates,
interaction frequency and task completion, is consistently observed when LLM
tools are purposefully integrated into learning activities. Meta-analytic evidence
reports a medium positive effect (Hedges’s g = 0.454; Heung & Chiu, 2025),
though this aggregate conceals substantial variation across tool types and
implementation contexts.

The clearest causal evidence comes from Polanco-Jimenez & De Witte (2026,
preprint), whose large-scale RCT in the Flemish secondary school system
(secondary education, Belgium, N = 2,440) compared a curriculum-tailored
chatbot against a generic chatbot and a control group. The tailored tool (built on
a 2024-era LLM that integrated the Flemish economics curriculum and was
designed to redirect errors rather than simply providing solutions) increased
module completion by 13.2 percentage points relative to the control. The generic
chatbot, running on the same underlying model without curricular integration,
produced a null effect on completion rates: students who given the untailored
LLM were no more likely to finish the task than those who did not use AI at all.
This within-study comparison shows that behavioural engagement depends on
tool design and curricular fit 9 , not on LLM access alone.

In an RCT involving 52 Chinese high school students over 8 weeks, Zhang &
Huang (2024) found that students using an LLM chatbot spontaneously asked
additional vocabulary questions that went beyond the designated curriculum, with
a higher proportion targeting productive knowledge (word usage and application)
rather than surface retrieval. In addition, Ng et al. (2024) conducted a 3-week
quasi-experimental study involving 74 students in Hong Kong. The intervention
compared a generative AI chatbot (“SRLbot”, built around ChatGPT) to a
traditional rule-based chatbot (“Nemobot”). The researchers found that the
ChatGPT-enhanced bot significantly outperformed the rule-based bot in
enhancing students’ science knowledge, behavioural engagement and
motivation. The authors noted that students appreciated in particular the
“personalised recommendations and flexibility” of the generative AI, which
adapted to their specific self-regulated learning needs (Ng et al., 2024).

However, behavioural volume alone is an unreliable indicator of productive
engagement. The same metric (high interaction frequency) can equally
reflect answer-seeking and content copying. Liu et al. (2025) studied 533
middle school students in the US who interacted with AI teachable agents in
mathematics. They found that those students whose learning declined were

9 Importantly, teacher intervention remained constant in this trial: students were randomised
individually within classrooms and teachers (present throughout, as the activity was part of the
mandatory lesson plan) were instructed to act as neutral supervisors and not to answer content-
related questions. The difference in completion rates therefore reflects tool design rather than
variation in teacher intervention. Whether active teacher mediation would strengthen or weaken
these effects is the open question, discussed in Section 1.4.

among the most behaviourally active; they completed more sessions and
generated more utterances per interaction, but their task completion rates were
low and much of their interaction was off-task. The two groups differed sharply in
interaction quality. Among students whose performance improved, 62.78 % of
interactions were constructive and 12.04 % passive; among those whose
performance declined, only 23.7 % were constructive while 41.5 % were passive
or off-task chat. Improving students also completed a higher proportion of
sessions (0.58 vs 0.35), despite completing fewer and shorter sessions overall
(Liu et al., 2025). Weatherholtz et al. (2025), whose large-scale analysis of
Khanmigo tutoring conversations was introduced above, add a critical
behavioural finding: median conversation length was similar across engagement
levels (roughly five turns), meaning that behavioural measures such as session
count or time on task would not have distinguished those students who were
learning from those who were not.

title: 3.1.2. Emotional engagement

paragraphs.text:
Emotional engagement (which encompasses motivation, interest, anxiety
reduction and affective responses to learning) is the domain in which LLM
interventions show the most consistently positive results. Meta-analytic evidence
reports a medium positive effect size (Hedges’s g = 0.512; Heung & Chiu, 2025).
However, this overall positivity warrants careful interpretation. Across the studies
reviewed, emotional engagement is the dimension in which positive
indicators most frequently co-occur with absent or weak learning gains – a
pattern examined in detail in Section 3.2 of this report. This makes it an especially
unreliable standalone indicator of productive engagement, which could be linked
to a “novelty effect” (Deng et al., 2025), wherein the initial excitement of
interacting with a new, conversational technology temporarily inflates students’
positive perceptions.

The strongest experimental evidence specific to secondary education comes
from Meyer et al. (2024), whose RCT involving 459 German upper-secondary
students of English as a foreign language tested feedback on argumentative
essays generated by GPT-3.5 Turbo. The LLM feedback group reported
significantly higher task motivation (d = 0.36) and positive emotions (curiosity,
enjoyment and pride) (d = 0.34) compared with a no-feedback control. Crucially,
these affective gains co-occurred with improved revision performance (d = 0.19),
meaning that emotional and cognitive engagement moved in the same direction.
This co-occurrence categorises the finding as active engagement rather than just
satisfaction. The authors interpret the motivational effect through a verbal reward
mechanism: structured feedback provided acknowledgement of effort and
invoked feelings of competence, generating a positive affect that helped to
sustain task investment . However, these findings are subject to two important
limitations: while the study did include a transfer measure (a second, new writing
task), the intervention yielded no significant transfer effects, leading authors to

conclude that a single feedback session is insufficient to support durable learning.
In addition, the positive emotion scale was only modestly reliable.

The anxiety-reduction pathway represents a distinct emotional engagement
mechanism with particular relevance to language learning. In their RCT, Zhang
& Huang (2024) found that their LLM chatbot created conditions in which foreign
language students could practise using vocabulary more freely than in
conventional classroom settings – a pattern the authors attribute to reduced
performance anxiety when interacting with a machine rather than a teacher
or peers . This finding echoes a broader pattern in the literature on language
learning: LLM-mediated interaction appears to lower the affective threshold for
participation, particularly for students who experience speaking anxiety. Whether
this reduced anxiety translates into deeper processing or simply more
comfortable surface-level interaction is a question the current evidence cannot
fully resolve. Nevertheless, the behavioural data from the same study
(spontaneous generative questioning beyond the curriculum) suggest the former,
at least for this sample.

The difficulties involved in analysing emotional engagement become visible when
these positive findings are set against the paradoxical evidence reviewed in
Section 3.2. Aptyka et al. (2025), in an RCT involving 241 German upper-
secondary biology students, found that the use of ChatGPT produced
significantly more positive attitudes towards AI-assisted learning, both
immediately and at a 7-week follow-up, but learning gains were minimal.
Kosmyna et al. (2025), studying 54 adult participants, found higher subjective
satisfaction in the ChatGPT condition, alongside objectively lower cognitive
engagement, as measured by EEG.

These contrasting findings suggest that emotional engagement with LLMs
operates through at least two distinct pathways.

• The first is pedagogically mediated , when positive affect comes from
structured feedback, reduced anxiety or a sense of competence gain (as
in Meyer et al. and Zhang & Huang). In this context, it co-occurs with
cognitive engagement and appears to support learning.
• The second is tool-mediated : when positive affect reflects the “novelty
effect”, fluency, or convenience of the AI interaction itself (as in Aptyka et
al. and Kosmyna et al.), it can persist without corresponding to any
cognitive or learning gains.

This distinction matters for interpretation: student satisfaction surveys and
attitudinal measures cannot differentiate between these pathways without a
concurrent assessment of cognitive engagement or learning outcomes.
