title: 3.1.3. Cognitive engagement

paragraphs.text:
Cognitive engagement 10 (which involves self-regulation, deep processing and
metacognition) is the most critical dimension for learning outcomes, and the most
difficult one to measure. It is also the dimension that is most sensitive to tool
design, as traditional behavioural metrics (such as time-on-task or session
counts) fail to capture the invisible metacognitive and inferential processes that
actually drive learning. Meta-analytic evidence reports a moderate-to-large
positive effect (Hedges’ g = 0.593; Heung & Chiu, 2025), but this aggregate figure
should be interpreted with caution. As the evidence reviewed in this chapter will
show, cognitive engagement is the area
in which productive and
counterproductive patterns differ most significantly: genuine deep processing can
occur alongside surface-level interaction that is mistaken for cognitive
engagement, within the same evidence base. An average that is taken across
such diverse patterns may not accurately describe either.

The most rigorous large-scale measurement of cognitive engagement in LLM-
mediated learning comes from the previously presented Weatherholtz et al.
(2025), who analysed over 34,000 authentic tutoring conversations between
secondary school students and Khanmigo (Khan Academy’s GenAI tutor) across
six US school districts. Using a validated ICAP-adapted rubric, they classified
student interaction turns as being either passive (perfunctory responses, answer-
mining), active (mechanically following procedural guidance), or constructive
(taking ownership, explaining thinking, making inferences). Only 1 % of
conversations achieved constructive engagement; 68 % were classified as
passive. Yet the learning outcome gradient was steep: constructive engagement
was associated with approximately a 10 percentage-point higher rate of
correctness on subsequent items when compared with passive engagement.
Active engagement fell between the two. Importantly, a panel analysis examining
within-learner differences showed that the same students engaged constructively
in some sessions and passively in others, suggesting that the quality of
cognitive engagement is not a fixed trait, but responds to contextual and
design conditions.

10 Chounta (2026), in a briefing for the European Parliament, grounds this dimension in cognitive
architecture: in order for young learners to meaningfully learn, they must construct durable
knowledge, develop reasoning, consolidate information in long-term memory, and build the
metacognitive and self-regulatory skills that underpin autonomous learning. Learning, from this
perspective, is a change in long-term memory. Durable knowledge is constructed only when new
information is effortfully processed in working memory (through retrieval practice, elaboration and
problem-solving under “desirable difficulty”) and thereby encoded. Tasks that feel difficult in the
moment produce stronger retention precisely because of the effort they demand. This explains
why cognitive engagement, rather than the volume of interaction or positive affect, predicts
durable learning: it is the level at which encoding happens or fails to happen. It also identifies an
AI-specific risk: AI tools that supply finished outputs short-circuit exactly this process, consistent
with the germane cognitive load mechanism identified by Stadler et al. (2024).

Two findings from higher education (HE) illuminate what drives cognitive
engagement when it does occur, with direct implications for the design of
secondary school education. Pallant et al. (2025; HE, Australia, N = 192) found
that the differentiating variable was not tool design but student goal orientation.
Students who approached general-purpose GenAI with an orientation towards
mastery (constructing and augmenting knowledge rather than reproducing AI
outputs) were more likely to demonstrate high critical thinking (94.3 %, vs. 33.9 %
among users regurgitating outputs) and learning autonomy (96.6 % vs. 63.4 %).
The implication of this is that cognitive engagement depends partly on what
the student brings to the interaction – the goals and expectations they bring
to the tool . M. Zhang (2025) (HE, China, N = 246) tested the complementary
hypothesis that structured scaffolding can shape those goals externally 11 . In a
three-arm experiment comparing guided LLM use (with explicit prompting
frameworks and metacognitive prompts), unguided LLM use, and a no-LLM
control, the guided condition produced significantly higher-quality writing than
both alternatives, alongside significantly greater academic engagement than the
control group. These two studies, taken together, suggest that productive
cognitive engagement requires either internal goal orientation on the part
of the student, or external scaffolding (whether embedded in the tool’s
design or delivered by the teacher). For a typical secondary school
population, in which an orientation towards mastery cannot be assumed,
such external scaffolding carries the greater policy relevance .

Evidence at the level of secondary education is thinner, but directionally
consistent. Dai et al. (2025), in their two sequential RCTs involving 387 Chinese
physics students, found that adding AI-generated heuristic hints (designed to
prompt independent reasoning rather than deliver answers) to conventional
worked answers improved achievement more than the worked answers alone,
particularly for low-achieving students receiving compulsory scaffolding 12 .
Interview data point to greater cognitive engagement being the mechanism:
students in the structured condition described working through problems with
guidance from AI, while students given voluntary access to the same system
reported glancing at materials without attempting problems independently (Dai et
al., 2025). The contrast between these two conditions (same tool, same feedback
quality, different cognitive engagement) reinforces the finding from Weatherholtz
et al. that cognitive engagement is design-responsive rather than tool-
inherent .

11 The scaffolding was instructional rather than being embedded into the tool: students used a
standard GPT-4 interface, but the guided group received a structured task prompt and a brief (10-
minute) orientation delivered by their course instructor from a standardised script, covering prompt
formulation, the critical evaluation of AI outputs, and ethical use.
12 “Compulsory” is the authors’ term for the delivery mode in their first experiment: as part of a
routine requirement to log daily homework errors, the system automatically sent each student
personalised review problems accompanied by AI-generated heuristic hints; students did not
choose whether or not to receive support. In the second experiment, support was “on demand”,
meaning students had to actively request it.

Deep cognitive engagement with LLMs is achievable and, when achieved,
strongly predicts learning (see Chapter 4. Guiding principles for integrating LLM-
based learning, in which we highlight the design conditions under which cognitive
engagement can be fostered). Deep cognitive engagement does not emerge
automatically from LLM access, however; its base rate in unstructured settings is
low, and it requires either deliberate pedagogical scaffolding or an existing
orientation towards mastery that secondary students cannot be presumed to
have.

students in the structured condition described working through problems with
guidance from AI, while students given voluntary access to the same system
reported glancing at materials without attempting problems independently (Dai et
al., 2025). The contrast between these two conditions (same tool, same feedback
quality, different cognitive engagement) reinforces the finding from Weatherholtz
et al. that cognitive engagement is design-responsive rather than tool-
inherent .
11 The scaffolding was instructional rather than being embedded into the tool: students used a
standard GPT-4 interface, but the guided group received a structured task prompt and a brief (10-
minute) orientation delivered by their course instructor from a standardised script, covering prompt
formulation, the critical evaluation of AI outputs, and ethical use.
12 “Compulsory” is the authors’ term for the delivery mode in their first experiment: as part of a
routine requirement to log daily homework errors, the system automatically sent each student
personalised review problems accompanied by AI-generated heuristic hints; students did not
choose whether or not to receive support. In the second experiment, support was “on demand”,
meaning students had to actively request it.
25
Deep cognitive engagement with LLMs is achievable and, when achieved,
strongly predicts learning (see Chapter 4. Guiding principles for integrating LLM-
based learning, in which we highlight the design conditions under which cognitive
engagement can be fostered). Deep cognitive engagement does not emerge
automatically from LLM access, however; its base rate in unstructured settings is
low, and it requires either deliberate pedagogical scaffolding or an existing
orientation towards mastery that secondary students cannot be presumed to
have.

title: 3.1.4. From engagement to learning

paragraphs.text:
The evidence reviewed above shows that LLM tools can make students more
active, more motivated and, under the right conditions, more cognitively engaged.
But engagement alone does not guarantee learning. The critical test is whether
students develop knowledge and skills that persist beyond the AI-supported
session, a distinction that proves central to interpreting the evidence that follows.
This is where the most significant gap in the evidence base is found. Most
studies in this field measure how students perform while using the AI tool,
which tells us about the tool’s effectiveness as a support. But they do not
tell us whether or not students have developed skills or knowledge that
they can use independently. Roughly half of the studies reviewed here include
some form of assessment carried out without AI, but most of these take place
immediately after the intervention, in the same session. Only a few studies test if
learning persists over a longer period 13 . With that caveat established, those
studies that do measure learning beyond the AI-supported session (all of which
involve tools that have a deliberately pedagogical design) point to a consistent
finding.

Polanco-Jimenez & De Witte (2026, preprint), whose findings on behavioural
engagement were discussed above, provide the strongest causal evidence. Their
instrumental variable analysis of complier students 14 found that completing the
tailored chatbot module produced a substantial long-term retention effect (0.309
SD at a two-month follow-up). This gain was mediated by engagement: students
who were behaviourally engaged learned more, and those gains proved durable.
The generic chatbot, running on the same underlying AI model but without
curricular integration, produced no retention effect; indeed, offering the generic

13 For example, Aptyka et al. (2025), who assessed students 7 weeks after the intervention, as
well as Polanco-Jiménez and De Witte (2026, preprint), whose 2-month follow-up lost over 94 %
of participants to attrition.
14 “Compliers” are the students whose behaviour was changed by the intervention: those who
would not have completed the module under traditional instruction, but who did so when offered
the tailored chatbot. The authors note these are “not just the highest-ability students, but a
broader, more representative group”. The instrumental–variable analysis estimates the effect of
completing the module for this subgroup in particular.

chatbot slightly discouraged module completion, so no comparable group of
engaged students exists for that arm.

A study by The LearnLM Team et al. (2025, preprint), conducted across five UK
secondary schools, provides the strongest evidence of transfer. Students guided
by a finely tuned pedagogical AI model were 5.5 percentage points more likely to
solve novel problems in subsequent topics that they had not practised during the
intervention (66.2 %, vs 60.7 % with human tutoring alone). The supervising
tutors attributed this transfer advantage to LearnLM’s Socratic questioning style,
which pushed students to explain their reasoning rather than receive answers.
Two caveats apply: the sample is modest (N = 165) and LearnLM was deployed
under direct human supervision 15 , and is a fine-tuned model not available as a
consumer product; however, the developers note that these specific pedagogical
capabilities have since been infused into consumer models such as Gemini 2.5
Pro, making this approach replicable for standard users.

Zhang and Huang (2024), whose behavioural and emotional engagement
findings were discussed in Sections 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 of this report, offer partial
corroboration for this. Their experimental group of 52 high school students
demonstrated significantly stronger retention of productive vocabulary at a post-
test two weeks after the intervention ended. While both groups experienced
typical memory decay, the performance gap between the two actually widened
over time, with the chatbot-assisted group outperforming the control by 12.4
percentage points at the delay. The retention window in this study is short and
the sample small, but this durable retention of productive knowledge suggests
that the behavioural patterns documented earlier (spontaneous generative
questioning beyond the curriculum) and the emotional conditions (reduced
performance anxiety enabling freer language output) jointly supported the
deeper processing needed for lasting learning.

The pattern emerging across these three studies points to a consistent structural
finding: productive engagement that converts into durable learning is tied
to tool architectures that maintain cognitive demand (through Socratic
questioning, scaffolded hints, error redirection, and curriculum alignment),
rather than reducing it. Notably, the strongest transfer result in this evidence
base (LearnLM) came from a deployment that, by design, built in human
oversight: tutors reviewed every message before it reached students. Well-
designed architecture and human mediation are complements, not alternatives.
Where engagement is generated by a tool that also offloads cognitive effort,
behavioural and emotional indicators may be high, but evidence of transfer is
absent. This distinction is directly relevant to the policy question of whether
providing students with access to general-purpose LLMs constitutes, in itself, an
educational investment. The evidence reviewed here suggests it does not, unless

title: 3.2.1. Engagement disconnect

paragraphs.text:
The previous section identified the conditions under which LLM-mediated
engagement translates into durable learning. This section examines what
happens when those conditions are not met. A recurring finding across the
emerging evidence base is that LLM-based tools can generate substantial
student engagement without producing corresponding learning gains. This
pattern – the engagement paradox – occurs when high behavioural and
emotional engagement coexists with low cognitive engagement, ultimately
impairing durable learning. The paradox is not a uniform phenomenon; it
manifests along a spectrum, from subtle dissociations between task performance
and transfer (Meyer et al., 2024) to stark disconnects between neurophysiological
engagement and subjective experience, as highlighted in “Your Brain on
ChatGPT” study below.

Indeed, the clearest demonstration comes from Kosmyna et al. (2025, preprint),
who used objective neurophysiological measurement to capture what self-report
cannot. In a between-subjects experiment, participants who used ChatGPT for
essay writing reported higher satisfaction and perceived their essays to be of
higher quality than the students in the control condition. Yet EEG data revealed
a different picture: cognitive engagement, measured through brain activity, was
significantly lower during ChatGPT-assisted writing. Instead of maintaining
sustained concentration, participants’ thought processes were intermittently
disrupted by the LLM’s suggestions, impairing the deep neural integration
necessary for semantic processing. Furthermore, while LLM-assisted essays
scored highly overall, expert human raters noted that they lacked uniqueness and
exhibited structural homogeneity. The study thus documents a critical disconnect:
students felt highly satisfied with their work, but experienced weaker
memory traces (failing to accurately quote their own essays), reduced
executive self-monitoring and a fragmented sense of ownership over the
text. Although this study involved adults rather than secondary school students,
it provides the only evidence in the database that measures this cognitive
offloading at the neurophysiological level, rather than inferring it from outcomes
data.

Similar patterns emerge in secondary education through behavioural and
attitudinal measures. Aptyka et al. (2025), in an RCT involving 241 German
upper-secondary biology students, found that the use of ChatGPT produced
significantly more positive attitudes towards AI-assisted learning (both

immediately and at 7-week follow-up), while learning gains were minimal. A small
effect on factual key concepts was found, no effect on threshold concepts
requiring conceptual restructuring, and no reduction in persistent misconceptions.
The authors flag the self-reinforcing risk that this creates: students who develop
positive attitudes towards a tool that does not improve their understanding
are likely to increase their use of it, deepening the paradox over time.

The disconnect operates at scale, not just in controlled settings. The
Weatherholtz et al. (2025) data discussed in Section 3.1.3 illustrate this directly.
In that study, the majority of students sustained multi-turn dialogues with
Khanmigo (behavioural engagement) while remaining cognitively passive,
showing minimal evidence of constructing understanding. Liu et al. (2025),
studying middle-school mathematics students, found that declining learners were
paradoxically among the most behaviourally active (completing more sessions
and generating more utterances), but they directed much of their interaction
towards off-task conversation with the AI rather than towards mathematical
content. In both studies, conventional engagement metrics (session count, time
on task, utterance frequency) would have classified these students as highly
engaged.

A final dimension of the disconnect is worth noting. Lieb & Goel (2024), studying
secondary physics students using NewtBot, found that students rated the tool as
efficient and easy to use but did not believe it improved their grades, yet still
intended to continue using it. This combination suggests that for some
students, the engagement paradox operates not through ignorance but
through a rational preference for convenience over cognitive effort . The
implication is that even students who are metacognitively aware of a tool’s limited
learning benefit may not self-correct – a finding that has implications for the
metacognitive miscalibration evidence examined in Section 3.2.3.

title: 3.2.2. Cognitive offloading and cognitive debt 16

paragraphs.text:
The engagement disconnect documented above raises a direct question: what
happens cognitively when students delegate thinking to LLMs? The evidence

16 The strongest causal evidence for cognitive offloading comes from secondary education
(Bastani et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2025), but the mechanistic evidence explaining how offloading
operates at a cognitive level draws primarily on studies on higher education. This reflects a
structural gap in the evidence base: research at the level of secondary education has
demonstrated that offloading occurs, and that it harms learning – but the experimental designs
required to isolate the underlying cognitive mechanisms (process mining, cognitive load
measurement, controlled variation of assistance levels) have so far been conducted only with
university students. The findings from higher education reviewed below are included because the
mechanisms they identify (germane cognitive load reduction, behavioural displacement of
independent problem-solving, non-linear assistance effects) are not population-specific; they
describe how human cognition responds to the delegation of effort to an external tool: a process
that applies across age groups and arguably with greater force to secondary students, whose
self-regulation capacities are still developing.

points to cognitive offloading – the process by which learners transfer mental
effort to an external tool – as the main mechanism through which the engagement
paradox functions. When offloading becomes habitual, it may create what
Kosmyna et al. (2025) have called “cognitive debt”, a cumulative deficit in skills
development that builds over time as students avoid the effortful processing
required for lasting learning . Two elements of this claim stand on different
evidential footings. First, the fact that offloading occurs and that each episode of
offloading carries a learning cost is well documented in the studies reviewed
below. Second, the accumulation itself is not: no study has yet tracked offloading
and skills development over one school year or longer, and the term rests largely
on a single, small experiment. “Cognitive debt” should therefore be read not as
an established finding, but as a plausible hypothesis as to where the short-term
effects documented might lead (one of the research gaps identified in Chapter 5).
The consequences that are now visible appear in both immediate performance–
learning dissociations and in the longer-term erosion of transfer capacity and
learner autonomy 17 .

The performance–learning dissociation: the strongest school-based evidence
for performance–learning dissociation comes from Bastani et al. (2025), who
conducted a large-scale RCT involving high-school mathematics students in
Türkiye. Students were randomly assigned to access a standard GPT-4 base
model (which provided direct solutions), a GPT-4 tutor with pedagogical
guardrails (Socratic questioning, hints rather than answers), or a control group
with no AI. During practice, both AI conditions dramatically outperformed the
control (GPT base +48 %, GPT tutor +127 %). But when AI access was removed
for a subsequent exam with conceptually similar problems, the pattern reversed:
students who had used the non-guardrailed GPT Base performed 17 % worse
than students who had never had AI access. The GPT tutor group showed no
significant difference from the control; the guardrails prevented harm, but did not
produce a learning advantage. Interaction analysis revealed the mechanism:
students quickly learned to treat the non-guardrailed model as an answer-
generator, with 67 % of initial interactions per problem in the GPT Base group
being superficial (copying solutions, repeating question text). Conversely, the
constraints built into the tutor forced more substantive engagement, with
superficial initial queries dropping to 37 % as students adapted to the guardrails.
This finding demonstrates that access to a powerful LLM can actively harm
learning when it enables students to bypass the problem-solving process.

Li et al. (2025; HE [programming], China, N = 55) make the offloading mechanism
visible at the behavioural level. Students using GPT-3.5 Turbo showed

17 Cognitive offloading is not unique to LLMs. The use of external tools to reduce cognitive
demand has been documented across a range of technologies, from calculators to spellcheckers
to web search (Pandey et al., 2024; Dawson, 2020). What distinguishes LLM-mediated offloading
is its scope: unlike earlier tools, which offloaded specific, bounded tasks (arithmetic, spelling,
information retrieval), LLMs can take over the core cognitive processes of reasoning,
argumentation and composition themselves (Kosmyna et al., 2025). This makes the offloading
harder to detect and potentially more consequential for learning.

dramatically improved performance during AI-assisted sessions (p < .001), but
the advantage disappeared entirely when AI was removed for transfer tasks
(p = .538). Process mining of student behaviour revealed why: GenAI users spent
their time in a loop of copying AI-generated code and retrieving information, while
independent coding was entirely absent from their visualised behavioural model.
By contrast, control students spent most of their time actively writing and revising
their own code. This study demonstrates not merely that cognitive offloading
occurred, but precisely how it displaced the productive struggle that learning
requires.

The cognitive load mechanism: Stadler et al. (2024; HE, N = 91, Germany)
provide the clearest experimental evidence as to why offloading impairs learning
at the cognitive level. In a socio-scientific enquiry task comparing ChatGPT with
Google search, ChatGPT significantly reduced cognitive load across all three
dimensions: intrinsic, extraneous and, critically, germane 18 (the largest effect).
Students using Google produced significantly higher-quality reasoning compared
with students using ChatGPT, and mediation analysis confirmed that this
difference in quality was fully explained by the reduction in germane cognitive
load. The direct effect of tool type on quality became non-significant once
germane load was accounted for. This is important theoretically: it shows that
the problem is not that ChatGPT provides bad information, but that it makes
information so accessible that the task no longer demands the deep self-
regulated processing through which learning occurs.

Chen et al. (2025; HE, USA, N = 30, preprint) extend this finding by showing a
non-linear relationship between the level of assistance and learning. This study
compared three conditions of AI-supported note-taking – minimal (real-time
transcripts), intermediate (summary building blocks) and automated (complete
structured notes). The intermediate condition produced the highest post-test
scores, while the automated condition produced the lowest. Students preferred
the automated condition for its convenience, but learned the least from it. This
finding illustrates a pattern that recurs across the evidence base: students’
preferences for AI assistance are inversely related to its educational effectiveness
when the assistance removes rather than scaffolds cognitive effort.

The frequency–dependence pattern: Gold & Geng (2025), analysing 127 US
university students’ interactions with a Socratic GPT-4 tutor in a data science
course, found that the students who asked the most questions performed worst
on subsequent mid-term examinations. This is not a simple selection effect (i.e.
weaker students asking more questions); the pattern held after controlling for
prior programming background. This suggests that high-frequency AI interaction
substituted for, rather than supplemented, independent problem-solving. Gerlich
(2025; mixed population, UK, N = 666) provides convergent correlational
evidence in a broader context: frequent AI use was strongly associated with
cognitive offloading (r = 0.72). This, in turn, predicted reduced critical thinking

compared three conditions of AI-supported note-taking – minimal (real-time
transcripts), intermediate (summary building blocks) and automated (complete
structured notes). The intermediate condition produced the highest post-test
scores, while the automated condition produced the lowest. Students preferred
the automated condition for its convenience, but learned the least from it. This
finding illustrates a pattern that recurs across the evidence base: students’
preferences for AI assistance are inversely related to its educational effectiveness
when the assistance removes rather than scaffolds cognitive effort.
The frequency–dependence pattern: Gold & Geng (2025), analysing 127 US
university students’ interactions with a Socratic GPT-4 tutor in a data science
course, found that the students who asked the most questions performed worst
on subsequent mid-term examinations. This is not a simple selection effect (i.e.
weaker students asking more questions); the pattern held after controlling for
prior programming background. This suggests that high-frequency AI interaction
substituted for, rather than supplemented, independent problem-solving. Gerlich
(2025; mixed population, UK, N = 666) provides convergent correlational
evidence in a broader context: frequent AI use was strongly associated with
cognitive offloading (r = 0.72). This, in turn, predicted reduced critical thinking

Gerlich’s evidence, however, is correlational and self-reported, and the evidence

study documented a non-linear pattern; beyond a threshold of AI reliance,
negative effects on critical thinking accelerated. Offloading is condition-
specific, not inevitable. The evidence reviewed above might suggest that
cognitive offloading is an inherent consequence of LLM use. However, evidence
suggests this is not the case. Indeed, Dai et al. (2025), in two sequential RCTs
involving 387 secondary school physics students in China, demonstrated that the
same AI feedback system produced radically different outcomes depending on
how students accessed it. When low-achieving students received compulsory
structured hints, they showed significant achievement gains with no decline in
autonomy. When this same demographic was given voluntary, on-demand
access to the same system, achievement gains disappeared, and significant
declines in learner autonomy emerged. Interview data confirmed the mechanism
for this: students in the voluntary condition glanced at materials without
attempting problems independently. High-achieving students showed the
opposite pattern, benefitting from autonomous access but experiencing a decline
in autonomy under compulsory recommendations. The core implication is that
cognitive offloading is triggered not by the AI tool itself but by the mismatch
between design choices (how access is structured) and learner characteristics
(what the student needs). Both dimensions matter: the same design that prevents
offloading for one group can induce it in another, a heterogeneity examined
further in Section 3.3.2.

habitually delegate cognitive work to an AI system, they may not only fail to
develop specific skills, but may also lose confidence in their capacity for
independent learning and self-regulation (Delikoura et al., 2025; Singh et al.,
2025). This is particularly concerning in secondary education, where the
development of self-directed learning capacity is itself a core educational
objective.

findings is echoed in the lived experience of European secondary schools, as
documented by Villar-Onrubia et al. (2025) in their exploratory JRC study, which
documented early AI adopters’ observations across five EU Member States.

title: 3.2.3. Metacognitive miscalibration

paragraphs.text:
One dimension of the engagement paradox that is particularly concerning is that
students who experience it are often unable to recognise it. If cognitive offloading
were accompanied by accurate self-awareness – that is, if students knew they
were learning less –, they might adjust their behaviour or seek alternative
strategies. The evidence suggests the opposite: use of LLMs can systematically
distort learners’ ability to evaluate their own understanding, creating a
metacognitive blind spot that effectively sustains the paradox.

Bastani et al. (2025) provide the most direct evidence of this metacognitive
miscalibration. In their RCT, secondary school students in the GPT base
condition, who performed significantly worse on the exam than the control group,
did not perceive that they had performed worse or learned less. Conversely,
students in the GPT tutor condition, who showed no significant improvement over
the control, perceived that they had performed significantly better. The gap
between actual and perceived learning was significant: students’ self-
assessments were notably inaccurate, indicating a failure in metacognitive
monitoring rather than mere imprecision. This finding has serious implications for
educational contexts that rely on student self-assessment, satisfaction surveys or
perceived usefulness as indicators of pedagogical effectiveness.

Fernandes et al. (2025; adult participants in laboratory settings, USA, N = 698
across two studies 20 ) extend this finding with a more granular analysis of the
metacognitive distortion. Participants who used ChatGPT-4o for logical reasoning
tasks overestimated their performance by approximately 4 points (on a 20-item
scale), compared with approximately 1 point for the no-AI condition. Their trial-
level metacognitive sensitivity (the ability to distinguish correct from incorrect
answers) fell significantly below the accepted benchmark (AUC = 0.62, vs. a 0.70
threshold). Most strikingly, the use of AI eliminated the Dunning-Kruger effect:
whereas low-performing participants without AI showed the classic pattern of
disproportionate overconfidence, AI use levelled performance enough that skill-
dependent variation in self-assessment disappeared. All participants, regardless
of actual ability, became equally overconfident. Counterintuitively, participants

20 Although this study was conducted outside of an educational setting, the metacognitive
mechanism it identifies is directly relevant to the use of LLMs in schools.

with higher AI literacy (measured via the SNAIL 21 scale) showed greater
overconfidence and lower metacognitive accuracy, suggesting that familiarity
with AI tools exacerbates rather than mitigates the distortion. The mechanism
proposed by the authors is misattribution: users mistake the fluency of AI-
generated explanations for proof of their own understanding, confusing the ability
of the system with their personal competence.

This combination of cognitive offloading and metacognitive miscalibration creates
a self-reinforcing cycle that is difficult to interrupt through student agency alone.
Students offload cognitive work to the LLM, experience the interaction as being
productive, overestimate what they have learned, and see no reason to change
their approach. Breaking this cycle requires external intervention by
teachers and schools, such as assessment designs that make the gap
between perceived and actual learning visible to students; pedagogical
guardrails that constrain offloading before it occurs; or explicit
metacognitive instruction that teaches students to monitor their own
cognitive engagement. These design features are examined in Chapter 4 22 .

title: 3.3.1. When LLMs fail to sustain engagement

paragraphs.text:
While much of the literature on LLMs in education focuses on the conditions
under which engagement is high (and on whether that engagement translates
into learning), a smaller but analytically important body of evidence documents
cases in which LLM-based interventions actively suppress engagement or fail to
generate it at all. This evidence is thinner than that for the engagement paradox
– in part, because publication bias works against null and negative results. As
previously noted, the fact that the most direct demonstration of disengagement
comes from a PhD thesis (Kline, 2024) is not incidental: grey literature may be
among the few avenues via which these findings reach the record.

Design-driven disengagement: the most direct evidence for this comes from
Kline (2024), who conducted a mixed-methods, quasi-experimental study
involving 52 high school students who used Google Gemini for writing tasks.

21 Scale for the Assessment of Non-experts’ AI Literacy.
22 It should be noted that not all students are unaware of these dynamics. Lieb and Goel (2024)
found that secondary school physics students, while rating their LLM tutoring tool as efficient and
easy to use, did not believe it improved their learning, yet still intended to continue using it.
Similarly, Gerlich (2025) reported qualitative evidence of users who simultaneously valued the
convenience of AI and expressed concern about its effects on their thinking. These findings
suggest a more complex picture in which some students possess a degree of metacognitive
awareness regarding the risk of cognitive offloading, even if this awareness does not consistently
translate into changed behaviour. The extent to which such awareness can be cultivated and
leveraged as a protective factor warrants further investigation.

Uniquely among the studies reviewed, the intervention group showed a
statistically significant decrease in behavioural, affective, and overall
engagement relative to baseline, while the control group’s engagement increased
over the same period. Students described the chatbot as an “inauthentic”
replacement for real interaction, capable of generating ideas but unable to
provide the kind of relational, contextualised response that makes writing feel
meaningful. This is not a case of cognitive offloading or surface engagement
masking the absence of genuine learning; it is a situation in which the tool itself
undermined the motivational conditions necessary for engagement to occur.

A different but related pattern appears in Polanco-Jiménez & De Witte (2026),
who used module attrition as a proxy for disengagement. A poorly designed,
generic AI chatbot caused such high dropout rates that only the most confident
students completed the assigned tasks. Disengagement was not a slow decline
but a threshold effect: the design of the tool actively excluded learners with lower
confidence, raising significant concerns about equity in AI-supported
learning environments when implementation is inadequate (this question will
be reviewed in further detail in Section 3.4).

A related form of design-driven disengagement emerges from Dai et al. (2025),
where the unpredictability of a GenAI feedback system’s responses led
secondary school students to disengage from it entirely. Student interviews
confirmed that not knowing what kind of feedback to expect (and therefore not
knowing how to act upon it) produced a disengagement response distinct from
the cognitive offloading observed elsewhere in the study’s data. This is
disengagement caused by feedback design failure rather than the AI technology
itself, a distinction with direct implications for implementation.

Motivational erosion: even when students remain formally on-task, the use of
LLMs can erode the motivational substrates of genuine engagement. Yang et al.
(2025, secondary education, N = 153, Taiwan) found, in a quasi-experimental
study, that students using ChatGPT experienced significantly lower levels of flow
and academic self-efficacy than peers who were taught via conventional
methods. Flow (the state of absorbed, intrinsically motivated task involvement) is
a strong predictor of sustained learning effort, and its suppression due to the use
of AI represents a qualitatively different form of disengagement than simple off-
task behaviour.

Liu et al. (2025) document a temporal dimension to this erosion. Tracking the
emotional states of middle school students using an teachable AI agent, they
found that among those students whose performance declined, boredom was the
most frequently occurring non-neutral emotion (50.4 %), and that it increased as
individual sessions progressed. The mechanism proposed by the authors is a
mismatch between the complexity of the problems faced by the students and the
absence of adequate pedagogical scaffolding. When the AI could not bridge that
gap, the result was not frustration redirected towards effort but progressive
withdrawal, with “unresolved frustration” escalating into boredom.

Relational displacement 23 : a third mechanism operates at the level of the social
ecology of learning. Two systematic reviews (Lo et al., 2024; Heung & Chiu,
2025) converge on the finding that the use of AI frequently produces emotional
disengagement through a reduction in peer interaction and human teacher
contact. Students reported missing the intellectual exchange and personal
connection characteristic of collaborative learning. As Delikoura et al. (2025) note
when framing this issue through the lens of self-determination theory, this
dynamic represents a direct threat to the basic psychological need for
relatedness. They conclude that when collaborative human dialogue and
feedback are replaced by solitary interactions with a machine, intrinsic motivation
is undermined at its foundation, regardless of the quality of the AI’s responses.

Taken together, these findings suggest that disengagement is not a single
phenomenon. It can be caused by concerns over authenticity, the erosion of
motivation, social displacement, or poor design – each of which has different
implications for what a productive intervention might look like. The evidence base
remains limited, and caution is needed when drawing strong conclusions from a
small number of diverse studies. However, the evidence shows that high
levels of engagement with LLMs should not be assumed to be an automatic
baseline; under certain conditions of design and context, introducing an
LLM tool can result in students being less engaged than they would have
been without it.

title: 3.3.2. Mixed and heterogeneous patterns

paragraphs.text:
If the evidence on disengagement establishes that under certain conditions,
LLMs can fail to sustain engagement, the evidence on heterogeneity establishes
something more structurally challenging: that the same tool, in the same
intervention, can simultaneously produce productive engagement for some
students, and the engagement paradox or disengagement in others . The
evidence reviewed here has direct implications for the way in which LLM-based
interventions should be designed, targeted and evaluated.

Two axes of heterogeneity emerge from the evidence: interaction style and
implementation mode.

Interaction style as a determinant of learning trajectory: the most direct
evidence that the same tool can produce opposite outcomes depending on how
students engage with it comes from Li et al. (2025), who conducted a quasi-
experimental study of GPT-3.5-supported programming education in higher
education. Behavioural clustering within the GenAI group revealed two distinct
learner types whose outcomes diverged sharply, despite having the same access
to the same tool. Type 2 students exhibited what the authors call “epistemic

23 This mechanism is documented primarily through student-reported experiences synthesised in
systematic reviews rather than through experimental designs that measure relational outcomes
directly. This limits causal claims, but identifies a consistent concern across multiple contexts.

agency”: they engaged in iterative questioning, critically evaluated AI outputs,
selectively applied suggestions, and achieved genuine learning improvements.
In contrast, Type 1 students engaged in passive copying, accepted AI-generated
code without critical analysis, and showed no transfer of learning when access to
AI was removed. Significantly, the study found that the entire GenAI group
performed noticeably worse than controls in terms of logical correctness and
functional completeness in the transfer task, suggesting that passive AI use was
not neutral but actively detrimental to skill development. The differentiating factor
was not prior ability (as students began with similar baseline level of proficiency),
but rather interaction quality. High-performing students demonstrated
epistemic agency by using the tool as a scaffold: they iteratively questioned
the AI, critiqued its outputs, and engaged in independent reflection before
selectively applying the code. Conversely, for low-performing students, the
AI functioned as a harmful cognitive substitute: they engaged in “negative
cognitive offloading” by directly copying and pasting AI-generated
solutions, allowing the tool to bypass the productive struggle required for
true knowledge mastery.

Weatherholtz et al. (2025) corroborate this pattern at scale. As discussed in
Section 3.1.3, their panel analysis examining within-learner differences
demonstrated that interaction quality is not a stable individual trait: the same
student engaged constructively in some sessions and passively in others. This
suggests that the quality of engagement is driven by contextual and temporal
factors (such as task difficulty, prior success or transient motivation) rather than
fixed student characteristics.

Content type as a moderator of engagement effects: heterogeneity operates
not only within students but within subjects. Aptyka et al. (2025), in an
experimental study involving upper-secondary biology students using ChatGPT-
3.5, found that learning outcomes varied depending on the cognitive demands of
the content. Key concepts (factual, well-defined knowledge targets) showed a
small improvement in the ChatGPT condition, although only at a 7-week follow-
up rather than immediately after the intervention. Threshold concepts, whose
mastery requires the restructuring of prior understanding, showed no significant
improvement at either time point. Intuitive concepts rooted in persistent
misconceptions showed no significant improvement either: students in the
ChatGPT condition were no more likely to correct flawed reasoning than those
using a traditional internet search. This pattern may have implications beyond
biology. In understanding the effectiveness of LLMs, it is possible that the type of
cognitive demand a task places on the learner matters more than the subject area
alone, though this remains to be tested across other domains and content types.

Section 3.1.3, their panel analysis examining within-learner differences
demonstrated that interaction quality is not a stable individual trait: the same
student engaged constructively in some sessions and passively in others. This
suggests that the quality of engagement is driven by contextual and temporal
factors (such as task difficulty, prior success or transient motivation) rather than
fixed student characteristics.
Content type as a moderator of engagement effects: heterogeneity operates
not only within students but within subjects. Aptyka et al. (2025), in an
experimental study involving upper-secondary biology students using ChatGPT-
3.5, found that learning outcomes varied depending on the cognitive demands of
the content. Key concepts (factual, well-defined knowledge targets) showed a
small improvement in the ChatGPT condition, although only at a 7-week follow-
up rather than immediately after the intervention. Threshold concepts, whose
mastery requires the restructuring of prior understanding, showed no significant
improvement at either time point. Intuitive concepts rooted in persistent
misconceptions showed no significant improvement either: students in the
ChatGPT condition were no more likely to correct flawed reasoning than those
using a traditional internet search. This pattern may have implications beyond
biology. In understanding the effectiveness of LLMs, it is possible that the type of
cognitive demand a task places on the learner matters more than the subject area
alone, though this remains to be tested across other domains and content types.
37

title: 3.4. Equity and access

paragraphs.text:
The evidence on heterogeneity reviewed above highlights that the same tool can
produce different outcomes, depending on who is using it and how – and who
ends up on which side of that distribution. Although the current evidence base is
limited, it is significant. Causal evidence on differential effects exists for one
moderator (prior achievement level), and is methodologically strong. For most
other dimensions relevant to equity-, such as gender, socioeconomic background
and digital literacy, the picture is less clear. Some studies have tested for these
moderators and found no significant differential effects (Meyer et al., 2024; Ng et
al., 2024; Polanco-Jimenez & De Witte, 2026). However, individual studies are
rarely powered to detect moderation effects, and for most dimensions that are
relevant to equity, the evidence is observational, qualitative or missing.

The strongest evidence comes from Dai et al. (2025), whose two sequential RCTs
involving secondary school physics students tested the same AI feedback system
under compulsory and voluntary access conditions. The interaction between the
implementation mode and prior achievement was sharp. Among low achievers,
compulsory scaffolded hints produced the largest achievement gains in the
dataset, with no decline in autonomy. Voluntary access to the same system
produced no achievement gains and significant erosion of autonomy for the same
subgroup. High achievers showed the opposite pattern. The mechanism
emphasises by the authors is self-regulation: the on-demand system delivered
useful feedback only when students could identify what they were struggling with
and were able to formulate explicit requests. Low-achievers typically lacked the
self-regulated learning and help-seeking skills this required. The same tool,
therefore, became either a genuine learning support or a driver of the erosion of
autonomy, depending on the learner’s existing self-regulatory capacity. This is
the clearest illustration of a broader risk: self-regulation and AI literacy do not
operate as neutral background variables, but as capabilities whose uneven
distribution can cause LLMs to amplify existing educational disadvantage rather
than reducing it. Equity-conscious implementation therefore requires active
structural choices, not simply making tools available

The evidence on gender, socioeconomic status, digital literacy and national
context is insufficient to draw causal conclusions. Villar-Onrubia et al. (2025) note
that socioeconomic status is a contextual factor, but do not quantify its effects –
a limitation echoed by Granström and Oppi (2025), whose large-scale survey also
could not account for socioeconomic variables.

Digital and AI literacy emerges across multiple studies as a plausible moderator,
but no study in the database provides causal evidence on this relationship within
a secondary school population. However, massive cross-sectional data from
Granström and Oppi (2025), who surveyed more than 15,000 Estonian students,
reveals a stark developmental divide in digital competence: upper-secondary
students demonstrated significantly greater critical awareness of AI risks, trust

calibration and metacognitive engagement than lower-secondary students. The
authors warn of a severe “implementation gap” in which students’ everyday use
of AI outpaces formal pedagogical guidance and AI literacy training, leaving
younger students especially vulnerable to uncritical reliance on AI.

These findings point to a single underlying capability rather than two separate
ones. The self-regulation that distinguished high- from low-achievers in the
evidence above (Dai et al., 2025) is itself a core element of AI literacy, as defined
by the joint OECD/European Union framework. This framework identifies
metacognition and self-regulation among its competences and warns that
offloading cognitive effort to AI can foster metacognitive laziness, weakening
critical thinking and self-regulation (OECD & European Union, 2026). Building on
this capability, captured in the framework’s foundational “Engage with AI”
domain 24 , is a central recommendation of the JRC study on early adopters of
GenAI in the EU. This is the organising purpose of the OECD/EU framework:
equipping learners to engage with AI critically rather than uncritically (European
Commission, Joint Research Centre et al., 2025; OECD & European Union,
2026). Beyond AI literacy, the digital divide in terms of access to capable AI tools
is acknowledged in the literature, but has not yet been experimentally
investigated. This includes the divide between free and subscription tiers of the
same tools, which differ in the capability of the model and in usage limits. A
student relying on a free tier interacts with a measurably less capable system
than a peer with a paid subscription, yet no study in this evidence base compares
learning outcomes between tiers. The temporal distinction drawn in Section 1.3
compounds this gap; several studies in this corpus tested free-tier GPT-3.5-class
models (e.g. Aptyka et al., 2025), and their findings may not be generalisable to
the tools accessed by paying users.

4. Guiding principles for integrating LLM-based learning

paragraphs.text:
The evidence in Chapter 3 shows that the results achieved through the use of
LLMs depend more on how they are implemented and who uses them, rather
than on the models themselves. For example, the same GPT-4 model caused
learning harm when offered as a standard chat interface, but had no negative
effect when deployed with teacher-designed pedagogical guardrails implemented
via its system prompt, providing Socratic hints rather than direct answers (Bastani
et al., 2025). A tailored chatbot improved engagement and retention, while a
generic one based on the same model led to students dropping out (Polanco-
Jiménez & De Witte, 2026). Similarly, an AI feedback system helped low-
achieving students to succeed when used in structured settings, but hindered
them when students were given greater independence (Dai et al., 2025). This
suggests that policymakers should focus on how AI tools are used, not just which
tools to adopt. The key question is what conditions are needed for these tools to
support learning effectively. This chapter outlines five simple design principles
based on the evidence reviewed. These principles concern implementation
choices rather than the AI models themselves, and can be made by educators,
schools or procurement bodies. Two system-level enablers cut across all five
principles: teacher preparation and the development of learners’ AI literacy.
These are addressed in the report’s recommendations (Chapter 5).

title: 4.1. Preserving cognitive demand

paragraphs.text:
Preserving cognitive demand is the single most consistent finding across the
database. Every study that documents productive engagement ties it to a tool
architecture that maintains the student’s cognitive workload through Socratic
questioning (LearnLM Team et al., 2025), providing scaffolded hints rather than
direct answers (Bastani et al., 2025; Kazemitabaar et al., 2024), redirecting rather
than correcting errors (Polanco-Jiménez & De Witte, 2026), or intermediate rather
than fully automated assistance (Chen et al., 2025). The mechanism behind this
is grounded in the finding on germane cognitive load from Stadler et al. (2024):
when AI makes information so accessible that the task no longer demands deep
processing, this results in a reduction in effort that feels like efficiency but is in
fact a reduction in learning.

When it fails: the principle of preserving cognitive demand fails when guardrails
are absent or easily circumvented. Bastani et al. (2025) demonstrate this directly.
Students who were given non-guardrailed access to GPT-4 developed superficial
interaction patterns within sessions, overwhelmingly using the tool as a crutch by
simply restating questions or asking for direct solutions. The principle also fails
when it is applied uniformly rather than adaptively: Dai et al. (2025) show that
compulsory scaffolding that preserves cognitive demand for low achievers can

simultaneously reduce autonomy for high achievers, whose cognitive demand is
better maintained through self-directed access.

title: 4.2. Alignment with the curriculum

paragraphs.text:
The “tailoring premium” documented by Polanco-Jiménez and De Witte (2026) is
the clearest causal evidence for the principle of curriculum alignment. A chatbot
specifically trained on the Flemish economics curriculum increased module
completion by 13.2 percentage points, while a generic chatbot based on the same
underlying model produced null or slightly negative completion effects. The effect
of the tailoring operated primarily through the channel of participation: the
curriculum-specific design determined whether or not students remained within
the learning environment at all, even before any question of interaction quality
arose. Aptyka et al. (2025) reinforce this point from a different angle: ChatGPT’s
inability to address threshold concepts and persistent misconceptions in biology
reflects its lack of domain-specific pedagogical knowledge: it can generate
plausible texts about evolution without understanding where student
understanding typically breaks down.

When it fails: tailoring to the curriculum requires substantial upfront investment
in aligning AI systems with specific educational contexts. This task is neither
cheap nor easily scalable across subjects, national curricula and languages. The
principle also creates a dependency on the quality of the curriculum materials
used for training: a tool tailored to a poorly designed curriculum will reproduce its
weaknesses.

title: 4.3. Matching scaffolding to the learner’s profile

paragraphs.text:
Dai et al. (2025) provide the most direct evidence that the effectiveness of
scaffolding depends on its calibration to the individual learner. For low-achievers,
compulsory structured hints produced the largest achievement gains in the
dataset. Voluntary access by low-achievers to the same system produced no
gains and a significant erosion of autonomy. For high-achievers, the reverse was
true: autonomous access was productive, while compulsory scaffolding was
counterproductive. The mechanism underlying this is that low-achievers who are
given the option to opt out of effortful engagement will do so, not because they
are incapable of learning, but because the voluntary design does not provide the
structural support they need to persist through difficulty.

When it fails: “one size fits all” scaffolding falls short in for both groups: it is too
structured for capable students, and too open for those who struggle. The low
base rate of constructive engagement documented by Weatherholtz et al.
indicates that even well-designed systems tend to default to low cognitive
demand when scaffolding is not actively calibrated. The implications of this for

equity are clear: implementations that offer uniform, voluntary access will mainly
benefit those students who already have the self-regulation skills to use them
effectively, thereby widening rather than narrowing achievement gaps. This might
appear paradoxical, since personalisation is GenAI’s most widely advertised
strength. But current tools personalise content (hints, feedback, diagnosis) rather
than the structure of access itself; the one condition in Dai et al. (2025) which
delegated that choice to the algorithm produced no measurable benefit. Thus,
calibrating access remains, on current evidence, a decision for schools and
teachers (see the concluding section of this chapter).

title: 4.4. Integrating teacher mediation by design

paragraphs.text:
The evidence for teacher mediation is largely qualitative, but consistent. Across
five EU Member States, Villar-Onrubia et al. (2025) document that teacher
mediation (i.e. helping students to formulate productive prompts, contextualising
AI outputs, maintaining the relational dimension of learning) distinguishes
effective implementations from ineffective ones. Experimental evidence points
the same way: the strongest transfer effect in this report’s evidence base
(LearnLM Team et al., 2025) was achieved not by a tool used autonomously but
deployed under direct human supervision, with tutors reviewing each message
before it reached students (see Section 3.1.4). In contrast, Bastani et al. (2025)
note zero teacher involvement during practice sessions as a contextual factor in
the failure of the non-guardrailed condition in their trial. The finding on
disengagement by Kline (2024) emerged from a context of independent chatbot
use without teacher framing. These negative cases suggest that teacher
involvement functions as a structural safeguard.

When it fails : teacher involvement fails when it is conceived as an add-on rather
than being integrated into the implementation design, or when teachers lack the
training to mediate AI-supported learning effectively. Villar-Onrubia et al. (2025)
report that educators across the five EU Member States studied needed
specialised support, and that existing policies and guidelines were insufficient.
Another important factor is the problem of so-called “hidden labour” – general-
purpose LLMs place the burden of pedagogical prompt engineering on teachers,
thus creating workload demands that purpose-built tools are designed to absorb
(European Commission. Joint Research Centre et al., 2025; Steiss et al., 2024).

title: 4.5. Learning assessment without AI access

paragraphs.text:
The engagement paradox can only be detected when assessment involves
students performing without the support of AI. Bastani et al. (2025), Li et al. (2025)
and Stadler et al. (2024) all include transfer tasks without access to AI, and it is
precisely these assessments that reveal the performance-learning dissociation.
Where studies measure performance only under AI-assisted conditions, the

paradox is invisible: such conditions appear to show high engagement, strong
task performance, and apparent success.

When it fails : assessment without access to AI fails as a design principle when
it is treated as a punitive policing mechanism, focusing merely on catching
cheating, rather than as a low-stakes diagnostic tool (European Commission,
Joint Research Centre et al., 2025). It fails when students experience it as an
abrupt withdrawal of support rather than a scaffolded opportunity to demonstrate
independent mastery. The principle also requires that assessments are
fundamentally redesigned to measure the kinds of understanding that cannot
easily be substituted by AI. As traditional recall-focused examinations lose
validity, assessments must target students’ application to novel problems,
conceptual restructuring, and critical reflection rather than the factual
reproduction that could equally be produced by an LLM (Deng et al., 2025).

The five principles above are summarised in the table that follows. For each
principle, the table shows the mechanism through which it operates, the
conditions under which it succeeds or fails, as well as key supporting evidence.
Two points should guide the reading of the table. First, the principles complement
each other, rather than being alternatives: the strongest implementations
combine several of the principles, while the most obvious failures typically violate
several at once. Second, the principles imply a division of labour. Content
personalisation rests with the AI tool; pedagogical differentiation and mediation
are provided by the teacher; decisions about access structure, procurement and
assessment lie with schools and systems. The failures documented in this report
typically arise when these levels are mismatched: the wrong tool, in the wrong
configuration, for the wrong learner. Whether AI tools could eventually take on
part of the structural calibration themselves remains untested beyond a single
null result (Dai et al., 2025). This question is identified as a research priority in
Chapter 5.

title: 5. Implications and recommendations

paragraphs.text:
The evidence reviewed in this report does not support a simple verdict on LLMs
in secondary education. Rather, the verdict it supports is a conditional one: LLM-
based interventions can generate genuine, durable learning, but only under
specific design conditions that are not met by default, and which require
deliberate investment to establish . The aggregate meta-analytic picture
(positive, but substantially inflated by publication bias; Bartoš et al., 2026,
preprint) obscures a distribution in which some implementations produce
meaningful learning gains while others produce cognitive offloading,
metacognitive distortion or outright disengagement.

title: Monitoring and evaluation

paragraphs.text:
Traditional indicators of success in adopting a technology, such as usage rates,
student satisfaction, session frequency and time on task, may systematically
overestimate the pedagogical value of integrating LLMs into education. The
engagement paradox documented in Chapter 3 shows that these metrics can
actually be high precisely when learning is weakest. Cognitive engagement – the
dimension that predicts learning outcomes – is neither evident in usage data, nor
is it reliably measured by student self-reporting.

•
Monitoring and evaluation frameworks for LLM-based interventions should
include measures of cognitive engagement quality and learning outcomes
assessed without AI support, not just behavioural and attitudinal
indicators.

•
The evaluation criteria developed for previous educational technologies
are inadequate for use with LLM-based interventions, and should be
updated to reflect the specific risks documented in this report.

•
Where Member States or schools report on the success of AI integration
in education, reporting frameworks should require evidence of learning
outcomes that are assessed independently of AI use, alongside
engagement and satisfaction data.
Procurement and quality assurance

The evidence consistently shows that design of AI tools matters more than a
given model’s capability. The same underlying model can produce learning gains
or harm learning, depending on whether it incorporates pedagogical guardrails,
curriculum alignment and structured interaction patterns.

•
Procurement frameworks for educational AI tools should evaluate whether
tools offer configurable pedagogical features, including guardrail settings

(constraints on the provision of direct answers), the ability to integrated
into the curriculum, and structured interaction modes, as well as if the
vendor provides institutional support for implementing these features.
Evaluating tools solely on the basis of the model’s capabilities or generic
functionality is insufficient.

•
Access to general-purpose LLMs should not be treated as equivalent to
accessing purpose-built educationally deployed tools. However, the
“purpose-built” label on its own should not be taken as a guarantee of
quality: the evidence behind individual products is uneven, and some offer
little more than a thin interface over a general-purpose model (Lindroos
Cermakova et al., 2026; also see Section 1.3 of the present report). Where
schools
or
education
systems
adopt
general-purpose
tools,
implementation plans should address how the compensatory pedagogical
structures will be developed and supported, rather than assuming that
access alone constitutes an educational investment.

•
Educational AI tools should be required to demonstrate positive learning
outcomes (as distinct from task performance) prior to their deployment in
compulsory education. No such requirement currently exists (European
Parliament & Chounta, 2026), leaving deployment decisions to be made
on the basis of vendor claims and usage metrics that, as shown in Chapter
3, may appear high precisely when learning is at its weakest.

•
The temporal dimension of the evidence base should inform procurement
decisions in both directions: negative findings from earlier-generation
models (GPT-3.5-era) may not be generalisable to current models.
Equally, positive findings from purpose-built systems should not be
extrapolated to the general-purpose tools most students actually use.

title: Teacher preparation

paragraphs.text:
The involvement of teachers appears as a key contextual factor that distinguishes
productive implementations of AI in education from counterproductive ones.
However, no study in the database isolates this factor experimentally. Teacher
involvement is present in most cases of productive engagement and is absent in
several cases of engagement paradox and disengagement. What this
involvement asks of teachers is substantial, and current levels of preparation fall
well short. In TALIS 2024, around one in three lower-secondary teachers across
OECD education systems reported using AI in their teaching, yet three in four
reported lacking the knowledge or skills to teach with it. AI was identified as the
content area in which there was the highest reported professional development
need (29 % of respondents). Participation in AI-focused training varies sharply,
from more than 60 % of teachers in the leading systems globally, to 9 % in France
and 16 % in the French Community of Belgium (OECD, 2025). Teacher
preparation is, therefore, a system-level investment in initial teacher education
(ITE) and continuing professional development (CPD) , not a demand that

individual teachers can absorb on their own. It is also the enabling condition for
the design principles set out in Chapter 4.

• Teacher preparation programmes (ITE and CPD) should develop three
specific competences: mediating student-AI interaction (prompt framing,
output contextualisation); recognising signs of cognitive offloading and
metacognitive distortion; and designing assessment that captures learning
with and without AI.

•
Digital literacy frameworks should encompass the critical evaluation of AI
outputs and the ethical dimensions of AI use, not just technical proficiency.

title: Reforming assessment practices

paragraphs.text:
The engagement paradox is visible only when assessment includes performance
without AI support. Where studies measure performance only under AI-assisted
conditions, the paradox is invisible: high engagement, strong task performance
and apparent success mask the absence of durable learning.

•
Schools
and
examination
systems
should
incorporate
transfer
assessments without access to AI, with this functioning not as a punitive
restriction but as a diagnostic tool that makes the gap between AI-assisted
performance and independent capability visible to both students and
teachers.

•
The evidence on metacognitive miscalibration shows that student self-
assessment and satisfaction surveys are unreliable proxies for learning
when AI tools are involved. External assessment of learning outcomes is
necessary to complement the self-reported data.

•
A formative-summative model in which AI tools provide formative feedback
on early-stage work, while human evaluation handles summative
assessment of independent capability, can prove highly effective.
Assessment design should increasingly focus on applying skills to novel
problems, restructuring concepts and encouraging critical reflection, rather
than on the reproduction of facts that an LLM could produce just as well.

title: Equity-conscious implementation

paragraphs.text:
Simply making LLM tools available does not constitute equitable provision. The
evidence
shows
that
voluntary
access
without
structural
support
disproportionately
harms
low-achievers,
while
appropriately
structured
scaffolding can produce the largest gains for precisely this group.

•
Equity-conscious implementation requires differentiated scaffolding: the
evidence indicates that more structured support benefits students with
lower prior achievement, while more autonomous access suits those with
demonstrated capacity for self-regulation. Education systems should

develop guidance and tools to help schools calibrate scaffolding to learner
profiles (dynamically and in a revisable manner, avoiding fixed ability
labelling), rather than deploying uniform voluntary access models that risk
widening achievement gaps.

•
AI literacy development for learners (anchored in the OECD/EU
framework’s foundational “Engage with AI” domain) should be treated as
a precondition for autonomous access models: the evidence shows that
voluntary access disproportionately harms students who lack the self-
regulation and critical engagement skills that AI literacy comprises (see
Section 3.4).

•
Evidence on the gender gap should be treated as a priority both for
research funding and reporting requirements. No study in the current
evidence base provides causal evidence on gender-differentiated
outcomes.

•
The dimensions of the socioeconomic and digital divides are
acknowledged in the literature, but remain unquantified. Precautionary
approaches are necessary pending such evidence, particularly with regard
to equitable access to purpose-built tools rather than only to free general-
purpose alternatives.

title: Research priorities

paragraphs.text:
The evidence base reviewed in this report, while sufficient for some of the
precautionary design principles outlined above, has significant gaps that limit the
confidence and specificity of policy recommendations. Three clusters of research
priorities emerge.

•
Most evidence comes from single-session or short interventions. Whether
or not the design principles identified in this report can sustain productive
engagement over extended periods (a full school year, for example)
remains untested. Funding bodies should prioritise longer-duration studies
that track engagement and learning trajectories over time, particularly for
the purpose-built tools that show the most promise.

•
The teacher’s role is the largest blind spot in the causal evidence base.
Experimental designs that vary teacher mediation (rather than isolating the
AI–student interaction) should be a funding priority, alongside research on
how teacher preparation shapes the effectiveness of LLM-based
interventions.

•
Whether AI tools can reliably take on part of the scaffolding calibration
themselves remains untested beyond a single null result; GenAI-enabled
scaffolding warrants being a standalone focus of research as the evidence
base matures.

•
Transfer and retention, assessed without access to AI, should become
standard outcome measures in research on LLMs in education. Gender-
disaggregated analysis should be adopted as a reporting requirement. The
field needs to move beyond assessing performance under AI-supported
conditions as the default learning metric, a measurement practice that
systematically obscures the engagement paradox.

•
Most RCTs in the current database are conducted in the United States,
China or Türkiye. European secondary school contexts are represented
by only a handful of studies. The evolving capability of AI tools must also
be acknowledged in research design: the tools studied in 2023 are not the
tools available in 2026, and research programmes need to account for
rapid improvement in models and the shifting boundary between what
general-purpose and purpose-built tools can do.

This report shows that LLMs are not neutral tools. The impact they have on
learning depends on how they are used. Factors such as teacher training,
scaffolding, curriculum fit, assessment design and safety measures influence
whether they help or harm students. The same model can improve or hurt
learning based on these decisions. The key question for policymakers is not
whether to integrate LLMs into secondary education – students are already using
them, in and out of school, at rates that outpace the guidance given by schools
as well as the preparedness of teachers (Granström & Oppi, 2025; OECD, 2025;
Vodafone Foundation, 2025). Instead, policymakers should focus on creating
conditions that ensure this integration leads to effective learning. Although the
evidence is still developing, and varies across different (often non-European)
contexts, it provides enough guidance to establish good principles and
precautions. By acting on this evidence, being aware of its limits and continuing
to gather more data, policymakers can guide this process responsibly.

title: Polanco- Jiménez & De Witte (2025/2026)

paragraphs.text:
The study shows a large “tailoring premium”: the generic
AI offered no learning gains, but a curriculum-tailored AI
boosted learning by 0.126 SD. Engagement is key: the
tailored AI increased module completion by 13.2 points,
while the generic AI acted as a “harsh filter”, causing less
confident students to drop out. For motivated students,
long-term retention rose by 0.309 SD. Importantly, the
tailored AI democratised learning, working equally well
across gender, achievement and socioeconomic groups.

paragraphs.text:
Two
5-week
periods

Effectiveness depends on matching the usage pattern to
achievement level. Under compulsory use, low achievers
improved (d = 0.673) while high achievers lost self-
regulated learning (d = −0.477) with no achievement gain.
Under autonomous on-demand access, high achievers
gained (d = 0.378) with no cost to autonomy, while lower
achievers' autonomy declined (d = −0.383). The risk is
"short-term gain, long-term loss": the access structure that
raises attainment for one group erodes self-direction in the
other.

LLMs reduced mental effort (cognitive ease) but also

reasoning without engaging cognitively. The study
identified that the drop in performance was fully mediated
by a reduction in germane cognitive load. Because the

was not cognitively challenging enough to demand deep
self-regulated processing. Strong experimental evidence
for paradox.

title: Abstract

paragraphs.text:
This
report
examines
how
demographic
change
and
technological progress (artificial intelligence - AI) will affect
economic growth and public finances. While declining fertility
rates and increasing longevity are driving population ageing, key
uncertainties remain around the extent of healthy ageing and the
role of migration in mitigating workforce decline. At the same
time, the adoption of AI will likely increase productivity, but
although the precise effects and timing remain uncertain, new
technologies will entail structural changes. Demographic and
productivity trends will therefore pose significant challenges for
labour markets and public finances through multiple channels.
