paragraphs.text: Long-term growth assumptions in the face of artificial intelligence (AI) and demographic change

text: Long-term growth assumptions in the face of artificial intelligence (AI) and demographic change

title: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

paragraphs.text:
This report discusses developments in and projections for demographics and productivity, two
essential factors in projections of GDP per capita and public finances.

Demographic changes driven by low fertility rates and increasing longevity have significant effects on
both the size and age structure of the population, although these effects are partly mitigated by
immigration. Today, fertility rates in the EU are below the replacement level, and there is uncertainty
about future trends, as some recent evidence points to further declines. The upward trend in longevity
is expected to continue, and the main uncertainty concerns the extent of healthy ageing, which is
important both for health expenditure and for the policy option of increasing the retirement age.
Migrant workers have played an important role in many countries in recent years and have contributed
to employment growth. Looking ahead, it may become more difficult to offset declining workforces
through labour migration, as demographic changes are global and many countries are competing for
the same pool of qualified labour.

Generative AI has the potential to affect productivity significantly. However, empirical findings suggest
a positive but moderate short-term effect on productivity, with country-specific impacts depending
on exposure and capacity to adopt the technology. These estimates are based on early evidence,
including surveys of AI use and assumptions about adoption rates, and are therefore subject to
considerable uncertainty. Moreover, they provide limited guidance on the long-run effects. If GenAI, in
a long-run perspective, leads to significantly higher productivity growth rates, it will also be associated
with significant structural changes; hence, such a scenario is not captured by simply increasing an
exogenously given productivity growth rate.

The effects of new technologies on labour markets are more uncertain in a medium-run perspective
and should be seen in the context of demographic factors reducing the relative size of the labour force.
However, both of these developments change the structure of labour demand and supply, thereby
testing the flexibility and adaptability of labour markets. A key question for medium- and long-run
projections is whether the structural unemployment rate increases (or, equivalently, reduces the
structural employment rate). This would have important implications not only for GDP, economic
growth, and income distribution, but also for public finances through lower tax revenues and higher
expenditure on income support and labour market programmes.

Demographic changes have direct implications for public finances via age-dependent spending and the
budget sensitivity to the employment rate. Higher productivity growth has more ambiguous effects
since, on the one hand, it increases revenues, while on the other hand it may also increase expenditures,
as public wages and transfer levels respond to the private wage increases triggered by productivity
growth. In addition, productivity growth may worsen Baumol’s cost disease (explained below) unless
new technologies offer opportunities to increase efficiency and productivity in public service
production and are effectively implemented. The upward trend in age-related expenditures implies an
increase in public employment which, given the relative decline in the workforce, adds to labour market
adjustment challenges.

title: INTRODUCTION

paragraphs.text:
Medium- and long-term projections have become increasingly integral to economic policy planning.
The main purpose is to provide a better planning basis, anticipate needed changes in a timely manner,
and consider policies that can influence future developments. This focus has been institutionalized in
fiscal rules to strengthen the long-term perspective in policy planning, including long-term trajectories
for public finances and fiscal sustainability analyses.

The purpose of such analyses is not to predict specific economic variables at a given point in the future,
but rather to gain insight into possible development paths, and in particular to identify warning signs
if, e.g., public finances are not on a sustainable path. They are a planning tool to guide policymakers on
the need to change economic policies to shape future outcomes. Such forward-looking analyses rely
on a number of assumptions, and it is important to understand their role and how changes in the
assumptions affect trajectories of economic variables.

The starting point for such long-term analyses is the development in economic activity, or value
creation, measured by GDP (gross domestic product) 0F 1 . By definition, GDP can be broken down into
value creation per employed person (or measured in working hours), multiplied by the number of
people employed (total hours worked). Average value creation per employed person (or per hour) is
generally referred to as labour productivity. Labour productivity in turn depends on overall productivity
(total factor productivity) and real capital. From this follows that GDP growth can be decomposed into
effects coming from changes in employment and changes in productivity. The former depends on
demographic factors and labour market institutions and structures, and the latter on development in
knowledge, human capital and technologies etc. and investments increasing capital per worker (capital
deepening).

GDP per capita is a measure of the average level of material living standards in the population. It is
given as GDP per employed times the number of employed relative to the population size. Labour
productivity and the size of the labour force (employment) determine total GDP, while population size
determines GDP per capita. The size and age composition of the population is thus of importance for
the size of the potential labour force and its share of the total population. These basic considerations
point to developments in demographic factors and productivity as essential for growth in GDP and GDP
per capita. These two basic building blocks—demographics and productivity—are also the foundation
for the long-term projections published by the European Commission, for example in the Ageing
Reports and Debt Sustainability Analyses; see, e.g., European Commission (2024, 2025).

As is well documented, significant demographic changes are unfolding as a consequence of declining
fertility rates and increasing longevity. These trend changes reduce the size of the labour force relative
to the population. Since the 1970s, productivity growth has exhibited a declining trend and combining
these two developments points to rather bleak economic prospects. However, recent technological
developments, in particular generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), are expected to have wide-
ranging societal and economic impacts, including effects on productivity growth. Against

this backdrop, this report discusses the macroeconomic implications of demographic change and
GenAI.

The size and age composition of the population is also crucial for public finances. In all countries, there
is a strong age dependency in both expenditures and revenues, although the strength of this

title: PE 784.027 11

paragraphs.text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

title: DEMOGRAPHICS

paragraphs.text:
Large demographic changes are unfolding, driven both by declining fertility rates, increasing longevity
and migration flows. These trends affect both population size and composition, with significant changes
in both the young- and especially old-age dependency ratios. These trends are well known and have
been described in, e.g., Bloom and Canning (2008), European Commission (2023), and United Nations
(2024). For the EU, the share of the population aged 0-19 is projected to decrease from 20% in 2022 to
18% in 2070 and for the share aged 20-64 from 59% to 52%, while the share of the population aged 65+
increases from 21% to 30% and the group aged 80+ from 6% to 13%, European Commission (2023).
While the population size has been steadily growing, the growth has been driven by net migration since
2011; see European Commission (2026a). The following discusses in more detail the future paths of
fertility, mortality, and migration to shed light on the demographic assumptions in long-term analyses
(growth and public finances).

and migration flows. These trends affect both population size and composition, with significant changes

While the population size has been steadily growing, the growth has been driven by net migration since

(growth and public finances).

title: 2.1. Fertility

paragraphs.text:
Fertility has generally been declining and has in many countries fallen below the replacement level of
2.1 children per woman. For the EU, the total fertility rate has declined from about 2.6 in 1960 to 1.5 in
2022, but is projected to increase to 1.6 in 2070, see European Commission (2023).

While the historic declines in fertility can be explained by improvements in living and health conditions
and societal changes, the fall of fertility rates below the reproduction level has raised concerns. The
more recent declines in fertility rates have been attributed to increasing costs of raising children,
changed attitudes towards parenthood and more intensive parenting norms than in the past, see e.g.
Doepke et al. (2023), Goldin (2025), Kearney and Levine (2025), and OECD (2024). These explanatory
factors are not likely to reverse, and this suggests that fertility rates would stay low or even fall further,
see e.g. Kearney and Levine (2025). It is also noteworthy that the decline is also seen in countries which
have pursued "family friendly policies" like the Nordics, see e.g. Hellstrand et al. (2021), and specific
measures aimed at increasing fertility rates in countries like Japan and China have not been successful,
see e.g. Jones (2024).

A permanent decline in fertility causes low frequency changes in the age composition of the population.
First, it decreases the number of children and young (and hence the youth dependency ratio), later the
working age population decreases (which increases both youth and old-age dependency ratios), and
then the number of old (for unchanged mortality) declines (reducing the old-age dependency ratio).
These changes will clearly impact macroeconomic variables and public finances.

This raises the question of whether a double demographic crisis evolves with low fertility rates adding
to preexisting fiscal challenges caused by increasing longevity, or whether it is a mitigating factor
reducing the pressure on public finances, see e.g. Bloom et al. (2025). In policy debates and analyses,
the answer to this question is not clear, since some find that lower fertility increases the pressure on
public finances (see e.g. Darvas et al. (2024)), while others argue that it reduces it (see e.g. the Danish
Economic Council (2024) and the Swedish Fiscal Council (2025)). Looking at public finances in more
detail, the budgetary position may at first improve and then deteriorate, thus leaving the long-run
effect ambiguous. The magnitude and direction of the effect depend on each country's welfare
institutions and policy design, in particular whether welfare arrangements are front-loaded in terms of
care and education offered to children and the young or back-loaded in terms of health care and
pensions offered to the old. If the former, fiscal sustainability may improve when fertility rates decline,
see Andersen (2026). The public finance implications are discussed further in Section 4.

First, it decreases the number of children and young (and hence the youth dependency ratio), later the
working age population decreases (which increases both youth and old-age dependency ratios), and
then the number of old (for unchanged mortality) declines (reducing the old-age dependency ratio).
These changes will clearly impact macroeconomic variables and public finances.
This raises the question of whether a double demographic crisis evolves with low fertility rates adding
to preexisting fiscal challenges caused by increasing longevity, or whether it is a mitigating factor
reducing the pressure on public finances, see e.g. Bloom et al. (2025). In policy debates and analyses,
the answer to this question is not clear, since some find that lower fertility increases the pressure on
public finances (see e.g. Darvas et al. (2024)), while others argue that it reduces it (see e.g. the Danish
Economic Council (2024) and the Swedish Fiscal Council (2025)). Looking at public finances in more
detail, the budgetary position may at first improve and then deteriorate, thus leaving the long-run
effect ambiguous. The magnitude and direction of the effect depend on each country's welfare
institutions and policy design, in particular whether welfare arrangements are front-loaded in terms of
care and education offered to children and the young or back-loaded in terms of health care and
pensions offered to the old. If the former, fiscal sustainability may improve when fertility rates decline,
see Andersen (2026). The public finance implications are discussed further in Section 4.

title: 2.2. Mortality

paragraphs.text:
Longevity is on an upward trend, and the increases have been astonishing, amounting to 2.5 years per
decade for females when assessed in terms of best ‐ practice countries; see Oeppen and Vaupel (2002)
and Vaupel et al. (2021) for an update and discussion on this topic. In 1960 life expectancy at birth in
the EU was 68.3 years for women and 63.2 years for men, 84.2 and 78.6 years, respectively, in 2021,
and projected to be 90.4 and 86.1 years, respectively, in 2070; see European Commission (2023). In
itself, this is an astonishing welfare improvement, but it raises some economic questions concerning
the labour market and the financial sustainability of public finances and pension schemes.

There are ongoing discussions about future developments in longevity, highlighting its dependence on
behavioural, political, epidemiological, and biological factors. Views range from pessimistic
assessments predicting that gains in longevity may level off or even reverse (for example, due to
lifestyle-related factors), to more moderate expectations of continued increases at a slower pace than
in recent decades, and optimistic perspectives anticipating further gains because an upper limit to
longevity has not yet been reached and additional biomedical breakthroughs are expected; see, e.g.,
Utkus and Mitchell (2025). Population projections generally assume that increases in longevity will
gradually level off and that life expectancy will converge across countries.

From both a labour market and public finance perspective, it is critical whether increases in longevity
are accompanied by healthy ageing. A key distinction is between extending life expectancy and adding
healthy years of life, that is, between improvements in mortality and morbidity. Ageing is generally
defined as a deterioration in function (mental and physical capabilities) and an increase in vulnerability.
Although this process is inevitable, it is not straightforward to relate individual capabilities and
opportunities to a specific age, since the ageing process depends on a range of factors, including
material living conditions, advances in health care, lifestyle, and the nature of work.

The concept of healthy ageing is widely used to describe the extent to which increases in longevity are
accompanied by additional years of good health. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines healthy
ageing 2F 3 as “the process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables wellbeing in
older age”. Functional ability refers to the capabilities that enable individuals to be and do what they
value. It encompasses an individual’s intrinsic capacity (their physical and cognitive abilities), relevant
environmental characteristics, and the interaction between the two.

Despite the widespread use of the term, healthy ageing is not straightforward to measure. One
common approach relies on self-reported assessments of health and functional status, while another
focuses on objective indicators such as the prevalence of chronic diseases, disability, hospital
admissions, and healthcare utilization. Each approach has advantages and limitations, and no single
measure fully captures the multidimensional nature of healthy ageing (see, for example, Christensen et
al., 2009; Beltrán-Sánchez et al., 2015).

Chang et al. (2019) develop a metric of age-related morbidity and mortality for 195 countries between
1990 and 2017 to analyse the disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs). They estimate an age-standardized
age-related health burden for each country using the global average of 65-year-olds as the reference
population. While there are large differences across countries, age-standardized age-related disease
rates have decreased over time for all countries between 1990 and 2017. This suggests that the physical
and mental capacity of a person at the age of, say, 65 is significantly larger today than it was 20 or 30
years ago, and this development can be expected to continue. Skirkekk et al. (2022) compute a health-

title: PE 784.027 13

paragraphs.text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

adjusted dependency ratio 3F 4 and compare it to the standard demographic old-age dependency ratios
for 188 countries and find large differences. For the EU, the demographic old-age dependency ratio is
significantly larger than the health-adjusted dependency ratio, suggesting that the demographic old-
age ratio is an imprecise measure for the economic and societal impact of an ageing population and
that it may exaggerate the ageing challenge.

For the present discussion, it is important how increasing longevity affects the ability to postpone
retirement and remain in work, as well as its implications for health expenditures (see section 4).
Healthy ageing makes it possible to increase the size of the labour force and alleviate pressures on
public expenditure. It therefore leaves the option of addressing the increase in the old-age dependency
ratio by raising retirement ages—as many countries have already implemented or are planning to
implement—with positive effects on both labour supply and the sustainability of public finances and
pension systems. Reforms in this area also raise questions of intergenerational distribution regarding
how the gains from higher longevity and the financing burdens are distributed across cohorts.

On the employment issue, recent experience shows that increases in statutory retirement ages are
associated with higher employment. Empirical evidence documents the very strong influence that
statutory retirement ages have on retirement decisions with so-called bunching of retirement ages at
the statutory retirement age; see Blundell et al. (2016), Gruber and Wise (2004), and Börsch-Supan et
al. (2018). Many countries have also experienced rather significant increases in employment rates for
seniors in recent years. On average for EU, the employment rate for the age group 55-64 has increased
from 53.5% in 2016 to 66.4% in 2025 (for women from 47.3% to 60.8%, and for men from 60.1% to 72.3%).
These increases can be interpreted as showing both that many people have the capability of prolonging
work life and that there is a demand for senior workers. It should be noted that these changes cannot
be attributed solely to policy, since some increase in the employment rate of seniors is to be expected
given the positive relationship between education and retirement age. Moreover, an increase in
longevity may also induce individuals to retire later to sustain a reasonable pension (in schemes where
the pension depends on the length of the work life).

title: 2.3. Migration

paragraphs.text:
Migration is an additional important demographic factor. The trend across EU countries has been an
increase in net migration, although with large variations across countries (some experiencing negative
net migration) and time. The share of people born in an EU Member State and living in another has
increased moderately (2014: 4%; 2024: 4.4%), but these aggregate numbers conceal larger gross flows.
Generally, there has been a larger increase in the share of EU working age population born outside the
EU (2014: 8%, 2024: 12%). The intra-EU flows also reflect economic developments, and the larger flow
is from East to West and the EU Member States with the strongest economic development and lowest
unemployment rates, see Kiss et al. (2026). The migration flows into EU depends on political
developments, war and natural catastrophes and migration policies, see e.g. EEAG (2020). The
experience in recent years is that labour immigration is associated with employment growth and thus
does not substitute for domestic labour, see e.g. Kiss et al. (2026).

In a forward-looking perspective, a key question is whether a shrinking workforce can be offset through
labour migration, a policy option currently under discussion in many countries. However, the prospects
for attracting qualified foreign workers are likely to be more limited than recent experience may
suggest. Demographic change is a global phenomenon, and many countries are experiencing declines

title: 14 PE 784.027

paragraphs.text: Long-term growth assumptions in the face of artificial intelligence (AI) and demographic change

in their working-age populations. As a consequence, competition for skilled migrants is intensifying,
while the pool of potential migrants with relevant qualifications is not expanding at a corresponding
rate. Moreover, some net-emigration countries - and others may follow - have introduced policies
aimed at retaining young and highly educated individuals, thereby reducing talent outflows and making
it harder for other countries to attract skilled labour.

It is also important to nuance the economic impact on migrant workers. While immigrant labour adds
to the labour force and thereby increases GDP, the population size also increases, and the effect on
GDP per capita for the incumbent population is less clear. If the average productivity of foreign and
domestic workers is the same, there would not be an effect to a first approximation. A positive effect
requires either that the migrant workers have higher productivity than the average incumbent work
force or that there is a positive synergy effect from a more diverse workforce 4F 5 .

It is well established that employment rates differ significantly among immigrants depending on the
reason for migrating (asylum, family reunification, work, studies), as would be expected. Labour
migrants who bring specialized skills can often enter the labour market directly, while refugees arriving
from different cultural backgrounds may face greater difficulties in labour market integration. Ensuring
high employment rates among refugees (and family reunification migrants) is particularly challenging,
and employment rates for this group are generally below those of the native population. Employment
rates are typically higher for men than for women and tend to increase with the duration of stay, but
they do not reach the levels observed for the native population. Many factors may explain these
differences, including qualifications, norms, culture, and economic incentives. The evidence on policies
aimed at increasing employment rates for these groups is mixed; see, e.g., Arendt et al. (2022).

The public finance implications of immigration are closely linked to its effects on labour market
outcomes. The reason is straightforward: non-employed individuals pay less in taxes than those in
employment and typically receive some form of public transfer. The long-term effects on public
finances are more complex, however, as they also depend on factors such as family reunification and
the labour market performance of descendants. For refugees, the same labour market performance as
that of labour migrants cannot generally be expected, and entry into employment may remain difficult
over time due to lack of qualifications, cultural and social norms, and adverse social conditions
(including trauma). This is one reason why many countries have adopted more restrictive immigration
policies.

The heterogeneity among migrants implies that the composition of the immigrant population is crucial
for its economic effects, making it impossible to draw general, unconditional conclusions about the
impact of immigration on either the labour market or public finances. A general trend is that countries
are adopting stricter rules for asylum seekers and family reunification, while at the same time facilitating
entry for labour migrants.

To sum up: Demographic changes driven by low (and possibly declining) fertility rates and increasing
longevity have significant effects on both the size and age structure of the population. This, in turn, will
impact the labour market and public finances requiring policy responses. Migrant workers have played
an important role in many countries in the recent past and have contributed to employment growth.
Looking ahead, it may become more difficult to mitigate declining workforces through worker
migration, since demographic changes are global and many countries are competing for qualified
labour.

5
For an analysis, see e.g. Olovsson et al. (2025). Empirical evidence points to worker immigrants having a positive effect on output and
productivity, while this is not the case for other types of immigrants, see e.g. IMF (2020).

title: PE 784.027 15

paragraphs.text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

title: TECHNOLOGY AND PRODUCTIVITY – AI

paragraphs.text:
Productivity growth is the source of increases in output per worker and thus a fundamental driver of
GDP growth and material living standards. The historical decline in productivity growth, combined with
population ageing, has raised concerns that future growth rates may remain low, leading to economic
stagnation; see, e.g., Jones (2022). This forms the backdrop for the current discussion of whether
generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) represents the next industrial revolution capable of reversing
this trend and boosting productivity growth.

Generative AI refers to technology that can generate new content in the form of text, audio, images, or
video. GenAI can not only collect, organise, and systematise large amounts of information, but also
solve problems and draw conclusions. GenAI can therefore affect non-routine and cognitive jobs,
including some that currently require high levels of qualifications. Examples include credit assessment
and lending, the resolution of legal questions, and medical diagnostics. Nordhaus (2021) formulate this
as a scenario in which it is possible to “increase productivity and breadth to the extent that human
labour and intelligence will become superfluous”.

General-purpose technologies like GenAI can have wide-ranging consequences since it may affect
productivity across multiple sectors. Historically, all major technological changes have been associated
with both job destruction and job creation and large changes across different sectors in the economy,
see e.g. Hötte et al. (2023). There is, however, an ongoing debate about whether GenAI represents
simply the latest addition to a long sequence of technological advances since the industrial revolution,
or whether it is qualitatively different and therefore likely to have more far-reaching societal and
economic implications, see e.g. Aghion et al, (2019), Nordhaus (2021), Trammel and Korinek (2023),
and Jones (2026).

The adoption of generative AI is still at an early stage—and the technology itself continues to evolve—
and it is therefore premature to draw firm conclusions about its qualitative and quantitative effects.
The diffusion of new technologies takes time, and their initial impact is often concentrated in the
development and deployment of the technology itself, which tends to be associated with employment
growth, while adoption and the resulting structural changes unfold more gradually. Effects arising at
the firm level are only slowly reflected in official statistics. This pattern is often referred to as the “J-
curve effect,” whereby productivity may initially decline during the implementation phase before the
full potential of the technology is realized and productivity increases; see, e.g., Brynjolfsson (2021).
Until data are available over a sufficiently long period, it remains difficult to distinguish temporary
fluctuations from trend changes in productivity growth.

title: 3.1. Productivity

paragraphs.text:
GenAI is an all-purpose technology that could have a positive effect on productivity, lead to
reallocations between labour and capital, and affect many jobs and sectors. The breadth and flexibility
of its applications make its implications uncertain, and the impact also varies across firms and sectors.
What has been observed so far is a spike in AI-related investments, but it is too early to draw firm
conclusions about the wider economic impacts (see e.g. OECD (2024)). GenAI is being explored and
introduced in many different contexts, revealing both its potential and its shortcomings (e.g. false
answers, hallucinations, and the propagation of fake news), as well as its threats (e.g. cyberattacks,
biological warfare, and autonomous weapons).

On the specific effects on productivity, some initial studies by Goldman Sachs Research (see Briggs
and Kodnani (2023)) and McKinsey (see McKinsey (2023)) estimated that AI over the medium run could
increase productivity by 1.5 percentage points (pp) and up to 3.3 pp per year; however more recent

assessments find the effects to be smaller, though still positive. Empirical research on the effect of
GenAI on productivity is rapidly expanding 5F 6 .

Acemoglu (2025) assesses the macroeconomic effects of AI from a task-based approach, combining
measures of the importance of AI-exposed sectors for GDP, the share of tasks for which it is cost-
saving to use AI, the average cost savings from AI adoption, and the labour share. Total factor
productivity growth is estimated for the United States to increase by about 0.1 pp per year over the
coming 10 years, but the effect may be smaller when considering that the early evidence is influenced
by easy-to-learn tasks. AI will widen the gap between capital and labour income, but it may not increase
income inequality as much as previous automation technologies because its impact is more equally
distributed across the income distribution.

Bergaud (2024) uses the same method and finds that TFP growth may increase by 0.29 pp per year
over a 10-year horizon, for the euro area. Similarly, Misch et al. (2025) find that productivity gains for
Europe as a whole are likely to be modest, at around 1 percent cumulatively over five years. Aghion and
Bunel (2024) find for the United States, using a method that draws a parallel between the AI revolution
and past technological revolutions, an increase in aggregate productivity growth of between 0.8 and
1.3 pp per year over the next decade. Using the same method as in Acemoglu (2025), but based on
different empirical analyses, the median estimate of additional annual total factor productivity (TFP)
growth is about 0.7 pp.

Filippucci et al. (2025) also build on the approach in Acemoglu (2025) but apply it at the sectoral level
and then aggregate the results to arrive at the macroeconomic effects for the G7 countries. The
aggregate labour productivity growth is assessed to be 0.4-1.3 pp in countries with high AI exposure
and adoption e.g. United States and United Kingdom. The range is 0.2 to 0.8 pp in countries with less
exposure and adaptation, e.g. Italy, Japan.

Additional effects arise via capital deepening, as GenAI boosts investments, which in turn increases the
capital-labour ratio. A higher capital-labour ratio, in turn, increases GDP per capita. One consequence
is the rise of capital income relative to wage income, which directly affects the functional distribution
of income but also has implications for public finance, as discussed below.

In summary, the empirical findings suggest a positive but moderate short-term effect of GenAI on
productivity, with country-specific impacts depending on exposure to and capacity to adopt the
technology. These estimates are based on early evidence, including surveys of AI use and assumptions
about adoption rates, and are therefore subject to considerable uncertainty. Moreover, they provide
limited guidance on the long-run effects. While there is growing evidence that GenAI can raise
productivity (through both total factor productivity and capital deepening), it remains difficult to
translate these findings into assumptions suitable for medium- and long-term analyses. A useful
approach is therefore to conduct scenario analyses, as in European Commission (2023), which
considers alternative assumptions for productivity growth. If GenAI, in a long-run perspective, GenAi
leads to significantly higher productivity growth rates, it will also likely be associated with significant
structural changes; hence, such a scenario is not captured by simply increasing an exogenously given
productivity growth rate.

title: 3.2. Labour market adjustments and structural employment

paragraphs.text:
Even when productivity gains are driven by general-purpose technologies, their effects differ across
sectors and occupations. Labour market adjustments are necessary both to realize the benefits of new
technologies and to accommodate the reallocations they trigger. New technologies may be substitutes
for labour but may also complement labour and hence benefit some occupations while disadvantaging
others. A particular concern regarding GenAI is that it could become a source of jobless growth, as it
has the potential to substitute for tasks and occupations with a substantial cognitive content.

The effects of new technology and globalisation on labour markets can broadly be divided into three
categories: skill bias, task bias, and artificial intelligence (GenAI). Historically, technological advances
have been associated with a skill bias in labour demand. Job creation has tended to concentrate in high-
skill occupations, while job destruction has primarily affected those in low-skill occupations. For the
latter groups, this has led to lower wages and/or employment, so the adjustment burden has largely
fallen on those already in weaker labour market positions. Conversely, highly qualified workers have
enjoyed better wage and employment prospects. The process driven by skill bias can be seen as a race
between education and technology, since an increase in the skill level of the labour force can mitigate
the effects of skill-biased technological developments on the level and structure of employment, as
highlighted by Tinbergen (1975) and supported by empirical evidence; for discussion and references,
see e.g. Deming (2023).

New technologies related to digitalization and automation may produce effects different from the
traditional skill-bias mechanism. A distinction can be made between routine and non-routine jobs.
“Routine jobs” can relatively easily be taken over by machines or robots and include both
manual/physical and cognitive/mental tasks 6F 7 . A job is routine if its tasks are well defined, unlike non-
routine jobs requiring flexibility, creativity, problem-solving, and human interaction. Automation, and
digitalisation (and offshoring) in particular affect routine jobs, and although this is not clearly correlated
with income/skill levels, the effects tend to be largest for a “middle group” in the wage distribution.
Routine-based technological change is thus considered a main reason for the relative decline of
employment in middle-wage occupations—so-called job polarization—in Europe and the United States
between 1980 and 2010; see e.g. Goos et al. (2014).

GenAI makes it relevant to distinguish jobs both in terms of the degree of routineness and their
cognitive content, yielding four broad categories: non-cognitive routine jobs, non-cognitive non-
routine jobs, cognitive routine jobs, and cognitive non-routine jobs. GenAI differs from skill- and task-
bias mechanisms in that it particularly affects routine cognitive jobs.

The debate on the labour market consequences of GenAI often focuses on which jobs are most exposed
to the new technology, and measures of such exposure are often used in policy debates as an indicator
of the labour market consequences, see e.g. Gimbel et al. (2026) and OECD (2026). However, exposure
may be both negative (substitution) or positive (complementarity). This leads to a two-by-two
classification with low or high exposure to GenAI and substitutability and complementarity with labour;
see e.g. Cazzaniga et al. (2024). The impact can thus vary between negative, neutral, and positive across
occupations and sectors. In cases of high exposure and substitutability, future job opportunities are
slim, and conversely with high exposure and complementarity. It should be noted that these measures
are focused on existing jobs and occupations and hence do not include the new types of jobs that may
arise as a result of these new technologies.

7
US evidence shows that manual routine jobs have long been declining, while cognitive routine jobs, after a period of growth, have also
begun to decline; see Restrepo (2024).

paragraphs.text: Long-term growth assumptions in the face of artificial intelligence (AI) and demographic change

New technologies create not only new possibilities but also new demands, which in turn are a source
of job creation. Moreover, the economy and the labour market are affected by relative scarcity. To the
extent that GenAI boosts productivity for certain products and services—and thus their supply—their
prices decline. If the price elasticity is not large, demand shifts to other products and services, e.g.
services intensive in human interaction that cannot easily be substituted by AI and have a high-income
elasticity (Wagner’s law). This is related to the so-called Baumol cost disease, which predicts that in
activities/sectors for which it is difficult to increase productivity (as for some services), the relative
price will increase and (provided demand is not sufficiently price elastic), therefore constituting an
increasing share of the economy and employing a larger share of the labour force. Hence, as argued by
Aghion et al. (2019), “growth may be constrained not by what we are good at but rather by what is
essential and yet hard to improve”. Alongside growth, there has been a trend increase in the size (both
absolutely and relatively) of the service sector, both private and public, and this trend may be expected
to continue. Extrapolating from the historical experience, this does not support the job pessimism often
associated with new technologies (GenAI). The bottom line is that pessimistic views regarding the
employment implications of GenAI are not broadly supported, although it is evident that the technology
is driving significant labour market adjustments.

GenAI – like technological advances in the past - creates both winners and losers in the labour market.
The challenge for labour market adjustment has both a short-run and a long-run dimension. In the short
run, the key issue is retraining and reskilling workers to facilitate transitions between jobs. Experience
shows that adjustments to technology-induced changes in labour demand can be frictional and may
lead to mismatches, with simultaneous vacancies for certain types of jobs and unemployment among
workers with other skill profiles, see e.g. Autor (2022). While technological change in the past has
largely benefited the upper part of the wage distribution, GenAI differs in that it may also affect highly
educated groups whose specific competencies become obsolete. However, the adjustment process
evolves over time, as workers’ reservation wages and job expectations need to adapt, and jobs and
occupations adapts to the new technologies. Traditionally, mismatch problems have affected young
workers and older workers approaching retirement most strongly. This pattern may change, since
younger generations are generally more familiar with and better trained in the use of AI than older
cohorts. Conversely, some highly exposed and potentially substitutable occupations serve as entry-
level positions for highly educated young workers. The disappearance or shrinking of such jobs may
reduce opportunities for on-the-job learning, thereby hampering future career progression and labour
mobility, see e.g. Cazzaniga et al. (2024). On the other hand, growth in service sectors may benefit
senior workers more if experience is more valuable in these sectors.

The race between technology and education is thus changing. The long-run challenge concerns
education. However, the future role and design of education in an AI-intensive economy remain highly
uncertain. It is still unclear which occupations will expand, how educational programmes should adapt,
and to what extent AI itself will transform both the content and methods of learning. However, this
uncertainty and the increased need for adjustments (also in the perspective of longer working lives due
to increasing longevity) point to the danger of making education too specialized and job-specific; a
broader educational background generally provides better opportunities for retraining and job finding,
including transitions to positions below previous qualification levels.

GenAI may also have implications for public finances through several channels. First, a shift in the
functional income distribution from labour to capital income reduces tax revenue, since average tax
rates are higher for wage income than for capital income. In 2024, the share of tax revenue from social
contributions and income taxation constituted about 57% of total tax revenue, while capital income
taxes contributed only 8% on average for EU countries; see European Commission (2026b). Secondly,
a decrease in structural employment over a prolonged period will lead to a deterioration of public

finances. Thirdly, if AI is associated with increasing inequality, the need for more redistributive policies
may rise. Finally, AI may help mitigate Baumol’s cost disease and thus reduce pressure on public
expenditures; see Section 4.

To sum up, the key question for medium and long-run projections is whether AI will increase the
structural unemployment rate (or, equivalently, reduce the structural employment rate). This would
have important implications not only for GDP, economic growth, the income distribution, but also for
public finances through lower tax revenues and higher expenditure on income support and labour
market programmes. While technological progress ultimately tends to create new tasks and
employment opportunities, the transition may be prolonged and difficult.

title: 3.3. Productivity and demographics

paragraphs.text:
Older people will not only make up an increasing share of the population; the composition of
employment is also shifting so that older workers account for a growing share of the labour force.
Standard findings point to an inverted U-shaped relationship between age and productivity—initially
increasing with age and then declining—though with large differences across occupations. This
distribution implies that an ageing workforce tends to reduce overall productivity. Aiyar et al. (2016)
find that an ageing workforce, through this effect, will reduce TFP growth by 0.2 pp over the coming
two decades. An analysis from the OECD finds that the increase in the old-age dependency ratio and
the lower employment rate of older workers will reduce GDP per capita growth by about 0.25
percentage points per year over the next three decades, see André et al. (2024). Higher employment
rates among older workers, including later retirement, could reduce this drag to about 0.1 percentage
points per year. Consequently, productivity growth will need to increase to offset the adverse effects
of demographic change.

The above discussion considers demographic developments solely in terms of age serving as a proxy
for mental and physical capacity. However, developments in life expectancy and healthy ageing
challenge this simple age-based perspective. The relation between demographics and productivity can
alternatively be approached by considering a forward-looking, prospective measure based on expected
remaining life expectancy. Empirical evidence shows a close relationship at the cohort level between
remaining life expectancy and a range of health conditions, physical and cognitive capacities, etc., see
also Section 2 and 4 on healthy ageing. Forecasts based on remaining life expectancy may therefore
provide better estimates of how ageing will affect the economy than projections based purely on age.
An empirical study based on data from 145 countries covering the period 1950–2015, Kotschy and
Bloom (2023), conclude that average growth in GDP per capita, in a hypothetical scenario without
demographic change, would be 2.5% per year from 2020 to 2050. Using a retrospective approach to
demographic developments, growth due to demographic change falls to 1.7% per year, whereas with
the prospective approach it is 2.1%. While the traditional approach suggests a reduction in growth of
0.8 percentage points, this is roughly halved when it accounts for the fact that age is not a good
indicator of physical and cognitive capacity across generations.

However, the relationship between age and productivity is complex and must also be considered in
relation to specific occupations and how the nature of work changes over time. In physically demanding
jobs, there will generally, from a certain age, be a negative relationship between age and productivity.
However, this is also mitigated by technological substitution for heavy physical workloads. In other
areas, where experience and social insight are highly important, no clear relation between age and
productivity may exist. Moreover, structural changes in the economy also includes a growing service
sector in which social skills and experience matter, and this may lead to different relationships than
those observed historically.

title: 20 PE 784.027

paragraphs.text: Long-term growth assumptions in the face of artificial intelligence (AI) and demographic change

The change in the age composition of the population may be an additional driver of such structural
changes. Elderly people possess substantial purchasing power, and it may increase due to the build-up
of funded pension schemes, combined with a desire to maintain their independence, retain control over
their own lives, and remain active. This creates demand for innovation and the development of assistive
technologies in a broad sense, helping to make everyday life easier and more independent. This trend
is associated with the so ‐ called “Internet of Things,” that is, products containing computing units that
enable connections and interaction within a person’s network, as well as easy access to information
exchange. Examples include internet ‐ connected, voice ‐ activated devices that facilitate both physical
and cognitive activities (although they also raise “big brother”-type surveillance concerns). In other
words, technological progress holds considerable potential for productivity gains and for
improvements in the living conditions of older people.

Technological developments thus feed back to the labour market through different channels. New
technologies will enable longer working lives by reducing physically demanding and strenuous work,
and it will offer new possibilities in healthcare and elderly care (welfare technologies), which can
strengthen personal autonomy and control over one’s own life. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2022), for
example, argue that AI technology will free up much of the labour that will be needed as populations
age.

Productivity may depend on demographics through other channels. Demographic changes imply a
relatively smaller labour force (and possibly an absolute decline), which, all else being equal, tends to
allocate labour according to its scarcity, which in turn leads to higher wages and lower returns on
capital. This is one of the main reasons why real returns on financial assets (shares and bonds) have
been declining and are also expected to remain low going forward. It follows that as labour becomes
scarcer, wages will increase. This strengthens incentives for innovation, particularly in areas with
growing demand and where recruitment challenges may be especially pronounced. In this way, it can
act as a driver of rising productivity. Acemoglu et al. (2026) present empirical evidence that
labour ‐ saving technologies respond elastically to labour scarcity (especially the scarcity of younger
workers), and this may fully offset or even reverse the negative direct effects of a shrinking labour
force. Opposite effects may be released from an increase in the service sector, since it exhibits lower
productivity growth than other sectors.

To sum up, while demographics tend to reduce the labour force, the effects of new technologies on
labour demand are more uncertain in a medium-run perspective, and the former effect is likely to be
dominant within a realistic policy time frame. However, both developments change the structure of
labour demand and supply, thereby testing the flexibility and adaptability of labour markets.

act as a driver of rising productivity. Acemoglu et al. (2026) present empirical evidence that
labour ‐ saving technologies respond elastically to labour scarcity (especially the scarcity of younger
workers), and this may fully offset or even reverse the negative direct effects of a shrinking labour
force. Opposite effects may be released from an increase in the service sector, since it exhibits lower
productivity growth than other sectors.
To sum up, while demographics tend to reduce the labour force, the effects of new technologies on
labour demand are more uncertain in a medium-run perspective, and the former effect is likely to be
dominant within a realistic policy time frame. However, both developments change the structure of
labour demand and supply, thereby testing the flexibility and adaptability of labour markets.

title: PE 784.027 21

paragraphs.text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

title: PUBLIC FINANCES – DEMOGRAPHICS AND PRODUCTIVITY

paragraphs.text:
Long-term analyses of public finances generally follow the principle of analysing trajectories for the
economy and public finances triggered by changing demographics, productivity increases, and other
trends, assuming unchanged policies. The purpose is to provide information for policy planning and not
to assess whether current policies are optimal or to evaluate specific policy proposals for the future.
The basic question is thus: what are the possible trajectories for the economy under unchanged policies,
to assess both their consequences and whether their financial basis is viable, or in other words, is fiscal
sustainability ensured? This, in turn, is a starting point for discussions of both existing policies and the
need to change policies to affect future developments. This ‘no-policy-change’ assumption is also
made by European Commission (2023, 2024).

It is important to stress that the “unchanged policy” assumption does not reflect the most realistic
scenario, as policy changes are to be expected, but it serves to clarify the consequences of current
policies as an input in discussing policy changes. Related, there are many reasons why public finances
may be affected on both, the revenue and the expenditure side in the future (e.g. advances in health
care driving health expenditures), but the perspective is that such changes would have to be addressed
by future generations; if there is a desire to expand health care, there is also an obligation to find ways
to finance it.

The following section discusses the public finance implications of demographic and productivity
changes. It should be noted that there are additional expenditure pressures not captured by the
“unchanged policy” assumption, including both defence and energy (to reduce reliance on imported
energy), as well as environmental and climate challenges, see e.g. Andersen (2024). There are also
potential new revenue sources, e.g. CO2 taxes. These are important issues, but they are not addressed
here. Another key issue in most countries is the adequacy and financial viability of pension systems,
and the need to strengthen private pension savings. The influence of demographics on public
expenditures is included in the analyses of fiscal sustainability via the “unchanged policy” assumption,
but changes in the structure of pension systems are not, and they are not discussed here.

title: 4.1. Age-related spending

paragraphs.text:
On average across EU countries, the so-called costs of ageing (comprising the effects of demographic
change on public expenditures for pensions, health care, long-term care, and education at current
standards) are projected to grow faster than GDP, see European Commission (2024). The total public
expenditure share of GDP is expected to increase by about 1.2 pp between 2022 and 2070 (ranging
from around −2 to 10 pp of GDP), with health care and long-term care accounting for on average about
two thirds of the total increase, see European Commission (2024).

In particular, the projections of future health and old-age costs raise important questions. While there
is, on the one hand, a clear relationship between expenditures and age (particularly pronounced for the
60+ age group), there are, on the other hand, effects of healthy ageing, which may reduce costs (or
postpone health expenditures to higher ages), see also the discussion above.

In the literature, there is a discussion of the so-called “red herring hypothesis” and the steeping effect,
see e.g., Buchner and Wasem (2006), Felder and Werblow (2008), and Kollerup et al. (2022). The former
argues that increasing longevity implies a postponement of the age at which morbidity appears and
thus the need for health care. This implies that time to death (the remaining time until death) , and not
age per se, is most important for health needs, and making this assumption reduces average health
costs at given ages (although there is still an effect of more people reaching higher ages). The steeping
effect refers to the basic relationship between age and need for health- and old age care, and that this

title: 22 PE 784.027

paragraphs.text: Long-term growth assumptions in the face of artificial intelligence (AI) and demographic change

relation may become steeper. While longevity is increasing, extension of life implies a larger prevalence
of other age-related, but non-mortal, diseases (e.g., diabetes). There is mixed evidence on the
importance of these two factors, but importantly they are not mutually exclusive. However, empirical
studies suggest that the steeping effect is dominating in net-terms, see e.g. Kallestrup-Lamb et al.
(2026). Moreover, productivity increases in life sciences may generally offer new and better treatments
and raise expectations of what the healthcare system can deliver. While this may be important in a
forward-looking perspective, it is an effect beyond the “unchanged policy” assumption.
However, service production in general is expected to have lower than average productivity growth.
Old-age care is an example of an area where it has historically been difficult to increase efficiency and
productivity. It is a prime example of the so-called Baumol cost disease. Since such care activities are
labour-intensive, and wages for care personnel, for recruitment reasons, must follow general wage
developments (or more, given increasing demand) driven by general productivity growth, unit costs
are increasing over time. While the Baumol cost disease affects service activities intensive in human
interactions, it becomes a particular problem for the public sector, since it in most countries assumes a
key responsibility for providing services such as child and old-age care and education, which are
particularly affected.

Finally, most analyses of the trajectory for public revenues and expenditures focus on the financing
issue. While this is the key question for fiscal sustainability analyses, it is important to recognise that
there is also a real ‐ economy dimension to these projections. Increasing public expenditures reflect both
transfers (e.g. pensions) and public consumption (e.g. health and old ‐ age care and education). The
flipside to the latter is public employment, and public consumption has a high service content and
therefore tends to be labour ‐ intensive. Returning to the above-mentioned analysis of the ageing costs,
the increase in the expenditure ratio of 1.2 pp of GDP between 2022 and 2070 can be decomposed as
follows (albeit with large cross-country differences): (i) an increase in pension expenditures of 0.4 pp,
(ii) an increase in health care expenditures of 0.4 pp, (iii) an increase in old-age care expenditures of
0.8 pp, and (iv) a reduction in education expenditures of 0.5 pp, see European Commission (2024).
Hence, expenditures on health care, old-age care, and education increase by about 0.7 pp of GDP in
total. This implies an increase in public employment (and also its composition), to be realised in a labour
market where the labour force is shrinking. Implicitly, this assumes a decline in total private-sector
employment. The required adjustment for this reallocation is likely to involve labour market frictions
and mismatch problems. and is therefore a policy challenge.

title: 4.2. Fiscal sustainability and GDP growth

paragraphs.text:
Higher productivity growth is essential for the development of material living conditions, but what are
the effects on public finances and fiscal sustainability?

Higher growth implies higher income and thus, for a given taxation system, an increase in tax revenue.
However, there are also effects on the expenditure side. Higher productivity growth results in higher
wages in the private sector (the primary channel through which productivity growth is transmitted in
the economy). In the medium to long run, it must be expected that public sector wages grow
proportionally—otherwise, the public sector would face recruitment problems (especially since ageing
increases public sector labour demand, see above). Since wage expenditures constitute the larger part
of public consumption spending, these expenditures increase alongside productivity growth in the
private sector (for an unchanged level of public employment). The other major expenditure item is
social transfers. If all types of income transfers adjust to wage developments (through either explicit
indexation or discretionary changes) to preserve income levels and avoid an increase in income
inequality, total expenditures on the social safety net will also increase proportionally with private

title: PE 784.027 23

paragraphs.text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

sector productivity 7F 8 . In short, unless it is politically acceptable to either reduce public employment or
increase income inequality, higher productivity growth in the private sector may affect public sector
revenues and expenditures proportionally. Growing the pie does not necessarily improve public
finances.

However, there are channels through which growth may worsen public finances. The starting point of
fiscal sustainability analyses is to project public revenues and expenditures for unchanged policies,
which in turn include current standards for welfare services like child and old-age care, education,
healthcare, etc. as discussed, these areas are labour-intensive, and human interaction is a core part of
the activity being subject to Baumol’s cost disease. While this problem is shared by both private and
public services, it poses particularly severe challenges for the public sector, since users/citizens are not
directly induced to make substitutions to the same extent as they are for private services that become
relatively more expensive over time.

Baumol cost disease may be muted by digitalization and GenAI. Digitalization has already resulted in
“productivity increases” in public administration, and GenAI may allow productivity increases more
broadly, not only in public administration but also in core activities—for example, AI ‐ assisted
diagnostics and triage in healthcare, personalized and adaptive learning tools in education, and
decision-support systems in social services. Technological changes may also affect citizens directly.
Digital technologies can increase autonomy and make it possible to substitute relatively high-cost care
inputs with technology ‐ enabled support. The evidence is strongest for telehealth/telecare, remote
monitoring, medication ‐ adherence technologies, and some socially assistive robotics.

An issue of implementation arises both in relation to incentives in the public sector to adopt new
technologies and from a user/citizen perspective. Budgeting rules may not give public institutions an
incentive to introduce cost ‐ reducing technologies (for unchanged standards) if this leads to lay ‐ offs
and budget reductions. Similarly, users may not find the substitution attractive. While it is a virtue of
public provision of services such as health and old-age care that there is no, or only limited, user
payment, it also implies that users do not observe the price and therefore have little incentive to
substitute towards new solutions. This contrasts with privately purchased services, where rising prices
and technological developments may create incentives and opportunities for substitution. Consider
two examples: social interaction and assistance with daily activities. Elderly care is not only about
meeting basic physical needs; it also has an important social dimension through regular contact and
interaction. Although older people would often prefer to communicate with family and friends, this is
not always possible. In such cases, care workers may partly fill this role, although they are not a perfect
substitute. Modern technologies enable online communication with family and friends. While virtual
contact is not a perfect substitute for face ‐ to ‐ face interaction, it may provide a more meaningful
alternative than relying solely on interactions with care personnel. Technology can also help older adults
manage everyday tasks, such as dressing themselves or remembering to take medication. By
supporting autonomy in daily activities, these innovations are welfare improving and also cost saving.
Of course, technology may also substitute for human interactions, lowering costs but also welfare.

8
While transfers are not necessarily formally indexed to wages in all countries, the key issue is whether they are, over time, adjusted
discretely to reflect general developments in wages and incomes. Assuming that transfers are adjusted by less than wages implies that
they, over time, decline relative to average income and that poverty rates increase (given standard poverty metrics based on median
income). In the Ageing Report, minimum pensions are assumed to be indexed to average wage developments; see European Commission
(2024, p. 95). For example, old-age care cash benefits are generally indexed to GDP per capita, while unit costs for in-kind transfers are
indexed to GDP per hour worked; see European Commission (2024, p. 105).

title: 24 PE 784.027

paragraphs.text: Long-term growth assumptions in the face of artificial intelligence (AI) and demographic change

Hence, organisational reforms (including budget reforms to ensure a supportive incentive structure) to
increase efficiency and productivity in public service production are important, and new technologies
may provide new opportunities for productivity gains in the provision of some types of services.

Finally, productivity growth and thus GDP growth affect the growth-corrected rate of return, which is
the relevant discount factor in sustainability analysis. Higher growth reduces, other things being equal,
the growth-corrected rate of return. A decline in the discount rate has an ambiguous effect on the fiscal
sustainability indicator, increasing the weight placed on developments in the near future and
decreasing the weight placed on developments in the distant future (see Andersen (2025)). If the
primary balance shows a trend toward deterioration, a decline in the discount rate worsens the
sustainability indicator, since the future receives a higher weight in the present value calculation, while
the opposite is the case if there is a trend toward improvement in the primary balance. If the
productivity increase is a global phenomenon, as is most likely, it should also be expected to raise the
rate of return (in a standard setting, the real rate of return increases with productivity growth). Hence,
the growth-corrected rate of return does not decline one-for-one with an increase in the growth rate
and may even remain unchanged.

text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

title: CONCLUDING REMARKS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

paragraphs.text:
Medium- and long-run projections are, by definition, associated with uncertainty. The aim is not to make
precise forecasts for particular variables at particular points in time in the future, but rather to inform
decision-makers about the trajectories the economy may follow and the need or desirability of policy
changes to alter those trajectories. Such analyses therefore provide guidance on the direction in which
the economy is likely to evolve in the absence of policy initiatives, as well as on the order of magnitude
of key variables. While discussions tend to focus on the main scenario, such analyses also typically
consider alternative scenarios to assess the robustness of the main conclusions, and thereby the
uncertainty associated with the projections.

Whether uncertainty regarding medium- to long-run developments is greater today than in the past
remains an open question. However, there are clear sources of uncertainty related to demographic
trends (in particular fertility), technological developments (notably the effects of GenAI), climate and
environmental challenges, and geopolitical developments. This underscores the importance of
considering alternative scenarios.

This paper has focused on the consequences of demographic developments and new technologies
(GenAI). While there is a tendency in policy debates to discuss these issues under the heading of
“problems”, it is important to keep in mind that the underlying changes expand the opportunity set.
Individuals can be expected to live longer and in better health, while productivity growth makes
improvements in material living standards possible. Options that were not available in the past are thus
becoming feasible. The policy challenge is to adjust policies and facilitate economic and social
adaptation to these changes to reap their benefits in the best possible way, given societal objectives.

Demographic changes (fertility and longevity) and technology (GenAI) simultaneously affect economic
developments, including productivity, employment, and public finances. While GenAI may increase
productivity, population ageing tends to have the opposite effect. Although it is likely that the former
effect dominates, the empirical evidence on the magnitude of these effects remains uncertain.
Sensitivity analyses presenting projections under alternative productivity growth assumptions
therefore remain a useful way to illustrate how changes in productivity growth may affect projections.
New technologies are also associated with structural change, implying that the potential effects of
GenAI may not be adequately captured by changes in aggregate productivity growth alone.

The structural employment level is important for potential output but also essential for public finances.
GenAI is often discussed from the perspective of concern about the future of work: will there be enough
jobs? Ageing populations, however, raise the opposite concern: will there be a shortage of labour? The
obvious question is whether these two trends will balance each other out, but equally importantly,
simple projections of labour demand and supply focusing on the aggregate effect may overlook
important adjustment mechanisms, including incentives to adopt new technologies (labour-saving
technologies) and to expand the labour force through postponed retirement, made possible by
increasing longevity (and healthy ageing).

This points to labour market policies as being essential, both to increase the labour force and to ensure
adaptability and flexibility. To increase employment rates, increases in the statutory retirement age are
an obvious option, made possible by healthy ageing. Experience also shows that this is a rather effective
instrument, since it essentially targets core workers (already in jobs) to extend their working careers.
Increasing employment rates for other groups is more difficult, especially for marginalized groups. The
scope for doing so differs markedly across EU countries. In some countries, employment rates for men
and women are on par, while in others there are significant differences. Likewise, there are differences
in NEET rates (young people who are neither in employment, education, nor training). Increasing

an obvious option, made possible by healthy ageing. Experience also shows that this is a rather effective
instrument, since it essentially targets core workers (already in jobs) to extend their working careers.
Increasing employment rates for other groups is more difficult, especially for marginalized groups. The
scope for doing so differs markedly across EU countries. In some countries, employment rates for men
and women are on par, while in others there are significant differences. Likewise, there are differences
in NEET rates (young people who are neither in employment, education, nor training). Increasing

employment rates will contribute not only to the workforce and GDP per capita but also improve public
finances and reduce income inequality.

However, the labour market response is not only a quantitative issue concerning the overall supply and
demand for labour. There is also an important qualitative dimension. New technologies are associated
with both job destruction and job creation, while ageing changes the structure of labour demand
through increasing demand for services, including health and old-age care. The adjustment challenges
for labour markets are therefore larger, and mismatch problems may arise. Historical experience shows
that job pessimism has not been vindicated in the medium to long run, but also that there can be
prolonged periods of high unemployment due to frictions and barriers to adjustment in the labour
market. This is a major source of uncertainty in projections of potential output and public finances over
a medium-run horizon.

Long-run analyses typically assume “unchanged policies”, not because this is considered realistic, but
because the purpose is to understand the implications of current policies when assessing the need for
and desirability of policy change. There are many reasons to anticipate future policy changes. For
example, productivity growth and the associated increase in incomes are likely to raise the demand for
services, including those provided by the public sector, since the income elasticity of demand is high
for many services, a phenomenon often referred to as the ‘Wagner effect’. This would add to
expenditure pressures but arguably falls outside the scope of an “unchanged policies” assumption. If
future generations or policymakers wish to accommodate such changes, they will also have to identify
ways of financing them. The same applies to advances in, for example, life sciences that offer new and
improved treatments for various illnesses. Likewise, higher living standards are likely to lead to shorter
working hours, as has been observed historically, which in turn would reduce public revenues under
unchanged tax policies. If shorter working hours are desired in the future, the associated financing
challenges will also need to be addressed.

Finally, for the use of long-term analysis in the process of EU policy decision-making, there are both
methodological and more general aspects to consider. The methodological considerations and
recommendations include the following:

1. For the projection of future demographic developments discussed in section 2, a key issue is
the future path of the fertility rate. The population forecast from Eurostat (EUROPOP2025)
takes into account the recently observed decline in fertility rates but maintains an assumption
of convergence to a higher level in the future. Revisions in the forecast of fertility rates since
the previous forecast therefore have only a minor influence on the overall projection of
population size and age composition. As discussed above, there are concerns that fertility rates
may remain low, while at the same time changes in fertility rates may have highly country-
specific effects. This points to the need for a careful analysis of this issue, greater use of
alternative fertility scenarios, and also the needed for future work on the underlying modelling
approach.

2. Key to projections of the path for potential output, which, as discussed in the introduction, in
the Ageing Reports and Debt Sustainability Analyses; see, e.g., European Commission (2024,
2025), follows a standard approach. More specifically, potential output is determined based on
a standard aggregate Cobb-Douglas production function. While this is a standard and tractable
approach, it is also restrictive and does not make it straightforward to capture essential effects
that may be induced by GenAI. First, the framework distinguishes only between the aggregate
capital stock and labour input. It is debatable whether GenAI can be modelled as part of the
(conventional) capital stock or should be treated as a separate input. Second, and related, the
rate of substitution between traditional physical capital and labour may differ from that

title: PE 784.027 27

paragraphs.text: ECTI | Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV)

between GenAI inputs and labour (and may also vary across sectors and tasks). In the existing
framework, the effects of GenAI may be introduced via changes in TFP growth, but this leaves
out essential aspects associated with GenAI, see discussion above. Finally, GenAI may reduce
the labour share of output (although this can be captured in the framework by changing the
beta parameter in the production function, this this implicitly assigns a larger role to
conventional real capital) which may have important effects, among other for tax revenues.
Therefore, this suggests a need to consider alternative modelling approaches that can capture
GenAI as a separate production input and its impacts.

3. Economic growth and increasing incomes may increase the demand for publicly provided
services through the income effect, known as the Wagner effect, discussed in Section 3.2.
Consistent with this mechanism, the Ageing Report includes an income effect (which fades out
towards 2070) in the projection of health care expenditure. While it is plausible that such an
income effect exists, the specific approach raises two issues. First, income effects may also
affect other variables, such as working hours (for which there is a clear downward trend). Yet,
weekly working hours by age group are assumed to remain fixed (with the increase in part-time
work driven by a higher female. This suggests a need for a more consistent treatment of income
effects on a range of variables, including a reassessment of whether working hours should
remain fixed over the long term.
More broad policy issues include the following:

1. This report has focused on demographics and GenAI, but in policy discussions on future growth,
it is important also to include climate change and broader environmental challenges. Climate
change, through higher temperatures and more volatile weather patterns, may both reduce the
capital stock (e.g. through flooding) and lower productivity (e.g. through heat waves). Some
recent work finds that a 1oC increase in temperature reduces world GDP by 20%, see Bilal et al.
(2026). While this estimate may be debated, significant effects are to be expected, with
important consequences for both GDP and public finances.

2. The analyses of the costs of ageing and fiscal sustainability are essential inputs to the policy
process. However, it should be kept in mind that they do not directly address “political
sustainability”. When the net costs of ageing imply lower expenditure on the young and higher
expenditure on the old (health and long-term care, and pensions), see European Commission
(2024), it is implicitly assumed that spending on the young can be reduced). While such
changes in expenditure levels and composition are technically possible, it remains an open
question whether they would have detrimental effects on the balance of the intergenerational
contract and the public support underpinning it.

3. Finally, as discussed in the main text, the efficiency and productivity in the public sector is
important both for the welfare solutions provided and public finances. In the reform discussions
not only to point to scope for improvements, but to find precise ways of implementing reforms
which deliver higher efficiency/productivity. It is a key element in solving the challenges public
finances are facing.

title: 32 PE 784.027

paragraphs.text: Long-term growth assumptions in the face of artificial intelligence (AI) and demographic change

This report examines how demographic change and technological progress (artificial intelligence -
AI) will affect economic growth and public finances. While declining fertility rates and increasing
longevity are driving population ageing, key uncertainties remain around the extent of healthy ageing
and the role of migration in mitigating workforce decline. At the same time, the adoption of AI will
likely increase productivity, but although the precise effects and timing remain uncertain, new
technologies will entail structural changes. Demographic and productivity trends will therefore pose
significant challenges for labour markets and public finances through multiple channels.

This document was provided by the Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit at the request of
the Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs (ECON).
