title: 4.3. Teachers, trainers and institutional capacity

paragraphs.text:
The successful integration of AI-related competences into education and training systems depends
heavily on the preparedness of teachers, trainers and institutions, whose capacity is essential for
implementation. Teachers and trainers need protected time, incentives and institutional support to
experiment with AI tools and redesign learning activities. Curriculum reform alone is insufficient if
education providers lack the human and institutional capacity required to implement new approaches
effectively, including guidance on the responsible use of AI in teaching, assessment and learning
support (UNESCO, 2023b).

Teachers and trainers need time and effort to develop the capacity to integrate AI-related tools and
approaches into teaching, learning and assessment practices. Their capacity must include
understanding the opportunities, limitations and risks of AI applications within their professional fields,
selecting appropriate pedagogical uses of AI tools, and guiding learners in critically interpreting AI-
generated outputs (UNESCO, 2024d). In TVET systems in particular, teachers and trainers require
familiarity with the evolving use of AI technologies in workplaces and occupations relevant to their
sectors, through industry placements, joint curriculum development and sectoral communities of
practice (OECD, 2021c).

This creates growing demand for continuous professional development systems that move beyond
one-off awareness-raising activities. Effective professional development increasingly requires
sustained approaches that include practical experimentation, peer learning, mentoring, collaborative
lesson design and opportunities to adapt teaching materials and assessment methods (OECD, 2024e;
2026). Institutional support structures are therefore critical to allow teachers and trainers sufficient

For TVET teachers, maintaining strong links with industry becomes even more important in the context
of AI adoption. Rapid technological change requires regular updating of occupational knowledge and
exposure to changing workplace practices. Partnerships between training institutions and employers
can therefore support teacher industry placements, workplace learning opportunities and joint
curriculum development activities (Gmyrek et al., 2023).

Institutional leadership and AI governance also play a crucial role. Education and training institutions
increasingly require clear strategies, rules and code of conduct regarding the adoption and use of AI
tools in their services, including policies related to ethics, data privacy, transparency and academic
integrity (UNESCO, 2023b). Educational institutions must have clear guidance on responsible use,
data protection, bias, copyright, academic integrity and accessibility. Without institutional guidance,
access to AI-related learning opportunities may become uneven across institutions and learner
groups, reinforcing existing inequalities in digital access and educational quality.

Infrastructure and resource gaps remain major constraints in many countries, particularly in low- and
middle-income contexts. Reliable connectivity, access to digital devices, appropriate software and
technical support remain unevenly distributed across institutions and regions (UNESCO, 2023c). As a
result, policy responses should not only focus on advanced AI adoption, but also on ensuring the
foundational digital infrastructure and institutional conditions necessary for equitable participation in
AI-enhanced learning environments.

title: 4.4. AI upskilling for adults and workers

paragraphs.text:
The relevance of AI literacy for the workplace is evident across sectors and occupations. Although
highly qualified workers are more inclined to use AI technology in their jobs, the need for AI upskilling
spans across all skill levels. For example, in education, teachers are expected to evaluate and adapt
content generated by AI tutoring platforms. In healthcare, nurses and technicians must understand
how diagnostic algorithms support (but do not replace) clinical judgement. In logistics and
manufacturing, workers interact with robots and wearables that require basic familiarity with
automation protocols and safety rules. These tasks do not always require advanced technical training
but depend on the situational awareness and ethical discernment that AI literacy enables (OECD,
2024f). Furthermore, improving AI literacy transversally can stimulate bottom-up use of AI technology
in work environments and help with its mainstreaming.

In spite of the wide consensus on its importance, existing evidence suggests a relatively low level of AI
literacy among workers, even in advanced economies. Despite the increasing need for both
specialised AI professionals alongside workers with a more general understanding of AI, according to
Orrell (2025), AI literacy is low in the US, for instance, as only 25% of workers are deploying AI on the
job, compared with 60% of workers in China and India in 2024. This skills gap is also reinforced by a
trust gap. According to the 2025 Edelman Trust Barometer, 77% of Chinese and 75% of Indian
respondents are reported to trust AI, compared to only 47% of Americans (Orrell, 2025). These figures
suggest that AI literacy is not only a matter of technical training but also of technological trust building,
especially among worker groups most vulnerable to AI-driven changes.

Cedefop’s AI skills survey carried out in 2024 included a specific AI literacy scale covering different
meta-aspects of it, ranging from whether workers can recognise an AI technology and its limits, to
understanding of the way in which AI systems and machines represent and learn from the world, and
awareness of the socioeconomic and ethical challenges implied by AI systems (Figure 2). The findings
of the survey show the low AI literacy in the European adult workforce, with between 40-60% of adult
workers surveyed possessing a relatively limited understanding of the diverse pillars of AI literacy
(Cedefop, 2025). This is important, since European workers with high AI literacy are found to have a
higher incidence of AI use and are, in general, more likely to enjoy positive labour market outcomes.

informally or in the workplace), this result suggests current training supply may not be sufficient to

consider ways to expand general AI literacy programmes for a wider population, as most workers will

Several short and diverse learning pathways exist regarding the AI skilling of the workforce, from
employer-led training and academic-industry hybrids to bootcamps and massive open online courses
(MOOCs). These are often for highly educated workers in more tech-savvy fields like ICT, who are
acquiring most AI skills on-the-job or through alternative routes such as digital portfolios, certifications,

administration, finance, and health are also beginning to offer AI awareness courses, often as part of

acquired outside traditional frameworks remain underdeveloped.

title: CHANGING LANDSCAPE OF SKILLS IN THE AGE OF AI | 44

paragraphs.text:
non-financial incentives, collaboration with industry, and the development of more inclusive learning
pathways (OECD, 2025d).

Considering the persistent ‘digital divide’ among social groups and countries, inclusion, equity and
linguistic diversity must be at the centre of education and training systems. Within countries, low-
skilled individuals face greater challenges, so access to AI-related training must be designed to meet
their needs. AI upskilling should complement rather than replace investments in foundational skills,
given growing concerns regarding literacy, numeracy and basic digital skills. Whereas continuous
lifelong learning becomes a must against rapidly changing skills demands for the AI era.

In low- and middle-income countries, poor internet connectivity is the single most important factor
preventing the use of AI, which requires significant investment in digital infrastructures (ETF, 2026).
Constraints related to informality, firm size, limited training provision and digital infrastructure mean
that AI skills policies need to prioritise accessible, work-based and publicly supported learning
pathways, rather than relying primarily on employer-led or market-based training solutions. Moreover,
promoting first-language-based multilingual education becomes even more important given that most
LLMs are designed in just a few languages. As well as affecting the AI model first, it can negatively
influence users in terms of access to and development of AI-related skills (ETF, 2026) 53 .

title: 4.5. Assessment, certification and quality assurance systems

paragraphs.text:
The growing use of AI technologies in education and workplaces also requires significant adaptation of
assessment, certification and quality assurance systems. It is important to distinguish between using
AI to support assessment processes and assessing AI-related competences themselves. Traditional
assessment approaches may become less effective in contexts where learners can use generative AI
tools to produce sophisticated outputs with limited demonstration of underlying understanding or
competence (UNESCO, 2023b).

Assessment systems increasingly need to emphasise not only final outputs, but also learners’
reasoning processes, problem-solving approaches, critical judgement, and ability to apply knowledge
in authentic contexts. The assessment itself could focus more on process, reasoning, verification,
occupational judgement and the ability to identify errors or bias in AI outputs. This is particularly
important in AI-enhanced environments where the capacity to interpret, validate and improve AI-
generated outputs becomes as important as producing content independently (OECD, 2023f, 2025e).

As a result, greater emphasis may be placed on performance-based and authentic forms of
assessment, including practical projects, workplace simulations, portfolios, oral examinations,
supervised problem-solving exercises and collaborative tasks. Such approaches can help assess
whether learners are able to apply occupational knowledge, exercise judgement and interact
responsibly with AI-supported tools in realistic settings (European Commission, 2025).

Recognition systems also need to evolve to reflect increasingly diverse forms of learning. Many AI-
related competences are acquired through workplace experience, online learning, short courses,
vendor certifications or non-formal training pathways. Recognition of prior learning and modular
certification systems can help make these competences more visible and portable within labour
markets. However, maintaining trust and transparency requires robust quality assurance
arrangements and clear descriptions of learning outcomes, assessment methods and qualification
levels (Council of the European Union, 2022).

Quality assurance systems therefore need to adapt to rapidly evolving AI-related programmes and
credentials, and they can be further strengthened by including equity considerations, since AI-
supported assessment may disadvantage learners with weaker access to digital tools, connectivity,
language support or prior exposure to AI. Overall, they must ensure the relevance of learning content
to labour market developments, the credibility of assessment practices, the preparedness of teaching
staff and the ethical use of AI within teaching and assessment processes (OECD, 2024e). Regular

title: 4.6. Shifting focus from specific ‘skills’ to broader ‘capabilities’

paragraphs.text:
It is important to note that AI is not the only factor changing labour markets, and other simultaneous
disruptions are occurring as well, such as demographic transitions, climate change, geopolitical/
economic tensions, to name a few. These concurrent changes happen at different speeds in every
region and from different starting points across geographies. The ways these trends coexist and
overlap ultimately determine the type and size of their ultimate effects. It is probably their combined
effects that will shape the eventual future skills demand. In the context of multiple disruptions and high
uncertainty, individuals will have to be agile with a broader set of skills beyond digital and technology-
related skills, such as skills for sustainability, entrepreneurial skills, career management skills, etc.

Some experts refer to ‘future-ready skills’ that enable individuals to adapt to a rapidly changing world,
remaining resilient and excelling in the 21st-century workplace (see OECD/Cedefop/European
Commission/ETF/ILO/ UNESCO, 2024). They often imply much stronger foundational skills and socio-
emotional skills that enable people to adapt, interact well, and be attuned to their own emotional
states. Within stronger cognitive and socio-emotional skills, future-ready skills emphasise, in
particular, digital and tech-savviness (understanding and utilising technology), proactivity and
adaptability (continuous professional development), and entrepreneurial mindset (risk-taking and
open-minded approach to new ideas). These transversal abilities and mindset for readiness, agility
and resilience are crucial in solving complex problems and working with people in an uncertain future.
They help to increase adaptability, encourage innovation and complement technology with human
skills.

Others use the terms ‘21 st century skills’ or ‘core skills’, emphasising the generic or transversal nature
of skills across sectors and occupations – different names with similar underlying abilities. Despite the
confusion with the terms, the critical importance of future-readiness and socio-emotional maturity is
widely recognised, alongside technical skills and academic knowledge. These are the glue of all skills,
essential in adapting to new developments and required at some level from every worker. Moreover,
the need for expanded digital and technology-related skills is growing beyond workplaces, becoming
key to access to public services, information, and rights.

Due to their high importance, some international frameworks provide a taxonomy for these skills, such
as ‘Global Framework on Core Skills for Life and Work in the 21 st Century’ (ILO, 2021a) and ‘Global
Framework on Transferable Skills’ (UNICEF, 2019). The European Commission has also developed
several EU frameworks that provide guidance for teaching similar qualities. Examples include the
European Key Competences for Lifelong Learning, the European Framework for Entrepreneurial
Competencies (EntreComp), the European Sustainability Competence Framework (GreenComp), the
European Framework for Personal, Social and Learning to Learn Key Competence (LifeComp),
alongside the European Digital Competence Framework for Citizens (DigComp 3.0).

There is a close connection between robust foundational skills, socio-emotional maturity, and future-
readiness, often fostered by access to good quality education. These broader skillsets are now

uncertain future. The vital importance of foundational learning/ skills could not be overstated. As

title: CHANGING LANDSCAPE OF SKILLS IN THE AGE OF AI | 46

paragraphs.text:
skills landscape in the age of AI. Learners must be equipped with stronger, and more solid
foundational skills so that they can succeed in skills programmes and workplaces.

With the advent of AI technologies, the demand for higher-order cognitive and metacognitive skills is
increasing beyond highly skilled professions; citizens increasingly need to use analytical and critical
thinking, problem-solving and decision-making or self-reflection in their work and lives alike. Similarly,
an enhanced level of socio-emotional skills becomes crucial in regulating thoughts, emotions and
behaviours and fostering endurance in uncertain times with big changes. Socio-emotional intelligence
can also provide safeguards for ethical and human-centred AI ensuring inclusivity, agency and
wellbeing (see Box 4). Hence, investing in socio-emotional learning is not just for learners’ personal
growth, but a strategic imperative for safe, effective, and equitable AI adoption (UNESCO, 2024b).
Box 4: Teaching socio-emotional skills for ethical and human-centred AI

Despite their increasing importance, teaching socio-emotional skills is less visible in education and
training. UNESCO defines ‘socio-emotional learning’ (SEL) as the process of acquiring competencies to
recognise and manage emotions, show care and concern for others, establish positive relationships,
make responsible decisions, and handle challenging situations effectively. Recently, it developed a policy
guide on how to mainstream SEL in education systems (UNESCO, 2024b). According to UNESCO, SEL
integrates cognitive, emotional, and relational dimensions to foster learners’ wellbeing, academic
attainment, and active global citizenship oriented towards positive social transformation. Capacities such
as self-control, critical reflection and social awareness are hallmarks of SEL (ibid).

Effective human–AI interaction depends on socio-emotional dispositions. Research shows that people
often either over-rely on AI outputs (automation bias) or under-use them (algorithm aversion). Avoiding
both extremes requires metacognition, reflective judgment, and emotional regulation, which are core SEL
competencies (ibid). SEL equips learners to calibrate trust in AI systems, question outputs critically,
recognise potential harm to others, manage uncertainty and act responsibly.

These higher-order and broadened skillsets have become essential to empower citizens, so that they
get the most out of changing labour markets and perform effectively in different work-related settings
as employees, self-employed and entrepreneurs. It is not only AI adoption shifting humans toward
cognitively and emotionally more demanding tasks; the shift from ‘curator’ to ‘editor’ is making AI’s
impact less visible, because AI can massively influence public discourse and the way people think
through algorithms and AI chatbots, often without independent oversight 54 . The surge in the new forms
of work and evolving employment structures also requires people to be more resourceful to manage
greater uncertainty and the prospect of multiple careers in one’s life. Coping with new forms of work is
a case in point for the increased importance of digital, self-management, and learning-to-learn skills,
especially in many developing countries (see ETF 2021a, 2021b, 2023a, 2024a, 2024b, 2024c).

This context calls for a shift from teaching narrow skill-sets to the cultivation of broader human
‘capabilities’ for citizens with higher agility, resilience and adaptability 55 . Human capabilities transcend
specific skill domains; they underlie the ‘human agency’ and ability to learn, apply and effectively
adapt knowledge and skills for meeting one’s own future needs 56 . New studies of human wellbeing
increasingly emphasise the importance of ‘subjective capacity’, with dimensions of agency, resilience,
optimism, and a sense of purpose (Lehmus-Sun, 2026). Agency reflects an individual’s capacity to act,
resilience pertains to their capacity to bounce back from challenges, optimism measures capacity to
have a positive outlook, and purpose captures the capacity to feel a sense of meaning in life.

generate and frame it. Whereas Facebook and Google decided which news articles to show you, tools like ChatGPT, Claude,
and Gemini synthesise that information into authoritative-sounding answers’, see Who’s Whispering in Your Chatbot’s Ear? by

55 For a good discussion of skills policies for resilient labour markets and societies, please see OECD/Cedefop/European
Commission/ETF/ILO/UNESCO, 2024.

alternative approach to welfare economics. Sen’s core focus (what individuals are able to do, i.e. as ‘agents’ who act and bring
about change) also emphasises the expansion of capability for development.

title: CHANGING LANDSCAPE OF SKILLS IN THE AGE OF AI | 47

paragraphs.text:
These enduring human capabilities are becoming much more important than skills themselves, but
they cannot be developed in a vacuum by individuals. Capabilities are built within skills ecosystems,
through coordinated and life-course education and training investments, firm practices, labour market
institutions, and social dialogue 57 . In the context of an evolving AI landscape, inclusive governance,
ethical considerations, and workplace safeguards (transparency, explainability, consent, and worker
voice) are essential to improve human capabilities alongside digital, data and AI literacies to augment
work and support decent outcomes.

Ongoing AI progress brings significant implications for learning and resonates with the discussions
regarding the direction of future education systems and new pedagogical approaches such as
experimental learning, reflection, collaboration and social interaction over content acquisition. For
example, scientific literacy becomes critical in an AI-driven future due to the complementarity between
AI literacy and STEM topics. According to OECD (2025e), the future science curricula must prepare
students to become flexible, adaptive, creative and socially aware problem solvers and curious about
the world around them 58 . This requires linking science learning to real-world phenomena to make the
relevance of scientific knowledge visible to learners but also placing greater emphasis on ethics and
civic responsibility in science education.

Although it is not the focus of this report, a highly capable AI system raises even more fundamental
questions about the priorities and assumptions that currently underpin education. For example, using
generative AI in writing urges education systems to consider which abilities are uniquely human and
the corresponding knowledge that remains valuable (OECD, 2025g). While offering many
opportunities, AI systems introduce risks that might challenge the basics of education in the long term.
Even in the current context, information is widely and instantly available thanks to AI technologies, so
‘knowledge’ in itself is less important than the higher-order skills needed for its selection, application or
implementation (e.g., communication, innovation, decision ‐ making, judgement) (see Box 5).
Box 5: ‘Knowledge is cheap, but wisdom is scarce’

In the words of an educationalist, Ulf-Daniel Ehlers, knowledge is no longer the scarce resource in the
age of AI. Generative AI, language models, machine tutors and recommendation engines have redefined
access to information. If the act of knowing is being dislocated from the human mind, externalised into
systems that simulate understanding, then the question is ‘what remains the unique domain of the
human’. Education should go beyond knowledge and instil wisdom – moving from information delivery to
cultivating judgement, reflection, ethical decision-making, imagination and co-creative capability. The
latter is becoming the true marker of human competence in the AI age. Education can be a tool to shape
the kind of futures people can imagine and pursue. Students must be prepared to be ready, with the
capacity to take responsibility and co-create solutions for the future of society (Ehlers, 2025).

These core competences or future-ready skills are not the mere accumulation of skills; it is the capability
to act responsibly and effectively in complex, uncertain, and evolving contexts. The future of human
competence does not lie in outperforming machines, but in doing what they cannot: exercising
judgement in ambiguous situations; taking moral responsibility for collective futures; engaging in
meaning-making and identity development; collaborating across diversity, systems, and disciplines;
imagining alternative realities and bringing them into being. These are not just soft skills, they are the
foundation of the ability to shape society ethically, sustainably and creatively; agility, reflection and
uncertainty navigation are the new excellence. Focusing on employability as the primary goal of
education is no longer enough, because the crises of our time—ecological, democratic, humanitarian—
demand something more (Ehlers, 2025).

(cognitive, socio-emotional, and manual skills). It often increases demand for cognitive and meta-

These enduring human capabilities are becoming much more important than skills themselves, but
they cannot be developed in a vacuum by individuals. Capabilities are built within skills ecosystems,
through coordinated and life-course education and training investments, firm practices, labour market

ethical considerations, and workplace safeguards (transparency, explainability, consent, and worker
voice) are essential to improve human capabilities alongside digital, data and AI literacies to augment
work and support decent outcomes.
Ongoing AI progress brings significant implications for learning and resonates with the discussions
regarding the direction of future education systems and new pedagogical approaches such as
experimental learning, reflection, collaboration and social interaction over content acquisition. For

AI literacy and STEM topics. According to OECD (2025e), the future science curricula must prepare
students to become flexible, adaptive, creative and socially aware problem solvers and curious about

relevance of scientific knowledge visible to learners but also placing greater emphasis on ethics and
civic responsibility in science education.

(cognitive, socio-emotional, and manual skills). It often increases demand for cognitive and meta-

title: CHANGING LANDSCAPE OF SKILLS IN THE AGE OF AI | 48

paragraphs.text:
cognitive skills, particularly higher-order analytical and critical thinking. Moreover, the value of socio-
emotional skills is amplified as human cognition, emotion, judgement, and creativity are key for
effective human-AI collaboration and the fair and human-centric adoption of AI. While manual skills
are less affected so far, the rise in demand for intermediate and advanced digital skills and data
literacy is growing in order to integrate and use AI tools. As a result, the need for individuals to
comprehend and safely use AI tools in an ethical manner has emerged as a new foundational skill.

Overall, most human skills will still be needed – but how people use them will change as they work
alongside intelligent machines. AI increases demand for new skillsets that blend technical, cognitive
and interpersonal abilities. This points to the need for a different approach to skills policy, centred on
building ‘hybrid intelligence’: combining technical AI literacy with domain expertise and uniquely
human capabilities and originality. This requires qualification systems to move from certifying tasks
and occupations towards recognising capabilities, agency and learning capacity, while skills
anticipation must shift from predicting job losses to understanding how AI reshapes skills, entry
pathways and job quality.

Besides the need for incorporating AI literacy into educational curricula, this report argues for
widespread AI upskilling of adults and workers, revising occupational standards, qualifications and
curricula, and adapting assessment, certification and quality assurance systems in education and
training. It also advocates shifting from teaching narrow skillsets to instilling broader capabilities, as
the AI-powered future calls for a human-centred approach and resourceful and adaptable citizens in
the face of growing uncertainties. Such capabilities underpin human agency and the ability to learn,
apply, and adapt knowledge and skills for future needs.

Finally, skills policy alone cannot ensure inclusive and fair AI outcomes. The benefits of AI
technologies are being unequally distributed, while persistent gender, racial and socio-economic
imbalances in the AI workforce risk embedding existing biases into AI systems and limiting the
inclusiveness of future labour market opportunities. Evidently, skills policies need to address access,
progression pathways and retention for underrepresented groups, not only aggregate supply, in order
to support vulnerable groups. However, investments in skills and AI literacy must be complemented by
labour market institutions, social protection, and governance arrangements that shape how AI is
introduced, how work is organised, and how the gains from technological change are shared.

title: Abstract

paragraphs.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a potential accelerator of human capital development in low- and
middle-income countries, with implications and opportunities for learning, technical skills development,
and labor market productivity. Unlike earlier education technologies, AI shifts spending from relatively
predictable purchases of hardware, software, and connectivity toward dynamic, usage-based
expenditures for inference, cloud compute, data integration, governance, and continuous teacher support.
These costs are volatile, cumulative, and often poorly captured in traditional education budgets. The paper
develops a planning lens for understanding AI adoption as a transition from products to services to tokens,
showing how this shift changes the fiscal risks facing ministries of education. It highlights why pilot costs
are especially misleading predictors of system-wide affordability, as subsidies disappear, integration
requirements expand, and equity obligations become more expensive at scale. It also examines pathways
that may make AI more feasible in resource-constrained settings.

The paper situates AI within the hard realities of infrastructure gaps, low digital skills, constrained public
education budgets, and weak evidence on learning impacts. Its core contribution is to reframe AI in
education as a problem of cost architecture, sequencing, and institutional readiness. For policymakers, the
implication is clear: cost-effective AI adoption will depend less on access to the latest model than on the
ability to govern recurrent costs, learn from carefully designed pilots, protect equity, and build flexible
systems that can adapt as technologies, prices, and evidence evolve.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence; AI in education; education finance; education technology; low- and
middle-income countries; digital infrastructure; total cost of ownership; AI inference costs; teacher
adoption; digital skills; education systems; cost-effectiveness; public procurement; small AI; generative AI;
educational planning; recurrent costs; digital divide; vendor lock-in; innovative financing.

title: 1. Introduction

paragraphs.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a potential accelerator of human capital development, with
implications and opportunities for learning, technical skills development, and labor market productivity .
A primary economic rationale for public investment in education technology lies in its potential to
strengthen workforce productivity and support inclusive growth. Recent advances in AI—particularly
generative and adaptive applications—offer new possibilities to improve teaching and learning processes,
support skills development at scale, and better align education systems with evolving labor market needs.
Beyond education, people-centered AI applications also show promise in expanding access to health and
mental health services, improving job matching, and facilitating broader economic participation (Comer
et al., 2025; Demombynes, 2023).

Within education systems, AI is in growing use among students, teachers, and administrators. AI-
enabled tools are personalizing instruction, reducing administrative burdens on teachers, expanding
access to learning materials, and supporting education systems in identifying students at risk of learning
loss or dropout. These capabilities are increasingly relevant in contexts where teacher shortages, large
class sizes, and fragmented data systems constrain education quality.

AI adoption in education is already widespread in many high- and middle-income countries. The
Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) reports that approximately one-third of teachers in
participating high- and middle-income countries are using AI in their professional practice (OECD, 2025),
while other surveys suggest even higher levels of uptake, with a recent Google–Ipsos study finding that 81
percent of teachers report using AI tools (Gomes, 2026). Students are also rapidly adopting AI, particularly
in post-secondary education, where 86 percent of surveyed students report using AI to answer questions
and conduct research. At the system level, education authorities are beginning to use AI to support teacher
deployment, curriculum planning, and the identification of students at risk of dropping out (Molina et al.,
2024).

Despite this momentum, the scalability and cost-effectiveness of AI use in education remain uncertain
in low- and lower-middle-income countries (LICs and LMICs). While AI tools are increasingly accessible
and affordable in high-income contexts, effective deployment in resource-constrained settings is limited
by gaps in electricity, connectivity, and device access, as well as often low levels of digital literacy and weak
institutional capacity. Education budgets in LICs and LMICs are often constrained and face competing
priorities, raising questions about whether AI investments represent the highest-return use of scarce
public resources.

Estimating costs associated with uses of new technologies in education has long been notably difficult
and complex for education policymakers and planners. Budgeting often focuses only on visible upfront
capital investments while ignoring much larger, ongoing total cost of ownership and operation. 'Hidden'
operational costs include regular hardware replacement cycles, software licensing, and substantial
infrastructure upgrades. Edtech tools require continuous teacher training to be effective, and teacher
professional development acts as a massive, ongoing variable cost that is rarely tracked accurately. This
complexity is compounded by rapid technological advances and obsolescence. In addition, there are
challenges associated with cross-sectoral investments, such as those related to connectivity and the

building out of the electricity grid, which are funded outside of traditional education budgets. Historically,
this mix of fluid and fragmented cost variables has challenged education ministries in their attempts to
establish reliable, reasonable, long-term expenditure baselines. Introducing AI further increases this
complexity. Costs related to uses of AI in education are dynamic, as business models change, new
applications and use cases emerge, and new forces shift related supply and demand.

This paper explores costs associated with integrating AI into education systems in low- and lower-middle
income countries. Drawing on emerging global evidence and currently available data across primary,
secondary, and tertiary education, it analyzes the preconditions for effective adoption, current cost
structures and associated risks. It does not seek to explore the nature or impact of this use, which are
topics of upcoming and ongoing analytical work at the World Bank. Instead, it aims to help policymakers
and planners better understand real and potential costs associated with uses of AI in education.
Highlighting phased, context-specific approaches to adoption rather than large-scale deployment, the
paper aims to inform pragmatic policy and planning choices related to the deployment of an exciting and
rapidly changing new technology – AI -- that balance innovation with equity, affordability, and institutional
readiness within broader education reform and human capital development strategies.

text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a potential accelerator of human capital development, with
implications and opportunities for learning, technical skills development, and labor market productivity .
A primary economic rationale for public investment in education technology lies in its potential to
strengthen workforce productivity and support inclusive growth. Recent advances in AI—particularly
generative and adaptive applications—offer new possibilities to improve teaching and learning processes,
support skills development at scale, and better align education systems with evolving labor market needs.
Beyond education, people-centered AI applications also show promise in expanding access to health and
mental health services, improving job matching, and facilitating broader economic participation (Comer
et al., 2025; Demombynes, 2023).
Within education systems, AI is in growing use among students, teachers, and administrators. AI-
enabled tools are personalizing instruction, reducing administrative burdens on teachers, expanding
access to learning materials, and supporting education systems in identifying students at risk of learning
loss or dropout. These capabilities are increasingly relevant in contexts where teacher shortages, large
class sizes, and fragmented data systems constrain education quality.
AI adoption in education is already widespread in many high- and middle-income countries. The
Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) reports that approximately one-third of teachers in
participating high- and middle-income countries are using AI in their professional practice (OECD, 2025),
while other surveys suggest even higher levels of uptake, with a recent Google–Ipsos study finding that 81
percent of teachers report using AI tools (Gomes, 2026). Students are also rapidly adopting AI, particularly
in post-secondary education, where 86 percent of surveyed students report using AI to answer questions
and conduct research. At the system level, education authorities are beginning to use AI to support teacher
deployment, curriculum planning, and the identification of students at risk of dropping out (Molina et al.,
2024).
Despite this momentum, the scalability and cost-effectiveness of AI use in education remain uncertain
in low- and lower-middle-income countries (LICs and LMICs). While AI tools are increasingly accessible
and affordable in high-income contexts, effective deployment in resource-constrained settings is limited
by gaps in electricity, connectivity, and device access, as well as often low levels of digital literacy and weak
institutional capacity. Education budgets in LICs and LMICs are often constrained and face competing
priorities, raising questions about whether AI investments represent the highest-return use of scarce
public resources.

and complex for education policymakers and planners. Budgeting often focuses only on visible upfront
capital investments while ignoring much larger, ongoing total cost of ownership and operation. 'Hidden'
operational costs include regular hardware replacement cycles, software licensing, and substantial
infrastructure upgrades. Edtech tools require continuous teacher training to be effective, and teacher
professional development acts as a massive, ongoing variable cost that is rarely tracked accurately. This
complexity is compounded by rapid technological advances and obsolescence. In addition, there are

title: 2.1. Education Budget Constraints

paragraphs.text:
Education budgets impose constraints on AI adoption across all income levels, as they do with
investments in edtech more generally, with the greatest constraints in the lowest income contexts. In
LICs, per-student education spending is around US$55 per year (EFW, 2024) and most education budgets
are absorbed by recurrent expenditures. Teacher salaries and related costs account for more than half of
recurring education expenditures in all countries (Arias & Kheyfets, 2023) and often up to 75 percent or
more of education spending in low-income countries (UNESCO, 2010). This leaves little fiscal space for new
investments in digital infrastructure and devices, let alone investments in educational software and AI
tools and the necessary training and maintenance needed to support their effective use.

The scale of investment needed to build the basic digital foundations for AI-enabled education far
exceeds current resources in many low- and lower-middle income countries. UNICEF estimates that
achieving universal digital learning would require about US$1.4 trillion between 2021 and 2030 (Yao et al.,
2021). This includes US$410 billion for electricity access, US$428 billion for internet connectivity, and
US$498 billion for data access. In addition, delivering digital learning—covering devices, initial teacher
education, continuous professional development, digital content, and institutional capacity—would cost
another US$46 billion, with Sub-Saharan Africa alone needing US$13.1 billion. These figures generally align
with UNESCO’s estimate that LICs would need to spend $21 billion per year between 2024 and 2030 to
achieve a limited level of digital learning and solar-powered electricity (UNESCO, 2023). While these are
estimates, they underscore the scale of the challenge facing education systems. In LICs, 2022 total
education spending from all sources was US$25.86 billion (EFW 2024).

In upper-middle- and high-income countries (UMICs and HICs), financial constraints are less binding, but
adoption challenges remain significant, particularly among teachers. World Bank analysis of Europe and

Central Asia (ECA) highlights uneven digital infrastructure within countries, persistent workforce skills
gaps, fragmented and low-quality data, and gaps in ethical and responsible AI governance as key barriers
to effective AI implementation. These constraints have resulted in uneven uptake of AI tools by teachers,
which underscores a lesson that policymakers have learned related to edtech more generally: Investments
in infrastructure are necessary but not sufficient conditions for the successful adoption of edtech –
including AI (Molina & Medina, 2025).

It is important to note that these calculations and cost projections are largely based on market,
infrastructure and institutional constructs from the pre-AI era. These realities imply that the affordability
of AI use in education, as with edtech more broadly, is not solely a function of income level, but also of
how fiscal space, infrastructure, and institutional capacity interact. Broadly speaking, in LICs and LMICs,
the initial constraint is financing complementary infrastructure and recurrent costs, while in UMICs and
HICs the challenge increasingly lies in teacher adoption, governance, and system alignment—an important
consideration for designing cost-effective and scalable AI strategies across contexts.

title: 2.2. Total Cost of AI Integration in Education Systems

paragraphs.text:
The total cost of deploying and integrating AI into education extend well beyond the retail price of
consumer AI tools themselves and depends on a combination of foundational investments,
implementation choices, and recurrent expenditures, many of which are outside the remit of ministries
of education. The World Bank identifies four foundational ecosystem investments— connectivity, compute,
context, and competency (4 Cs)—as essential for countries to benefit from AI. Connectivity encompasses
reliable digital infrastructure, energy, and device access; compute covers AI chips, servers, data centers,
and cloud services; context refers to locally relevant data and content, and competency is the set of digital
skills that are indispensable for adopting, adapting, and innovating with AI (World Bank, 2025). Where
these foundations are weak, introducing AI risks exacerbating existing inequalities by benefiting only
already-connected schools, teachers, and students – or perhaps, in a worst-case scenario, not benefitting
anyone at all.

To plan effectively for the future of digital education in an age of AI, policymakers can benefit from
understanding how related business models and technologies are evolving. The edtech sector has
transitioned through three distinct but overlapping paradigms. Initially, procurement focused on one-off
purchases of hardware and software. Over time, the introduction of subscription models for software and
education content (and, in some places, including leased hardware as part of bundled services) resulted
in an evolution away from what were largely capital expenditures to increasingly include various types of
recurrent operating expenditures (Trucano, 2012). The introduction of AI represents a new phase that
disrupts traditional cost considerations related to edtech. This evolution does not just alter accounting
classifications; it alters some of the defining questions a ministry must ask—and introduces new fiscal
vulnerabilities.

title: 2.2.1. Training an AI Model

paragraphs.text:
Developing a foundation AI model is an extraordinarily expensive undertaking that is well beyond the
financial and technical capacities of individual education systems, both now and for the foreseeable
future. In the commercial sector, building, or "training", a cutting-edge Large Language Model (LLM) is
computationally expensive, costing tens of millions, and increasingly hundreds of millions, of dollars. For
instance, training OpenAI's GPT-4 required an estimated $100 million, Google's Gemini Ultra was almost
twice that, and industry trends points toward multi-billion-dollar single training runs in the near future
(Stanford HAI, 2026; Epoch AI 2026). These figures do not account for the staggering costs of hiring
specialized AI researchers and engineers, data curation, or the massive energy infrastructure needed to
keep clusters of thousands of high-end graphics processing units (GPUs) running 24/7 for months at a time.
Because of this prohibitive financial barrier, ministries of education will not be building their own core
foundational models.

That said, a small number of countries are pursuing state-funded development of their own foundation
models as part of a broader push for "Sovereign AI", the general term for national strategies to build, own,
and govern independent digital infrastructure and AI capabilities rather than relying entirely on foreign
technology companies. While these massive investments are led by central governments or ministries of
science and technology, national education systems potentially stand to be major beneficiaries. By tapping
into these 'sovereign' resources, the hope is that schools can eventually access AI models that are aligned
with local languages, cultural heritage, and national curricula, optimized for use consistent with local
contexts and needs that run on local infrastructure at lower, more predictable costs.

title: Box 1 . Small Language Models in Education

paragraphs.text:
While Large Language Models (LLMs) capture global headlines, a parallel revolution is occurring with
Small Language Models (SLMs). These compact, highly efficient and greener AI models, sometimes
referred to as “Small AI", are designed to perform specific tasks exceptionally well, rather than trying,
like LLMs, to know everything about everything. If you think of an LLM as a massive, expensively built
public library, a small AI model is, in contrast, a highly curated, specialized textbook. Many of these small
models are being released with "open weights" which means that they can be downloaded and
customized; the resulting small AI is owned by the group who performed this customization, who can
host it locally. This means that a foreign tech company cannot shut off access to it, nor change the way
it works or what they charge to host and run it. Notably, many of these small models are coming out of
China (Meinhardt et al., 2025). For ministries of education, especially in LICs, small models potentially
offer many advantages: lower operating costs; off-line use; and localized customization, optimized for
use with local curricula, in local languages, more consistent with local cultural norms and histories,
greater control over data privacy and ownership, with fewer risks of generating content that is
inappropriate in learning environments. Among the tradeoffs are that SLMs typically deliver lower
performance on complex reasoning tasks and have more limited general knowledge than LLMs.

title: 2.2.2. AI Inference

paragraphs.text:
While the massive capital investment expenditures (capex) required to 'train' or develop an AI model
are well-recognized, the ongoing costs of actually using the model, which is known as 'inference', are
often less understood. Inference is the recurring operational cost of running an AI model. Every time a
user submits a prompt, the system performs an inference to produce a response. While the cost per
individual query is small, these costs, which are measured in 'tokens', accumulate into a continuous,
variable operational expenditure (opex) that needs to be monitored and managed by education systems.

An analogy can be helpful: Think of AI inference as a chef preparing and tasting a dish right before it’s
served to a customer. Up until this point, the chef has spent years in culinary school learning the rules of
flavor, practicing techniques, and studying recipes. This long, intense, and highly expensive educational
phase is what AI engineers call "training." When a customer sits down at a restaurant and places a specific
order, the chef doesn't go back to school. Instead, she instantly applies everything she has learned and
draws on her experience of what she knows how to cook and makes a new plate of food which is delivered
to an eager customer. In the world of generative AI, inference is that live moment of application. It happens
when a fully educated AI model receives a brand-new prompt or question from a user, runs it through its
existing repository of knowledge, and instantly generates and presents a resulting response.

Viewed from an historical perspective, the AI industry has moved from what was predominantly a
"construction phase" (building and training models) and into an increasingly "operational phase" (running
AI models at scale). At a macro level, the financial bottleneck for the AI economy is no longer teaching the
AI how to 'think,' but rather paying for the necessary compute every time a user prompts it to do so, i.e.
for inference. Training an AI model is a one-time capital expenditure. To date, education systems have not
paid for the creation of their own AI models, this has been done by private companies. Paying for inference
represents an on-going, operational expenditure. Users of AI within education systems, from education
ministries down to individual users, have been paying for inference, directly and indirectly, both bundled
with subscriptions to AI tools and on a per unit (or, in the language of AI, on a per token ) basis, and will
continue to do so for the foreseeable future.
Box 2 . Projecting Future Costs for AI Inference: Wright’s Law Meets Jevons’ Paradox

A key consideration for assessing the affordability of AI-enabled education solutions is that AI unit costs
for inference, especially costs tied to usage, prompt length, model complexity, and related infrastructure
requirements (known as ‘variable inference costs’) are declining rapidly. This pattern is consistent with
experience-curve dynamics, often summarized as Wright’s Law : many technologies become cheaper by
a roughly constant percentage with each doubling of cumulative production or installed capacity (Roser,
2023).

Recent data illustrate the speed of this change. The cost to query a model with GPT-3.5–equivalent
performance fell from $20 per million tokens in Nov 2022 to $0.07 per million tokens in Oct 2024 --
about a 280× decline in roughly 18 months (Maslej et al., 2025)! Epoch AI similarly finds that inference-

price declines vary substantially by task and by the performance milestone considered, decreasing from
roughly 9× to 900× per year across the benchmarks they analyzed (Cottier et al., 2025).

These trends are directly relevant to the variable costs of AI usage. Declining per unit costs of generating
outputs at scale using AI suggest that cost estimates based on current inference prices may quickly
become outdated, and that what is expensive today may be materially less expensive in the near term.

That said, projections of future costs of AI inference based on simple linear or even geometric
reductions in price consistent with Wright’s Law may fall victim to Jevons’ Paradox . This economic
theory holds that as technological progress increases the efficiency with which a resource is used, the
total consumption of that resource tends to go up, rather than down. In other words, there is a ‘rebound
effect’: as the cost of AI inference falls, people may purchase a lot more of it, and so, while per unit
costs decrease, overall spend may increase.

If Jevons’ Paradox holds, costs and total expenditure on AI inference may resemble what happened
previously with lighting and internet data. Tsao and Saunders showed that the historical demand for
lighting has been highly elastic: Every gain in efficiency that made light cheaper was met with an equal
increase in its total use. In other words, technological breakthroughs (such as the widescale introduction
of LEDs for lighting) do not automatically reduce overall energy consumption, because consumers
consequently take advantage of cheaper light to illuminate spaces that were previously dark. (Tsao &
Saunders, 2010) Similarly, Coroama and Hilty demonstrated that declines in costs of gigabytes of data
catalyzed the growth of data-intensive services like video streaming and cloud computing, which
contributed to explosive growth in internet usage and which, in turn, off-set per unit savings in energy
consumption. (Coroama & Hilty, 2014)

When planning for AI use at scale in an education system, policymakers are pulled in opposite directions
as they contend with the implications of both Wright's Law and Jevons’ Paradox. Which costs are likely
to rise and which are likely to fall? The fact that there are no simple answers to this question underscores
the need for adaptive approaches to planning and budgeting for uses of AI in education, including
piloting, iterative design, and periodic cost re-estimation, as model performance improves and related
costs of AI inference evolve.

AI-related costs in education can be broadly divided into eight general categories and characterized as
either capital expenditures (capex) or operating expenditures (opex). It is important to note that many
AI-related costs are recurrent and cumulative rather than one - off. Pilot programs may underestimate

long - term financial implications by focusing on initial licensing or setup costs, while underfunding
maintenance, retraining, device replacement, data governance, and system upgrades. As systems scale,
these recurring costs dominate total costs of ownership and operation. Affordability cannot be assessed
based on simple extrapolations from the retail costs of subscriptions to popular AI chatbots. Sustainable
AI adoption requires multi - year planning and financing, careful sequencing, and cost - aware design—

especially in LICs and LMICs, where education budgets are severely constrained while AI continues to
evolve rapidly.

Most ministries of education utilize established frameworks to categorize and budget for educational
technology. With the expectation that all edtech will soon have “AI inside”, it will be possible to analyze
how AI shifts cost dynamics within these existing structures, allowing policymakers and planners to future-
proof their strategic thinking. This approach highlights how AI transforms the underlying economics of
current budgeting models: While the general taxonomy remains unchanged, the internal financial
plumbing does change, introducing highly variable, recurring expenditures that now run alongside costs
that were historically fixed and predictable.

with subscriptions to AI tools and on a per unit (or, in the language of AI, on a per token ) basis, and will
continue to do so for the foreseeable future.
Box 2 . Projecting Future Costs for AI Inference: Wright’s Law Meets Jevons’ Paradox
A key consideration for assessing the affordability of AI-enabled education solutions is that AI unit costs
for inference, especially costs tied to usage, prompt length, model complexity, and related infrastructure
requirements (known as ‘variable inference costs’) are declining rapidly. This pattern is consistent with
experience-curve dynamics, often summarized as Wright’s Law : many technologies become cheaper by
a roughly constant percentage with each doubling of cumulative production or installed capacity (Roser,
2023).
Recent data illustrate the speed of this change. The cost to query a model with GPT-3.5–equivalent
performance fell from $20 per million tokens in Nov 2022 to $0.07 per million tokens in Oct 2024 --
about a 280× decline in roughly 18 months (Maslej et al., 2025)! Epoch AI similarly finds that inference-
6
price declines vary substantially by task and by the performance milestone considered, decreasing from
roughly 9× to 900× per year across the benchmarks they analyzed (Cottier et al., 2025).
These trends are directly relevant to the variable costs of AI usage. Declining per unit costs of generating
outputs at scale using AI suggest that cost estimates based on current inference prices may quickly
become outdated, and that what is expensive today may be materially less expensive in the near term.
That said, projections of future costs of AI inference based on simple linear or even geometric
reductions in price consistent with Wright’s Law may fall victim to Jevons’ Paradox . This economic
theory holds that as technological progress increases the efficiency with which a resource is used, the
total consumption of that resource tends to go up, rather than down. In other words, there is a ‘rebound
effect’: as the cost of AI inference falls, people may purchase a lot more of it, and so, while per unit
costs decrease, overall spend may increase.
If Jevons’ Paradox holds, costs and total expenditure on AI inference may resemble what happened
previously with lighting and internet data. Tsao and Saunders showed that the historical demand for
lighting has been highly elastic: Every gain in efficiency that made light cheaper was met with an equal
increase in its total use. In other words, technological breakthroughs (such as the widescale introduction
of LEDs for lighting) do not automatically reduce overall energy consumption, because consumers
consequently take advantage of cheaper light to illuminate spaces that were previously dark. (Tsao &
Saunders, 2010) Similarly, Coroama and Hilty demonstrated that declines in costs of gigabytes of data
catalyzed the growth of data-intensive services like video streaming and cloud computing, which
contributed to explosive growth in internet usage and which, in turn, off-set per unit savings in energy
consumption. (Coroama & Hilty, 2014)
When planning for AI use at scale in an education system, policymakers are pulled in opposite directions
as they contend with the implications of both Wright's Law and Jevons’ Paradox. Which costs are likely
to rise and which are likely to fall? The fact that there are no simple answers to this question underscores
the need for adaptive approaches to planning and budgeting for uses of AI in education, including
piloting, iterative design, and periodic cost re-estimation, as model performance improves and related
costs of AI inference evolve.
AI-related costs in education can be broadly divided into eight general categories and characterized as
either capital expenditures (capex) or operating expenditures (opex). It is important to note that many
AI-related costs are recurrent and cumulative rather than one - off. Pilot programs may underestimate
long - term financial implications by focusing on initial licensing or setup costs, while underfunding
maintenance, retraining, device replacement, data governance, and system upgrades. As systems scale,
these recurring costs dominate total costs of ownership and operation. Affordability cannot be assessed
based on simple extrapolations from the retail costs of subscriptions to popular AI chatbots. Sustainable
AI adoption requires multi - year planning and financing, careful sequencing, and cost - aware design—
7
especially in LICs and LMICs, where education budgets are severely constrained while AI continues to
evolve rapidly.
Most ministries of education utilize established frameworks to categorize and budget for educational
technology. With the expectation that all edtech will soon have “AI inside”, it will be possible to analyze
how AI shifts cost dynamics within these existing structures, allowing policymakers and planners to future-
proof their strategic thinking. This approach highlights how AI transforms the underlying economics of
current budgeting models: While the general taxonomy remains unchanged, the internal financial
plumbing does change, introducing highly variable, recurring expenditures that now run alongside costs
that were historically fixed and predictable.

title: 2.3.1. Infrastructure Constraints

paragraphs.text:
Infrastructure constraints inhibit the potential adoption of AI in education systems in LICs and LMICs.
Access to AI in education depends first on access to electricity, connectivity, and devices at the school and
user level. Where these foundations do not exist, high costs to build out supporting basic technology
infrastructure greatly exceed all other cost components.

In HICs, integrating AI into classrooms is, comparatively speaking, more operationally feasible due to
mature digital infrastructure and institutional readiness. With widespread access to reliable electricity,
fast internet connectivity, and high levels of device access, the marginal cost of integrating AI into
education systems including the classroom is fiscally manageable. Across OECD countries with available
data, for instance, 96.1 percent of students said a desktop or laptop computer was available to them at
school (Boeskens and Echazarra, 2025). Initial AI adoption typically requires limited additional investment
beyond teacher training, policy development including data - privacy safeguards, and classroom
management adjustments.

By contrast, in low- and lower-middle income countries, the cost of introducing AI is driven primarily by
infrastructure gaps rather than by the price of AI tools themselves. While AI tools may be low cost, their
effective use depends on access to electricity, sufficient internet bandwidth, and access to digital devices,
all of which remain scarce in many low-income settings. As shown in Table 3, only 38 percent of primary
and secondary schools in LICs have electricity, 27 percent have computers, and 23 percent have internet
access, compared with near - universal access across all three infrastructure types in UMICs and HICs. These

gaps sharply limit the feasibility of equitable, system - wide AI deployment. Annex 2 further shows that
access to infrastructure increases with education level.

Closing infrastructure gaps at scale implies large financing allocations that extend well beyond current
national education budgets in low income and lower-middle income countries. In Sub-Saharan Africa
alone, achieving affordable universal connectivity is estimated to require US$91 billion, equivalent to 4.5

AI” use would cost tens of billions of dollars to be financed by governments, the private sector, and donors.
While these estimates include society more broadly rather than only the education sector and will change
with time and technological advances, the magnitude of the cost makes them difficult to achieve. For
education systems, UNESCO estimates that enabling electricity, connectivity, and devices for all schools in
LICs and LMICs would require more than US$125 billion, with additional annual maintenance costs of
about US$12 billion (UNESCO, 2023). Against this backdrop, “Small AI” may enable access at lower cost,
but with highly constrained budgets, use-at-scale will require additional sources of finance.

title: 2.3.2. Innovative Financing for Infrastructure

paragraphs.text:
Innovative approaches for financing AI in education at scale are necessary. Traditional approaches to
procurement and financing fall short as education ministries shift their spending. Instead of funding
predictable capital expenditures like infrastructure and fixed operating costs for digital content and
training, they must now navigate the dynamic, token-based usage economies that characterize the age of
AI. Relying on standard approaches to budgeting and financing risks potentially bankrupting ministries or
shutting down access for schools when, for example, token usage spikes. Policymakers do not need to
invent entirely new financing mechanisms from scratch. A potential path forward can be found in adapting
funding streams such as national Universal Service Funds (USFs), which are massive financial pools
generated by a compulsory regulatory fee on domestic telecommunications revenues. M any countries
have successfully deployed USF monies to finance the infrastructure needed to connect rural and
disadvantaged schools to the internet (Trucano, 2015). By legally updating the scope of USFs, governments
can shift their focus from supporting the extension of telephony and the Internet to, for example, help to
subsidize cloud compute data and offline ‘edge’ hardware. Pairing USF capital with proven financial
instruments borrowed from the global health sector, such as front-loaded capital facilities that utilize
donor pledges to issue bonds, which raise fund the development of vaccines (Barder & Yeh, 2006); from
the climate sector, which has utilized debt-for nature swaps to support conservation efforts (Green Climate
Fund, 2024); and from results-based financing approaches increasingly common in international
development (Lee & Medina, 2019); can allow governments to systematically de-risk the unique cost
dynamics of AI deployment in education.

The table below maps how established, successful financing mechanisms can be repurposed to fund
national, scalable, and equitable educational AI infrastructure. It is important to note that, at this point in
time, these ideas remain conceptual and have not yet been tested. In some cases —such as the "compute-
for-data" swap — these concepts may prove controversial, but their inclusion here is intentionally meant
to spark innovative thinking and debate among policymakers. Ultimately, financing educational technology
only using traditional mechanisms is unlikely to be sufficient to meet the financial realities of the AI era.

Infrastructure costs remain a binding, first-order constraint to AI adoption in education for LICs and
many LMICs. Without sustained investment in electricity, connectivity, and devices, AI use will remain
limited to a small subset of schools and users, and risk deepening existing inequalities.
Infrastructure-aware design choices—including phased rollouts and selective use of lower-compute, ‘small
AI’—are therefore critical to making AI adoption feasible and fiscally sustainable.
Box 3 . Why the Costs of AI Pilots in Education are Not Good Predictors of AI Costs at Scale

The vast majority of current AI initiatives in education in low- and middle-income countries take the
form of pilot projects. These are typically small-scale, localized initiatives designed to explore how AI
tools function in challenging operating environments. While a few pilots are designed to reflect the
realities of an intervention at scale, most are heavily subsidized by corporate partners, who may donate
free API tokens or waive cloud compute fees, and international donor agencies and nonprofits, these
pilots can appear at first glance to be remarkably cheap to run. Many of these projects utilize global
Large Language Models (LLMs), though a growing number are experimenting with compact, localized
"Small AI". However, education planners must face a hard truth: The costs incurred during an AI pilot
project cannot be simply extrapolated to budget for the rollout of AI in education at scale. While some

cost components may benefit from economies of scale (e.g. bulk discounts on subscriptions to AI
chatbots), many costs may only become apparent at scale:

The Disappearance of Subsidies : A tech company may happily donate free AI access for 500 students in
a controlled trial to generate good public relations. They are unlikely to absorb the data and token costs
for 5 million students nationwide. When a project scales, the ministry transitions from a "free trial" to
the dynamic volatility of the token economy.

From Apps to Platforms : A pilot can run on a standalone app or a basic web interface. Scaling AI across
a national education system requires building secure data pipelines to connect an AI model with the
national Education Management Information System (EMIS). The costs of data integration,
cybersecurity, and cloud infrastructure are entirely absent from a small-scale pilot budget.

Equity at Scale : In a small pilot, technical support and teacher troubleshooting are often handled directly
by the partner organization's engineers or a few dedicated, highly capable project staff, conducted in
major urban centers or standard languages of instruction to minimize variables. When scaling the use
of AI, the Ministry of Education must ensure equity by funding large-scale, ongoing teacher professional
development and support, providing new infrastructure and additional technical support for rural
schools and in some cases deploying AI in minority languages and regional dialects.

Many ministries of education fund pilot edtech projects because they can't afford to do something at a
large scale for financial reasons, and they can’t afford to do nothing for political reasons, so instead they
fund something small. Ideally, these small initiatives can serve as 'pilot' projects, explicitly designed and
implemented to understand what works, and what does not, when implementing a new technology.
Such pilots can have value in supporting system readiness as well, serving as sandboxes for ministries
to develop the core institutional capacities of their personnel. Crucially, a pilot project can enable a
ministry of education to observe and understand the peculiar, variable cost dynamics of AI usage in real
time. By watching how teachers and students actually interact with the tool, and closely monitoring
associated costs, planners can gain vital insights in order to make more informed decisions before
committing to a costly, system-wide rollout.
