title: Explainability of AI systems in education

paragraphs.text:
Explainability in educational AI refers to making the outputs of an AI system, its predictions,
recommendations or classifications understandable to the people affected by them –– by showing
clearly how those outputs were generated and on what basis. It involves providing human-readable
insight into the factors and reasoning a system uses, so that teachers, learners and administrators can
judge whether to rely on a result, rather than accept it by default (Khosravi et al., 2022; Türkmen,
2025). Definitions in the field remain unstandardized. Explainability is increasingly understood to be not
only a technical property of a model, but also as a pedagogical and ethical requirement, which supports
human judgement, oversight and accountability in education (Altukhi and Pradhan, 2024).
The debate on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in education has largely emerged from concerns
about the use of algorithmic systems in high-stakes educational decisions. These decisions include
automated grading, dropout prediction, admissions, content recommendation and learning analytics.
The implications of explainability extend beyond technical governance to the protection of the right to
education . International human rights instruments recognize education not only as a service to which
individuals are entitled, but as a fundamental right that must be available, accessible, acceptable and
adaptable to the needs of all learners. As AI systems become increasingly embedded in educational
decision-making, opacity may directly affect the realization of this right. Automated systems that
influence learner assessment, progression, admissions, access to support services, or personalized
learning pathways may shape educational opportunities in ways that remain difficult for learners,
parents, teachers and public authorities to understand or contest. Where decisions cannot be
meaningfully explained, individuals may be unable to identify errors, challenge discriminatory
outcomes or seek effective remedies. All this weakens the procedural safeguards that underpin the
right to education. The Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (UNESCO, 2022)
identifies transparency, explainability, accountability and human oversight as fundamental principles
for the responsible governance of AI systems. In parallel, it emphasizes the protection of human rights
and human dignity across all sectors, including education.
This connects explainability directly to the argument that AI should support rather than displace the
professional judgement of teachers. A teacher can only exercise judgement over an AI output, and
choose whether to override it, if that output can be understood. Explainability is, in this sense, a
condition of the teacher agency and public authority.
These concerns become even more significant in the context of emerging frontier and agentic AI
systems which often have unexplainably baked into the model design. The issue is not only whether AI
can enhance educational access, efficiency or personalization, but whether public education systems
can continue to exercise democratic oversight over technologies that increasingly shape educational
experiences. UNESCO and United Nations reports have repeatedly emphasized that AI governance must
serve the public interest, protect human rights, and reduce rather than deepen global
inequalities (United Nations, 2026). When educational authorities rely on opaque systems supplied by a
small number of commercial actors, there is a risk that crucial decisions affecting learners may become
inaccessible to public scrutiny. In such circumstances, explainability becomes a prerequisite for
safeguarding the right to education itself, ensuring that learners retain the ability to understand
decisions that affect them, obtain human review when necessary, and hold institutions accountable for
educational outcomes.
From this perspective, the right to explanation should be understood as an emerging procedural
safeguard for the protection of the right to education in AI-mediated environments . The fundamental

question is no longer simply whether a developer can provide a technical explanation of an algorithm. It
is about whether learners and educators can: obtain meaningful explanations for decisions that affect
educational opportunities; exercise the right to contest those decisions; and secure human review
where significant educational interests are at stake. As AI systems become more capable and
potentially less interpretable, protecting the right to education may increasingly depend on governance
mechanisms that guarantee accountability and meaningful human oversight. This must be the case
even in situations where full technical explainability is unattainable.
The legal basis for the right to an explanation
The Convention on the Rights of the Child (United Nations, 1989) provides an implicit legal and
normative foundation for a right to explanation through its emphasis on participation, access to
information and developmental support (Articles 5, 12, 17, 29). Explanation is not framed as a
standalone right but is essential to ensuring that children can understand, express views on and
meaningfully engage with decisions that affect them, in line with their evolving capacities.
The legal basis for the ‘right to an explanation’ in European Union law derives primarily from the
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (European Union, 2016), applied across the
European Union since 2018 and supplemented by later digital regulations. Under the GDPR, the right is
not explicitly named but it emerges from several provisions. Article 22 establishes a right not to be
subject to decisions based solely on automated processing when these have legal or similarly significant
effects. Supporting this, Recital 71 highlights safeguards against such decisions and implies that
individuals should understand how they are made. Additionally, Articles 13, 14, and 15 require data
controllers to provide ‘meaningful information about the logic involved’ and the expected
consequences of automated decisions. This foundation is reinforced by more recent EU legislation. The
AI Act explicitly introduces a ‘right to explanation’ (Article 86) for high-risk AI systems (European
Commission, 2024). This requires the provision of clear and meaningful information about how the
system has influenced a decision Similarly, Article 27 of the Digital Services Act imposes transparency
obligations, requiring platforms to explain the main parameters of recommender systems (European
Union, 2022).
Technical background
Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI) that investigates
approaches that provide people with the opportunity to exercise human oversight over AI systems. The
main focus is on the reasoning behind the decisions or predictions made by the AI algorithms, to make
them more understandable and transparent. XAI seeks to help users of AI systems to perform more
effectively by improving their understanding of how those systems reason. XAI might be an example of
the social right to explanation being put into practice. XAI has the potential to enhance the user
experience of a product or service by assisting end-users in developing trust in the AI's decision-making
capabilities. XAI seeks to clarify past, present and future actions of an AI system, as well as the
information that informs those actions.
Two main approaches are used:

•
Global explainability: The ability to understand how the model functions generally and how
input features drive outputs at an overall level.
•
Local explainability: The ability to understand why a particular output occurred for a specific
individual, such as why a customer was denied a financial service.

Usually, they use methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), 1 LIME (Local Interpretable Model-
agnostic Explanations) 2 and PDP (Partial Dependence Plots). 3
However, the explainability challenge is evolving rapidly. The emergence of increasingly
autonomous, agentic and multimodal frontier AI systems raises questions that go beyond the
traditional XAI. In these systems, opacity is not merely a limitation that can be addressed through
post hoc explanations or model interpretation techniques. Rather, it increasingly appears to be a
structural feature of the technology itself. In that context the notion of a right to explanation
becomes especially significant.

Policy concern about explainability of AI systems
in education
As AI models expand in capability, complexity and autonomy, understanding how specific outputs,
recommendations or actions are generated becomes progressively more difficult, even for their
developers. Recent United Nations reports have noted that AI capabilities are advancing faster than
scientific understanding and governance mechanisms can adapt, creating significant challenges for
accountability, reliability and public oversight (United Nations, 2026). While these developments are
not yet fully expressed within education systems, they represent an emerging issue that educational
policy-makers cannot ignore.
A second dimension of the problem concerns the political economy of AI development. The opacity of
many contemporary and emerging AI systems is not solely a technical issue; it is also shaped by
commercial incentives, proprietary business models and highly concentrated control over
computational resources, training data and model architectures. UNESCO has consistently highlighted
the concentration of AI development within a small number of companies and countries, warning that
such asymmetries risk deepening global inequalities and limiting the capacity of many institutions to
exercise meaningful oversight. For ministries of education, particularly in low-resource contexts, the
challenge is acute (United Nations, 2026). Educational authorities may lack access to independent
auditing capacity , technical expertise, regulatory infrastructure or specialized AI supervisory bodies
capable of scrutinizing systems before they are deployed.
The implications extend beyond technical governance to the fundamental public purposes of
education . UNESCO's vision of education emphasizes human development, equity, inclusion,
democratic participation, learner agency and the cultivation of human judgment. Decision-making
processes that cannot be adequately explained, contested or reviewed risk undermining these
purposes. If learners, teachers, parents and educational authorities cannot understand how
consequential decisions are made, it becomes more difficult to ensure fairness, protect rights, identify
discrimination or hold institutions accountable. Explainability therefore should not be understood
merely as a technical property of AI systems; it is a condition for preserving public trust, democratic
oversight and the human-centred mission of education itself.
Against this backdrop, explainability must be reconsidered as a policy and governance challenge rather
than solely a technical one. Existing definitions often assume that AI systems are, in principle,

General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (European Union, 2016), applied across the
European Union since 2018 and supplemented by later digital regulations. Under the GDPR, the right is
not explicitly named but it emerges from several provisions. Article 22 establishes a right not to be
subject to decisions based solely on automated processing when these have legal or similarly significant
effects. Supporting this, Recital 71 highlights safeguards against such decisions and implies that
individuals should understand how they are made. Additionally, Articles 13, 14, and 15 require data
controllers to provide ‘meaningful information about the logic involved’ and the expected
consequences of automated decisions. This foundation is reinforced by more recent EU legislation. The
AI Act explicitly introduces a ‘right to explanation’ (Article 86) for high-risk AI systems (European
Commission, 2024). This requires the provision of clear and meaningful information about how the
system has influenced a decision Similarly, Article 27 of the Digital Services Act imposes transparency
obligations, requiring platforms to explain the main parameters of recommender systems (European
Union, 2022).
Technical background
Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI) that investigates
approaches that provide people with the opportunity to exercise human oversight over AI systems. The
main focus is on the reasoning behind the decisions or predictions made by the AI algorithms, to make
them more understandable and transparent. XAI seeks to help users of AI systems to perform more
effectively by improving their understanding of how those systems reason. XAI might be an example of
the social right to explanation being put into practice. XAI has the potential to enhance the user
experience of a product or service by assisting end-users in developing trust in the AI's decision-making
capabilities. XAI seeks to clarify past, present and future actions of an AI system, as well as the
information that informs those actions.
Two main approaches are used:
•
Global explainability: The ability to understand how the model functions generally and how
input features drive outputs at an overall level.
•
Local explainability: The ability to understand why a particular output occurred for a specific
individual, such as why a customer was denied a financial service.
5
Usually, they use methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), 1 LIME (Local Interpretable Model-
agnostic Explanations) 2 and PDP (Partial Dependence Plots). 3
However, the explainability challenge is evolving rapidly. The emergence of increasingly
autonomous, agentic and multimodal frontier AI systems raises questions that go beyond the
traditional XAI. In these systems, opacity is not merely a limitation that can be addressed through
post hoc explanations or model interpretation techniques. Rather, it increasingly appears to be a
structural feature of the technology itself. In that context the notion of a right to explanation
becomes especially significant.
Policy concern about explainability of AI systems
in education
As AI models expand in capability, complexity and autonomy, understanding how specific outputs,
recommendations or actions are generated becomes progressively more difficult, even for their
developers. Recent United Nations reports have noted that AI capabilities are advancing faster than
scientific understanding and governance mechanisms can adapt, creating significant challenges for
accountability, reliability and public oversight (United Nations, 2026). While these developments are
not yet fully expressed within education systems, they represent an emerging issue that educational
policy-makers cannot ignore.
A second dimension of the problem concerns the political economy of AI development. The opacity of
many contemporary and emerging AI systems is not solely a technical issue; it is also shaped by
commercial incentives, proprietary business models and highly concentrated control over
computational resources, training data and model architectures. UNESCO has consistently highlighted
the concentration of AI development within a small number of companies and countries, warning that
such asymmetries risk deepening global inequalities and limiting the capacity of many institutions to
exercise meaningful oversight. For ministries of education, particularly in low-resource contexts, the
challenge is acute (United Nations, 2026). Educational authorities may lack access to independent
auditing capacity , technical expertise, regulatory infrastructure or specialized AI supervisory bodies
capable of scrutinizing systems before they are deployed.
The implications extend beyond technical governance to the fundamental public purposes of
education . UNESCO's vision of education emphasizes human development, equity, inclusion,
democratic participation, learner agency and the cultivation of human judgment. Decision-making
processes that cannot be adequately explained, contested or reviewed risk undermining these
purposes. If learners, teachers, parents and educational authorities cannot understand how
consequential decisions are made, it becomes more difficult to ensure fairness, protect rights, identify
discrimination or hold institutions accountable. Explainability therefore should not be understood
merely as a technical property of AI systems; it is a condition for preserving public trust, democratic
oversight and the human-centred mission of education itself.
Against this backdrop, explainability must be reconsidered as a policy and governance challenge rather
than solely a technical one. Existing definitions often assume that AI systems are, in principle,

explainable and that sufficient technical effort can reveal the basis for their decisions. Yet this
assumption may become increasingly untenable as educational institutions begin to encounter more
capable agentic systems whose internal processes remain only partially understandable. The central
policy question is therefore not simply how to explain AI, but how to ensure that increasingly opaque
systems remain compatible with human rights, educational values and democratic accountability .
This concern aligns closely with emerging international discussions on rights-based AI governance,
including questions about the right to information, meaningful human oversight, human review of
automated decisions, public accountability and procurement requirements that make transparency and
explainability conditions for the adoption of AI systems in education.
Agentic AI represents the next evolution of AI systems. Agentic AI builds on advances in machine
learning and generative AI to create systems that can autonomously pursue goals, plan actions, use
tools and adapt their behaviour based on feedback. Whereas explainability in ‘traditional’ AI often
focuses on understanding predictions and in generative AI on explaining generated outputs,
explainability in agentic AI is more complex. It requires transparency about goals, planning
processes, tool selection, data sources, intermediate reasoning steps and the actions taken by the
system. As AI systems become more capable of acting independently within educational
environments, explainability must evolve to help educators and learners understand not only what
the AI produced but also how and why it made particular decisions, ensuring trust, accountability
and responsible use of AI technologies in education . While existing governance principles for
trusted AI such as transparency, accountability and fairness continue to apply, they need to be
translated in practice for agents.
Policy concerns around AI explainability in education are closely tied to broader issues of
transparency, accountability and human rights. Transparency and explainability are essential
preconditions for ensuring that AI systems respect fundamental rights and ethical principles. When
AI-driven tools in education operate as ‘black boxes’ or when agentic AI is automating some
processes, it becomes difficult for students, teachers and institutions to fully understand how
decisions are made. Decisions may relate to grading, adaptive learning recommendations and
behavioural predictions, or to admissions and other administrative processes. This lack of clarity
undermines trust and limits the ability to challenge potentially unfair or incorrect outcomes –– thus
posing risks to the right to a fair process and effective remedy. Policy-makers therefore face the task
of ensuring that AI systems used in educational contexts are auditable, interpretable and subject to
meaningful oversight.
A related concern is the question of responsibility and accountability. While AI systems may assist in
decision-making, they cannot replace ultimate human responsibility . Educators and institutions
should have opportunities to interfere with and change AI systems decisions that affect learners’
academic pathways and personal development. Additionally, meaningful human control and
oversight need to be integrated into the agentic AI life cycle .
Children and young learners present a particularly sensitive case: where decisions cannot be
meaningfully explained or challenged, learners may be deprived of the opportunity to understand
the reasons behind outcomes that shape their educational experiences. Many children and young
learners may not fully understand that they are interacting with AI systems or how these systems
generate recommendations about their learning. This lack of awareness raises serious concerns
about informed consent, privacy and safety. Furthermore, AI systems that monitor, assess abilities
or predict behaviours carry significant risks because such outputs can be life-altering . Decisions
influenced by AI may affect educational placement, assessment outcomes, access to learning
opportunities, support services or future educational trajectories.

Finally, explainability is critical in addressing bias and inequality in education. AI systems can
reproduce and reinforce existing prejudices and stereotypes embedded in training data, potentially
exacerbating educational disparities . Without transparent mechanisms to understand how these
systems operate, it becomes nearly impossible to detect and mitigate discriminatory patterns (as
mentioned in Māori language AI example).
In this context, the right to explanation becomes an important safeguard for the right to education ,
enabling learners and their families to seek justification for significant decisions, contest potential
errors or discrimination and secure meaningful human review. Without such safeguards, AI systems
risk undermining the principles of equity, inclusion, agency and accountability that are essential to
the realization of the right to education.
From a UNESCO and broader United Nations perspective, the issue is not whether every technical
aspect of a frontier model can be fully explained. Rather, the question is whether individuals and
institutions affected by AI-mediated educational decisions can obtain meaningful information about
how decisions are made, challenge outcomes, secure human review and hold decision-makers
accountable.

Suggestions for policy actions ensuring the
explainability of AI systems in education
The following actions frame explainability as a matter of governance and human oversight, not only
technical design. They fall to different actors. Policy-makers govern and supervise the overall
system, defining the laws and policies that frame the development and use of explainable AI.
Technology developers and vendors must ensure that educational tools provide practical,
meaningful explanations to non-technical users by design, from the start of development. They must
also integrate meaningful human control into the agentic AI life cycle, in collaboration with
educators. Learners and educators need clear, simplified explanations to understand AI
recommendations and act on them. They should be aware of, and exercise, the rights they hold.
Together, these policy actions, through ensuring transparency, accountability, technical robustness,
data protection, institutional oversight and protection of vulnerable groups, will create a
comprehensive framework for making AI systems in education explainable, trustworthy and aligned
with fundamental rights.
1. Guarantee the right to explanation and human review
Learners, parents and educators should be fully informed whenever decisions such as grading,
placement or behavioural predictions are made or supported by AI. Policies should require that
individuals can request clear, accessible explanations from the responsible institution or provider,
including the reasoning behind decisions that affect their rights, opportunities or safety. This right
must include the ability to seek human review, so that AI-driven decisions can be challenged and
corrected by qualified staff. Such measures strengthen procedural fairness and help ensure that
decisions rest on merit rather than discriminatory characteristics.
2. Establish clear accountability and responsibility frameworks
UNESCO Member States should ensure that ethical and legal responsibility for AI systems can always
be attributed to identifiable individuals or legal entities across the entire life cycle of the system.
Policies must define who is responsible when AI systems produce harmful, biased or incorrect

outcomes. This is essential in education, where algorithmic decisions can significantly influence life
trajectories, and it becomes more complex with agentic AI. While AI agents may act autonomously,
human responsibility continues to apply: responsibility must be defined clearly across all the
multiple actors involved in the agent's life cycle –– within and outside the institution.
3. Mandate technical transparency and traceability
Policy frameworks should require developers and providers to maintain robust technical
documentation, including data sources, model design and training processes. Standardized
documentation and traceability logs allow independent audits and ensure that decisions can be
reconstructed and evaluated. For high-risk educational applications, policy-makers should
encourage or require explainability tools, such as interpretable models or post hoc explanation
techniques, that make outputs understandable to educators and learners. Regular auditing and bias
testing should be compulsory for detecting and addressing discriminatory outcomes.
4. Strengthen data governance and protection
Regulatory requirements should govern how learner data is collected, processed, stored and shared.
This is to ensure that data is not misused or exploited for commercial purposes without
authorization, and transparency obligations should inform users clearly how their data is used within
AI systems. Systems that monitor or assess student abilities must meet high standards of
explainability, to prevent harmful effects on learning or cognitive development.
5. Make explainability a condition of procurement
Explainability should not fall to end-users alone, given the significant imbalance of power between
teachers and learners on one side and system developers and vendors on the other. At the
procurement stage, education authorities at the national or regional level should ensure that
developers provide appropriate explanations and that the relevant information is available to
teachers and learners. Procurement is the key point at which an education system can make
explainability a condition of adoption. It can include the requirement that a system disclose the basis
for its decisions before it is bought, rather than seeking explanations after deployment, when
leverage is weakest.
6. Invest in awareness, capacity and institutional oversight
The effectiveness of explainability depends not only on technical design but on users’ ability to
understand explanations. UNESCO Member States should invest in AI literacy for educators,
students and the broader public, drawing on the AI competency frameworks for teachers (UNESCO,
2024) and AI competency framework for students (UNESCO, 2024). At the institutional level, policies
should promote independent oversight structures, such as AI ethics officers or review boards, to
monitor compliance with explainability standards. There should also be capacity-building within the
judiciary and regulatory authorities for resolving disputes involving AI effectively. Ministries, school
leaders, teachers, inspectors and regulators need the knowledge, skills and resources to evaluate AI
systems critically, interpret automated outputs and identify any risks to learners’ rights.
7. Protect children and vulnerable groups
Explainability requirements should ensure that users can always identify when they are interacting
with an AI system rather than a human. Special safeguards are needed to address the limited
capacity of children to understand AI processes, including clear, age-appropriate explanations and
restrictions on deceptive or manipulative design. AI systems should be prohibited from exploiting
cognitive biases or engaging in practices that could harm vulnerable users.

Key insight
The ultimate goal of explainable AI in education is not just legal accountability –– it is agency. When
educators understand why an AI made a recommendation, they can choose to override it. When
students understand exactly how they are being evaluated, they can adapt their learning strategies
to succeed.
Explainability should not be the responsibility of end users (teachers and students) only because
there is significant misbalance in power between end-users and AI systems developers and vendors.
Education authorities at national or regional levels should be responsible for ensuring appropriate
explanations from AI-system developers during the process of procurement and ensure that all
relevant information is available for teachers and students.
Keep asking, keep requesting and exercise your right to an explanation!

Questions for further exploration
The decisions that lie ahead are the responsibility of UNESCO Member States, their social partners and
education communities, and they will differ by context. Three questions follow from this paper.

1. As frontier and agentic systems become less interpretable even to their developers, how
should an education system govern the use of tools whose decisions cannot be fully
explained, and at what point should it refuse to use them at all?
2. Where the capacity to inspect, audit and contest AI systems is uneven, how can that capacity
be built and shared, so that the right to an explanation is real for learners and teachers in
low-resource settings and not only in well-resourced ones?
3. If explainability is to be a condition of procurement rather than a request made after
deployment, what must an education system be able to specify and verify at the point of
purchase, and what can it realistically require of a global provider on its own?

A few examples from different countries
Different countries are tackling the explainability problem of AI in education through varying levels
of regulation, ranging from legally binding audits to voluntary technical testing toolkits. Examples
from the education context are still not widely available. The examples that follow are of a general
or business nature, but they can be mapped onto the educational context.

The European Union: The legally binding ‘high-risk’ audit
The European Union has the most stringent and legally binding approach globally, treating
educational outcomes as a matter of fundamental rights. Under the AI Act (Article 6 and Annex III,
European Commission, 2024), AI systems used in education are officially classified as ‘high-risk.’ This
specifically applies to tools that determine admission to educational institutions, evaluate learning
outcomes (like automated grading or essay scoring) or monitor student behaviour during exams (like
AI proctoring). Before a high-risk educational AI tool can be legally sold or deployed in the EU, the
provider must complete a rigorous conformity assessment. This is a mandatory audit requiring
developers to prove their system's transparency. They must compile detailed technical

documentation and activity logging so that the logic behind an AI's decision can be traced,
reconstructed and explained to both educators and students if a decision is challenged. More
specific details are described in the European Commission’s Draft Commission guidelines on the
classification of high-risk AI systems (2026 a ) and Guidelines on transparency obligations for
providers and deployers of AI systems (2026 b ), which describe obligations related to the disclosure
of AI interaction, marking AI-generated content and labelling deepfakes.
Singapore: The ‘AI Verify’ software toolkit
Singapore has developed actual software infrastructure to help companies test their AI tools against
governance principles, including those used in its highly digitized school system. The Model AI
Governance Framework (IMDA, 2026a) and the AI Verify testing toolkit, 4 are developed by the
Infocomm Media Development Authority. The toolkit specifically includes an explainability test, which
technically assesses whether the factors contributing to the AI model's output can be identified and
clearly communicated to end-users. The software does not issue a ‘Pass’ or ‘Fail’ grade for
explainability. Instead, it produces a comprehensive, interactive governance report. A human auditor
then reviews this report. If the AI Verify report shows that a model deciding university admissions is
heavily weighting a proxy variable for race or zip code, or if the explanations for individual rejections
are mathematically inconsistent, the developer fails the explainability check and must retrain their
model.
Singapore's Ministry of Education actively pilots AI, such as machine-learning-enhanced adaptive
learning and automated English marking systems. The national framework mandates that decisions
made by AI in these public sectors must be ‘explainable, transparent, and fair.’
In June 2026, Singapore published the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (IMDA, 2026b),
which addresses new concerns from agentic AI and helps organizations to assess and prevent risks. Four
dimensions of the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI are: assess and bound the risks
upfront; make humans meaningfully accountable; implement technical controls and processes; and
enable end-user responsibility. To enable responsible use, as a baseline, users should be informed of
the agent’s range of actions, access to data and the user’s own responsibilities.
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland: The ‘Inspect’ Framework
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland government's Inspect platform 5 is the
leading public-sector toolkit for testing frontier models and large language models (LLMs).
Developed and open-sourced by the AI Security Institute (AISI), Inspect is a software library hosted
publicly on GitHub that allows developers to run rigorous, automated safety and behaviour audits
on AI systems. It uses algorithms to check data distributions, Inspect runs over 200 pre-built
technical evaluations. It sets up parallel ‘sandbox’ environments to test models for specific
algorithmic risks, such as behavioural auditing, transparency and explainability.
Spain: AESIA sandbox and compliance toolkits

regulator, the Spanish Artificial Intelligence Supervision Agency (AESIA). To help companies prepare
for the European Union’s AI Act, they launched a national regulatory sandbox that resulted in a

which addresses new concerns from agentic AI and helps organizations to assess and prevent risks. Four
dimensions of the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI are: assess and bound the risks
upfront; make humans meaningfully accountable; implement technical controls and processes; and
enable end-user responsibility. To enable responsible use, as a baseline, users should be informed of
the agent’s range of actions, access to data and the user’s own responsibilities.
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland: The ‘Inspect’ Framework
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland government's Inspect platform 5 is the
leading public-sector toolkit for testing frontier models and large language models (LLMs).
Developed and open-sourced by the AI Security Institute (AISI), Inspect is a software library hosted
publicly on GitHub that allows developers to run rigorous, automated safety and behaviour audits
on AI systems. It uses algorithms to check data distributions, Inspect runs over 200 pre-built
technical evaluations. It sets up parallel ‘sandbox’ environments to test models for specific
algorithmic risks, such as behavioural auditing, transparency and explainability.
Spain: AESIA sandbox and compliance toolkits
Spain was the first country in the European Union to establish a dedicated, independent AI
regulator, the Spanish Artificial Intelligence Supervision Agency (AESIA). To help companies prepare
for the European Union’s AI Act, they launched a national regulatory sandbox that resulted in a

title: 5 See https://inspect.aisi.org.uk

paragraphs.text:
highly operational compliance toolkit with 16 practical technical guides and checklist tools designed
to help developers move away from the technological ‘black box.’ 6 The AESIA framework directly
targets ‘high-risk’ AI deployments (such as those in education or hiring). There are detailed protocols
ensuring that an AI’s decisions are always interpretable by human operators (e.g. teachers), offering
specific technical recommendations on how interfaces must present explanations, so users know
when to safely override an automated decision.
New Zealand: Indigenous language learning system
Māori Speech AI Model 7 is a successful indigenous AI project (Dang, 2026). Te Hiku Media 8
developed Māori language AI tools while maintaining community ownership of language data and
providing transparent AI processes. It combines the Principles of CARE (Collective Benefit, Authority
to Control, Responsibility and Ethics) for Indigenous Data Governance with Explainable AI in
Education (XAI-ED). CARE asks: ‘Who controls and benefits from the AI?’ while XAI-ED answers: ‘How
does the AI make its decisions?’. Together, they create an educational AI model that is transparent,
culturally respectful, community-governed and equitable. The central message is that educational AI
should not only explain its decisions but also respect indigenous data sovereignty, community
ownership and cultural values. This shows that successful XAI is not only about making algorithms
understandable, but also about ensuring that communities trust, govern and benefit from the
technology. Te Hiku Media's Māori language AI initiatives demonstrate that community-led and
explainable systems can improve both educational outcomes and trust.
Paraguay: designing explainable conversational agentic systems for Guaraní speakers
This case study on Paraguay’s Guaraní-speaking population illustrates why AI systems should be
designed for oral-first interaction, and not simply as text-based systems with speech input (Adomo
et al., 2026). Because Guaraní is widely spoken in daily life while Spanish dominates written and
digital contexts, many technologies offer only superficial language support and fail to align with how
people actually communicate. The authors propose a multi-agent conversational architecture that
separates speech processing, language understanding, dialogue memory, permissions and actions –
– making AI decisions more transparent and controllable. Their main contribution to XAI is the idea
that explainability should be delivered through conversation itself — by verbally clarifying what the
system understood, what it plans to do, what uncertainties exist, and why actions are allowed or
blocked. This is much more effective and accurate than a reliance on written explanations,
dashboards or visual interfaces that may not fit oral-language communities.
Latin America and the Caribbean
In April 2026, UNESCO launched the Observatory on Artificial Intelligence in Education for Latin
America and the Caribbean, a regional platform designed to support UNESCO Member States in
integrating artificial intelligence into their education systems, with a focus on equity, quality and
sustainable development (UNESCO, 2026). The Observatory emerges as the first multi-stakeholder
platform and a space for regional cooperation aimed at supporting countries in the growing
incorporation of these emerging technologies into teaching, learning and educational management
processes.

Further exploration
Recent academic and policy literature has shifted from asking if we need XAI in education to how we
implement it to protect student rights and improve pedagogy.
The Recommendation on the ethics of artificial intelligence and Guidance for generative AI in
education and research addresses AI explainability as a non-negotiable prerequisite for protecting
human rights, equity and agency, especially within educational systems. Because UNESCO
approaches technology from a humanistic perspective, its publications consistently warn that
unexplained algorithms undermine a person’s ability to challenge unfair decisions.
The UNESCO Ethical Impact Assessment (EIA) is a comprehensive tool designed for policy-makers
and other stakeholders to examine whether a specific AI system is in line with the values and
principles of UNESCO’s Recommendation on the ethics of artificial intelligence . The EIA
helps teams assess potential positive and negative impacts of the AI system, identify and engage
with relevant stakeholders, and develop mitigation strategies to address adverse outcomes.
The UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology includes a range of quantitative and qualitative
questions designed to gather information about different dimensions related to a country’s AI
ecosystem. The dimensions include: legal and regulatory; social and cultural; economic; scientific
and educational; and technological and infrastructural.
The UN Preliminary Report of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI : Evidence-based
assessment of opportunities, risks and impacts of AI is a first-of-its-kind independent, scientific
assessment of the capabilities, emerging opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence.
UNICEF AI Strategy 2025–2030: AI for Every Child : This strategy outlines how UNICEF utilizes and
advocates for AI globally. The entire strategy is anchored by five guiding principles, prioritizing
human oversight and explainability directly beside safety.
The UNICEF policy brief When AI becomes a friend: Child rights risks, harms, and regulatory
responses to AI chatbots and companions examines the growing use of AI chatbots and AI
companions by children and young people, and the opportunities and risks these technologies
create for children's rights, safety and well-being.
Explainable AI in education: Fostering human oversight and shared responsibility (2025): This
landmark policy report argues that XAI is essential for compliance with the GDPR and the AI Act. It
emphasizes that technical transparency is not enough; educational tools require ‘socio-technical
transparency’ where explanations are tailored to the digital literacy levels of the students and
teachers using them.
Explainability in Educational AI: A Critical Systematic Review (2026): This massive review of over 100
empirical studies found a critical flaw in current systems: most AI explanations serve technical
purposes (helping developers debug) rather than educational ones. The authors argue that XAI must
be grounded in learning theory so that explanations actually foster critical inquiry rather than just
checking a transparency box.
Beyond transparency: why explainable AI is essential for educational equity in low-resource language
communities : This paper highlights XAI as an ethical imperative. When AI models are used for
language assessment, marginalized communities are often penalized by biased models.

Explainability is required to expose these biases, allowing educators to intervene and ensure
equitable grading.
A.I. Regulation in Singapore: A Comprehensive Review : This article explains that Singapore adopts a
non-binding, governance-focused approach to AI regulation, relying on strategies, frameworks and
guidelines that promote human-centric, transparent and trustworthy AI development rather than
strict legislation.
Singapore’s Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI , addresses new concerns from agentic
AI and helps organizations to assess and bound risks upfront.
OECD Digital Education Outlook 2023 : In this document, explainability is presented as the primary
bridge to building user trust. The document argues that to maintain ‘human-in-the-loop’ oversight,
dashboards must be designed transparently. Explainable interfaces allow teachers to combine their
contextual, real-world knowledge of a student with the AI’s data-driven insights, giving them the
confidence to either accept or safely override the AI’s recommendations.
Not One Size Fits All: A Stakeholder-Differentiated Framework for Explainable Agentic AI in
Education : This conference paper proposes a stakeholder-differentiated framework for students,
teachers and policy-makers around three dimensions: temporal scope, abstraction level and the
accountability function –– drawing on the HCXAI community's inquiry into the who and why of
explainability.
6th Human-Centered Explainable AI (HCXAI) workshop : Re-examining XAI in the era of agentic AI.
This workshop includes lightning talks and poster spotlights from researchers, practitioners and
policy makers to reimagine explainability for agentic systems — not just algorithmic transparency,
but understanding who needs to know what, when and why.

title: PANOS IPEIROTIS , New York University, USA KONSTANTINOS RIZAKOS, New York University, USA

paragraphs.text:
Large language models have broken take-home exams. Students generate polished work they cannot ex-
plain under follow-up questioning. Oral examinations are a natural countermeasure—they require real-time
reasoning and cannot be outsourced to an LLM—but they have never scaled. Voice AI changes this. We
describe a system that conducted 36 oral examinations for an undergraduate AI/ML course at a total cost of
$15 ($0.42 per student), low enough to attach oral comprehension checks to every assignment rather than
reserving them for high-stakes finals. Because the LLM generates questions dynamically from a rubric, the
entire examination structure can be shared in advance: practice is learning, and there is no exam to leak. A
multi-agent architecture decomposes each examination into structured phases, and a council of three LLM
families grades each transcript through a deliberation round in which models revise scores after reviewing
peer evidence, achieving inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff’s α = 0 . 86) above conventional thresholds. But
the system also broke in instructive ways: the agent stacked questions despite explicit prohibitions, could not
randomize case selection, and a cloned professorial voice was perceived as aggressive rather than familiar. The
recurring lesson is that behavioral constraints on LLMs must be enforced through architecture, not prompting
alone. Students largely agreed the format tested genuine understanding (70%), yet found it more stressful than
written exams (83%)—unsurprising given that 83% had never taken any oral examination. We document the
full design, failure modes, and student experience, and include all prompts as appendices.

CCS Concepts: • Social and professional topics → Student assessment ; • Human-centered computing
→ Natural language interfaces ; • Computing methodologies → Natural language processing .

Additional Key Words and Phrases: oral examination, voice agents, educational assessment, large language
models, automated grading, academic integrity, LLM-as-judge

title: 1 The Problem

paragraphs.text:
In our AI/ML Product Management course, we noticed a pattern we suspect is now common across
higher education: pre-class written submissions appeared thoughtful and well-structured, yet when
students were called upon randomly during discussion, many could not explain basic choices in
their own submissions after follow-up questions. The gap between written artifact quality and
demonstrated understanding was too consistent to attribute to performance anxiety. The problem
was compounded by the capstone group project: when students distribute work across teammates
and polish contributions with an LLM, written artifacts reveal almost nothing about comprehension.

paragraphs.text:
This is a measurement problem. If students cannot defend their written work in real time, the
written artifact is measuring something other than what we think it measures [ 2 , 8 , 11 ]. And it is
a structural problem, not a cheating problem. LLM-generated text is difficult to distinguish from
human writing even by expert raters [ 7 ], and detection tools produce unacceptable false-positive
and false-negative rates with systematic bias against non-native speakers. The detection arms race
is not one educators can win.

Reverting to proctored in-class written exams is one response, but it forecloses exactly the open-
ended, project-specific assessment that courses like ours require. Oral examinations sidestep the
problem entirely—a point increasingly recognized as educators confront generative AI [ 4 , 5 ]. They
require real-time reasoning, application of knowledge to novel prompts, and defense of specific
decisions. They have been used for centuries (the Latin “viva voce” tradition dates to medieval
universities), and research consistently shows that structured oral formats achieve high validity

and reliability, with Cronbach’s α of 0.75–0.80 versus 0.50 for unstructured formats [ 10 , 12 ]. The
reason they fell out of favor is not that they don’t work. It’s that they don’t scale.

A 25-minute oral examination for a class of 36 students, evaluated by two graders, requires 30
hours of faculty or teaching assistant time. For a class of 36, human-administered orals are feasible;
for a class of 100, they are challenging. Bayley et al. [ 1 ] addressed this by having 600+ students
simultaneously record video responses through an LMS—scaling the examination itself, though
with pre-set questions and human grading. The value proposition of AI automation goes further: it
reduces the marginal cost enough to make oral exams routine , deployable across courses multiple
times per semester, including low-stakes practice that no department would staff with human
examiners.

Conversational AI platforms now bundle the components required for natural spoken interaction
(speech-to-text, text-to-speech, turn-taking, and interruption handling) into systems that are good
enough to conduct a structured examination [ 3 ]. Nitze [ 13 ] explored text-based LLM oral exam
simulations in STEM but without voice interaction or automated grading. Concurrently, Jabarian
and Henkel [ 6 ] showed that AI-conducted voice interviews in hiring can match or exceed human-
administered interview quality, suggesting the technology is mature enough for high-stakes spoken
evaluation. We decided to find out if voice AI could deliver both the examination and the grading.

title: 2.1 Platform Requirements and Architecture

paragraphs.text:
A voice examination system requires six core capabilities: (1) speech-to-text with adequate accuracy
for domain terminology, (2) text-to-speech with natural prosody, (3) turn-taking that tolerates think-
ing pauses without interpreting silence as disconnection, (4) multi-agent workflows to decompose
the examination into phases, (5) per-session variable injection to personalize each conversation
with student-specific context, and (6) transcript export for downstream grading. These can be
assembled from individual components (an LLM API paired with a separate speech pipeline and
custom orchestrator) or obtained from integrated conversational AI platforms. We used ElevenLabs
Conversational AI [ 3 ], where capabilities (4) and (5) mapped to platform-native features: workflow
capabilities for multi-agent routing and dynamic variables for per-student context injection. The
architecture itself is platform-independent; what matters is that these six capabilities are present.
Figure 1 shows the end-to-end flow.
Rather than having one agent handling the entire examination, we decomposed it into three:

Scalable and Personalized Oral Assessments Using Voice AI
3
(1) Authentication Agent: Requests and validates student identification before proceeding. (In

production, this would integrate with institutional single sign-on.)
(2) Project Discussion Agent: Receives the student’s capstone project context via parameters

and conducts structured questioning about their specific work: goals, data choices, modeling
decisions, evaluation approaches, and failure modes. This targets the gap between LLM-
generated written work and genuine understanding: students cannot improvise consistent
answers about decisions in work they did not personally complete.
(3) Case Discussion Agent: Selects a case study from the semester and asks questions spanning
course topics. Questions are generated dynamically during the examination.

The decomposition prevents conversational drift and simplifies debugging. When something fails
in Phase 2, it does not contaminate Phase 3. Prompts are available in the supplementary materials.

title: 2.2 Grading: A Council of LLMs

paragraphs.text:
We implemented a “council of LLMs” (three models from different families that independently score
the same transcript, then revise after seeing each other’s reasoning) using Claude, Gemini, and
GPT-5. This “LLM-as-judge” approach, where language models evaluate open-ended work in place
of human raters [ 15 , 16 ], extends a long history of automated scoring [ 14 ] to oral examination
transcripts. The process has three steps:
(1) Round 1 (Independent): Each model receives the full examination transcript and the

grading rubric, then independently scores it on five dimensions (Problem Framing, Metrics
& Economics, Risk & Ethics, Experimentation, Communication), each 0–4, with verbatim
transcript evidence for each score. The three models run in parallel with no shared context.
(2) Round 2 (Deliberation): Each model receives a compiled summary of all three Round 1

assessments (scores, justifications, and cited evidence) and is asked to revise its evaluation in
light of the other models’ reasoning. Models may change scores or reaffirm them, but must
justify either decision with transcript evidence.
(3) Chair Synthesis: A designated chair model (Claude) receives all Round 1 and Round 2

outputs and produces the final grade: one score per dimension, a total score (0–20), and a
structured feedback report with strengths, weaknesses, and verbatim evidence.

Why not use a single model? Because initial independent assessments showed poor agreement.
The deliberation phase proved essential: without it, the system does not produce reliable grades.
A known risk of this design is anchoring bias : when models see each other’s Round 1 scores,
they may converge toward a shared (possibly wrong) answer rather than genuinely revising their
assessments. We cannot fully rule this out. However, deliberation transcripts show substantive
engagement (models citing specific transcript evidence to argue for score changes, not merely
splitting differences), suggesting the convergence reflects reasoning rather than pure anchoring.
More on this in Section 3 . The full grading prompt is included in the supplementary materials.

title: 3 Deployment and Results

paragraphs.text:
We deployed the system as the final examination for an undergraduate AI/ML Product Management
course at NYU Stern. Thirty-six students completed the examination over nine days (Table 1 ),
scheduling their own times, a logistical property worth emphasizing. Even with only 36 students and
two instructors, human-administered orals generated accommodation conflicts: flights, overlapping
finals, family events, time zones. The AI system eliminated scheduling as a constraint; students
chose any time during the nine-day window. Students recorded themselves (webcam and audio)
during the examination to discourage outsourcing or real-time assistance.

3.1
Cost
The total marginal cost was $15: Claude (grading chair) $8, Gemini $2, OpenAI $0.30, ElevenLabs
voice minutes approximately $5. The comparable human cost (36 students, 25 minutes each, two
graders at $25/hour) would be approximately $750. This represents a roughly 50 × reduction in per-
administration cost, though initial deployment required significant engineering effort for prompt
design, debugging, and pipeline construction. These fixed costs amortize across semesters and
courses (the infrastructure is reusable), but they are not zero.

3.2
Grading Reliability
Initial independent grading revealed a problem. Gemini averaged 16.3/20 while Claude averaged
13.0/20, a gap of 3.3 points (OpenAI fell between at 13.7/20, within one point of Claude on 64% of
students). Without deliberation, the council was useless. After the deliberation phase, convergence
was asymmetric: Gemini dropped its mean by 1.3 points after seeing stricter peer assessments,
while Claude rose by 0.9 points and OpenAI by 0.3 points, all three converging toward the 14–15
range. That the largest shift came from the most lenient model suggests genuine revision rather
than simple score-splitting. Overall, grades converged substantially (Table 2 ).

At the dimension level (5 dimensions × 36 students = 180 assessments), agreement was even
stronger: 74% perfect agreement, 25% within one point, and only 1% (2 of 180) with two-or-more-
point disagreement. Figure 2 illustrates this distribution. To enable comparison with human inter-
rater reliability benchmarks, we computed Krippendorff’s alpha [ 9 ] on the ordinal 0–4 dimension
scores. Before deliberation, α = 0 . 52 (dimension-level), indicating poor agreement. After delibera-
tion, α = 0 . 86 (dimension-level) and α = 0 . 83 (overall 0–20 score), both above the 0.80 threshold
conventionally considered “good reliability.”

These reliability metrics (Krippendorff’s alpha, agreement rates, convergence after deliberation)
measure consistency among raters , not correctness against ground truth . The distinction matters:
reliability (do raters agree?) is necessary but not sufficient. Validity (do grades reflect actual student
competence?) requires comparison to expert human judgment. Three models agreeing on a wrong
grade is still a wrong grade.

We conducted a partial validity check. The instructor and teaching assistant independently
graded all 36 examinations and compared their scores to the council output. The instructor’s
holistic grades aligned with the most lenient model (Gemini), but upon reviewing the stricter
models’ evidence (verbatim transcript excerpts supporting each deduction), conceded most of the
stricter scores. The strict grading surfaced teaching deficiencies (particularly in Experimentation,
Section 3 ) that the instructor’s own grading had obscured: when you grade your own students,
it is easy to give credit for what you know they understood rather than what they demonstrated .
Only two students requested regrading, and neither challenge succeeded; the transcript evidence
backing each grade was too specific to dispute.

This comparison was informal, not a controlled validation study; the instructor’s leniency was
partly driven by awareness of teaching gaps, a confound we did not control for. Rigorous validation

would require blinded expert re-grading of a random subset with pre-defined scoring criteria. A
practical interim safeguard is flagging examinations for human review when council disagreement
is high. In our data, 2 of the 180 dimension-level assessments with 2+ point disagreement and 14%
of students (5/36) with overall scores diverging by 3+ points are natural candidates for audit. This

Agreement varied by topic in a revealing way: after deliberation, Problem Framing, Metrics,
Risk/Ethics, and Communication all reached 100% agreement within 1 point, while Experimentation
(the topic where students performed worst) lagged at 94%. Before deliberation, the gap was starker:
Experimentation agreement was 64% in Round 1 versus 100% for Problem Framing. Vague responses
create legitimate disagreement about partial credit, whether the graders are human or artificial.

3.3
Diagnostic Power
Scores by topic revealed significant variation (Figure 3 ): Experimentation (A/B testing) averaged
1.94/4, compared to Problem Framing at 3.39/4. The Experimentation breakdown was striking: 8%
of students scored 0 (unable to discuss the topic at all), 19% scored 1 (superficial understanding),
42% scored 2 (basic understanding), and zero students demonstrated mastery.
This was a mirror held up to the instructor, not just the students. A/B testing had received
insufficient class time—easy to overlook with written exams, where students can produce plausible-
sounding answers by rephrasing textbook content. The oral format made the teaching gap impossi-
ble to ignore.

3.4
Duration and Performance
Duration showed no meaningful correlation with score (Figure 4 ; r = − 0 . 09, 95% CI [− 0 . 41 , 0 . 25 ] ,
p = 0 . 60). The shortest exam (9 minutes) received the highest score (19/20); the longest (41 minutes)
received 12/20. Confident understanding manifests as efficient communication; duration reflects
articulation difficulty, not thoroughness.

Paraphrasing During Clarification. When students asked the agent to repeat a question, it would
paraphrase rather than repeat verbatim, inadvertently changing the question. This is the LLM
doing what it was trained to do (being helpful by rephrasing), but exactly wrong in an examination
context. We added explicit prompt instructions (“repeat the exact previous question”) which reduced
but did not eliminate the behavior.

After 5 seconds of silence, the agent would ask “Are you there?”, precisely when the student was
formulating an answer. We increased the timeout to 10 seconds. Thinking time is not silence; it is
cognition.

prompt listed eight case studies and instructed the agent to “randomly select ONE case.” From

the end of December 18, we removed Zillow from the prompt. The agent immediately shifted to

Student Experience
We surveyed students after the examination but before grade release ( n = 30, 83% response rate).
The 17% who did not respond may differ systematically: dissatisfied students may have avoided a
post-exam survey, or satisfied students may not have felt the need to respond. The headline finding

actual understanding” (the highest-rated item), but only 33% found questions clear, and 83% found

it is unclear how much stress reflects the AI format versus the oral format itself.

Format preferences were revealing: 57% preferred traditional written exams, 27% preferred
human-administered oral exams, and 13% preferred AI-administered oral exams. That 40% were
open to oral formats despite documented problems suggests that fixing the failure modes could shift

two regrading requests, and did not concede a single point in either case. The transcript-backed
evidence for each grade was specific enough that students could see exactly what they said (or
failed to say) and why it earned the score it did. Actions around grades (which were strict but
documented) paint a different picture than pre-grade survey sentiment.

title: 6 Discussion

paragraphs.text:
6.1
Transparency and Incentive Alignment
The most underappreciated property of this approach is full transparency. Because the system
is powered by guidelines rather than specific secret questions, we shared the entire examination
structure with students beforehand: the format, the skills being assessed, the types of questions.
The LLM generates questions dynamically, so there is no exam to leak.

This inverts the traditional incentive structure. Students can practice repeatedly, and such practice
is legitimate learning. Articulating your understanding out loud (to a practice partner, to an AI,
to yourself) is one of the most effective study techniques we know. The assessment rewards the
preparation behavior we want to encourage. This is not a technological fix to cheating but a redesign
of assessment that makes cheating structurally difficult while rewarding genuine understanding.

6.2
Feedback Quality
The grading council produced feedback exceeding what human graders typically deliver in both
structure and specificity. Each evaluation included strengths, weaknesses, and action items with
verbatim evidence from the transcript. For the highest-scoring student: “Your understanding of
metric trade-offs and Goodhart’s Law risks was exceptional; the hot tub example perfectly illustrated
how optimizing for one metric can corrupt another.” For a lower-performing student: “Practice
articulating complete A/B testing designs: state a hypothesis, define randomization unit, specify
guardrail metrics, and establish decision criteria for shipping or rolling back.”

Human graders rarely generate such detailed, evidence-linked feedback for every student. The
automated system produces it as a byproduct.

title: 6.3 What Is Lost

paragraphs.text:
Automating assessment is not a free lunch. A human examiner develops real-time intuition about
student understanding—noticing by the third or fourth exam which topics the class systematically
struggles with. Our Experimentation gap (Section 3 ) was only visible after analyzing aggregate
scores from the AI system; a human examiner might have noticed it sooner.

That said, this concern can be mitigated by other feedback channels. In our course, students
complete a brief exit survey after every session (what they learned, already knew, and found
unclear), and an LLM analyzes responses to generate pedagogical recommendations within minutes.
We apply the same approach to assignments before grading, identifying class-wide patterns early
enough to address in subsequent sessions. These mechanisms are orthogonal to the exam format
and provide the continuous pedagogical feedback that automated assessment alone lacks.

There is also real value in the human relationship between examiner and student. A professor
can read body language, offer encouragement, and exercise contextual judgment that no rubric

Scalable and Personalized Oral Assessments Using Voice AI
9

fully captures. We do not claim AI-administered assessment is superior to well-resourced human
assessment. The claim is narrower: it is superior to no oral assessment, the realistic alternative for
most courses.

6.4
What This System Cannot Do
Several caveats are important for anyone considering adoption. We compared AI oral exams to
written assessments, not human-administered orals, so we cannot claim equivalence with faculty
orals—only that the format provides assessment properties unavailable through written exams at
dramatically lower cost. As discussed in Section 3 , the grading council’s high agreement establishes
reliability (consistency among AI raters), not validity (correctness against expert judgment); our
informal instructor comparison is encouraging but is not a formal validation study. The self-recorded
video requirement deters but does not prevent cheating; the format is more resistant than take-home
written work but not immune.

Voice-based assessment introduces accessibility challenges that institutions must address before
deployment, not after. Students with speech-related disabilities or conditions affecting verbal
fluency face barriers that written formats avoid; non-native speakers face compounded difficulty:
as the international student quoted in Section 5 reported, the challenge was articulating knowledge
under time pressure in a second language, not lacking the knowledge itself. Students should be
informed in advance about how the system works, what is recorded, and who accesses their
transcripts. The format is not uniformly exclusionary, however: students with anxiety-related
accommodations found the AI examiner less stressful than facing a senior professor, suggesting
voice AI may simultaneously create and remove accessibility barriers depending on the population.

Finally, data governance deserves attention. The system transmits student voice recordings
and transcripts to four third-party vendors. FERPA and GDPR impose requirements on such
arrangements: data processing agreements, retention limits, and deletion rights. We operated
under IRB approval with informed consent, but broader deployment will require alignment with
institutional data governance policies.

title: 6.5 Beyond Education

paragraphs.text:
The architecture described here is not specific to university courses. Technical hiring is an obvious
application: phone screens follow structured formats similar to our examination, recruiter time
is expensive, scheduling is a bottleneck, and multi-model grading could provide more consistent
evaluation than individual interviewers. Jabarian and Henkel [ 6 ] demonstrated in a field experiment
with 70,000 applicants that AI-conducted interviews increased job offers by 12% and retention by
16–18%, with 78% of applicants preferring the AI interviewer. Professional certification (medical
boards, legal competency, regulatory compliance) presents similar opportunities. The key insight
transfers: decompose the interaction into phases, enforce behavioral constraints in code, and use
multi-model consensus to reduce individual model biases.

title: 8 Conclusion

paragraphs.text:
The spread of LLMs has disrupted traditional assessment. Rather than pursuing a detection arms race,
we can adopt assessment formats that inherently reward genuine understanding. Oral examinations
have always had this property but never had scalability. Voice AI restores scalability.

Our deployment demonstrates feasibility: 36 students examined at $0.42 each, with grading
validated against every transcript, diagnostic feedback exceeding typical human output, and well-
characterized, fixable failure modes. Student experience was mixed: effective at testing understand-
ing but stressful and unfamiliar, particularly for a cohort where 83% had never taken any oral exam.
The documented problems (voice tone, question stacking, thinking time) are engineering issues,
not fundamental limitations. The full prompts are included in the supplementary materials as the
core deliverable. Adapt them, improve them, and share what breaks.
